recipes.name: Andhra Kodi Kura
recipes.subtitle: bone-in chicken curry, fiercely red and thick with browned onion

ingredients.note: bone-in only; boneless breast has nothing to give this gravy
pounded with the garlic to a coarse paste
Guntur chilli powder; drop to 1.5 tsp if that is more heat than you want
added at the end
ground with 3 tbsp water to a smooth paste; thickens the gravy the Andhra way

prepNotes: Rub the chicken with 1/2 tsp turmeric, 1/2 tsp salt and 1 tsp of the chilli powder then cover and refrigerate it 30 minutes.
Pound the ginger and garlic together in a mortar rather than blitzing them. The coarse paste browns better and does not go watery.
Soak the poppy seeds in warm water for 20 minutes before grinding, or they stay gritty.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a kadhai until it shimmers, add the cloves, cinnamon and bay leaf and let them swell for 30 seconds.
Add the sliced onion with a pinch of salt and fry over medium heat for 14 to 16 minutes, until deep brown at the edges and shrunk to a third of the volume.
steps.tip: This is the backbone of the curry and the one step you cannot shorten. Pale onion means a thin, sharp gravy.

steps.text: Stir in the ginger-garlic paste, green chillies and curry leaves and cook 3 minutes until the raw garlic smell has gone completely.
Add the tomato and cook 6 minutes, pressing it against the pan, until it breaks down and the mixture pulls together.
Add the chilli powder, coriander powder, remaining turmeric and crushed pepper and fry 2 minutes over low heat with a splash of water so the spices do not catch.
steps.tip: Powdered spices burn in about 40 seconds on a dry hot pan. The splash of water is your insurance.

steps.text: Tip in the marinated chicken and turn it in the masala over high heat for 8 minutes, until every piece is coated and the edges have seized and browned.
Stir in the poppy seed paste and the salt, then pour in 400ml water and bring to a boil.
Lower the heat, cover, and simmer 20 minutes, until the chicken is tender and a thigh piece comes off the bone easily.
Uncover and cook 8 minutes more on medium heat, until the gravy clings to the chicken and a slick of red oil rises to the top.
steps.tip: The oil separating is when it is done. Serve it before that and it tastes unfinished.

steps.text: Sprinkle over the garam masala and coriander leaves, cover, and rest 5 minutes off the heat.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated and is better on day two. Freezes for 2 months. Reheat over low heat with 3 tbsp water, stirring gently so the chicken does not shred.

recipes.name: Ariselu
recipes.subtitle: rice flour and jaggery discs fried for Sankranti, chewy and dark

ingredients.qty: 400g, soaked 4 hours then dried and ground
ingredients.note: the flour must be slightly damp, which is why it is ground at home

prepNotes: The jaggery syrup stage decides everything. Too soft and the discs dissolve in the oil; too hard and they are inedible.
Test it: a drop of syrup in cold water should form a ball you can roll between your fingers.

steps.text: Melt the jaggery with the water and boil to the soft-ball stage, about 8 minutes.
steps.tip: Drop a little into cold water. It should gather into a soft ball, not a thread and not a brittle sheet.

steps.text: Take off the heat and stir in the rice flour, sesame and cardamom quickly, while the syrup is still hot.
Knead into a soft dough while just cool enough to handle. Rest it 4 hours or overnight.
steps.tip: The rest lets the flour drink the syrup. Skipping it gives a hard ariselu.

steps.text: Pat portions into 8cm discs between two greased sheets of plastic.
Fry one at a time on medium, spooning oil over the top, until deep brown, about 3 minutes.
steps.tip: One at a time. They are fragile and stick to each other.

steps.text: Press each one between two flat spoons as it comes out to squeeze the oil back.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 weeks in an airtight tin at room temperature and firms up over the first few days, which is normal.

recipes.name: Avakaya
recipes.subtitle: the raw mango pickle Andhra households measure the year by

ingredients.qty: 1kg, firm and sour, cut into 3cm pieces with the shell of the stone
ingredients.note: the stone shell is traditional and holds the pieces together
a coarse, deep red pickle chilli, not the fine hot kind
avakaya means mustard; this is the flavour
iodised salt clouds the pickle and softens the fruit
Indian gingelly oil, and enough to cover

prepNotes: Everything must be bone dry. One drop of water and the jar spoils within a week.
This is not a same-day pickle. It needs three days to come together and is better after a month.

steps.text: Wipe the mango pieces with a dry cloth and spread them on a towel for an hour. There must be no moisture at all.
steps.tip: Do not wash and use immediately. Wash the whole fruit, dry it thoroughly, then cut.

steps.text: Mix the chilli powder, ground mustard, salt, turmeric and fenugreek in a wide dry bowl.
Add half the oil and work it into a thick paste. Fold in the mango pieces and the garlic until every piece is coated.
Pack into a dry glass or ceramic jar, pressing down to remove air pockets. Pour the remaining oil over so the surface is covered.
steps.tip: The oil layer is the seal. If the pickle drinks it, top it up.

steps.text: Close and leave three days at room temperature, turning the jar once a day, then refrigerate.
steps.tip: Three days is the traditional cure. After that keep it cold: a jar left out all summer is a tradition, not a tested method.

recipes.storage: Keeps 6 months refrigerated under a covering film of oil, using only a dry spoon. Traditionally kept in a cool larder for a year, but that rests on the salt and oil levels being judged by eye, which is not something this recipe can verify for your batch.

recipes.name: Bandar Laddu
recipes.subtitle: the coarse gram-flour laddu of Machilipatnam, more crumb than sphere

ingredients.note: coarse besan is the point; fine flour gives a dense, pasty laddu

prepNotes: The boondi is made loose and coarse rather than as neat pearls, which is what gives Bandar laddu its crumbly bite.
It is a GI-tagged sweet from Machilipatnam, which the British called Bandar.

steps.text: Whisk the besan with the water into a thick batter that falls in ribbons.
Heat half the ghee. Pour the batter through a slotted spoon so it falls in irregular drops and fry until pale gold.
steps.tip: Pale gold, not brown. It cooks again in the syrup.

steps.text: Drain and crush the fried boondi coarsely between your palms.
Fry the cashew and raisins in a spoonful of ghee and stir them through with the sugar and cardamom.
Pour over the remaining warm ghee and mix. While still warm, press firmly into balls.
steps.tip: Warm is essential. Cold mixture will not hold and you will be left with sweet crumbs.

recipes.storage: Keeps 10 days in an airtight tin at room temperature. The ghee firms up but the laddu stays crumbly, which is how it should be.

recipes.name: Bobbatlu
recipes.subtitle: thin griddled flatbreads stuffed with sweet chana dal and jaggery

ingredients.note: dark jaggery gives the proper colour and depth
a little wholewheat keeps the dough manageable; all maida is the traditional choice
for colour in the dough only

ingredients.qty: 6 tbsp, melted, plus more for the griddle

prepNotes: Make the dough at least 3 hours ahead. An underrested bobbattu dough will not stretch and will tear every time.
Soak the chana dal 30 minutes before cooking so it softens evenly.
Cook the filling and cool it completely before stuffing; warm filling turns the dough sticky and unworkable.

steps.text: Knead the maida, atta, salt, turmeric and about 120ml water into a very soft, sticky dough. Softer than chapati dough, almost batter-like at the edges.
Pour 4 tbsp of the melted ghee over the dough, cover, and leave it 3 hours at room temperature. It should be slack and silky when you come back.
steps.tip: The dough must be soft enough to spread with your fingers. If it holds a firm ball shape, work in another tablespoon of water.

steps.text: Pressure cook the drained chana dal with 400ml water for 4 whistles, until a grain crushes to paste between two fingers.
steps.tip: Cook it soft but drain it hard. Wet dal makes filling that will not hold together.

steps.text: Drain the dal thoroughly, then blitz or mash it to a smooth paste.
Cook the dal paste with the jaggery in a heavy pan over medium heat for 12 to 15 minutes, stirring constantly, until it thickens and comes away from the sides in a single mass.
steps.tip: It will loosen and go watery when the jaggery melts. Keep going. It stiffens again, and that is when it is ready.

steps.text: Stir in the cardamom and nutmeg, spread the filling on a plate and cool it completely, then roll it into 8 equal balls.
Oil your palms, take a lump of dough the size of a lime, flatten it on a greased sheet of banana leaf or baking paper, place a filling ball in the centre and gather the dough over it.
With greased fingertips, pat the parcel out to a thin 15cm round. Do not use a rolling pin, it will tear.
steps.tip: Work from the centre outwards in small pats. If the filling shows through in one spot, patch it with a scrap of dough.

steps.text: Heat a tawa over medium heat and flip the bobbattu onto it, paper side up, then peel the paper away.
Cook 60 to 90 seconds a side, brushing with ghee, until brown spots appear and the surface puffs in patches.
steps.tip: Medium heat only. High heat browns the outside before the filling warms through.

steps.text: Slide it onto a plate, brush with more ghee, and repeat with the rest.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days at room temperature in an airtight box, or 8 days refrigerated. Warm on a dry tawa for 30 seconds a side before eating; microwaving makes them chewy.

recipes.name: Chepa Vepudu
recipes.subtitle: fish steaks rubbed with chilli and shallow fried until the edges crisp

ingredients.note: a firm fish; soft fillets break up
the crust; without it the spice slides off in the pan

prepNotes: Rub the fish with the turmeric, salt, chilli, ginger, garlic and lemon juice, then cover and refrigerate 30 minutes.
Pat the pieces dry before they touch the oil. Wet fish steams instead of frying.

steps.text: Toss the marinated fish in the rice flour so each piece carries a thin, even coat.
Heat the oil until a pinch of flour sizzles at once. Lay the fish in without crowding the pan.
steps.tip: Crowding drops the temperature and you get grey fish.

steps.text: Fry 4 minutes without moving it. Turn once, add the curry leaves to the oil, and fry 3 minutes more.
steps.tip: Turning it repeatedly is how the crust ends up in the pan instead of on the fish.

steps.text: Drain on paper, squeeze over the rest of the lemon and serve hot with rice and a pulusu.

recipes.storage: Best within the hour. It keeps a day refrigerated but the crust goes soft; crisp it briefly in a dry pan rather than a microwave.

recipes.name: Chepala Pulusu
recipes.subtitle: fish simmered in a dark tamarind gravy sharpened with fenugreek

ingredients.qty: 600g firm steaks such as seer or kingfish, cut 2cm thick
ingredients.note: a firm fish that will not fall apart; soft fillets disintegrate in the gravy
dry-roasted and powdered. The signature note of a pulusu
slaked in 3 tbsp cold water to thicken the gravy

prepNotes: Rub the fish with 1/4 tsp turmeric and 1/2 tsp salt and refrigerate 20 minutes, then bring it back to room temperature before it goes into the pan.
Soak the tamarind in 300ml hot water for 25 minutes and extract a thick, dark pulp.
Dry-roast the fenugreek seeds until deep brown and powder them. Do this first, while the pan is still cool enough to control.

steps.text: Heat the sesame oil in a wide kadhai and crackle the mustard seeds, then add the cumin, dried red chillies and curry leaves.
Add the onion and cook 10 minutes over medium heat until soft and golden brown.
Stir in the garlic, ginger and green chillies and fry 2 minutes until fragrant.
Add the tomato and cook 6 minutes until it collapses completely.
Add the chilli powder, coriander powder and remaining turmeric with 2 tbsp water and fry 2 minutes until the paste darkens to brick red.
steps.tip: Keep the heat low here. Chilli powder scorches fast and a burnt pulusu cannot be rescued.

steps.text: Pour in the tamarind pulp and 500ml water, add the salt and jaggery, and boil hard for 12 minutes to cook off the raw tamarind edge.
steps.tip: Twelve minutes of real boiling, not a lazy simmer. This is what turns sharp tamarind into a rounded gravy.

steps.text: Stir in the rice flour slurry and cook 2 minutes until the gravy thickens enough to coat a spoon.
Slide the fish steaks in in a single layer, spoon gravy over them, and simmer uncovered on low heat for 8 to 10 minutes.
steps.tip: Never stir once the fish is in. Tilt and swirl the pan instead, or you will end up with fish flakes in soup.

steps.text: Sprinkle over the fenugreek powder, shake the pan once, and take it off the heat.
Scatter the coriander leaves and leave it to stand at least 2 hours before serving.
steps.tip: A pulusu is genuinely better hours later, once the fish has drunk the gravy.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated and tastes best the next day. Reheat gently over low heat without stirring. Do not freeze. The fish turns woolly.

recipes.name: Dosakaya Pappu
recipes.subtitle: everyday toor dal cooked down with yellow cucumber and tamarind

ingredients.qty: 200g, rinsed until the water runs clear
400g, peeled, deseeded and cut into 2cm cubes
ingredients.note: dosakaya is the squat yellow Andhra cucumber; ordinary cucumber is the closest catalogued stand-in. Choose a firm one and it holds its shape
use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free

prepNotes: Rinse the dal in three changes of water and soak it 20 minutes. It cooks faster and creamier.
Soak the tamarind in 80ml hot water for 15 minutes and squeeze out the pulp.
Taste a raw sliver of the cucumber first; if it is bitter at the stem end, cut that part away.

steps.text: Pressure cook the dal with the cucumber, tomato, green chillies, turmeric and 600ml water for 4 whistles, then let the pressure drop naturally.
steps.tip: Add the cucumber at the start. It should be soft enough to crush, not crunchy.

steps.text: Open the cooker and mash the dal lightly against the side with the back of a ladle, leaving some cucumber cubes whole.
Stir in the tamarind pulp, chilli powder, salt and the remaining 100ml water, and simmer uncovered for 8 minutes.
steps.tip: Tamarind goes in after the dal is cooked. Added early it keeps the lentils grainy.

steps.text: Meanwhile heat the oil in a small pan and crackle the mustard seeds until they pop, about 30 seconds.
Add the cumin, dried red chillies, garlic and curry leaves and fry 1 minute until the garlic is golden and the leaves go crisp.
Take the pan off the heat, stir in the asafoetida, and let it sizzle for 5 seconds.
steps.tip: Asafoetida burns instantly on direct heat. Off the flame is the only safe moment.

steps.text: Pour the tempering into the dal, add the raw onion if using, and simmer 2 minutes more.
Finish with the coriander leaves and check the salt. It should taste sour, then hot, then savoury.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated. It thickens a lot as it sits; loosen with hot water when reheating and simmer 2 minutes so it comes back together. Do not freeze.

recipes.name: Gongura Mamsam
recipes.subtitle: mutton braised with sour sorrel leaves, the dish Andhra is judged by

ingredients.note: bone matters here, the gravy is thin without it
standing in for gongura (sorrel); if you find gongura use it and cut the tamarind by half
only to make up the sourness the substitute lacks
Guntur if you can get them

prepNotes: The greens go in twice. Half early, to melt into the gravy, half at the end so something still tastes green.
Gongura is aggressively sour. If you are using amaranth, the tamarind is doing the work the leaf would.

steps.text: Wilt the greens in a dry pan until they collapse and give up their water, about 5 minutes. Set aside.
steps.tip: No oil. You want them dry, not fried.

steps.text: Brown the onion in the oil until properly dark. Add the ginger and garlic pastes and cook out the raw smell.
Add the mutton, turmeric, coriander powder and chillies. Fry on high until the meat is sealed and colouring.
steps.tip: Do not add salt yet, it draws water and stews the meat.

steps.text: Add 250ml water and the tamarind, cover and cook 50 minutes until the mutton yields, or 5 whistles in a pressure cooker.
Stir in half the wilted greens and simmer uncovered 10 minutes until the gravy tightens around the meat.
Fold in the rest of the greens, salt to taste, and rest 10 minutes before serving with rice.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated and improves overnight as the sourness settles into the meat. Reheat gently with a splash of water. Freezes well for a month.

recipes.name: Gongura Pachadi
recipes.subtitle: fierce sour-leaf chutney, eaten by the spoonful with hot rice

image.alt: Gongura pachadi, the sour-leaf chutney of Andhra

ingredients.note: standing in for gongura (sorrel), which is not in the catalogue; amaranth has the same soft body but none of the sourness, so the tamarind below is doing that job
not optional here. It replaces the acidity real gongura would bring
Guntur chillies if you have them
Indian toasted gingelly oil, not the East Asian kind
a quarter teaspoon and no more
use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free

prepNotes: Soak the tamarind in 100ml of hot water for 20 minutes, then squeeze it to a thick pulp and discard the fibres.
Wash the greens and spread them on a cloth until bone dry. Wet leaves steam instead of frying and the chutney turns watery.
Have a clean, completely dry glass jar ready; any moisture and this will not keep.

steps.text: Heat 2 tbsp of the sesame oil in a kadhai and fry the dried red chillies, fenugreek seeds and half the cumin over low heat for 2 minutes, until the chillies darken by a shade and smell toasty.
steps.tip: Fenugreek burns from tan to black in about ten seconds. Pull the pan off the moment it colours.

steps.text: Lift the spices out onto a plate and set them aside to cool completely.
In the same pan add another 2 tbsp oil and the garlic, and fry 2 minutes until the cloves are pale gold at the edges.
Add the greens a large handful at a time with the green chillies and turmeric, and cook over medium-high heat for 8 to 10 minutes, stirring, until the leaves collapse and the pan goes almost dry.
steps.tip: Keep cooking past the point where they look done. Any water left behind will spoil the chutney within days.

steps.text: Stir in the tamarind pulp and salt and cook another 4 minutes, until the mixture pulls away from the sides of the pan in a single mass.
Cool the greens fully, then grind them with the toasted spices to a coarse paste. No water at all, and it should still have some texture.
steps.tip: Grind in short pulses. A smooth purée loses the rustic bite this is meant to have.

steps.text: Heat the last tbsp of oil, crackle the mustard seeds and remaining cumin, add the curry leaves and asafoetida, and pour the whole tempering over the chutney.
steps.tip: Wait for the mustard to actually pop before the curry leaves go in, or the tadka tastes raw.

steps.text: Fold the tempering through and taste for salt and sourness. It should hit sour first, then heat.

recipes.storage: Packed into a dry jar with a thin film of oil on top, it keeps 3 weeks refrigerated. Always use a dry spoon. It is traditionally left out for several days and the sourness of the gongura does a lot of the work, but that is custom rather than a tested figure, so keep it in the fridge and take out what you need. Serve at room temperature.

recipes.name: Gutti Vankaya Kura
recipes.subtitle: small eggplants stuffed with a peanut, sesame and coconut masala in tamarind gravy

ingredients.note: the little purple ones; large aubergine will not hold a stuffing
Guntur chilli powder for the proper heat

prepNotes: Soak the tamarind in 150ml hot water for 20 minutes and squeeze out the pulp.
Slit each eggplant into quarters from the base down, stopping 1cm short of the stem so it stays in one piece, and drop them into salted water while you make the masala.
Dry-roast the peanuts, sesame and coconut separately (they colour at very different speeds) and cool them before grinding.

steps.text: Dry-roast the peanuts over medium heat for 4 minutes until blistered, then the sesame for 1 minute until they jump, then the coconut for 1 minute until sandy gold.
steps.tip: Coconut goes from gold to bitter in seconds. Take it off while it still looks underdone.

steps.text: Grind the cooled peanuts, sesame and coconut with the coriander powder, cumin, chilli powder, turmeric and 1 tsp salt to a coarse, dryish powder.
Drain the eggplants, pat them dry, and press about a tablespoon of the masala into each one, prising the quarters apart with your thumb. Keep the leftover masala.
steps.tip: Do not overfill. The eggplant needs room to soften or it splits open in the pan.

steps.text: Heat 4 tbsp of the oil in a wide kadhai, lay the stuffed eggplants in a single layer and fry them 6 to 8 minutes, turning gently, until the skins blister and go glossy. Lift them out.
Add the remaining oil, crackle the mustard seeds, then add the curry leaves, onion, garlic and ginger and cook 8 minutes until the onion is soft and lightly browned.
Stir in the leftover masala powder and fry it for 3 minutes, until it darkens and smells nutty rather than raw.
steps.tip: This is the step people skip. Raw ground peanut tastes chalky in the finished gravy.

steps.text: Pour in the tamarind pulp and 300ml water, add the jaggery and remaining salt, and bring to a simmer.
Slide the eggplants back in, spoon gravy over them, cover and cook on low heat for 15 to 18 minutes, until a knife slips into an eggplant with no resistance.
steps.tip: Do not stir once they are back in the pan. Tilt and shake it instead, or the stuffing falls out.

steps.text: Uncover and simmer 5 minutes more until the gravy thickens and oil beads on the surface.
Scatter the coriander leaves over and rest it 10 minutes off the heat before serving with rice.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated and improves on the second day. Reheat covered over low heat with 2 tbsp water, shaking the pan rather than stirring. It does not freeze well, the eggplant collapses.

recipes.name: Kodi Vepudu
recipes.subtitle: chicken fried dry with curry leaves and pepper until the masala clings to the bone

ingredients.note: small pieces, this is eaten with fingers
crushed, not powdered, you want to meet it

prepNotes: Vepudu means fry. There is no gravy at the end and there should not be.
Rub the chicken with the turmeric and salt and refrigerate 20 minutes while you slice the onion.

steps.text: Heat the oil, splutter the dried chillies and one sprig of curry leaves, then add the onion and fry until golden.
Add the ginger and garlic pastes, cook 2 minutes, then the chicken and chilli powder. Fry on high 5 minutes.
Cover and cook 15 minutes on low. The chicken releases its own water and cooks in it.
steps.tip: No added water at any point.

steps.text: Uncover, raise the heat and fry until every drop has gone and the masala is stuck to the meat, about 10 minutes.
steps.tip: This is the whole dish. Stop too early and it is a curry.

steps.text: Add the crushed pepper and the remaining curry leaves, toss 2 minutes, and serve.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated. Reheat dry in a pan rather than a microwave, which softens the crust you just built.

recipes.name: Menthi Kura Pappu
recipes.subtitle: toor dal cooked with fenugreek leaves, bitter and soft and eaten every week

ingredients.note: bitter; do not try to cook it out, it is meant to be there

prepNotes: Wash the fenugreek in several changes of water. Grit hides in the leaf and there is no rescuing it later.
The dal should be soft enough to smear, not soupy.

steps.text: Pressure cook the dal with the turmeric, tomato, onion, green chilli and 500ml water for 4 whistles, or simmer 40 minutes.
Stir in the fenugreek leaves and the tamarind and simmer 10 minutes uncovered until the leaves are soft.
Mash the dal roughly against the side of the pan. Season.
steps.tip: Roughly. A completely smooth dal loses the texture of the leaf.

steps.text: Heat the oil, splutter the mustard seeds, then the cumin, dried chillies, garlic, curry leaves and asafoetida.
Pour the tempering over the dal, stir once, and cover for 5 minutes before serving.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated. It thickens considerably; loosen with hot water and re-season. Do not freeze, the leaves turn slimy.

recipes.name: Natu Kodi Pulusu
recipes.subtitle: country chicken in a thin tamarind gravy, cooked long enough to matter

ingredients.note: free-range or older bird if you can, it is the point of the dish

prepNotes: Pulusu means sour. The tamarind is not a background note, it is the dish.
Country chicken is tougher and better flavoured than broiler. If you use broiler, cut the cooking time by half.

steps.text: Fry the onion in the oil until deep brown. Add the curry leaves and dried chillies.
Add the chicken, turmeric and coriander powder and fry on high until the pieces colour, 8 minutes.
Add the tomato and cook until it breaks down completely.
Strain in the tamarind water, bring to a boil, then cover and simmer 40 minutes until the chicken is tender.
steps.tip: It should stay thin. This is a gravy for pouring over rice, not for coating it.

steps.text: Season and rest 10 minutes. The sourness rounds out as it stands.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated and tastes better on day two. The tamarind keeps it stable. Reheat to a full simmer.

recipes.name: Perugu Vada
recipes.subtitle: urad dal vadas soaked soft and drowned in seasoned yogurt
prepNotes: Grind the dal with as little water as possible. A wet batter gives flat, oily vadas.
The soak in warm water after frying is what makes them spongy. Skip it and you get bread in yogurt.

steps.text: Drain the dal and grind to a thick, fluffy paste, adding water a spoonful at a time. Beat it by hand for 2 minutes to aerate.
steps.tip: A spoonful of batter dropped in water should float. If it sinks, beat it more.

steps.text: Mix in the green chilli, ginger and salt. Shape into flat rounds with a hole in the middle and fry until golden.
Drop the hot vadas into warm salted water for 10 minutes, then squeeze each one gently between your palms.
steps.tip: Gently. You are pressing out water, not flattening them.

steps.text: Season the yogurt with salt and pour it over the squeezed vadas. Refrigerate at least an hour.
Heat 2 tbsp oil, splutter the mustard and cumin seeds with the dried chillies, curry leaves and asafoetida, and pour it over. Finish with coriander.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated. The vadas go on drinking the yogurt, so add a few spoonfuls of fresh whisked yogurt before serving on day two.

recipes.name: Pesarattu
recipes.subtitle: a green whole-moong crepe topped with raw onion, ginger and chilli

image.alt: Pesarattu, the green gram crepe of coastal Andhra

ingredients.note: just enough for crispness; more and it stops being pesarattu
4 ground into the batter, 2 finely chopped for the topping

ingredients.qty: 1 large, very finely chopped, for topping

prepNotes: Soak the whole moong and rice together for 6 hours or overnight. The skins must be soft enough to grind smooth without being removed.
Pesarattu batter is not fermented. Grind it and cook straight away, which makes it a good same-morning breakfast.
Chop the onion for the topping as fine as you can and keep it dry, ready beside the stove.

steps.text: Drain the soaked moong and rice and grind with the whole green chillies, ginger, 1 tsp of the cumin and the salt to a smooth batter, adding water gradually.
steps.tip: Aim for a batter a shade thinner than dosa batter. It should coat the ladle but pour freely.

steps.text: Stir in the remaining cumin seeds whole, for texture.
Heat the tawa over medium-high, then rub it with half an onion dipped in oil.
steps.tip: The onion-rub seasons the pan and stops sticking better than oil alone.

steps.text: Lower the heat slightly, pour a ladleful in the centre and spread outward in a slow spiral to a 22cm round.
Scatter a generous tablespoon of chopped onion, chilli and coriander over the wet surface and press it down with the ladle.
steps.tip: Press the topping in while the surface is still wet or it falls off when you fold the crepe.

steps.text: Drizzle 1 tsp oil around the edge and cook 3 minutes until the base is crisp and speckled brown and the edges curl away.
Flip and cook 1 minute only, just to set the onion.
steps.tip: One minute on the onion side. Longer and the topping burns while the crepe goes leathery.

steps.text: Fold in half and serve hot with allam pachadi or a plain coconut chutney.

recipes.storage: Eat immediately; pesarattu softens as it sits. The ground batter keeps 2 days refrigerated but the green dulls to olive. Stir well and use within that window.

recipes.name: Pootharekulu
recipes.subtitle: paper-thin rice sheets layered with ghee and sugar, the sweet that looks like parchment
prepNotes: This is the hardest sweet in the collection and the reason is the sheet: it has to be thin enough to read through.
The traditional method lifts the film off an inverted clay pot. A heavy non-stick tawa held upside down over low heat is the workable substitute.

steps.text: Grind the soaked rice with water to a very thin, pourable batter, about the consistency of milk.
steps.tip: Too thick and the sheet will not be translucent.

steps.text: Heat a tawa on low. Dip a clean muslin cloth in the batter and wipe it across the hot surface in one pass.
steps.tip: One pass. Going over it twice tears the film.

steps.text: Within seconds the film lifts at the edges. Peel it off whole and lay it on a dry surface.
steps.tip: If it sticks, the tawa is too cool. If it browns, too hot.

steps.text: Brush a sheet with ghee, dust generously with the sugar and cardamom, scatter cashew, and lay a second sheet on top.
Brush again, fold in the sides and roll into a loose cylinder. Repeat with the rest.
Leave 20 minutes for the sugar to draw and settle before eating.

recipes.storage: Keeps 4 days in an airtight tin at room temperature, layered with greaseproof paper so the sheets do not fuse. Do not refrigerate: the ghee sets and the sheets crack.

recipes.name: Pulihora
recipes.subtitle: sour, peppery tamarind rice, the temple food of the telugu country

ingredients.qty: 300g raw sona masuri or any short-grain, rinsed

ingredients.note: gingelly oil; pulihora genuinely needs this much
dry-roasted and powdered separately
dry-roasted and coarsely powdered
use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free
just enough to round the sourness, not to sweeten

prepNotes: Soak the tamarind in 250ml hot water for 30 minutes and extract a thick, dark pulp.
Dry-roast the fenugreek seeds until deep brown and the sesame until they pop, then powder each separately and keep aside.
Cook the rice so the grains stay separate (1 part rice to 1.6 parts water) and spread it on a wide tray to cool to room temperature before you dress it.

steps.text: Spread the cooked rice on a large tray, drizzle over 2 tbsp of the sesame oil and 1/2 tsp turmeric, and fork it through gently.
steps.tip: Hot rice will break into paste when you mix it. Wait until it is barely warm.

steps.text: Heat the remaining 4 tbsp oil in a kadhai over medium heat and fry the peanuts for 3 minutes until they turn a shade darker and smell roasted, then scoop them out.
Into the same oil add the chana dal and urad dal and fry 2 minutes until both are reddish-gold and crisp. They are the crunch in the finished rice.
Add the mustard seeds and let them pop, about 30 seconds, then the dried red chillies, green chillies, curry leaves and asafoetida.
Pour in the tamarind pulp with the rest of the turmeric and the salt, and bring it to a hard simmer.
Cook the tamarind mixture for 10 to 12 minutes, until it thickens, darkens and the oil separates and pools at the edges of the pan.
steps.tip: The oil separating is the signal. Stop before it and the rice tastes raw and thin.

steps.text: Stir in the jaggery and the powdered fenugreek, cook 1 minute more, then take the pan off the heat.
steps.tip: Fenugreek powder goes in at the end. Boiled hard, it turns the whole pot bitter.

steps.text: Pour two-thirds of the tamarind paste over the rice and fold it in with a flat spoon, lifting rather than stirring, until every grain is pale gold.
Scatter over the fried peanuts and the sesame powder, fold once more, and taste. Add the rest of the paste if you want it sharper.
Cover and leave it 30 minutes before serving so the rice absorbs the dressing evenly.
steps.tip: Pulihora is better an hour later than it is straight away.

recipes.storage: Cool it quickly and refrigerate within two hours in a covered steel container; it keeps 3 days. Do not leave it out overnight, however well it seems to hold. Do not reheat in a pan. Let it come back to room temperature, or microwave 60 seconds with a sprinkle of water.

recipes.name: Punugulu
recipes.subtitle: crisp fermented-batter fritters, the roadside snack of the coast

ingredients.note: adds crispness, but it is wheat semolina. Omit it to keep the punugulu gluten-free
only if the batter is young and not properly sour

prepNotes: Soak the rice and urad dal separately for 5 hours, then grind them together to a slightly coarse batter and leave it to ferment 8 to 10 hours somewhere warm.
The batter should be thicker than dosa batter and smell pleasantly sour. Day-old dosa batter is exactly what most Andhra kitchens use.
Take the batter out of the fridge an hour before frying; cold batter drinks oil and stays heavy.

steps.text: Stir the rice flour and rava into the fermented batter and let it sit 15 minutes to hydrate.
steps.tip: This is what makes them crisp rather than bready. Do not skip the resting.

steps.text: Fold in the onion, green chillies, ginger, cumin, curry leaves, coriander leaves and salt.
steps.tip: Salt the batter just before frying. Added early it thins the batter and the onion weeps.

steps.text: Check the consistency: it should drop off a spoon in a thick lump, not a ribbon. Add the baking soda only if the batter tastes flat.
Heat the oil in a kadhai to 170C. A drop of batter should sink briefly and rise within 3 seconds, fizzing.
steps.tip: Too hot and they brown outside while staying raw in the middle. This is the single most common failure.

steps.text: Drop in walnut-sized spoonfuls of batter, 8 or 10 at a time, keeping the pan uncrowded.
Fry 4 to 5 minutes, turning them once they float, until deep golden brown all over and audibly crisp when tapped with the spoon.
Lift them out onto a rack, not paper. Paper traps steam and softens the bottoms.
Let the oil come back up to temperature for a minute before the next batch, and serve hot with coconut or peanut chutney.

recipes.storage: Eat within the hour. Punugulu are a fresh-fried snack and go leathery once cool. The batter itself keeps 2 days refrigerated, so fry only what you will eat.

recipes.name: Ragi Sangati
recipes.subtitle: finger millet and rice pounded into a smooth ball, the working staple of Rayalaseema

ingredients.note: cooked soft with the millet, not separately

prepNotes: Sangati is eaten with a hot, thin curry, usually natu kodi pulusu or a chilli and onion chutney. On its own it is deliberately plain.
The pounding is the technique. A whisk gives lumps; a sturdy wooden spoon and some force gives the smooth, heavy texture the dish is named for.

steps.text: Boil the rice in the water until completely soft and collapsing, about 20 minutes. Do not drain it.
Lower the heat. Rain the ragi flour in with one hand while stirring hard with the other.
steps.tip: All at once and you get a lump you will never break up.

steps.text: Cook 8 minutes, stirring constantly, until it pulls away from the sides of the pan.
Take it off the heat and pound it against the side of the pan with a wooden spoon until glossy and smooth, about 3 minutes.
Wet your hands and shape into balls. Serve at once with a hot curry.
steps.tip: It sets firm as it cools, so shape while hot.

recipes.storage: Best eaten straight away. It keeps a day refrigerated but sets hard; steam it briefly to soften rather than microwaving, which dries the surface.

recipes.name: Royyala Iguru
recipes.subtitle: prawns cooked dry in a thick masala until it clings to every one

ingredients.qty: 500g medium, shelled and deveined, tails on

prepNotes: Toss the prawns with 1/4 tsp turmeric and 1/2 tsp salt and leave them 15 minutes, then rinse and pat them completely dry.
Chop the onion finer than feels necessary. Iguru is a dry curry and the masala has to melt into a coating, not sit in lumps.
Have everything cut and measured before you start; from the moment the prawns go in you have four minutes.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a kadhai over medium-high heat and fry the onion for 10 minutes, until soft and browning at the edges.
Add the garlic, ginger, green chillies and curry leaves and cook 2 minutes until the garlic loses its raw edge.
Add the tomato and cook 8 minutes, mashing it down, until it is completely broken and the oil starts to show at the sides.
steps.tip: Iguru has no added water, so all the moisture must come out of the tomato now.

steps.text: Stir in the chilli powder, coriander powder, remaining turmeric and crushed pepper and fry 2 minutes on low heat.
Add the salt and cook the masala another 3 minutes until it is thick enough to hold the mark of a spoon.
Raise the heat to high, tip in the dried prawns and stir them through the masala for 3 to 4 minutes, until they curl into loose Cs and turn opaque coral.
steps.tip: Prawns go from tender to rubbery in about 60 seconds. A tight O shape means you have gone too far.

steps.text: Take the pan off the heat and sprinkle over the garam masala.
Squeeze in the lemon juice, scatter the coriander leaves and toss once.
steps.tip: Lemon off the heat only. Boiled, it goes bitter and flat.

recipes.storage: Best eaten the day it is made. It keeps 1 day refrigerated; reheat quickly in a hot pan for 90 seconds rather than a slow simmer, which overcooks the prawns. Do not freeze.

recipes.name: Royyala Vepudu
recipes.subtitle: prawns tossed dry with onion, curry leaf and a lot of chilli
prepNotes: Prawns take four minutes and not a minute more. Have everything else finished before they go in.
Toss the prawns with the turmeric and salt and refrigerate 15 minutes while the masala cooks down.

steps.text: Fry the onion in the oil until golden and soft, 8 minutes. Add the ginger and garlic and cook 2 minutes.
Add the chilli powder, coriander powder and one sprig of curry leaves. Fry 2 minutes until the oil separates.
Raise the heat, add the prawns and toss constantly for 4 minutes until they curl and turn opaque.
steps.tip: They are done the moment they curl. Past that they tighten into rubber.

steps.text: Add the remaining curry leaves, toss once, check the salt and finish with coriander.

recipes.storage: Eat the same day. Reheated prawns toughen, and the dish is dry enough that a day in the fridge does it no favours.

recipes.name: Tomato Pappu
recipes.subtitle: andhra everyday toor dal cooked soft with sour tomato and garlic

ingredients.note: sour tomatoes make the dish
Andhra pappu is meant to be hot
only if the tomatoes are not sour enough
use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free

prepNotes: Rinse the toor dal until the water runs clear, which stops the dal frothing over.
Chop the tomatoes coarsely; they go into the cooker with the dal and melt away.
Crush the garlic with the flat of a knife rather than mincing it. You want soft sweet cloves at the end.

steps.text: Pressure cook the dal with the tomatoes, green chilli, turmeric and 2.5 cups water for 5 whistles.
steps.tip: Cooking the tomato with the dal, not after, is what makes it pappu rather than dal with tomato.

steps.text: Let the pressure drop naturally, open, and mash the dal against the side of the pot until smooth.
Add the salt, chilli powder and tamarind if using, with 1/2 cup water, and simmer 5 minutes.
Adjust with hot water until it pours thickly off the ladle.
Heat the oil in a small pan and pop the mustard seeds, then add the cumin.
Add the crushed garlic and fry until the cloves turn golden at the edges, about 1 minute.
steps.tip: Garlic browned properly here is most of the flavour; pale garlic tastes raw in the dal.

steps.text: Add the onion and fry 3 minutes until soft and lightly browned.
Add the red chilli, curry leaves and hing and let them crackle for 15 seconds.
Pour the tempering into the dal, stir once, scatter the coriander and serve over hot rice.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated and thickens as it stands. Reheat with a splash of water and a fresh squeeze of lemon if it tastes tired.

recipes.name: Ulavacharu
recipes.subtitle: the dark, smoky horse gram broth of the coast, sour and deeply savoury

ingredients.note: balances the sourness; ulavacharu should not taste sweet

prepNotes: Soak the horse gram in plenty of water overnight, at least 8 hours. It is an unforgivingly hard lentil and takes a very long time unsoaked.
Soak the tamarind in 200ml hot water for 20 minutes and extract a thick pulp.
Set aside a full afternoon-ish window: the broth needs a long, slow reduction and cannot be hurried.

steps.text: Drain the soaked horse gram, rinse it, and pressure cook with 1.5 litres of fresh water and the turmeric for 8 whistles, then let the pressure fall on its own.
steps.tip: If the grains still resist a fingernail, cook another 3 whistles. Undercooked horse gram gives a thin, gritty broth.

steps.text: Strain the cooked gram over a bowl, keeping every drop of the dark cooking liquid. That liquid is the dish.
steps.tip: Do not throw the drained grains away; they make a fine dry stir-fry with onion and chilli the next day.

steps.text: Crush about a quarter of the cooked grains to a paste and stir it back into the liquid to give the broth body.
Pour the broth into a heavy pan with the remaining 500ml water and bring it to a steady simmer.
Heat the sesame oil in a small pan, crackle the mustard seeds, then add the cumin, fenugreek, dried red chillies and curry leaves and fry 1 minute until fragrant.
steps.tip: Fenugreek here is a quarter teaspoon. Any more and the broth turns bitter as it reduces.

steps.text: Add the onion and garlic to the tempering and cook 6 minutes until soft and just golden, then tip the whole lot into the simmering broth.
Add the tamarind pulp, green chillies, chilli powder, coriander powder, jaggery and salt, and simmer uncovered.
Let it reduce for 45 to 60 minutes over low heat, stirring occasionally, until it darkens to the colour of strong coffee and coats the back of a spoon.
steps.tip: The colour change is the whole point. Stop early and you have brown water instead of ulavacharu.

steps.text: Taste and adjust. It should be sour and smoky first, with the heat arriving after.
Scatter the coriander leaves over and serve hot in bowls alongside plain rice.

recipes.storage: Keeps 4 days refrigerated and freezes well for 2 months. It thickens on cooling, so reheat with a splash of water over low heat. Traditionally a spoon of cream or ghee is stirred in at the table, which is worth doing if you are not keeping it vegan.

recipes.name: Ball Curry
recipes.subtitle: beef meatballs poached in a thin red coconut gravy, the Sunday lunch of Calcutta Anglo-Indian homes

ingredients.note: mutton mince works equally well
the binder; soak it and squeeze it dry

ingredients.qty: 3 medium: 1 grated for the balls, 2 sliced for the gravy

ingredients.note: kashmiri chilli if you want the colour without the heat
traditional, and they soak up the gravy

prepNotes: Soak the bread in the milk for 5 minutes, then squeeze it almost dry before working it into the mince. Wet bread makes balls that fall apart.
Chill the shaped balls for 20 minutes before they go into the gravy; cold balls hold together far better.
Have the gravy simmering before you start dropping the balls in, so they set on contact rather than sitting in warm liquid.

steps.text: Mix the mince with the squeezed bread, beaten egg, grated onion, half the ginger-garlic paste, the chopped green chilli, 2 tbsp coriander leaves, the black pepper and 1 tsp salt.
steps.tip: Mix with your hand until it just comes together. Overworking makes the balls rubbery.

steps.text: Roll into balls the size of a walnut, about 20 of them, and chill 20 minutes.
Heat the oil in a wide pan and cook the sliced onion until soft and gold, 10 to 12 minutes.
Add the remaining ginger-garlic paste and fry 2 minutes.
Add the chilli powder, turmeric, coriander and cumin powders with a splash of water and fry 2 minutes until the oil takes on colour.
Add the tomato and cook until it collapses and the oil separates at the edges, 7 to 8 minutes.
Pour in the water, add the potato and salt, and bring to a steady simmer for 10 minutes.
Lower the balls in one at a time. Do not stir for the first 5 minutes; shake the pan instead.
steps.tip: Stirring too early is how ball curry becomes mince curry.

steps.text: Simmer uncovered 15 minutes, turning the balls gently once, until they are firm and cooked through.
Stir in the coconut milk and simmer very gently 5 more minutes. Check the salt, scatter the remaining coriander leaves and serve with yellow coconut rice.
steps.tip: Never let it boil after the coconut milk goes in.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated and tastes better the next day. Reheat gently in a pan, not a microwave, so the balls stay whole. Freezes for a month.

recipes.name: Bread Pudding
recipes.subtitle: stale bread, milk and dried fruit baked into the household dessert

ingredients.note: stale is not a compromise, fresh bread turns to paste

prepNotes: Every Anglo-Indian household made this and no two made it the same way. What is constant is stale bread, milk and whatever dried fruit was in the tin.
Soak the bread properly. Twenty minutes, not five.

steps.text: Warm the milk with the sugar until it dissolves. Pour it over the torn bread and leave 20 minutes.
Mash the soaked bread roughly with a fork. It should be lumpy, not smooth.
Beat in the eggs, melted butter, cardamom and nutmeg, then fold in the raisins and apricot.
Pour into a greased dish and bake at 180C for 50 minutes until set with a browned top and a slight wobble at the centre.
steps.tip: A slight wobble. Baked until firm all through, it is dry.

steps.text: Cool 20 minutes before cutting. It firms as it settles.

recipes.name: Coconut Toffee
recipes.subtitle: coconut and milk boiled to a fudge, cut in diamonds at Christmas
prepNotes: This is the Anglo-Indian Christmas sweet, made alongside kul kuls and rose cookies and given away in tins.
It is a sugar-stage recipe. Stop at the wrong moment and you get either syrup or a brick.

steps.text: Boil the sugar and milk together until the sugar dissolves completely.
Add the coconut and cook on medium, stirring constantly, for 20 minutes.
steps.tip: Constantly. The bottom catches the moment you look away.

steps.text: Add the butter and cardamom and keep going until the mixture leaves the sides of the pan in one mass and a drop set in cold water holds its shape.
Pour into a greased tray, scatter the cashew and press down flat.
Mark into diamonds while still warm and cut through when cold.
steps.tip: Mark warm, cut cold. Cutting it hot smears it; cutting it fully cold shatters it.

recipes.name: Country Captain Chicken
recipes.subtitle: dry-fried chicken buried in browned onion and whole red chillies, barely any gravy

ingredients.note: yes, four; they cook down to almost nothing
broken open if you want the heat
the Anglo-Indian sourness, added at the end

prepNotes: Rub the chicken with the turmeric, half the black pepper, 1 tsp salt and the ginger-garlic paste then cover and refrigerate it 30 minutes.
Slice the onions as thinly and evenly as you can. They are half the dish, and uneven slices give you burnt shreds next to raw ones.
This is a dry curry, so use a wide kadhai or frying pan rather than a deep pot.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a wide kadhai and fry three-quarters of the sliced onion over medium heat until brown and crisp at the edges, 15 to 18 minutes. Lift out and drain.
steps.tip: Brown, not black. Burnt onion turns the whole dish bitter and there is no rescuing it.

steps.text: In the same oil, fry the whole dried chillies and curry leaves for 20 seconds until the chillies darken and smell toasty.
Add the remaining raw onion and cook 5 minutes until soft and translucent.
Turn the heat high, add the marinated chicken and fry hard for 10 minutes, turning the pieces so every side takes colour.
steps.tip: Crowding the pan steams the chicken. Do it in two batches if your pan is small.

steps.text: Lower the heat, cover and cook 12 to 15 minutes, stirring once or twice. The chicken releases its own liquid and cooks in it.
Uncover, raise the heat and cook off the liquid until the pieces are coated and shining rather than sitting in sauce, about 5 minutes.
Crush most of the reserved fried onion between your fingers and stir it in with the remaining black pepper, the slit green chillies and the sugar.
Splash in the vinegar, toss for 1 minute and take the pan off the heat.
steps.tip: Vinegar at the end, off the boil, keeps its brightness. Added early it just cooks away.

steps.text: Scatter the rest of the fried onion and the coriander leaves over the top and serve with plain rice or bread.

recipes.name: Dak Bungalow Curry
recipes.subtitle: the chicken curry cooked in colonial rest houses, thickened with a boiled egg and a potato

ingredients.note: fried before it goes in, which is what makes it a dak bungalow curry
pepper rather than chilli leads this curry

prepNotes: Dak bungalows were the rest houses on the mail routes. The khansama cooked whatever was to hand, which is why the dish carries a potato and an egg.
Fry the potato and the boiled eggs before they go in. That browning is the difference between this and an ordinary curry.

steps.text: Fry the halved potatoes in the oil until golden on all sides. Lift out. Fry the boiled eggs until blistered. Lift out.
In the same oil, brown the onion deeply with the bay leaves. Add the ginger and garlic and cook out.
Add the chicken, turmeric and half the pepper. Fry on high until sealed and coloured, 8 minutes.
Add 400ml water, cover and simmer 25 minutes. Return the potatoes for the last 15.
Add the eggs, the rest of the pepper, the garam masala and the vinegar. Simmer uncovered 5 minutes.
steps.tip: The vinegar goes in at the end. Boiled long it just tastes sour.

steps.text: Rest 10 minutes before serving with bread or rice.

recipes.subtitle: lamb kidneys in a sharp, peppery sauce, eaten on toast at breakfast

prepNotes: Devilled means hot and sharp: pepper, mustard and something acid. It is a breakfast dish and a fast one.

steps.text: Soak the cored kidneys in salted water 20 minutes, then rinse and pat completely dry.

Raise the heat, add the kidneys and sear 2 minutes without moving them.

recipes.name: Duck Buffath
recipes.subtitle: duck stewed with vinegar and whole spice, a Christmas table dish

ingredients.note: buffath is a vinegar stew; this is not a place to economise

prepNotes: Buffath is close kin to Goan vindaloo and sorpotel: meat, vinegar, garlic and long keeping. It sat on Anglo-Indian Christmas tables because it improved for days.
Render the duck fat off first and cook the onions in it. Nothing else gives the same depth.

steps.text: Brown the duck pieces skin down in a dry heavy pot until the fat runs and the skin is deep gold. Lift out.

steps.text: Pour off all but 4 tbsp of the fat. Fry the onions in it until soft and brown, 15 minutes.

steps.text: Rest overnight if you can. It is a better dish on day two.

the Anglo-Indian signature; it is what separates this from a stir fry

prepNotes: Jalfrezi is a leftovers dish by design. The name comes from a Bengali word for hot frying, and the method is fast and dry.
Everything is cut large and stays distinct. It should not collapse into a curry.

steps.text: Heat the oil until nearly smoking. Add the garlic and ginger and fry 30 seconds.
Add the onion petals and capsicum and fry on high 4 minutes. They should char at the edges and stay crisp.

recipes.name: Kalkals
recipes.subtitle: little curls of coconut-milk dough deep-fried crisp and frosted with sugar, the Christmas sweet

ingredients.note: gives the shell its bite
or butter

ingredients.qty: 3 tbsp for the dough, plus 250g for the glaze

prepNotes: Kalkals are rolled on the back of a fork, and it takes a few to get the knack. Make one, see how it curls, then adjust how hard you press.
The dough must rest at least 2 hours, or overnight refrigerated. Unrested dough is slack and the curls unravel in the oil.
Have everything ready before you start the sugar syrup at the end; it goes from clear to grainy in under a minute.

steps.text: Rub the melted ghee into the maida, rava, 3 tbsp sugar, cardamom and salt with your fingertips until it looks like coarse breadcrumbs.
Work in the beaten egg, then add the coconut milk a little at a time until you have a firm, smooth dough. You may not need all of it.
steps.tip: Firm, like a stiff chapati dough. A soft dough will not hold the ridges.

steps.text: Knead 5 minutes, cover and rest at least 2 hours.
Pinch off marble-sized pieces. Roll each into a tiny ball, press it flat on the back of a greased fork, then roll it away from you with your thumb so it curls into a shell.
steps.tip: Press lightly. Bear down and the dough sticks to the fork instead of curling.

steps.text: Spread the shaped kalkals on a tray in a single layer and leave them to dry, uncovered, for 30 minutes.
Heat the oil in a kadhai to a steady medium. A scrap of dough should rise slowly and sizzle, not brown in seconds.
steps.tip: If they brown fast they will be raw inside. Low and slow gives an even, pale gold crisp.

steps.text: Fry in batches for 4 to 5 minutes, turning, until pale gold and hard. Drain on paper and cool completely.

Take the syrup off the heat, tip in the cooled kalkals and stir constantly as the syrup crystallises into a white frosting, 2 to 3 minutes.
steps.tip: Keep stirring right through the grainy stage or they will set in one solid lump.

steps.text: Spread them out on a tray to dry and harden for an hour before storing.

recipes.name: Mulligatawny Soup

ingredients.note: the bones make the stock; shred the meat back in
the thickener that makes this a soup rather than a broth
a spoonful goes into each bowl
the pepper in the pepper water
squeezed in at the table
or ghee

prepNotes: Rinse the toor dal until the water runs clear, then soak it 20 minutes so it collapses on time.

steps.text: Tip the fried mixture into the dal pot and simmer everything together 10 minutes.

recipes.name: Mutton Cutlets

ingredients.note: binds the mix; keep the mash dry

ingredients.qty: 2, beaten with a pinch of salt
ingredients.note: for the coating
dry, fine crumbs, not fresh soft ones

prepNotes: Boil the potatoes in their skins and let them steam dry for 10 minutes before mashing. Wet mash makes cutlets that split in the pan.

steps.tip: Keep going until the pan is properly dry. Any moisture left here ends up in the cutlet.

recipes.name: Pepper Water

ingredients.note: coarsely crushed, not powdered

ingredients.qty: 2 tbsp pulp, soaked in 200ml warm water

prepNotes: Soak the tamarind in warm water for 15 minutes, then squeeze it out and strain. The fibres will ruin the texture otherwise.

steps.text: Stir in the pounded pepper-cumin-garlic paste and simmer 8 minutes.

In a small pan heat the coconut oil, crackle the mustard seeds, then add the dried red chillies, the remaining bruised garlic and the curry leaves.
steps.tip: Wait for the mustard to actually pop before the rest goes in, or the tempering tastes raw.

steps.text: Stir in the asafoetida off the heat for 5 seconds and pour the whole tempering into the pepper water.
Cover at once and let it stand 2 minutes so the aromatics steep, then scatter the coriander leaves.

recipes.name: Railway Mutton Curry
recipes.subtitle: the mild dining-car mutton curry, loosened with coconut milk and sharpened with tamarind

ingredients.note: shoulder and neck give the best gravy
the railway version is deliberately mild
added late, for the catch at the back of the throat

ingredients.qty: 1 tbsp pulp, soaked in 100ml warm water

prepNotes: Bring the mutton to room temperature for 30 minutes before cooking; straight from the fridge it seizes and takes longer to tenderise.
Soak the tamarind in warm water while you slice the onions, then squeeze and strain out the fibres.
This curry was cooked to be reheated on a moving train, so make it a few hours ahead if you can.

steps.text: Heat the ghee in a pressure cooker and drop in the bay leaf, cinnamon and cloves. They should fizz and smell sweet within 30 seconds.
Add the sliced onion with a pinch of salt and cook over medium heat until deep gold and collapsed, 12 to 14 minutes.
steps.tip: This is the body of the gravy. Pale onion means a thin, watery curry.

steps.text: Stir in the ginger and garlic pastes and fry 2 minutes, until the raw edge is gone.
Add the coriander, chilli, turmeric and cumin powders with 3 tbsp water and fry 2 minutes.
steps.tip: The splash of water stops ground spice catching on the base and turning bitter.

steps.text: Add the tomato and cook until it breaks down and ghee glosses the edge of the pan, 6 to 8 minutes.
Turn the heat high, add the mutton and brown it in the masala for 8 minutes, stirring so every piece is coated and the surface has sealed.
steps.tip: Do not add salt to the meat yet; salt draws out water and the pieces stew rather than brown.

steps.text: Pour in the water, salt to taste, close the cooker and cook 20 minutes at full pressure. Let the pressure fall on its own.
Open, add the potato halves and simmer uncovered 12 to 15 minutes until a knife slides through them without resistance.
Stir in the strained tamarind water, the coconut milk and the crushed black pepper. Simmer gently 6 to 8 minutes.

steps.text: Fry the curry leaves in a teaspoon of ghee until they crackle and pour them over the curry. Rest 10 minutes before serving with bread or yellow rice.

recipes.name: Rissoles

ingredients.qty: 2, one for the dough and one for sealing

ingredients.note: beef or chicken mince works equally

steps.text: Rub the butter into the flour with a pinch of salt, bind with one beaten egg and a little cold water, and rest the dough 30 minutes.

steps.tip: Dry. Any moisture left will burst the pastry.

Roll the dough thin, cut 10cm rounds, place a spoonful of filling on each and fold into a crescent.
Seal the edges with beaten egg and crimp firmly with a fork.

recipes.name: Yellow Coconut Rice

ingredients.note: for the colour the dish is named after
or coconut oil
the Calcutta touch, optional

prepNotes: Rinse the rice in three changes of water until it runs clear, then leave it to drain in a sieve for 20 minutes. Do not soak it: coconut milk rice goes sticky if the grain is waterlogged.

Tip in the drained rice and turn it in the fat for 2 minutes, until every grain is coated and glossy.
Pour in the coconut milk and water, add the salt and sugar, and bring to a boil.

steps.tip: Lifting the lid lets out the steam that is doing the cooking. Trust the clock.

steps.text: Take the pan off the heat and leave it covered for 10 minutes more.
Fork the grains apart gently from the edge inwards, scatter the reserved onion over and serve.
steps.tip: Fork, never spoon. A spoon crushes coconut-milk rice into paste.

steps.text: Pour in the hot water, bring to a rolling boil, then taste for salt and let it boil uncovered 4 minutes until the water level drops to the rice.

Take off the heat, sprinkle over the garam masala, and rest covered 10 minutes before opening.

recipes.name: Arhar ki Dal

recipes.name: Awadhi Kheer

ingredients.note: broken coarsely between the palms for a thicker set

added at the end

steps.text: Tip the hung yogurt into a bowl and mash in the grated paneer until smooth and even.

steps.text: Work in the roasted besan a tablespoon at a time until the mixture just holds a shape when pressed. It should feel soft, almost too soft.

Heat 2 tbsp ghee on a tawa over medium-low heat. Lay in half the kebabs, leaving space between them.

steps.text: Fry undisturbed 3-4 minutes, until the underside is set and deep gold, then turn once with a thin spatula and give the second side 3 minutes.
steps.tip: Turn once only. Every flip after that is a chance for them to break.

steps.text: Drain briefly on paper, repeat with the rest, dust with chaat masala and serve hot with mint chutney.

recipes.name: Dum Aloo Lucknowi

ingredients.qty: 500g baby potatoes, boiled 10 minutes and peeled

ingredients.note: use compounded-free hing to keep the dish gluten-free

steps.text: Prick the boiled, peeled potatoes deeply all over and pat them dry.
Deep fry them in hot oil until golden and lightly blistered, 4–5 minutes. Drain and set aside.
steps.tip: Dry potatoes only. Wet ones spit violently in hot oil.

steps.text: Whisk the yogurt with the coriander powder, kashmiri chilli, turmeric, fennel powder and dry ginger powder to a smooth, lump-free mix.

Add the asafoetida, count to five, then immediately pour in the spiced yogurt.
steps.tip: Hing burns in seconds. It goes in last and the yogurt follows straight after.

steps.text: Cook on the lowest flame, stirring without stopping, for 7–8 minutes until the mixture thickens and the ghee separates.
steps.tip: Stop stirring and it curdles. This is the one step that needs your full attention.

steps.text: Add the fried potatoes and salt and turn them through the masala for 3 minutes.
Pour in 250ml warm water, bring to a simmer, then cover tightly and cook on the lowest heat for 15 minutes.

recipes.name: Gulab Jamun
recipes.subtitle: milk-solid dumplings fried slowly and soaked in cardamom syrup

ingredients.note: for deep frying

prepNotes: The oil must be barely warm when the jamuns go in and rise slowly over ten minutes. Hot fat browns the outside while the centre stays raw dough.

steps.text: Make the syrup: 500g sugar to 500ml water with the crushed cardamom, boiled 8 minutes to a slightly sticky, one-string syrup. Keep it warm.

steps.tip: Overworked dough gives hard jamuns. Stop as soon as it is smooth.

steps.text: Roll into 18 smooth balls with no cracks, rolling between your palms with a little ghee.
steps.tip: Any crack becomes a split in the oil.

steps.text: Heat the ghee to only 120C, barely warm, and slide the balls in.
steps.tip: Barely warm. If they sizzle, the ghee is too hot.

steps.text: Let them rise on their own and colour slowly over 10 minutes, turning gently, until deep brown all over.
Lift out, rest 2 minutes, then drop into the warm syrup.

steps.text: Grind the drained dal with as little water as possible into a smooth, stiff paste.

steps.text: Grill over medium charcoal or in an oven at 220C, turning every 3 minutes and basting with ghee, for 12–15 minutes total.

ingredients.note: crush it fresh, the whole dish rests on this

ingredients.note: boiling keeps the gravy pale

ingredients.note: oil your hands and the knife first, the sap is glue
4 for frying the jackfruit, 2 for the masala

Add the sliced onion and fry 10-12 minutes over medium heat until deep brown at the edges.

heat without staining the gravy

colour without heat

recipes.name: Muzaffar
recipes.subtitle: saffron-yellow fine vermicelli fried in ghee and glazed with syrup, khoya and slivered nuts

ingredients.note: grated paneer is a poor but workable stand-in

ingredients.qty: a good pinch, soaked in 2 tbsp warm milk

ingredients.note: for the saffron

prepNotes: Soak the saffron in warm milk at least 20 minutes ahead so the colour is deep, not streaky.

steps.text: Tip the roasted vermicelli onto a plate so it stops cooking.

steps.tip: Do not stir while it cooks or the strands break into mush.

steps.text: Fry the almonds, pistachios and raisins in the remaining 2 tbsp ghee in a small pan for 90 seconds, until the nuts are gold and the raisins swell.

Sprinkle the kewra water, cover off the heat and rest 5 minutes.

recipes.name: Nalli Nihari
recipes.subtitle: marrow bones and shank stewed overnight, eaten at dawn

ingredients.note: the marrow is the point; ask for nalli specifically

ingredients.qty: 3 tbsp paste, plus julienne to finish

ingredients.note: the thickener; nihari gravy is flour-bound, not reduced

prepNotes: Nihar means dawn. It was cooked overnight on dying coals and eaten at first light, and the long cook is not negotiable.
Nalli is the marrow bone. Serve it with a thin skewer so people can get the marrow out.

steps.text: Brown the onions in the oil until deep and dark. Lift half out and reserve for the top.
Add the ginger and garlic pastes, then the fennel, dry ginger, chilli, turmeric and black cardamom. Fry 3 minutes.
Add the meat and bones and fry hard until sealed and coloured, 10 minutes.
Add 2 litres water, bring to a boil, then cover and cook on the lowest heat for 3 hours.
steps.tip: The lowest heat you can hold. A hard boil makes the meat stringy rather than soft.

steps.text: Slake the flour in cold water and stir it in. Simmer uncovered 30 minutes until the gravy coats a spoon.
steps.tip: Slaked in cold water, always, or it lumps.

steps.text: Finish with garam masala. Serve topped with the reserved onions, ginger julienne and lemon.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated and is famously better the next day. Reheat to a full simmer, loosening with hot water.

recipes.name: Nargisi Kofta
recipes.subtitle: boiled eggs sheathed in spiced mutton mince, fried and halved into a korma gravy

ingredients.note: binds the mince around the egg
one for the kofta, two for birista

ingredients.qty: a pinch in 2 tbsp warm milk

prepNotes: Boil the eggs 9 minutes, cool under running water and peel carefully. A torn white makes a kofta that splits in the oil.
Cook and grind the mince at least an hour ahead and chill it. Cold mince wraps cleanly, warm mince slides off.
Have the gravy finished and waiting before you fry. The koftas go in only at the last moment.

steps.text: Simmer the mince with the drained chana dal, one sliced onion, ginger and garlic pastes, salt and 150ml water until dry, about 20 minutes.
steps.tip: Cook it down until the pan is genuinely dry. Damp mince will not seal around the egg.

steps.text: Cool, then grind to a stiff paste and knead in the roasted besan, green chilli, chopped coriander and half the garam masala. Refrigerate 45 minutes.
Divide into 6, flatten each into a disc on your wet palm and wrap it around an egg, sealing every seam.
steps.tip: Hunt for cracks with your fingertips before frying. One gap and the kofta bursts.

steps.text: Deep fry two at a time in medium-hot oil, turning, until an even deep brown, 3–4 minutes. Drain and set aside.
For the gravy, fry the two remaining sliced onions in 2 tbsp ghee until deep brown, 12 minutes. Drain, cool and grind with the soaked cashews and 4 tbsp water.
Heat the remaining ghee with the cardamom, cinnamon and cloves for 30 seconds, then add the onion-cashew paste and cook 5 minutes.
Off the heat, whisk in the yogurt in three additions, return to a low flame and stir 6 minutes until the fat separates.
steps.tip: Adding cold yogurt to a hot pan in one go is how this gravy splits.

steps.text: Add the coriander powder, kashmiri chilli, mace, remaining garam masala and salt and cook 3 minutes, then pour in 350ml warm water and simmer 12 minutes.
Halve each kofta lengthways with a sharp knife so the egg shows, and lay them cut side up in the gravy.
Spoon the gravy over, add the saffron milk, cover and rest off the heat 5 minutes before serving.
steps.tip: Do not simmer the koftas in the gravy. They go soggy and fall apart.

recipes.storage: The gravy keeps 3 days refrigerated on its own. Store koftas separately and reheat them 5 minutes in a hot oven, then combine at the table. Do not freeze.

recipes.name: Navratan Korma
recipes.subtitle: nine jewels: mixed vegetables, paneer, nuts and fruit in a pale sweet cream gravy
prepNotes: Navratan means nine gems, and the count is the point: vegetables, paneer, nuts and dried fruit should all be identifiable.
No tomato and no chilli powder. The gravy is deliberately pale and mild; heat belongs in a different dish.

steps.text: Boil the onion, ginger, cardamom and soaked cashews in 200ml water for 12 minutes, then blend to a smooth white paste.
Blanch the carrot, beans, cauliflower and potato until just tender and refresh in cold water so they keep their colour.
steps.tip: Refreshing matters. Vegetables left to sit hot go grey.

steps.text: Fry the paneer cubes in ghee until pale gold and set aside.
Cook the white paste in the remaining ghee for 8 minutes without letting it colour.
steps.tip: It must not brown. The colour of this dish is its signature.

steps.text: Add the milk, sugar and salt, and simmer to a coating consistency.
Fold in the vegetables, paneer, almonds and raisins and warm through for 4 minutes.
Finish off the heat with the cream and garam masala, and scatter pomegranate over.

recipes.name: Nihari
recipes.subtitle: Overnight shank stew, thickened with wheat flour and finished with ginger and lime

ingredients.qty: 1kg shank on the bone, with marrow

ingredients.note: the traditional thickener

prepNotes: Nihari comes from nahar, meaning morning: it was cooked overnight and eaten at dawn. The long, low cook is not optional. It is what turns shank into something spoonable.
Shank with marrow bones is the cut. Boneless meat makes a curry, not nihari.

steps.text: Brown the sliced onion in ghee, then add the ginger and garlic pastes and cook until the raw smell goes.
Add the powdered spices with a splash of water so they do not scorch, then the mutton. Turn it in the masala over high heat until sealed.
Add 2 litres of water and the whole spices. Bring to a boil, then drop to the barest simmer, cover, and cook 4-5 hours until the meat slides off the bone.
steps.tip: A trembling surface, not a rolling boil. Boiling makes the meat stringy.

steps.text: Whisk the atta into a cup of cold water until perfectly smooth and stir it into the pot. Simmer 30 minutes more, stirring often, until the gravy coats a spoon.
steps.tip: Cold water and hard whisking, or you will get lumps you cannot remove.

steps.text: Rest off the heat 20 minutes; the fat will rise. Do not skim it. That layer is the point.
Serve with julienned ginger, green chilli, coriander and a hard squeeze of lemon at the table.

recipes.storage: Improves for two days refrigerated and is arguably better on day two. Reheat gently with hot water. Freezes 2 months.

recipes.name: Paneer Do Pyaza
recipes.subtitle: paneer with onion twice over, once melted into the gravy and once in soft petals

ingredients.qty: 5, two chopped fine and three in petals
ingredients.note: the name means two onions, and it is literal

prepNotes: The two onions do different jobs. The chopped one dissolves into the gravy; the petals go in at the end and must stay separate and sweet.
Take the yogurt off the heat before it goes in, or it splits.

steps.text: Fry the chopped onion in oil for 12 minutes until deep brown, then add ginger and garlic.
Add the ground spices with a splash of water, then the tomato, and cook until the oil separates.
Take the pan off the heat, whisk in the yogurt, and only then return it to a low flame.
steps.tip: Off the heat, always. Yogurt added to a hot pan curdles instantly.

steps.text: Simmer 5 minutes with a little water to a thick gravy.
In a separate pan sear the onion petals hard for 2 minutes so they colour but keep their bite, and add the paneer for a minute.
Fold the petals and paneer through the gravy, add kasuri methi and garam masala, and rest 5 minutes off the heat.

recipes.name: Rabri
recipes.subtitle: milk reduced for an hour with the skin folded back in at every stage

ingredients.note: full fat, and nothing less; skimmed milk will not layer

prepNotes: Rabri is not thickened milk, it is collected milk skin. The layers are the dish, so it should never be smooth.
Use the widest pan you own. More surface area means more skin, which means better rabri.

steps.text: Bring the milk to a boil in a wide heavy pan, then lower to a bare simmer.
As a skin forms, push it to the side of the pan with a spatula and leave it stuck there.
steps.tip: Do not stir it back in. You are collecting layers on the wall of the pan.

steps.text: Keep going for about an hour, until the milk has reduced by three quarters.
Add the sugar, cardamom and saffron and stir to dissolve.
Scrape all the collected skin off the sides back into the milk and fold once, no more.
steps.tip: Once. Stirring it smooth undoes the entire hour.

steps.text: Cool and refrigerate. Serve cold, topped with the nuts.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated. It is reduced dairy, so keep it cold and do not leave it out.

recipes.name: Shahi Tukda
recipes.subtitle: ghee-fried bread soaked in saffron syrup under a blanket of thick rabri

ingredients.qty: 8 slices of white bread, crusts cut off
ingredients.note: day-old bread fries crisper than fresh
for the rabri; there is no shortcut to reducing it
thickens the rabri faster

ingredients.qty: 150g for the syrup, plus 3 tbsp for the rabri
a generous pinch, steeped in 2 tbsp warm milk

prepNotes: Reduce the milk for the rabri first. It takes 45 minutes and cannot be hurried.
Use day-old bread and leave the slices uncovered for an hour so they dry out; fresh bread soaks up ghee and goes soggy.
Steep the saffron in warm milk for 20 minutes.

steps.text: Simmer the milk in a wide heavy pan over medium-low heat, scraping the cream back in from the sides every few minutes, until reduced to about a third, 40–45 minutes.
steps.tip: A wide pan, not a tall one. Surface area is what reduces milk.

steps.text: Stir in the grated khoya, 3 tbsp sugar, half the saffron milk and half the cardamom powder and cook 5 minutes more. Set the rabri aside to cool a little.
Meanwhile boil the 150g sugar with 150ml water for 5 minutes to a thin one-string syrup, then stir in the remaining saffron milk and the rose water.
steps.tip: Thin syrup. A thick one turns the bread to candy.

steps.text: Cut each bread slice into two triangles.
Fry them in ghee over medium heat until deep golden and crisp on both sides, 2 minutes a side, adding ghee as needed. Drain on paper.
steps.tip: Fry to properly crisp. Bread that is only pale will collapse in the syrup.

steps.text: Dip each fried triangle into the warm syrup for 5 seconds a side and lift it straight out onto a serving plate.
steps.tip: Five seconds, no more. Any longer and it disintegrates.

steps.text: Arrange the soaked bread in a single overlapping layer and spoon the warm rabri over the top.
Scatter with pistachios, almonds and the remaining cardamom powder.
Chill 1 hour before serving so the rabri sets and the bread softens through.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated, covered. It is served chilled or at room temperature, never reheated. The bread turns to mush. Assemble on the day you plan to eat it.

recipes.name: Shami Kebab
recipes.subtitle: dense little mutton and chana dal patties, smooth inside and crisp at the edge

ingredients.note: the binder. Nothing else does the same job

ingredients.qty: 1 medium quartered for the boil, 1 small very finely chopped for the mix

ingredients.note: helps the patties hold when frying
to squeeze at the table
neutral oil works but tastes flatter

prepNotes: Soak the chana dal 1 hour in warm water. Undersoaked dal stays gritty and the kebab will crumble.
The cooked mince must be bone dry before grinding. Any moisture and the patties fall apart in the pan.
Chill the shaped kebabs 30 minutes before frying. They firm up and turn far more easily.

steps.text: Pressure cook the mutton, drained dal, quartered onion, garlic, ginger, whole chillies, black cardamom, green cardamom, cinnamon, cloves, peppercorns, salt and 250ml water for 5 whistles, about 20 minutes.
steps.tip: In a pan instead, allow 50 minutes covered on low.

steps.text: Open the lid and boil hard, stirring, until every trace of liquid has gone and the mix looks dry and sandy, 8–10 minutes.
steps.tip: This is the step people skip. Wet mince equals kebabs that disintegrate.

steps.text: Cool completely, then pick out the cinnamon stick and black cardamom shell and grind the rest to a smooth, tight paste with no added water.
Knead in the finely chopped onion, green chilli, coriander, mint, garam masala and the beaten egg. Taste for salt now.
Divide into 12 and shape into flat discs 5cm across and 1.5cm thick. Refrigerate 30 minutes.
Heat 2 tbsp ghee on a tawa over medium heat and lay in the kebabs without crowding.
Fry 3–4 minutes a side until a deep brown crust forms, adding the remaining ghee as you turn.
steps.tip: Turn once only, with a thin spatula. Fiddling breaks them.

steps.text: Drain on paper, rest 2 minutes and serve hot with lemon wedges and sliced onion.

recipes.storage: Cooked kebabs keep 3 days refrigerated and reheat well on a dry tawa over low heat. The raw ground mix freezes for a month; thaw fully before shaping.

recipes.name: Sheermal
recipes.subtitle: slightly sweet saffron-milk flatbread, soft as brioche, brushed with ghee

ingredients.note: the shir in sheermal. This is what makes it
helps the crumb stay soft
traditionally sheermal is yeast-leavened; soda with yogurt gives a similar soft crumb in less time

ingredients.qty: a generous pinch, steeped in 3 tbsp warm milk

prepNotes: Steep the saffron in warm milk for at least 20 minutes so it gives up its full colour.
The dough must rest 1 hour covered at room temperature. Skipping the rest gives a tough, cracker-like bread.
Preheat the oven with the tray inside for 20 minutes; sheermal wants immediate bottom heat.

steps.text: Dissolve the sugar and salt in the warm milk and stir in the yogurt.
steps.tip: Warm, not hot. Hot milk cooks the yogurt into lumps.

steps.text: Mix the maida with the baking soda, rub in 60g of the melted ghee until it looks like breadcrumbs, then add half the saffron milk.
Add the milk mixture gradually and knead 10 minutes to a soft, smooth, slightly sticky dough.
steps.tip: Softer than a chapati dough. Resist adding extra flour.

steps.text: Cover with a damp cloth and rest 1 hour at room temperature.
Knock back, divide into 8 and roll each into a disc 15cm across and 5mm thick. Prick all over with a fork.
steps.tip: The fork holes stop it ballooning into a puri.

steps.text: Bake at 220C on a preheated tray for 6–7 minutes, until the surface is set and just speckled.
Pull the tray out, brush each bread generously with the remaining saffron milk and melted ghee, and return for 3 minutes.
steps.tip: The saffron glaze goes on partway through, not at the start, or it scorches.

steps.text: Dust with cardamom powder, stack under a cloth and serve warm with korma or kebabs.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days wrapped in a cloth at room temperature, or 5 days refrigerated. Revive on a hot tawa for 30 seconds a side; the microwave makes them chewy.
