recipes.name: Kadhi Bari
recipes.subtitle: fried gram-flour dumplings soaked soft in a tart yogurt gravy with a mustard-oil temper

ingredients.note: 150g for the bari, 50g to thicken the kadhi
the sourer the better; fresh sweet yogurt makes a flat kadhi

ingredients.qty: 3 tbsp, for the kadhi and the temper

ingredients.note: use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free
makes lighter bari, but a well-beaten batter works without it

prepNotes: Take the yogurt out of the fridge 30 minutes ahead. Cold yogurt hitting a hot pan splits instantly.
Whisk the yogurt, the 50g besan and the water together completely smooth before any of it goes near heat. Lumps set hard and never disperse.
Beat the bari batter for a good 5 minutes; a spoonful should float in a bowl of water when it is aerated enough.

steps.text: Whisk 150g besan with 1/2 tsp salt, 1/4 tsp turmeric, the baking soda and about 120ml water into a thick batter, then beat hard for 5 minutes until it is pale and fluffy.
steps.tip: Drop a little into water. If it floats, the batter is ready; if it sinks, keep beating.

steps.text: Heat the neutral oil to 170C and drop in walnut-sized spoonfuls of batter. Fry 4-5 minutes, turning, until deep golden and hollow-sounding.
Drain the bari on paper, then soak them in warm water for 10 minutes and squeeze gently.
steps.tip: This soak is what makes bari spongy rather than chewy. Do not skip it, and squeeze softly or they tear.

steps.text: Whisk the sour yogurt with the remaining 50g besan, the rest of the turmeric, the chilli powder and 1.2 litres water until absolutely smooth.
Heat 2 tbsp mustard oil in a kadhai until it smokes, then lower the heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds and the fenugreek seeds for 15 seconds.
Add the chopped onion, garlic, ginger and green chillies and fry 6-8 minutes until the onion turns golden.
Pour in the yogurt mixture and bring it to a boil over medium heat, stirring constantly in one direction.
steps.tip: Stir without stopping until it boils. The moment you walk away is the moment it curdles.

steps.text: Once boiling, lower the heat and simmer uncovered 25 minutes, stirring every few minutes, until the kadhi coats a spoon and the raw besan smell is gone.
Add salt and slip in the squeezed bari. Simmer another 8 minutes so they drink up the gravy.
In a small pan heat the remaining 1 tbsp mustard oil, crackle the mustard seeds, remaining cumin, nigella, broken red chillies and asafoetida for 20 seconds, and pour it over the kadhi.
steps.tip: Pour the temper over at the table so the aroma survives to the plate.

steps.text: Scatter with coriander leaves and serve with plain rice.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated and tastes better on day two. It thickens considerably. Reheat over low heat with 100ml water, stirring, and never boil it hard on reheating.

recipes.name: Litti Chokha
recipes.subtitle: baked wheat balls stuffed with spiced roasted gram, dipped in ghee and crushed over smoky brinjal mash

image.alt: Litti served with chokha, lemon and green chilli

ingredients.note: roasted gram flour; the filling depends on it
the litti is not finished until it has drunk ghee

ingredients.qty: 10 cloves, crushed to a coarse paste

ingredients.note: for the chokha

prepNotes: Sattu is sold already roasted, so it goes straight in. If you are standing in besan, dry-roast it over low heat for 8-10 minutes until it darkens a shade and smells like roasted grain, then cool it completely. Unroasted besan tastes raw and pasty.
Make the dough first and let it rest a full 30 minutes so it seals around the filling instead of tearing.
Char the vegetables for the chokha while the litti bake, so both land hot at the same time.

steps.text: Rub 2 tbsp mustard oil and 1 tsp salt into the atta until a squeezed handful holds its shape, then add water a little at a time to make a stiff, smooth dough.
steps.tip: Stiffer than roti dough. A soft dough splits open as the filling steams.

steps.text: Cover the dough and rest it 30 minutes.
Mix the sattu with the garlic, ginger, 4 chopped green chillies, the ajwain, nigella, juice of half the lemon, 3 tbsp mustard oil and 1 tsp salt, rubbing it through your fingers.
steps.tip: It should end up damp and crumbly, never a paste. Wet filling makes a heavy, soggy litti.

steps.text: Divide the dough into 10 balls. Cup each in your palm, press a hollow, pack in a heaped tablespoon of the sattu mix, then pinch the seam closed and roll smooth.
steps.tip: Roll seam-side down and check for cracks; an open seam leaks filling and scorches.

steps.text: Bake at 200C for 25 minutes, turning once at the halfway mark, until the litti are dry, cracked across the top and pale brown.

Meanwhile rub the brinjal with a little oil and hold it directly over a gas flame, turning, for 10-12 minutes until the skin blisters black and the flesh slumps. Char the tomatoes the same way for 5 minutes.
steps.tip: The smoke is the whole flavour of chokha. Take it to the open flame, not to a covered pan.

steps.text: Boil the potatoes 15 minutes until a knife slides in without resistance, then drain and peel.
Peel the charred brinjal and tomatoes and mash them with the potato, chopped onion, remaining 2 green chillies, 1 tbsp mustard oil, the juice of the remaining lemon half and salt.
Fold in the coriander leaves and taste. Chokha should be sharp with lemon and raw mustard oil, not bland.
Dip each hot litti in the melted ghee, holding it under for a few seconds so it soaks, then crush it open and serve over the chokha.
steps.tip: Dip while the litti is still hot; a cooled one will not take the ghee.

recipes.storage: Chokha keeps 2 days refrigerated and is good cold. Litti keep 2 days in an airtight tin. Refresh them 6 minutes in a 200C oven and dip in fresh ghee before serving.

recipes.name: Machhli ka Jhor
recipes.subtitle: river fish simmered in a thin, fiery mustard-oil gravy sharpened with ground mustard seed

ingredients.qty: 700g rohu or katla, cut into 2cm steaks on the bone
ingredients.note: any firm freshwater fish on the bone; boneless fillets fall apart in this gravy
not negotiable here. The pungency is the dish

ingredients.qty: 2 tsp, ground to a paste with 2 green chillies and a splash of water

ingredients.note: for colour without extra heat

prepNotes: Rub the fish steaks with 1 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt then cover and refrigerate 15 minutes. This firms the flesh so it survives frying.
Grind the mustard seeds with green chilli and a little water and use the paste within the hour. Mustard turns bitter if it sits ground and warm.
Pat the fish completely dry before it goes into the oil, or it will spit and stick.

steps.text: Heat 5 tbsp mustard oil in a kadhai until it smokes and the sharp smell dies down, then lower the heat.
steps.tip: Mustard oil must be taken to smoking point first; used raw it tastes bitter and thin.

steps.text: Fry the fish steaks in batches, 2 minutes a side, until the surface is set and pale gold. Lift out and set aside.
steps.tip: Do not move the fish for the first two minutes. It releases from the pan by itself once a crust forms.

steps.text: In the same oil add the remaining 2 tbsp, then crackle the cumin seeds and nigella for 20 seconds.
Add the onion paste and fry 8-10 minutes over medium heat until it loses its raw smell and turns light brown at the edges.
Stir in the ginger and garlic pastes and cook 2 minutes, until the oil starts to bead at the sides.
Add the chopped tomato and cook 6 minutes, mashing it down, until it collapses completely.
Mix the remaining 1 tsp turmeric, the chilli powder, kashmiri chilli and coriander powder with 3 tbsp water and fry this paste for 3-4 minutes until the oil separates and floats clear.
Stir in the ground mustard paste and cook exactly 1 minute, no longer.
steps.tip: Mustard paste goes bitter if fried hard or long. One minute over low heat is all it needs.

steps.text: Pour in 500ml water with the slit green chillies and 1 tsp salt and bring to a boil. The gravy should be thin, like a light broth.
Slide the fried fish back in, lower the heat and simmer uncovered 8-10 minutes, spooning gravy over the pieces rather than stirring.
steps.tip: Never stir a fish curry with a spoon; tilt and swirl the pan or the steaks break up.

steps.text: Rest 5 minutes off the heat, scatter with coriander leaves and serve with plain rice.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated and the flavour deepens overnight. Reheat gently over low heat without stirring, adding a little hot water if the gravy has tightened. Do not freeze. The fish goes woolly.

recipes.name: Mithila Machh Posto
recipes.subtitle: river fish simmered in a ground poppy seed and mustard gravy, no onion or garlic

ingredients.qty: 700g rohu or katla, cut into 2cm steaks
ingredients.note: any firm freshwater fish works
soak with the poppy seeds
1 tsp for rubbing the fish, the rest for the gravy

prepNotes: Soak the poppy seeds and mustard seeds together in 100 ml warm water for 30 minutes before grinding, or the paste will stay gritty.
Rub the fish steaks with 1 tsp turmeric and a good pinch of salt and leave 15 minutes. It firms the surface so the pieces do not break.
Pat the fish completely dry before it meets the oil.

steps.text: Grind the soaked poppy and mustard seeds with 2 of the green chillies and 3 tbsp of their soaking water to a smooth pale paste.
steps.tip: Grind in short bursts. Mustard turns bitter if the blender heats it up.

steps.text: Heat the mustard oil in a kadhai until it smokes, then lower the flame.
Slide in the fish and fry 2 minutes a side until the surface is set and pale gold, then lift out onto a plate.
steps.tip: Do not brown it hard. The fish finishes cooking in the gravy.

steps.text: Crackle the nigella seeds in the remaining oil for 20 seconds until they smell smoky.
Add the ground paste with the remaining turmeric and the chilli powder and cook on low for 4 minutes, stirring constantly.
steps.tip: Keep the heat low and keep it moving; mustard paste scorches in seconds.

steps.text: Pour in the water, add the remaining slit chillies and salt, and simmer 5 minutes until the gravy thickens enough to coat a spoon.
Return the fish, spoon gravy over each piece, cover and simmer 6 minutes on low.
Drizzle over 1 tsp raw mustard oil, scatter the coriander and rest 5 minutes off the heat before serving with plain rice.

recipes.storage: Best eaten the day it is made. Keeps 1 day refrigerated; reheat covered on low heat without stirring so the fish stays whole.

recipes.name: Namkeen Sattu Sharbat
recipes.subtitle: savoury roasted gram drink with black salt, lemon and roasted cumin, drunk cold through the summer

ingredients.note: roasted gram flour, the whole point of the drink
the sulphurous note that makes this taste right

prepNotes: Sattu is sold already roasted, so it goes straight in. If you are standing in besan, dry-roast it over low heat for 8-10 minutes until it darkens a shade and smells like roasted grain, then cool it completely (unroasted besan tastes raw and pasty. It must be cold either way) hot flour will not disperse in cold water.
Chill the water beforehand. This is drunk cold, and a lukewarm sattu sharbat is heavy and dull.
Roast and crush the cumin fresh; pre-ground cumin powder has none of the smokiness this needs.

steps.text: Dry-roast the cumin seeds in the same pan for about 1 minute, until they darken and pop, then crush them coarsely.
Whisk the sattu with just 100ml of the chilled water to a completely smooth, thick paste.
steps.tip: Paste first, then thin. Pour all the water in at once and you get lumps that never break up.

steps.text: Whisk in the remaining 400ml chilled water in a steady stream until the drink is thin and even.
Stir in the black salt, plain salt, roasted crushed cumin and the juice of the whole lemon.
Add the green chilli, onion, mint and coriander leaves and stir once.
Taste and adjust. It should be sour and salty first, with the roasted flour underneath. Serve immediately in tall glasses.
steps.tip: Sattu settles fast; give the glass a stir between sips or serve straight from the jug.

recipes.storage: Drink within 20 minutes of mixing, before the flour settles and thickens. The roasted flour itself keeps a month in an airtight jar at room temperature, so only the mixing is last-minute.

recipes.name: Sarson Wala Aloo
recipes.subtitle: boiled potatoes turned through a sharp ground mustard paste, no onion or garlic

ingredients.qty: 700g, boiled, peeled and broken into rough chunks

ingredients.note: for the paste
2 ground into the paste, 2 slit
softens the mustard's edge

prepNotes: Soak the mustard seeds and poppy seeds in 100 ml warm water with a pinch of salt for 30 minutes. Unsoaked mustard grinds bitter.
Boil the potatoes ahead and let them cool completely so they break into craggy chunks instead of mush.
Grind the paste just before cooking; it turns acrid if it sits.

steps.text: Grind the soaked mustard and poppy seeds with 2 green chillies, a pinch of salt and 3 tbsp of the soaking water to a smooth paste.
steps.tip: Pulse rather than run the blender. Heat is what makes mustard bitter.

steps.text: Heat the mustard oil until it smokes, then lower the flame and let it settle 30 seconds.
Crackle the nigella seeds for 20 seconds until they pop and smell smoky.
Add the potato chunks and fry 6 minutes, turning gently, until the edges are crisp and golden.
steps.tip: Give them a proper crust now; once the mustard paste goes in they will not brown any further.

steps.text: Push the potatoes to one side, add the turmeric to the clear oil and let it bloom for 10 seconds.
Stir in the ground mustard paste and cook on low for 3 minutes, stirring constantly, until it loses its raw smell.
steps.tip: Low heat and constant stirring, or the paste catches and the whole dish tastes burnt.

steps.text: Pour in the water, add the slit chillies and salt, and simmer 6 minutes until the gravy clings to the potatoes.
Take off the heat, scatter the coriander and drizzle over 1 tsp raw mustard oil before serving with rice or puri.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated. Reheat gently with a splash of water; the mustard sharpens as it sits, so add a pinch of salt to balance it.

recipes.name: Sattu ka Paratha
recipes.subtitle: wheat flatbread packed with garlicky roasted gram flour, sharp with mustard oil and ajwain

ingredients.note: roasted gram flour; the stuffing depends on it
for extra sourness if the lemon is weak

prepNotes: Sattu is sold already roasted, so it goes straight in. If you are standing in besan, dry-roast it over low heat for 8-10 minutes until it darkens a shade and smells like roasted grain, then cool it completely (unroasted besan tastes raw and pasty. Either way it must be cold) warm flour steams inside the paratha and turns it gluey.
Knead the dough and rest it 20 minutes so it rolls out without tearing over the filling.
Chop the onion as fine as you can; coarse pieces puncture the dough while rolling.

steps.text: Knead the atta with 1 tsp salt, 1 tbsp mustard oil and enough water to make a soft, pliable dough, about 6 minutes.
Cover with a damp cloth and rest 20 minutes.
Mix the sattu with the garlic, ginger, green chilli, onion, ajwain, nigella, amchur, coriander leaves, lemon juice, 2 tbsp mustard oil and 3/4 tsp salt.
steps.tip: Squeeze a fistful. It should just clump and then fall apart. If it is dry, add a teaspoon of water at a time, not more oil.

steps.text: Divide the dough into 8 balls. Roll one into a 10cm disc, mound 2 tbsp of filling in the centre, gather the edges over the top and pinch shut.
Flatten the sealed ball gently with your palm, dust with flour and roll out to about 18cm, pressing lightly and evenly from the centre.
steps.tip: Light hands. Bearing down forces the filling through and it sticks to the rolling pin.

steps.text: Cook on a hot tawa for 1 minute until pale spots appear, flip, and cook the second side 1 minute.
Brush both sides with mustard oil and cook another minute a side, pressing the edges with a cloth, until brown blisters form.
steps.tip: The tawa must be properly hot before the paratha goes on or the bread dries out before it browns.

steps.text: Serve straight off the tawa with plain yogurt, chokha or a spoon of pickle.

recipes.storage: Best eaten hot off the tawa. Cooked parathas keep 1 day wrapped in a cloth at room temperature; reheat on a dry tawa for a minute a side. The filling keeps 3 days refrigerated.

recipes.name: Silbatte ki Chutney
recipes.subtitle: tomato, chilli and garlic crushed on a stone, not blended
prepNotes: Silbatta is the stone and roller. A blender gives you a smooth sauce; the stone gives you a chutney with texture, which is the whole difference.
If you must use a blender, pulse two or three times only.

steps.text: Char the tomatoes, chillies and unpeeled garlic directly over a flame until blackened and blistered.
Rest them under a cloth for 5 minutes, then rub off the burnt skins. Do not rinse them.
steps.tip: Rinsing washes away the smoke, which is the point of roasting.

steps.text: Crush the garlic and chillies first with the salt, then work in the tomatoes.
Add the coriander and crush briefly so it is bruised, not pulped.
Beat in the raw mustard oil and sharpen with lemon if the tomatoes were sweet.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated. The raw garlic strengthens overnight. Serve at room temperature with litti or rice.

recipes.name: Tamatar Chokha
recipes.subtitle: charred tomatoes crushed with garlic, chilli and mustard oil into a smoky relish

ingredients.note: 3 roasted, 3 crushed raw

prepNotes: Use ripe tomatoes with taut skin; watery ones turn the chokha into soup.
Thread 3 garlic cloves onto a skewer so you can char them on the flame alongside the tomatoes.
Have the onion and chilli chopped before you start roasting. This comes together in two minutes once the tomatoes are off the flame.

steps.text: Set the tomatoes directly on a medium gas flame, resting them on the trivet.
Roast 10 to 12 minutes, turning with tongs, until the skins are blackened and split and the tomatoes slump.
steps.tip: Let them blacken properly. Pale roasting gives you sauce, not chokha.

steps.text: Char the skewered garlic for the last 3 minutes until the cloves are spotted brown and soft.
Rest 5 minutes, then slip off and discard the blackened skins, saving any juice on the plate.
Mash the tomato flesh and roasted garlic together with a fork into a coarse pulp.
Crush the 3 raw garlic cloves with a pinch of salt and stir them in with the ginger.
steps.tip: Raw garlic is what separates this from a cooked chutney. Do not skip it.

steps.text: Fold in the onion, green chilli, coriander leaves, salt, black salt and the raw mustard oil.
Taste and serve at room temperature with litti, sattu paratha or a plate of khichdi.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated. Serve at room temperature and stir in a little fresh mustard oil before serving; it separates as it sits.

recipes.name: Thekua
recipes.subtitle: hard, jaggery-sweetened wheat biscuits fried in ghee, made in every home for Chhath

ingredients.note: coarse-milled atta gives thekua its characteristic crunch
traditionally ghee; oil is the everyday version

prepNotes: Dissolve the jaggery in hot water and strain it. Unstrained jaggery carries grit that burns black in the frying oil.
Let the jaggery water cool to lukewarm before it touches the flour. Hot syrup makes a sticky dough that will not hold a pattern.
Do not rest this dough. Thekua dough should be mixed stiff and fried straight away, or the jaggery draws out moisture and it slackens.

steps.text: Heat the water with the jaggery over low heat for 4-5 minutes, stirring, until it dissolves completely, then strain and cool to lukewarm.
Rub the melted ghee into the atta with the salt for 3-4 minutes, until the flour looks damp and clumps when pressed.
steps.tip: This moyan of ghee is what makes thekua short and crisp. Skimp on it and you get a rock.

steps.text: Mix in the crushed fennel, ground cardamom and grated coconut.
Add the jaggery water a little at a time and bring it together into a very stiff dough. Do not knead it smooth.
steps.tip: Stop adding liquid while the dough still looks slightly crumbly; a soft dough soaks up oil and goes soggy.

steps.text: Pinch off lime-sized pieces, roll into balls, then flatten each to about 1cm thick.
Press each disc onto a thekua mould, or score a criss-cross pattern with the back of a fork.
Heat the frying oil to 150C. Low, not hot. A piece of dough should rise slowly after a few seconds.
steps.tip: Frying too hot browns the surface while the middle stays raw. Low and slow is the whole technique.

steps.text: Fry in batches for 8-10 minutes, turning often, until the thekua are a deep even brown and float high in the oil.
Lift out and drain on a rack, not on paper, and let them cool completely. They harden as they cool.
steps.tip: Judge doneness by colour, not by feel; thekua are soft in the pan and only crisp up once cold.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 weeks in an airtight tin at room temperature, and this is a sweet that improves after a day or two. Do not refrigerate, the crunch goes.

recipes.name: Tilkut
recipes.subtitle: gaya's winter sweet of pounded roasted sesame and jaggery, dry and shattering

image.alt: Tilkut, sesame and jaggery pounded into discs

prepNotes: Pick the sesame over for grit and have it completely dry before roasting.
Grease your palms, the rolling surface and a broad knife before you start on the jaggery syrup. Once it sets you have about two minutes to work.
Work on a cool day or in a cool kitchen; tilkut refuses to set crisp in humidity.

steps.text: Dry-roast the sesame in a heavy kadhai on medium heat for 6 to 8 minutes, stirring constantly, until the seeds turn pale gold and start popping.
steps.tip: Take them off while they are still blond. Browned sesame turns the tilkut bitter.

steps.text: Tip the roasted sesame onto a cold plate to stop the cooking and cool it completely.
Pound about two-thirds of the sesame coarsely in a mortar, or pulse briefly in a grinder, leaving the rest whole.
steps.tip: Stop before it turns to paste. Sesame releases oil fast.

steps.text: Melt the jaggery with the water in the same kadhai on low heat, stirring until it dissolves, about 5 minutes.
Boil the syrup for 6 to 8 minutes to the hard-ball stage: a drop into cold water should set into a firm ball you can snap.
steps.tip: This is the make-or-break test. Soft syrup gives you chewy chikki, not tilkut.

steps.text: Take the pan off the heat, stir in the crushed cardamom, then work in all the sesame quickly until evenly coated.
Turn the mass out onto a greased surface and, while it is just cool enough to handle, pinch off walnut-sized pieces.
Flatten each piece into a 6cm disc with your greased palm and press the pounded sesame in firmly.
steps.tip: Press hard. The pounding is what makes tilkut crumble rather than stick to your teeth.

steps.text: Leave the discs to cool and harden on a rack for 30 minutes before stacking.

recipes.storage: Stores 3 weeks in an airtight tin at room temperature, layered with paper. Keep it away from the fridge and from any moisture, which turns it sticky.

recipes.name: Alsande Tonak
recipes.subtitle: black-eyed peas in a roasted coconut masala, the everyday Goan Hindu curry

ingredients.note: alsande
rounds off the tamarind

prepNotes: Soak the black-eyed peas in plenty of cold water for 4 hours, or overnight if that is easier. They cook unevenly unsoaked.
Soak the tamarind in 3 tbsp hot water and press out the pulp.
Grate the coconut before you start cooking. The roasting step wants your full attention.

steps.text: Drain the soaked peas and pressure-cook them with 3 cups water and 1/2 tsp salt for 3 whistles, about 12 minutes. They should give completely under a thumb but hold their shape.
steps.tip: Undercooked alsande stays chalky in the middle no matter how long the curry simmers afterwards.

steps.text: Dry-roast the grated coconut in a heavy pan over low heat 10 minutes, stirring, until it is evenly brown and smells toasted.
steps.tip: Stop when it looks like coarse brown sugar. Darker than that and the curry turns bitter.

steps.text: Add the chillies, coriander powder, cumin, pepper, cloves and cinnamon to the pan and roast 90 seconds more.
Grind the roasted coconut and spices with the turmeric and 200ml warm water to a smooth thick paste.
Heat the coconut oil in a pot and fry the onion 8 minutes until soft and light gold, then add the garlic for 1 minute.
Stir in the ground masala and cook 6-8 minutes until it darkens by a shade and oil separates at the edges.
Tip in the cooked peas with their liquid, add 200ml hot water and salt, and simmer uncovered 12 minutes until the gravy thickens.
Stir in the tamarind pulp and jaggery, simmer 3 minutes, then taste. It should read sour first, then sweet, then hot.
Finish with coriander leaves and serve with rice or with pav.

recipes.storage: Keeps 4 days refrigerated and thickens as it sits. Loosen with hot water when reheating. Freezes well for 2 months.

recipes.name: Ambot Tik
recipes.subtitle: a sharp coconut-free fish curry that is exactly what its name says, sour and hot

ingredients.note: traditionally shark or catfish; kingfish or monkfish hold up well
the tik half of the name

ingredients.qty: lime-sized ball, soaked in 200ml hot water

ingredients.note: the second sour note

prepNotes: Rub the fish with salt and 1/4 tsp turmeric and rest it 15 minutes. A firm fish takes salt slowly.
Soak the tamarind in hot water while you grind the masala, then squeeze and strain.
There is no coconut in this curry. Do not add any to soften it. The sharpness is the dish.

steps.text: Grind the chillies, garlic, ginger, cumin, pepper, turmeric and coriander powder with the vinegar and 3 tbsp water to a fine paste.
Heat the oil and fry the chopped onion over medium heat for 8 minutes, until soft and pale gold.
Add the masala paste and fry 6-7 minutes until it darkens and the oil beads at the edge of the pan.
steps.tip: Frying the vinegar out is what stops the curry tasting raw. Give it the full seven minutes.

steps.text: Pour in the tamarind water and the rest of the water, add the kokum and salt, and bring to a simmer.
Simmer uncovered 10 minutes so the gravy reduces slightly and turns glossy.
Taste and balance: it should be assertively sour and hot. Add a pinch of salt or a splash of vinegar rather than sugar.
steps.tip: Balance it before the fish goes in. You cannot stir it properly afterwards.

steps.text: Slide in the fish, shake the pan to settle the pieces, and simmer 7-8 minutes until opaque through.
Rest 10 minutes off the heat before serving with plain rice.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated and the sourness mellows usefully by day two. Reheat gently to a bare simmer; never boil hard or the fish shreds.

recipes.name: Baath Cake
recipes.subtitle: dense semolina and coconut cake, rested overnight and eaten in thin slices with tea

ingredients.note: frozen grated coconut, thawed, is fine
unsalted
deepens the coconut flavour

prepNotes: The batter must rest at least 6 hours, and overnight is better. This is not optional: the semolina has to swell completely or the cake bakes gritty.
Bring the eggs, milk and coconut to room temperature before mixing. Cold ingredients seize the melted butter into lumps.
Baath is a Christmas kuswar sweet in Goan Catholic homes, but it is baked year round. It is meant to be dense and moist, not light. Do not expect a sponge.

steps.text: Whisk the sugar into the melted butter until the mixture looks like wet sand, about 2 minutes.
Beat in the eggs one at a time, then the milk and coconut milk, until smooth and pourable.
Fold in the semolina, grated coconut, nutmeg, cardamom and salt. The batter will be thick and slightly grainy at this stage.
Cover and rest at room temperature 6 hours or overnight in the refrigerator. It will thicken considerably as the semolina drinks.
steps.tip: If it has set too stiff to pour by morning, slacken it with 2-3 tbsp of milk, no more.

steps.text: Heat the oven to 170C. Grease a 20cm round tin with ghee and line the base with paper.
Stir the baking soda through the rested batter and pour it into the tin, levelling the top with a spatula.
steps.tip: Add the soda only at this point. Mix it in the night before and the lift is gone by morning.

steps.text: Bake 55-65 minutes until the top is deep golden brown and a skewer comes out with a few moist crumbs.
steps.tip: Tent the top with foil at 40 minutes if it is browning faster than the centre is setting.

steps.text: Cool in the tin a full hour before turning out. The cake is fragile while warm.
Cool completely, then cut into thin wedges or squares. It slices cleanly only when cold.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate it in an airtight tin, up to a week; there is egg and coconut in it and the counter-top keeping is traditional practice rather than anything we have tested. It settles and improves over the first two days either way. Bring it back to room temperature before eating.

recipes.name: Batata Song
recipes.subtitle: quick potato curry sharp with vinegar and slow-browned onion, a weeknight standby

ingredients.qty: 500g, boiled, peeled and cut into 2cm cubes

ingredients.note: song is really an onion dish with potato in it
coconut or palm vinegar if you have it
takes the edge off the vinegar

prepNotes: Boil the potatoes ahead and let them cool completely before cubing; warm potato crumbles into the gravy.
Soak the dried chillies in hot water for 15 minutes so they grind smooth.
Chop the onion as finely as you can manage. It has to melt, not stay in pieces.

steps.text: Grind the soaked chillies with the garlic and 2 tbsp of the vinegar to a smooth thick paste. Use no water.
steps.tip: Grinding in vinegar rather than water is what gives song its keeping quality and its sharp edge.

steps.text: Heat the coconut oil in a kadhai and fry the onion over medium heat 12-14 minutes, stirring often, until deep brown and jammy.
steps.tip: This is the only real work in the dish. Stop at brown, not black. Burnt onion turns the whole pan bitter.

steps.text: Add the chilli paste and turmeric and fry 4 minutes until the raw vinegar smell burns off and oil shows at the edges.
Add the potato cubes and turn them gently until every piece is coated red.
Pour in 100ml hot water with the salt and sugar and simmer 5 minutes so the potato takes up the masala.
Taste and add a splash more vinegar if it needs lifting. Song should be noticeably sour.
Cook uncovered 2 minutes more to leave it thick and clinging rather than saucy, then scatter over the coriander.

recipes.storage: Keeps 4 days refrigerated. The vinegar preserves it and the flavour sharpens. Reheat in a pan with a spoonful of water. Do not freeze.

recipes.name: Bebinca
recipes.subtitle: Goa's layered coconut and egg cake, one grilled layer at a time
prepNotes: Bebinca is a test of patience: each layer is baked separately, and a traditional one runs to sixteen. Seven still tastes right.
Ghee is brushed between layers. That fat is what lets them separate cleanly when sliced.

steps.text: Whisk the yolks with the sugar until pale, then beat in the coconut milk, flour, nutmeg, cardamom and salt to a smooth, pourable batter. Rest 30 minutes.
Heat the oven to 180C with the grill element on. Brush a deep tin generously with ghee and warm it.
Pour in a thin ladle of batter (about 5mm) and grill 8-10 minutes until the top is browned and set.
steps.tip: Browned, not merely set. The colour contrast between layers is the whole look.

steps.text: Brush the baked layer with ghee, pour the next ladle over, and grill again. Repeat for at least seven layers.
Cool completely in the tin, then turn out. Slicing warm will tear the layers apart.
steps.tip: At least 3 hours. Overnight is better.

steps.text: Serve at room temperature in thin wedges.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate it in an airtight tin, up to a week. Goan kitchens keep bebinca on the counter for days and it is very good that way, but this is egg and coconut milk baked soft, and we have not tested how long that keeps warm. Bring it back to room temperature before serving, or the ghee is still set hard and the texture reads waxy.

recipes.name: Chicken Cafreal
recipes.subtitle: chicken marinated green with coriander, chilli and vinegar, then fried dry

ingredients.qty: 800g, legs and thighs, skin off, slashed to the bone
ingredients.note: on the bone only, breast dries out
the stalks carry most of the flavour
fried alongside, the standard accompaniment

prepNotes: Marinate the chicken at least 4 hours, ideally overnight. Cafreal is a marinade dish. An hour gives you green chicken with plain meat underneath.
Slash each piece to the bone in two or three places so the paste gets inside.
Take the chicken out of the fridge 30 minutes before cooking so it cooks evenly.

steps.text: Grind the coriander with stalks, green chillies, garlic, ginger, cumin, pepper, cloves, cinnamon, turmeric, vinegar, lemon juice, sugar and 1 tsp salt to a thick green paste. Use no water.
steps.tip: Water dulls the colour and thins the marinade. The vinegar and lemon are enough liquid.

steps.text: Rub the paste hard into the slashed chicken, working it into the cuts. Cover and refrigerate 4 hours or overnight.
Heat the oil in a heavy kadhai and lay in the chicken in a single layer, scraping the marinade back into the bowl.
Fry 4 minutes a side over medium-high heat until the surface is seared and patchy brown.
steps.tip: Sear first, marinade later. If you tip everything in together the paste burns before the chicken cooks.

steps.text: Add the reserved marinade and 4 tbsp water, cover, and cook on low for 20 minutes, turning the pieces twice.
Meanwhile fry the quartered potatoes in a separate pan until gold and cooked through, about 12 minutes.
Uncover, raise the heat and cook 5-6 minutes more until the sauce has reduced to a thick coating that clings to the chicken.
steps.tip: Cafreal is a dry dish. If there is a pool of gravy in the pan, keep going.

steps.text: Check with a knife at the thickest part of the thigh. The juices should run clear. Squeeze over lemon and serve with the potatoes and pav.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated. Reheat in a covered pan with 2 tbsp water over low heat; the microwave makes it stringy. The marinade freezes well for 2 months.

recipes.name: Chicken Xacuti
recipes.subtitle: dark roasted-coconut curry heavy with whole spice, the Goan Catholic Sunday chicken

ingredients.note: frozen grated works; desiccated does not
thickens the gravy
the spice that makes xacuti smell like xacuti
dagad phool, for the earthy back note

prepNotes: Marinate the chicken with the turmeric, half the ginger-garlic paste and salt for 30 minutes in the refrigerator.
Soak the tamarind in 3 tbsp hot water and squeeze out the pulp before you start; you will want it at the end.
Grate the coconut fresh if you possibly can. The whole dish is built on the flavour of coconut browned in a dry pan.

steps.text: Dry-roast the coconut in a kadhai over low heat, stirring constantly, 10-12 minutes until it is the colour of milk chocolate. Tip it out onto a plate.
steps.tip: Low heat and never stop stirring. Coconut goes from golden to burnt in under a minute, and burnt coconut cannot be rescued.

steps.text: In the same pan roast the chillies, coriander powder, cumin, poppy seeds, pepper, cloves, cinnamon, star anise, mace and stone flower for 2 minutes until fragrant.
steps.tip: Add the coriander powder last. Ground spice scorches far faster than whole seed.

steps.text: Grind the roasted coconut and spices with the nutmeg and about 200ml warm water to a very smooth, thick paste. Give it a full 3-4 minutes in the blender.
steps.tip: Any grittiness left now stays gritty in the finished curry.

steps.text: Heat the coconut oil and fry the sliced onion 12 minutes until deep gold and collapsing.
Add the remaining ginger-garlic paste and fry 2 minutes until the raw smell lifts.
Add the marinated chicken and turn it over high heat 6-8 minutes until the pieces are sealed and no longer pink outside.
Stir in the ground masala and cook it down 8-10 minutes, stirring, until it darkens and oil beads at the edges.
steps.tip: This is where xacuti gets its depth. If it catches, add a splash of water rather than lowering the flame.

steps.text: Pour in 400ml hot water, season with salt, cover and simmer 20 minutes until the chicken is tender and the gravy coats a spoon.
Stir in the tamarind pulp, simmer 3 minutes more, and taste for salt and sourness. Finish with coriander leaves.

recipes.name: Fish Caldine
recipes.subtitle: gentle yellow coconut curry, turmeric-led and barely chilli-hot

ingredients.qty: 600g firm steaks such as kingfish or pomfret

ingredients.note: caldine is a yellow curry; do not be shy with it
the only heat in the dish
or the juice of half a lemon

prepNotes: Rub the fish with 1/2 tsp turmeric and salt and leave 20 minutes, then pat dry.
Caldine is the mild curry of the Goan Catholic table, the one made when there are children or convalescents eating. Slit green chillies give perfume without heat, so leave them whole.
Grind the coconut with warm water, not cold. It extracts more thickly.

steps.text: Grind 1 cup of the coconut with the cumin, coriander powder, pepper and 150ml warm water to a very smooth paste. Strain if your blender is not powerful.
Grind the remaining coconut with 250ml warm water and set this thinner second extraction aside separately.
steps.tip: Keeping the two extractions apart is the whole technique: the thin one cooks the fish, the thick one finishes the curry.

steps.text: Heat the coconut oil in a wide pan and fry the onion 6 minutes until soft and just turning gold at the edges.
Add the garlic, ginger and slit green chillies and cook 2 minutes until fragrant.
Stir in the turmeric off the heat for 20 seconds so it blooms without burning, then return the pan to a low flame.
steps.tip: Turmeric burns fast and turns bitter and dusty. Off the heat is the safe way.

steps.text: Pour in the thin coconut extraction, season with salt and simmer 8 minutes until slightly reduced.
Lower the fish in one layer, cover and cook 6-7 minutes, spooning gravy over it, until the flesh flakes at the thickest point.
Pour in the thick coconut paste and warm it through 3 minutes without letting it boil.
steps.tip: A boil at this stage splits the coconut and leaves a grainy, oily curry.

steps.text: Take off the heat, stir in the vinegar, and rest 10 minutes. Finish with coriander leaves and serve with plain rice.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated. Reheat over low heat only until steaming. Boiling splits the coconut. Do not freeze.

recipes.name: Goan Dodol
recipes.subtitle: a dark, dense coconut and palm jaggery fudge stirred until it leaves the pan

ingredients.note: first-press from 4 coconuts is the real thing; good tinned works
palm, not cane. It makes the colour and the flavour

ingredients.qty: 2 tbsp, for greasing the tray and scraper

prepNotes: Set aside 90 minutes of near-continuous stirring. Dodol cannot be left, and this is the entire difficulty of the recipe.
Grease the setting tray and a flat scraper before you start. At the end you will have about 40 seconds to get it in.
Whisk the rice flour into 2 cups of the cold coconut milk until completely lump-free, before any heat goes near it.

steps.text: Melt the jaggery with 200ml water over low heat, then strain through a fine sieve to remove the grit.
steps.tip: Never skip the straining. Palm jaggery always carries sand and it is unpleasant in a set sweet.

steps.text: Whisk the rice flour into 2 cups of the cold coconut milk until smooth, then combine with the rest of the coconut milk, the strained jaggery syrup and the salt in a heavy kadhai.
Bring to a simmer over medium-low heat, stirring constantly with a flat wooden spoon that reaches the corners.
After about 25 minutes it will thicken to the consistency of a thick custard and turn light brown.
Keep stirring over low heat. At around 50 minutes it darkens to milk chocolate and starts to come away from the sides in sheets.
steps.tip: Do not raise the heat to hurry it. Scorched dodol tastes bitter all the way through and there is no fixing it.

steps.text: At around 75-85 minutes the oil separates and glistens on the surface and the mass rolls as one lump behind the spoon.
steps.tip: That oil separating is the finish line. Pull it then, not before and not much after.

steps.text: Stir in the cashews and crushed cardamom and cook 2 minutes more.
Tip it immediately into the greased tray and press flat with a greased scraper to about 2cm thick.
Cool completely at room temperature, 4-6 hours, until firm enough to cut into diamonds.
steps.tip: Do not refrigerate it to set faster. It sweats and goes sticky on the surface.

recipes.name: Goan Fish Curry
recipes.subtitle: the everyday coconut and kokum curry that gets eaten with rice twice a day

ingredients.note: on the bone tastes better than fillet
frozen grated coconut, thawed, works
for colour without ferocity

ingredients.qty: walnut-sized ball, soaked in 1/2 cup hot water

ingredients.note: the sourness Goan cooks actually reach for
a common addition, adds body
or any neutral oil

steps.tip: Grind longer than feels necessary. Three or four minutes. Grainy coconut makes a curry that never looks silky.

steps.text: Pour in the ground masala and cook 4 minutes, stirring, until it darkens a shade and smells toasted rather than raw.

Simmer uncovered 8 minutes, until the surface carries a thin rim of orange oil.
Slide in the okra, if using, and cook 3 minutes until just tender.
Lower the fish in a single layer. Do not stir. Shake the pan instead.

steps.text: Cook 6-7 minutes, until the flesh turns opaque and pulls from the bone when nudged.

steps.tip: The resting is not optional. The curry thickens and the fish takes up the sourness.

recipes.name: Goan Sausage Pulao
recipes.subtitle: smoky vinegary chouriço cooked through rice until every grain is stained red

ingredients.qty: 300g Goan chouriço sausage, casings removed and chopped
ingredients.note: or 300g diced pork belly tossed with 2 tbsp vinegar, 1 tsp chilli powder and 1 tsp crushed garlic

ingredients.qty: 2 cups, rinsed until the water runs clear

ingredients.note: the traditional filler, soaks up the fat
chouriço is already salty. Salt at the end

prepNotes: Soak the rinsed rice 20 minutes and drain it well. Wet rice and a fatty sausage together give you a sticky pulao.
Goan chouriço is cured and heavily salted. Taste a piece once fried before you add any salt at all.
If your sausage is very lean, keep 1 tbsp oil to hand; if it is fatty you will need none.

steps.text: Fry the chopped sausage in a dry heavy pot over medium heat for 6-8 minutes, until the fat runs out red and the edges crisp.
steps.tip: That rendered red fat is the entire flavour base. Do not drain it away.

steps.text: Lift out the sausage with a slotted spoon, leaving the fat behind.
In the same fat, fry the bay leaves, cloves and cinnamon for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the sliced onion and cook 8 minutes, until deep gold.
Stir in the tomato, green chillies, pepper and turmeric and cook 4 minutes, until the tomato collapses.
Add the potato cubes and the drained rice and turn them through the fat for 2 minutes, until every grain is coated and glossy.
steps.tip: Turn with a folding motion, not a stir. Broken grains make mush.

steps.text: Return the sausage, pour in the water, taste for salt and bring to a hard boil.
Cover tightly, drop to the lowest heat and cook 12 minutes without lifting the lid.
Rest off the heat, still covered, for 10 minutes, then fork through the coriander and serve with lemon.
steps.tip: The rest is what separates the grains. Opening the pot early undoes it.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated. Reheat covered with 2 tbsp water over low heat or steam it for 5 minutes; the fat re-melts and it comes back well.

recipes.name: Goan Xacuti
recipes.subtitle: Chicken in a dark roasted-coconut masala with poppy seeds and star anise

ingredients.note: the roast on this is the whole dish

prepNotes: Xacuti is defined by how far you take the coconut. It must go past golden to a genuine deep brown, which is where the colour and the smoky depth come from. Stop early and the curry is pale and flat.
Roast the coconut and the whole spices separately. They brown at very different rates and burnt spices cannot be rescued.
Star anise and poppy seeds are unusual in Indian coastal cooking and are what mark this out as Goan.

steps.text: Dry roast the grated coconut over medium-low heat, stirring constantly, until deep brown and nutty, 10-15 minutes. Be patient and do not walk away; it turns from brown to burnt in seconds. Tip onto a plate to stop the cooking.
In the same pan, roast the dried chillies, coriander seeds, cumin, poppy seeds, star anise, cinnamon, cloves and pepper separately until fragrant, about 2 minutes. Cool.
Blend the roasted coconut and spices with the ginger, garlic, turmeric and enough water to make a very smooth, thick paste. Take your time here; grittiness will not cook out.
Heat the oil and fry the sliced onion until well browned, 10 minutes. Add the masala paste and cook, stirring, until it darkens and the oil separates, 8-10 minutes.
Add the chicken and salt and turn it in the masala over high heat until sealed all over. Add about 2 cups of hot water, bring to a simmer, cover and cook 25-30 minutes until the chicken is tender.
Stir in the tamarind pulp and the nutmeg. Simmer uncovered 5 minutes to balance the sourness. Rest before serving; xacuti is better after an hour.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated and improves markedly overnight. Freezes 2 months. Reheat gently, adding water as the coconut masala thickens on standing.

recipes.name: Khatkhate
recipes.subtitle: the Saraswat temple stew of eight vegetables in coconut, no onion or garlic anywhere

ingredients.note: boil separately first if the variety is itchy
standing in for teppal, the Goan Sichuan pepper, which is hard to source

prepNotes: Cut the vegetables large and roughly equal, about 3cm. Khatkhate is a chunky stew and small dice disappears into it.
Add the vegetables in order of hardness (yam and colocasia first, beans and pumpkin last) or half of them collapse.
If you can find teppal (triphal), use 6 berries crushed instead of the pepper and add them in the last two minutes.

steps.text: Boil the toor dal in 400ml water for 20 minutes, until soft enough to crush against the side of the pot.
Meanwhile grind the coconut, dried chillies and coriander powder with 150ml water to a coarse-ish paste. A little texture is right here.
steps.tip: Do not grind this one glass-smooth. Khatkhate should feel like coconut, not like sauce.

steps.text: Add the yam, colocasia and raw banana to the dal with the rest of the water and 1 tsp salt. Simmer 10 minutes.
Add the sweet potato and drumstick and simmer 6 minutes.
Add the pumpkin and french beans and cook 5 minutes, until everything yields to a knife but still holds its shape.
steps.tip: Test the pumpkin first. It goes from firm to mush in about ninety seconds.

steps.text: Stir in the ground coconut paste, the tamarind extract and the jaggery.
Simmer gently 8 minutes, stirring only occasionally so the pieces stay whole.
Crush in the pepper, check the salt, and take it off the heat. It should be sweet, sour and mildly hot in that order.
Trickle over the raw coconut oil just before serving with rice.
steps.tip: Raw, not heated. That last spoonful of coconut oil is the signature of a Saraswat kitchen.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated. Reheat gently over low heat with a splash of water; do not boil, as coconut gravies split and the vegetables break down.

recipes.name: Kismur
recipes.subtitle: dry prawn and coconut salad, crunchy and sour, eaten alongside rice and curry

ingredients.note: galmbo; dried Bombay duck is the other classic choice
or the juice of half a lemon

prepNotes: Pick over the dried prawns for grit and shell fragments, then rinse them twice in cold water and squeeze dry. They are salty, so hold back on salt until the end.
Soak the tamarind in 2 tbsp hot water and press out the pulp.
Everything is combined off the heat, so have the onion chopped and the coconut grated before you turn on the stove.

steps.text: Dry-roast the drained prawns in a kadhai over medium heat 4-5 minutes until they are crisp and rattle in the pan.
steps.tip: They must be properly dry and brittle. Any softness left and the kismur goes soggy within the hour.

steps.text: Tip them onto a plate to cool, then crush lightly with your fingers into coarse pieces.
In the same pan warm the coconut oil and fry the broken dried chillies 30 seconds until they darken.
Add the grated coconut and toast 3-4 minutes, stirring, until it is dry and pale gold at the edges.
steps.tip: Only lightly toasted. Kismur wants the fresh sweetness of coconut, not the deep roast of a tonak masala.

steps.text: Stir in the chilli powder and turmeric and take the pan off the heat immediately.
Let the coconut cool to room temperature, then fold in the crushed prawns, chopped onion and green chilli.
Add the tamarind pulp and toss thoroughly with your hands. Taste, then salt. The prawns may have brought enough.
Finish with coriander leaves and serve within a couple of hours, while the onion is still crunchy.

recipes.storage: Best within 2 hours of mixing. It keeps 2 days refrigerated but the onion softens and weeps; refresh with a little extra raw onion and tamarind before serving.

recipes.name: Mackerel Uddamethi
recipes.subtitle: saraswat mackerel curry built on toasted urad dal and fenugreek, sour and slightly bitter

ingredients.qty: 4 mackerel, cleaned and cut into thick halves
ingredients.note: bangda; pomfret or seer also work
the udda of uddamethi
the methi; more than this turns the curry bitter

prepNotes: Rub the mackerel with 1/4 tsp turmeric and salt and leave 15 minutes; rinse and pat dry. This firms the flesh so it does not break up in the pot.
Soak the tamarind in 3 tbsp hot water and press out the pulp.
Have the masala fully ground before the fish goes anywhere near the heat. From that point the curry takes eight minutes.

steps.text: Warm 1 tbsp of the coconut oil and roast the urad dal over low heat 3 minutes until it turns reddish and smells nutty.
steps.tip: Urad dal keeps browning after you take it off the heat, so pull it a shade early.

steps.text: Add the fenugreek seeds and roast 30 seconds only, then the chillies and coriander powder for another minute.
steps.tip: Fenugreek turns acrid the moment it goes dark brown. Thirty seconds, not sixty.

steps.text: Grind the roasted mixture with the grated coconut, turmeric and 200ml water to a smooth, pourable paste.
Heat the remaining oil in a wide pan and soften the onion 5 minutes until translucent but not coloured.
Pour in the ground masala with another 150ml water, add the green chilli and salt, and bring to a gentle simmer.
Simmer 6-7 minutes, stirring, until the raw coconut smell is gone and the surface glistens.
Slide in the mackerel in a single layer, spoon gravy over it, and cook 6 minutes without stirring.
steps.tip: Shake the pan by the handle instead of stirring. A spoon will shred the fish.

steps.text: Add the tamarind pulp, simmer 2 minutes more, and take it off the heat. Rest 10 minutes before serving with rice.
Scatter over the coriander leaves at the table.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated. Reheat only to steaming, never boiling, or the mackerel falls apart. Not suitable for freezing.

recipes.name: Patoleo
recipes.subtitle: steamed rice parcels of coconut and jaggery, made for the feast of the Assumption

ingredients.note: or 2 cups raw rice soaked 4 hours and ground thick
dark palm jaggery is the traditional one
optional but traditional in some homes

prepNotes: You need 12 fresh turmeric leaves, washed and wiped dry, with the thick centre rib shaved flat. They are seasonal and not something a shop stocks year round. Banana leaf cut into 20cm x 15cm rectangles and softened over a flame is the standard substitute, though it gives none of the perfume.
Make the filling first and let it cool. Hot filling melts through the rice layer.
Mix the dough with water as hot as you can handle. Cold water gives a dough that cracks when you spread it.

steps.text: Melt the jaggery with 4 tbsp water over low heat until it dissolves, about 3 minutes, then strain out the grit.
Return it to the pan with the grated coconut and cook 8-10 minutes, stirring, until the mixture pulls together and leaves the sides of the pan.
steps.tip: Stop while it is still moist. Cooked to dryness it turns hard and grainy in the parcel.

steps.text: Stir in the crushed cardamom and roasted sesame and set the filling aside to cool completely.
Bring the water to a boil with the salt, pour it over the rice flour and mix with a spoon, then knead into a soft, smooth dough once cool enough to touch.
steps.tip: The dough should feel like soft clay. Too stiff and it tears on the leaf; too wet and it slumps.

steps.text: Rest the dough 10 minutes under a damp cloth.
Spread a thin, even layer of dough over half of each turmeric leaf with wet fingers, about 3mm thick, leaving a clear border.
Spoon 2 tbsp of the coconut filling along the centre and fold the leaf over to close the parcel.
steps.tip: Do not overfill. Filling that escapes at the edges welds the parcels to the steamer.

steps.text: Stack the parcels in a steamer, not too tightly, and steam over rolling water for 20-25 minutes.
They are done when the leaf has darkened and the rice looks translucent and pulls away cleanly. Rest 5 minutes before opening.
steps.tip: Serve them in the leaf and let people unwrap their own. That first hit of turmeric-leaf steam is the point of the dish.

recipes.storage: Best the day they are made. Keep leftovers wrapped and refrigerated up to 2 days and re-steam 5 minutes to soften; they harden badly if left uncovered.

recipes.name: Pork Indad
recipes.subtitle: sweet-sour vinegar pork lifted with dates and jaggery, the milder cousin of vindaloo

ingredients.qty: 900g shoulder, in 4cm cubes with the fat left on

ingredients.note: palm or coconut vinegar if you can get it
indad's signature sweetness

prepNotes: Marinate the pork in half the ground masala with salt for at least 4 hours, or overnight refrigerated. This is where the sourness gets into the meat rather than sitting on top of it.
Soak the dried chillies in hot water 20 minutes before grinding.
Bring the marinated pork back to room temperature for 30 minutes before it goes in the pot, or it will seize and toughen.

steps.text: Grind the soaked chillies, garlic, ginger, cumin, pepper, cinnamon, cloves and turmeric with the vinegar to a smooth thick paste. Use no water at all.
steps.tip: Vinegar, not water. It is both the flavour of the dish and what keeps it for a week.

steps.text: Rub half the paste into the pork with 1 tsp salt and leave it to marinate as above.
Heat the oil in a heavy pot and fry the sliced onion 12 minutes until soft and evenly gold.
Add the remaining masala paste and cook 6-8 minutes over medium heat until it darkens and oil pools at the sides.
Add the marinated pork and turn it over high heat 8 minutes until sealed on all sides and coated in masala.
Pour in 300ml hot water, bring to a boil, then drop to a bare simmer, cover and cook 50 minutes until a knife slides into the meat without resistance.
steps.tip: Barely a bubble breaking the surface. A hard boil makes pork shoulder stringy instead of soft.

steps.text: Add the dates and jaggery and simmer uncovered 12 minutes more, until the dates have softened and the gravy is glossy and thick.
Taste and balance: indad should land sweet, then sour, then warm with pepper. Add vinegar or jaggery a teaspoon at a time.
steps.tip: Adjust while it is hot but taste after a minute's cooling. Heat flattens sourness on the tongue.

steps.text: Rest off the heat 20 minutes before serving, with sannas or crusty pav.

recipes.storage: Improves for 3-4 days refrigerated; the vinegar preserves it and day two is genuinely better. Reheat gently, adding hot water if it has tightened. Freezes 3 months.

recipes.name: Pork Vindaloo
recipes.subtitle: Vinegar-and-garlic pork, descended from Portuguese carne de vinha d'alhos

ingredients.qty: 800g shoulder, in large cubes with some fat

ingredients.note: palm vinegar if you can find it
balances the vinegar

prepNotes: Vindaloo is not simply 'very hot'. The name is vinha d'alhos (wine and garlic) and the defining flavours are sour and garlicky, with Kashmiri chillies for colour rather than fire.
Grind the masala with vinegar, never water. The vinegar is both the flavour and the preservative that let this dish travel.

steps.text: Grind the soaked chillies, garlic, ginger and whole spices with the vinegar to a smooth, thick paste. Use no water.
Rub half the paste into the pork with salt and marinate at least 4 hours, ideally overnight refrigerated.
Fry the onion in oil until soft and golden, then add the remaining masala paste and cook until the oil separates.
Add the pork with its marinade and turn it over high heat until sealed and coated.
Add a cup of hot water, cover, and simmer 60 minutes until the pork is tender and the fat has rendered into the gravy.
Balance with jaggery and salt. Rest overnight if you can. Vindaloo is markedly better on day two.

recipes.storage: Genuinely improves for 3-4 days refrigerated; the vinegar preserves it. Freezes 3 months.

recipes.name: Prawn Balchao
recipes.subtitle: a fierce vinegar-and-chilli prawn pickle eaten a spoonful at a time

ingredients.note: small prawns hold up better than large
adjust to your tolerance
Goan coconut vinegar if you can find it, else cider vinegar
balances the vinegar, do not skip
a pickle needs the oil to seal it

prepNotes: Soak the chillies in the vinegar for 30 minutes before grinding. This is what makes balchao red rather than brown.
Pat the prawns bone dry on a cloth. Wet prawns weep water and the pickle will not keep.
Use a scrupulously dry glass or ceramic jar. Any water in the jar and it spoils within the week.

steps.text: Grind the soaked chillies, garlic, ginger, cumin, pepper, cloves, cinnamon and turmeric to a thick paste using only the soaking vinegar, no water.
steps.tip: No water at any stage. Vinegar is the only liquid in this recipe.

steps.text: Toss the prawns with 1/2 tsp salt and a pinch of turmeric and fry them in 2 tbsp of the oil over high heat for 2 minutes, until they just turn pink. Lift them out.
steps.tip: Two minutes only. They cook again later and rubbery prawns are the usual failure here.

steps.text: Pour the rest of the oil into the same kadhai and fry the chopped onion over medium heat for 12-15 minutes, until dark gold and jammy.
Add the ground masala and fry 10 minutes, stirring often, until the oil separates and pools clearly at the edges.
steps.tip: This is the long, unglamorous part. Under-fried masala tastes raw and sharp for days.

steps.text: Stir in the sugar and salt and cook 2 more minutes.
Return the prawns, stir to coat, and cook 3 minutes on low.
Take it off the heat and cool completely, uncovered, in the pan.
Pack into a dry jar, pressing down so the oil covers the surface. Leave 2 days before eating.
steps.tip: It is harsh on day one and rounded by day three. Wait.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 weeks refrigerated as long as a film of oil covers the top and you only ever use a dry spoon. Goan kitchens keep balchao far longer, on the strength of the vinegar and the oil seal, and that may well be right, but the acidity here has not been measured and prawn is not a forgiving thing to be wrong about. Serve at room temperature with rice and dal or in a pao. Discard it if the oil layer breaks or it smells at all sharp.

recipes.name: Prawn Rissois
recipes.subtitle: crisp half-moon pastries with a creamy prawn filling, the standard Goan party snack

ingredients.note: for the crumb coating

prepNotes: The dough is a hot-water pastry made in a pan, not a rolled shortcrust. It must be worked while hot, so have a bowl and a wooden spoon ready.
The filling has to be cold and stiff before you fill anything. Make it first and refrigerate it an hour.
These freeze beautifully at the crumbed stage, which is how most Goan households actually make them. Assemble one day, fry the next.

steps.text: For the filling, cook the onion, garlic and green chilli in 1 tbsp butter over medium heat for 5 minutes until soft and translucent.
Add the chopped prawns, pepper and salt and cook 3 minutes, until just pink, then stir in 2 tbsp of the flour and 1/2 cup of the milk.
steps.tip: Three minutes maximum. The prawns cook again in the fryer.

steps.text: Cook 3-4 minutes more, stirring, until it thickens into a stiff paste that holds a ridge. Finish with lemon and coriander and chill 1 hour.
For the dough, bring the water, remaining milk, remaining butter and 1 tsp salt to a rolling boil.
Tip in the rest of the flour all at once and beat hard with a wooden spoon until it forms a single ball that leaves the pan clean, about 2 minutes.
steps.tip: All at once and beat immediately. Adding it gradually gives you lumps you will never get out.

steps.text: Turn it out, and as soon as you can bear the heat, knead 5 minutes until smooth and elastic. Cover and rest 15 minutes.
Roll the warm dough thin, about 2mm, and cut 9cm rounds.
steps.tip: Work with a quarter of the dough at a time and keep the rest covered. It stiffens fast and cracks when cold.

steps.text: Place a heaped teaspoon of filling on each round, fold into a half-moon and seal the edge firmly, pressing out any air.
Dip each in beaten egg, then press into the breadcrumbs to coat evenly. Chill 20 minutes.
Heat the oil to 175C (a crumb dropped in should sizzle and rise at once) and fry in batches of five for 3 minutes, until deep gold.
steps.tip: Too hot and the crumb burns before the pastry cooks; too cool and they drink oil. Adjust between batches.

steps.text: Drain on a rack, not paper, and serve hot.

recipes.storage: Fry to order. Crumbed, unfried rissois keep 3 months frozen on a tray then bagged. Fry from frozen, two minutes longer. Fried ones go soft within a few hours.

recipes.name: Recheado Mackerel
recipes.subtitle: whole mackerel stuffed with red vinegar masala and shallow-fried crisp

ingredients.qty: 4 whole mackerel, about 200g each, cleaned and slit along the belly
ingredients.note: pomfret or lady fish work the same way
Goan coconut vinegar preferred
swap for rice-flour if you need this gluten-free

prepNotes: Make the recheado paste a day ahead if you can. It sharpens as it sits, and a jar in the fridge turns a weeknight into dinner in 20 minutes.
Soak the chillies in the vinegar 30 minutes before grinding.
Rub the cleaned fish with salt and turmeric and rest 15 minutes, then wipe dry. Dry skin is the whole game for a crisp fry.

steps.text: Grind the soaked chillies, garlic, ginger, cumin, cloves, cinnamon, pepper, turmeric, tamarind, sugar and 1 tsp salt with the vinegar to a thick, smooth paste.
steps.tip: It should be spreadable, like tomato puree. Not pourable. Add vinegar a spoon at a time, never water.

steps.text: Slit each mackerel along the belly and, with a small knife, open a second pocket along the backbone from the outside.
Pack 1.5 tbsp of paste into each fish, inside the belly and into the pocket, and smear a thin film over the skin.
Rest the stuffed fish 20 minutes on a plate in the fridge.
steps.tip: This sets the paste so it stays in the fish rather than in the pan.

steps.text: Spread the rava on a plate and press each fish into it on both sides, shaking off the loose grains.
Heat the oil on a flat tawa over medium heat until a grain of rava sizzles on contact.
Lay in the fish and fry 5-6 minutes without moving it, until the underside is crusted and deep red-brown.
steps.tip: Do not poke or shuffle. Let the crust form or it will stick and tear.

steps.text: Turn once with a wide spatula and fry another 4-5 minutes.
Drain briefly on paper and serve hot with lemon wedges, rice and a plain dal.

recipes.storage: Fried fish is best within the hour and does not reheat well. The recheado paste itself keeps 2 months refrigerated under a layer of oil in a dry jar.

recipes.name: Sanna
recipes.subtitle: soft spongy steamed rice cakes, faintly sweet, eaten with sorpotel

ingredients.qty: 2 cups par-boiled rice soaked 5 hours, plus 1/2 cup cooked rice
ingredients.note: idli rice is the right kind; the cooked rice helps the batter ferment and stay soft
feeds the ferment as well as sweetening
insurance if the batter has not risen enough overnight

prepNotes: Sanna are traditionally leavened with fresh toddy. Without it, an overnight ferment of the coconut-rice batter in a warm place does the same job. Start this the night before.
Soak the par-boiled rice at least 5 hours; it should crush easily between your fingernails.
Keep the batter somewhere genuinely warm, around 28-30C. In a cold kitchen, an oven with only the light on works.

steps.text: Drain the soaked rice and grind it with the grated coconut, cooked rice and just enough water to a thick, smooth batter. Thicker than pancake batter, like idli batter.
steps.tip: Add water a splash at a time. A thin batter gives flat, rubbery sanna and cannot be rescued.

steps.text: Stir in the sugar, cover loosely, and leave in a warm place for 8-10 hours, or overnight.
By morning it should have risen by half, smell yeasty and sweet, and be full of small bubbles.
steps.tip: If it smells sharply sour rather than sweet it has gone too far. Use it now and expect a tangier cake.

steps.text: Stir in the salt gently, from the edges inwards, keeping as much air in as you can.
If the batter never rose, fold in the eno now and steam immediately.
Grease small steel bowls or idli moulds and fill each two-thirds full.
Steam over rolling water for 12-15 minutes, with the lid wrapped in a cloth to stop condensation dripping back.
steps.tip: Drips make craters and soggy tops. The cloth is worth the trouble.

steps.text: Test with a skewer at the centre. It should come out clean and the surface should spring back.
Rest 5 minutes, then run a knife around each and turn them out. Serve warm with sorpotel or a pork curry.

recipes.storage: Best warm from the steamer. Keep 2 days refrigerated in a closed box and re-steam 5 minutes to bring back the softness; they go dense and dry in the fridge otherwise.

recipes.name: Solkadhi
recipes.subtitle: cool pink kokum and coconut milk, drunk at the end of a fish meal to settle it

ingredients.note: the souring fruit that gives solkadhi its colour
or 400ml tinned coconut milk, thinned
for the optional tempering
only if the kokum is very sharp

prepNotes: Soak the kokum petals in 200ml warm water for 30 minutes, then squeeze them out. The soaking liquid is the drink; do not throw it away.
Grind and strain the coconut ahead and chill it. Solkadhi is served cool, never cold from the freezer and never warm.
Taste your kokum first. Some batches are salted and some are sharply sour, and both change how much you add.

steps.text: Grind the coconut with 400ml of the warm water for 3 minutes, then strain through muslin, squeezing hard. This is the thick first extraction.
Return the pressed coconut to the blender with the remaining 200ml water, grind again and strain into the same bowl.
steps.tip: The second pressing carries most of the volume. Skipping it gives you a claggy drink rather than a light one.

steps.text: Crush the garlic, green chilli and cumin to a rough paste in a mortar.
steps.tip: Pound rather than blend. You want the garlic to perfume the drink, not to dominate it.

steps.text: Stir the crushed paste and the squeezed kokum water into the coconut milk. It should turn a soft rose pink.
Season with salt, and a pinch of sugar only if it tastes harsh. Rest 20 minutes for the colour to deepen and the garlic to bloom.
For the optional tempering, heat the coconut oil, pop the mustard seeds, throw in the curry leaves and pour it over the top.
Chill 30 minutes and stir well before serving, in glasses on their own or ladled over hot rice.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated in a covered jug; stir before pouring as it separates. Do not heat it. Coconut milk splits and the drink goes grainy.

recipes.name: Sorpotel
recipes.subtitle: the vinegary pork and liver stew that gets cooked days before a Goan wedding

ingredients.qty: 700g belly and shoulder in one piece, plus 200g pork liver
ingredients.note: some fat is essential. Do not use lean loin, and do not leave out the liver
Goan coconut vinegar, else cider vinegar

prepNotes: Sorpotel is cooked three days before it is eaten. Plan for that. The flavour needs the wait and it is genuinely worse on day one.
Soak the chillies in half the vinegar for 30 minutes before grinding.
Everything that touches the pot must be dry and non-reactive. Use a ceramic or steel pot, never aluminium, and a dry spoon each time you go back in.

steps.text: Boil the pork and liver together in the water with 1 tsp salt and 1/2 tsp turmeric for 25 minutes, until firm but not falling apart. Keep the stock.
steps.tip: Save every drop of that stock. It is the only water this dish gets.

steps.text: Cool the meat, then cut it into small 1cm dice. It should be knife-cut, never minced.
Fry the diced pork and liver in 3 tbsp of its own rendered fat over high heat, in batches, until the edges brown, about 5 minutes a batch.
steps.tip: Crowding the pan steams the meat grey. Do it in two or three goes.

steps.text: Grind the soaked chillies, cumin, cloves, cinnamon, pepper, turmeric, garlic and ginger with the remaining vinegar to a fine paste.
In the same pot, cook the chopped onion in the fat over medium heat for 10 minutes, until soft and gold.
Add the ground masala and fry 8-10 minutes until the oil separates and the raw vinegar smell has gone.
steps.tip: Taste it. If it still stings the back of your throat, keep frying.

steps.text: Return the meat, add the reserved stock, green chillies, sugar and salt. Simmer uncovered 30 minutes, stirring now and then.
Stop when the gravy is thick enough to coat the meat and a distinct layer of red fat sits on top.
steps.tip: That fat cap is what preserves it. Do not skim it off.

steps.text: Cool completely and refrigerate. Reheat and simmer 5 minutes each day for three days before serving with sanna or crusty pav.

recipes.storage: Keeps 10 days refrigerated, and improves for the first four. Reheat to a full simmer each time, always with a dry spoon, and add a splash of vinegar if it tastes flat.

recipes.name: Sungtachi Kodi
recipes.subtitle: everyday prawn and drumstick curry in a thin red coconut masala

ingredients.note: adds the sweetness that makes this curry
for colour more than heat
or 1 tbsp tamarind pulp

prepNotes: Toss the prawns with 1/4 tsp turmeric and a pinch of salt and leave 15 minutes, then rinse and drain well.
Rinse the kokum petals and soak them in 3 tbsp warm water while you grind the masala.
Peel the drumsticks with a knife, leaving the tender inner rib. The tough outer skin never softens.

steps.text: Grind the coconut, Kashmiri chillies, coriander powder, cumin, turmeric and garlic with 250ml warm water to a completely smooth paste.
steps.tip: Blend for a full four minutes. A gritty masala is the commonest fault in a home coconut curry.

steps.text: Boil the drumstick pieces in 250ml salted water for 8 minutes, until a fingernail marks the flesh easily. Keep the water.
Heat the coconut oil in a wide pan and soften the onion 5 minutes until translucent.
Pour in the ground masala along with the drumstick and its cooking water, add the green chillies and salt, and bring to a simmer.
Simmer 8 minutes, stirring now and then, until the raw smell of the coconut has gone and the curry looks glossy rather than chalky.
steps.tip: Do not let it reach a rolling boil once the coconut is in, it will split.

steps.text: Add the kokum with its soaking water and simmer 2 minutes.
Slide in the prawns and cook 3-4 minutes only, until they curl and turn opaque.
steps.tip: Prawns go from done to rubbery in about a minute. Pull the pan as soon as they curve into a C.

steps.text: Take off the heat, check the salt and sourness, and rest 5 minutes before serving with rice.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated, though the prawns firm up. Reheat over low heat just to steaming. Do not freeze.

recipes.name: Tondak
recipes.subtitle: dried white peas in a roasted coconut and cashew masala, thick and faintly sweet

ingredients.note: in Goa these would be fresh green cashew in season
whole coriander seed, 1 tbsp, is better if you have it. Roast it with the coconut

prepNotes: Soak the white peas overnight in plenty of water. They roughly double, and an under-soaked pea cooks slowly and unevenly.
Soak the cashews separately for 30 minutes so they grind smooth.
Roast the coconut and spices dry before grinding. That roasting is the difference between tondak and an ordinary coconut curry.

steps.text: Pressure cook the drained peas with 400ml water and 1/2 tsp salt for 3 whistles, about 12 minutes, until soft but not split. Keep the cooking water.
steps.tip: Salt the peas from the start. Added later it never gets inside them.

steps.text: Dry-roast the grated coconut in a pan over medium heat for 6-8 minutes, stirring constantly, until it turns the colour of weak tea.
steps.tip: It goes from golden to burnt in seconds at the end. Keep the pan moving and pull it early.

steps.text: Add the dried chillies, coriander seeds, cumin, pepper, cloves and cinnamon to the pan and roast 1 minute more, until fragrant.
Grind the roasted coconut and spices with the soaked cashews, turmeric, garlic and 150ml water to a thick, smooth paste.
Heat the coconut oil and fry the chopped onion 8 minutes, until well browned at the edges.
Add the ground masala and fry 6 minutes, stirring, until it thickens and the oil shows at the sides.
Tip in the cooked peas with their water and the remaining water. Simmer 12 minutes.
Stir in the tamarind and jaggery, check the salt, and simmer 5 minutes more until the gravy is thick enough to hold a spoon mark.
steps.tip: Tondak is a thick curry, not a soup. If it looks loose, keep reducing.

steps.text: Rest 10 minutes and serve with rice or pao.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated and thickens considerably; loosen with hot water when reheating over low heat. Freezes well for a month.

recipes.name: Bajra no Rotlo
recipes.subtitle: thick hand-patted pearl-millet flatbread, nutty and dense, eaten hot under melting butter

ingredients.note: freshly milled if you can get it; bajra flour goes bitter with age
the classic pairing. Rotlo, gud and butter

prepNotes: Bajra has no gluten, so the dough is held together by heat and water alone. Use water as hot as your hands can bear and knead while it is warm.
Mix only as much dough as you will cook in the next twenty minutes. Bajra dough cracks and dries fast, and cold dough will not pat out at all.
Have the tawa heating before you shape the first rotlo. A patted rotlo cannot be moved twice.

steps.text: Warm the flour in a bowl with the salt, then add the hot water in stages, mixing with a spoon at first, then your hand.
Knead 3-4 minutes into a smooth, warm, slightly tacky dough. It should hold a ball without cracking at the edges.
steps.tip: If the edges crack, it is too dry. Wet your palm and knead again rather than pouring more water in.

steps.text: Heat a heavy tawa over medium heat until a drop of water skitters across it.
Take a lemon-sized ball, wet your palms, and pat it flat on a clean board or a sheet of plastic, rotating a quarter turn between pats, into a disc about 12cm across and 8mm thick.
steps.tip: Pat with the flat of the fingers in one direction and rotate. Slapping it randomly makes it tear.

steps.text: Lift it on your palm and lay it flat on the hot tawa in one movement.
Cook 90 seconds until the underside is speckled, then flip and cook the second side 2 minutes, pressing the edges with a cloth so it puffs.
Lift the rotlo with tongs and hold it 20-30 seconds directly over the flame, first side down, until it balloons.
steps.tip: It puffs only if both sides are properly cooked first. A rotlo that stays flat is still good. Do not chase it over the flame until it burns.

steps.text: Repeat with the rest, stacking them under a cloth.
Serve hot with a knob of butter pressed into the centre and a lump of jaggery, or alongside ringan no olo.

recipes.storage: Rotla are only good hot. Eat within an hour; leftovers can be crumbled the next morning into hot milk with jaggery, which is how Kathiawadi households use them up.

recipes.name: Bataka Poha
recipes.subtitle: flattened rice tossed with potato, peanuts and lemon, ready in twenty minutes

ingredients.note: thin poha dissolves. It must be the thick kind

ingredients.qty: 2 medium, peeled and cut into 1cm dice

ingredients.note: use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free

prepNotes: Rinse the poha in a colander under running water for 20 seconds, then leave it to drain for 10 minutes. It should be damp and separate, never sitting in water.
Mix the sugar, salt and turmeric into the drained poha with your fingertips before it goes in the pan. Seasoning it in the kadhai always ends up patchy.
Have everything chopped before you start; the whole cook takes under fifteen minutes.

steps.text: Fry the peanuts in the oil over medium heat for 3 minutes until they darken and smell toasted, then lift them out and set aside.
In the same oil pop the mustard seeds, then add the cumin, curry leaves, green chilli and asafoetida.
Add the diced potato, cover, and cook on medium-low 8 minutes, shaking the pan, until tender and lightly golden.
steps.tip: Cover the pan. The potato steams tender without needing more oil.

steps.text: Add the onion and fry 3 minutes until soft and translucent.
Tip in the seasoned poha and fold it through gently with a flat spatula, lifting rather than stirring.
steps.tip: Stirring hard mashes poha into paste. Lift and fold, three or four times only.

steps.text: Cover and steam on the lowest heat 3 minutes, until the poha is hot, plump and pale yellow throughout.
steps.tip: If it looks dry, sprinkle over two tablespoons of water before covering.

steps.text: Turn off the heat, add the lemon juice and the fried peanuts, and fold once.
Scatter the coriander and coconut over and serve hot with a wedge of lemon.

recipes.storage: Best within the hour. Keeps a day refrigerated; revive it in a covered pan over low heat with a sprinkle of water and a fresh squeeze of lemon.
