recipes.name: Kadala Curry
recipes.subtitle: black chickpeas in dark roasted coconut gravy, the breakfast partner to puttu

ingredients.note: black chickpeas, kadala
for roasting and grinding

prepNotes: Soak the black chickpeas at least 8 hours or overnight. They are much harder than white chana and take far longer without it.
The colour and depth of this curry come from roasting the coconut almost to the point of burning. Do it first, while the chickpeas cook.
Grind the roasted coconut with 1/2 cup water to as smooth a paste as your blender will manage. This gravy should not be gritty.

steps.text: Pressure cook the soaked chickpeas with 3 cups water, the turmeric and 1 tsp salt for 5 whistles, then 10 minutes on low. Release naturally and keep the cooking liquid.
steps.tip: The cooking water is dark and flavourful. Never throw it away. It is the base of the gravy.

steps.text: Heat 1 tbsp coconut oil in a heavy pan and fry the sliced shallots for 4 minutes until browning at the edges.
Add the grated coconut and roast on medium-low, stirring constantly, for 10-12 minutes until it is a deep chocolate brown.
steps.tip: Ten minutes feels long and the last two are where it happens. Do not walk away.

steps.text: Add the coriander powder, chilli powder and fennel seeds and roast 1 minute more, until the spices darken and smell toasted.
Cool slightly, then blend with 1/2 cup water to a fine dark paste.

In the same pan heat the remaining 2 tbsp oil, pop the mustard seeds, then add the broken red chillies, curry leaves, chopped onion, ginger and garlic. Cook 6 minutes until the onion is soft and gold.
Stir in the ground coconut paste and fry 4 minutes until the oil begins to separate at the edges.
Add the cooked chickpeas with their liquid and the garam masala. Simmer uncovered 12-15 minutes until the gravy thickens enough to coat a spoon.
steps.tip: Mash a spoonful of the chickpeas against the side of the pan to thicken the gravy naturally.

steps.text: Taste for salt and rest 10 minutes off the heat before serving with puttu or appam.

recipes.name: Kappa and Meen Curry
recipes.subtitle: mashed tapioca with a fierce red fish curry, the pairing Kerala argues about

ingredients.note: cassava is what is meant; yam is the closest thing in this pantry
sardine or kingfish traditionally
kudampuli, the smoked fish tamarind, is authentic; kokum is the nearest available

prepNotes: Two separate pots. The tapioca is boiled and mashed with coconut; the fish curry is cooked in a clay pot and stays thin and sharp.

steps.text: Boil the tapioca in salted water until a knife slides through, about 25 minutes. Drain well.
Crush the coconut with half the shallots, the green chilli and turmeric, and mash it through the hot tapioca.
For the curry, soak the kokum in 200ml warm water.
Fry the remaining shallots, fenugreek and curry leaves in the coconut oil, add the chilli powder and fry 1 minute.
Add the kokum with its water, bring to a boil, then slide in the fish and simmer 10 minutes without stirring.

steps.text: Rest 15 minutes before serving alongside the mashed tapioca.

recipes.name: Karimeen Pollichathu
recipes.subtitle: pearl spot masala-rubbed and steamed inside a banana leaf

ingredients.note: karimeen (pearl spot) is the fish; pomfret or tilapia stand in
coconut oil, not a substitute; it is half the flavour

prepNotes: Pollichathu means charred. The leaf is not a serving conceit; it scorches and perfumes the fish while trapping the steam.
If you cannot get banana leaf, foil works for the steam but you lose the aroma entirely.

steps.text: Score the fish to the bone on both sides. Rub with the turmeric, half the chilli powder, salt and lemon, then refrigerate 30 minutes.
Shallow fry the fish 3 minutes a side in 3 tbsp of the coconut oil. Lift out.
In the same pan, fry the shallots until soft, then the ginger, garlic, green chilli and curry leaves.
Add the remaining chilli powder, pepper and tamarind with a splash of water and cook to a thick masala.
Soften a banana leaf over a flame. Spread masala on it, lay the fish down, cover with more masala and wrap tightly.
Cook the parcel on a tawa 6 minutes a side on low heat until the leaf blackens and the kitchen smells of it.

recipes.name: Kerala Idiyappam
recipes.subtitle: steamed rice string hoppers, soft and threadlike, served with coconut milk

ingredients.note: boiling
for greasing the plates and hands

prepNotes: You need an idiyappam press (sevanazhi) with the finest disc. A potato ricer with a fine plate will do at a push.
If your rice flour is not pre-roasted, dry-roast it on low for 6-8 minutes until warm and fragrant without colouring, then cool.
Work the dough while it is hot. Hot enough to be just bearable. Cold dough will not extrude and comes out as broken worms.

steps.text: Bring the water to a full rolling boil with the salt and 1 tsp of the coconut oil.
Pour the boiling water over the rice flour all at once, stirring hard with a wooden spoon until it comes together as a shaggy mass.
steps.tip: All at once, not gradually. Half-scalded flour makes a dough that cracks.

steps.text: Cover and rest 5 minutes so the flour absorbs fully.
Oil your palms and knead the warm dough for 3-4 minutes until it is completely smooth, soft and non-sticky. Like fresh play dough.
steps.tip: If it cracks when rolled, sprinkle in a tablespoon of hot water and knead again.

steps.text: Grease the idiyappam plates and scatter a teaspoon of grated coconut on each.
Load the press and squeeze the dough onto the plates in tight overlapping spirals, about 1cm thick.
Scatter a little more coconut on top and stack the plates in a steamer over rapidly boiling water.
Steam 6-8 minutes, until the strings look glossy and set and no longer taste of raw flour.
steps.tip: Over-steaming makes them gummy. Six minutes is usually enough for a single layer.

steps.text: Lift off and let them cool for 2 minutes before easing them off the plate, or they will tear.

recipes.storage: Best within a few hours. Keeps 2 days refrigerated in a covered box; re-steam 3 minutes to bring the softness back. Reheating dry turns them to string.

recipes.name: Kerala Meen Curry
recipes.subtitle: Fish simmered in coconut milk and kokum, tempered with curry leaves and coconut oil

ingredients.note: kingfish, seer, pomfret or any firm white fish
kudampuli / gambooge; soak in warm water 10 min
or 1 small onion

prepNotes: Kokum (locally kudampuli) is the defining sour note. Tamarind will work but gives a rounder, sweeter sourness and a different colour.
Never boil a coconut milk curry hard after the thick milk goes in; it will split. Keep it at a bare tremble.
Traditionally cooked in a clay meen chatti, which holds heat gently. A heavy pan is fine.

steps.text: Heat the coconut oil. Splutter the mustard seeds and fenugreek, then add the curry leaves, shallots, ginger, garlic and green chillies. Fry until the shallots soften and turn pale gold.
Lower the heat, add the turmeric and Kashmiri chilli and stir for 30 seconds only. Powdered chilli scorches fast and turns bitter.
Add the soaked kokum with its water, the thin part of the coconut milk and salt. Simmer 8 minutes to build the base.
Slide in the fish in a single layer. Do not stir; shake the pan instead so the pieces stay whole. Simmer 6-8 minutes until just opaque.
Pour in the thick coconut milk, swirl the pan and heat through without letting it boil. Take it off the heat as soon as it steams.
steps.tip: Finish with a teaspoon of raw coconut oil and a fresh sprig of curry leaves.

steps.text: Rest at least an hour before eating. This curry is markedly better after resting, and better still the next day.

recipes.name: Koottu Curry
recipes.subtitle: yam, plantain and chana dal in a sweet-peppery roasted coconut gravy

ingredients.note: half ground into the gravy, half roasted for the finish
koottu curry is meant to be faintly sweet

prepNotes: Soak the chana dal 1 hour in warm water so it cooks in step with the vegetables.
Oil your hands before peeling the yam to avoid the itch, and drop the cut plantain into water so it does not blacken.
Grate the coconut and divide it into two equal piles before you start. One for grinding, one for roasting.

steps.text: Pressure-cook the drained chana dal with 250ml water and 1/4 tsp turmeric for 3 whistles, then let the pressure drop naturally. The dal should be soft but not collapsed.
steps.tip: Undercooked chana dal cannot be rescued later, but mushy dal ruins the texture. Test one grain between your fingers.

steps.text: In a separate pot, boil the yam and plantain with the remaining turmeric, black pepper, green chillies, salt and 250ml water for 12-15 minutes until just tender.
Grind half the coconut with the cumin seeds and 100ml water to a coarse, thick paste. A few seconds only, this should stay slightly textured.
Add the cooked dal with its liquid to the vegetables and simmer 5 minutes so the two come together.
Stir in the ground coconut and the jaggery, and cook 8 minutes on medium-low until the gravy is thick and barely runs off a spoon.
steps.tip: Koottu curry is a thick, almost dry curry. If it looks like a soup, keep reducing.

steps.text: Taste and adjust salt, pepper and jaggery. It should read sweet first, then peppery.
In a kadhai heat the coconut oil and crackle the mustard seeds, then add the dried red chillies and curry leaves.
Add the remaining grated coconut to the tempering and roast over medium heat 6-8 minutes, stirring, until it is a deep golden brown and smells toasted.
steps.tip: This roasted coconut is what separates koottu curry from every other coconut curry. Take it darker than feels comfortable.

steps.text: Tip the whole tempering, coconut and all, over the curry and fold it through.
Rest 10 minutes covered before serving as part of a sadya or with plain rice.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated. Reheat on the stovetop with a splash of water; the roasted coconut softens overnight but the flavour deepens.

recipes.name: Kozhi Porichathu
recipes.subtitle: crisp fried chicken in a pepper-and-fennel masala with fried curry leaves

ingredients.qty: 800g, bone-in pieces, skin removed and slashed twice each
ingredients.note: thighs and drumsticks stay juicier than breast
coarse, not fine. You want it to crunch
the crust; do not substitute wheat flour
fried alongside as garnish

prepNotes: Slash each chicken piece to the bone twice so the masala reaches the middle.
Marinate for at least 2 hours, ideally 6, in the fridge, 30 minutes gives you seasoned skin and bland meat.
Take the chicken out of the fridge 20 minutes before frying so it cooks through without burning outside.
Pat the marinated pieces to shed loose liquid just before they go into the oil.

steps.text: Crush the ginger and garlic to a rough paste with a little salt.
Mix the paste with the kashmiri chilli, chilli powder, turmeric, black pepper, fennel powder, garam masala, lemon juice and salt into a thick marinade.
Rub it into the slashed chicken, working it into the cuts, cover and refrigerate at least 2 hours.
steps.tip: Get the marinade inside the slashes with your fingers. Coating the outside only is why fried chicken tastes hollow.

steps.text: Just before frying, sprinkle the rice flour over the chicken and toss so each piece wears a thin, even dusting.
steps.tip: Add the rice flour at the last moment. Left to sit it goes gluey and slides off in the oil.

steps.text: Heat the coconut oil in a kadhai to about 170C. A pinch of rice flour should sizzle steadily, not violently.
Slide in the chicken in a single uncrowded layer and fry over medium heat 7-8 minutes on the first side without moving it.
steps.tip: Leave it alone. Turning early tears the crust off the meat.

steps.text: Turn and fry 6-7 minutes on the second side until deep red-brown and the juices at the thickest part run clear.
Lift onto a rack, not paper, and let the pieces drain while you fry the rest.
Drop the curry leaves, slit green chillies and sliced shallots into the hot oil for 20-30 seconds until the leaves stop spluttering and turn glassy.
steps.tip: Stand back and cover with a lid for the first few seconds. Curry leaves in hot oil spit hard.

steps.text: Scatter the fried aromatics over the chicken, squeeze over a little more lemon and serve hot.

recipes.storage: Best eaten within the hour. Keeps 2 days refrigerated; re-crisp in a 200C oven for 8 minutes rather than the microwave.

recipes.name: Kozhukatta
recipes.subtitle: steamed rice dumplings filled with jaggery and coconut

ingredients.note: the roasted kind sold as puttu podi gives the smoothest dough
dark jaggery gives a better colour
traditional in the filling and worth keeping

ingredients.qty: 1 tbsp, plus extra for your palms

prepNotes: Grate the coconut and jaggery before you start. Once the dough is made it must be shaped while warm.
Keep a small bowl of coconut oil beside you for greasing your palms as you shape.
Have the steamer full and already at a rolling boil before the dumplings are formed, so they go straight in.

steps.text: Make the filling first: melt the jaggery with 3 tbsp water in a pan over medium heat until it dissolves into a syrup, about 4 minutes, then strain out any grit.
Return the syrup to the pan, add the grated coconut, crushed cardamom and cumin seeds, and cook 6-8 minutes, stirring, until the mixture pulls away from the sides and holds its shape when pressed.
steps.tip: Stop while it is still slightly moist. Cooked too dry, the filling turns hard and sandy inside the dumpling.

steps.text: Spread the filling on a plate to cool completely.
Bring the 400ml water to a full boil with the salt and 1 tbsp coconut oil.
Take the pan off the heat and tip in the rice flour all at once, stirring hard with a wooden spoon until no dry flour remains and the mass comes together.
steps.tip: All the flour at once, off the heat. Sprinkling it in gradually gives you lumps you will never work out.

steps.text: Cover and leave 5 minutes, then knead the warm dough with oiled palms for 3-4 minutes until it is completely smooth and does not crack when you press a ball flat.
steps.tip: Knead it as hot as you can bear. Cold dough cracks open in the steamer and spills the filling.

steps.text: Divide the dough into 14-16 balls, keeping the rest covered with a damp cloth while you work.
Flatten each ball into a 7cm disc in your oiled palm, place a heaped teaspoon of filling in the middle, and gather the edges up over it, sealing and rolling into a smooth ball.
Arrange the dumplings in a greased steamer basket with space between them.
Steam over rapidly boiling water for 10-12 minutes, until the surface turns glossy and slightly translucent.
steps.tip: The shift from matte to shiny is the doneness cue. Overcooked kozhukatta go gummy.

steps.text: Rest 5 minutes before lifting them out. Straight from the steamer they tear.

recipes.storage: Best the day they are made. Keep 2 days refrigerated in an airtight box and re-steam 5 minutes to soften; they harden badly in the fridge and do not revive in a microwave.

recipes.name: Malabar Parotta
recipes.subtitle: layered, flaky flatbread slapped and coiled so it pulls apart in sheets

ingredients.note: optional, for softness; leave out for an egg-free parotta
or water; omit for a dairy-free parotta

prepNotes: The layers come from oil, stretching and coiling, not from folding like a paratha. The dough must be rested long enough to stretch paper thin without tearing.
Rest twice: once after kneading, once after shaping into balls. Two hours total is the minimum.

steps.text: Knead the maida with salt, sugar, egg and milk into a very soft dough, adding water as needed. Work it 10 minutes.
Coat with oil, cover, and rest 1 hour.
Divide into 8, roll each into an oiled ball, and rest another hour.
steps.tip: The second rest is what lets the dough stretch without tearing.

steps.text: Flatten a ball on an oiled surface and stretch it outward with your palms until nearly transparent.
steps.tip: Stretch, do not roll. A rolling pin cannot make it thin enough.

steps.text: Pleat the sheet like a fan along its length, then coil the strip into a spiral and tuck the end under. Rest 15 minutes.
Flatten the coil gently to a 15cm round and cook on a hot tawa with oil, 2 minutes a side, until golden and blistered.
While hot, clap the parotta between your palms to loosen the layers.
steps.tip: The clap is not showmanship. It is what separates the sheets.

recipes.storage: Best hot. They keep a day wrapped and reheat on a dry tawa. Coiled uncooked dough keeps 24 hours refrigerated and cooks straight from cold.

recipes.name: Meen Varuthathu
recipes.subtitle: chilli-and-pepper crusted fish shallow fried in coconut oil until the edges blister

ingredients.qty: 600g, 4 steaks or whole small fish, slashed
ingredients.note: seer, pomfret or mackerel
for colour without ferocious heat
for the crust

prepNotes: Pat the fish bone dry with paper towel and cut two deep slashes into each side, right down to the bone. Wet fish will never crisp.
Mix the chilli powders, turmeric, pepper, ginger, garlic, lemon juice and salt into a thick paste with 1 tbsp water and rub it into the slashes.
Marinate 30 minutes in the refrigerator, or up to 2 hours. Longer than that and the lemon starts to cook the flesh.

steps.text: Bring the marinated fish back to room temperature for 15 minutes if it has been in the fridge.
Dust each piece lightly with rice flour on both sides and shake off the excess.
steps.tip: A thin film only. A thick coat turns pasty in the pan.

steps.text: Heat the coconut oil in a heavy tawa over medium-high until a pinch of flour dropped in sizzles instantly.
Slide in the fish, laying it away from you, and do not touch it for 4 minutes.
steps.tip: Moving it early tears the crust off. Wait until it releases on its own.

steps.text: Turn once and fry the second side 3-4 minutes until the crust is deep brick red and the flesh at the slash is opaque.
Throw the curry leaves into the hot oil around the fish for the last 30 seconds until they crisp.
steps.tip: Stand back. Wet leaves in hot oil spit hard.

steps.text: Lift onto a plate, scatter the crisped leaves over, and serve within minutes with rice and a wedge of lemon.

recipes.storage: Eat hot from the pan. Leftovers keep 1 day refrigerated; re-crisp in a dry hot pan for 2 minutes a side rather than reheating in a microwave.

recipes.name: Mutta Roast
recipes.subtitle: boiled eggs in a dark slow-fried onion masala, breakfast alongside appam

ingredients.note: the volume looks absurd and then it collapses
for colour

prepNotes: Boil the eggs 9 minutes from a rolling boil, then cool them in cold water before peeling. The yolks stay just set and the shells slip off.
Slice the onions as thin as you can manage. Thin slices melt into the masala; thick ones stay as visible strands.
Score each peeled egg with 3 shallow slits so the masala gets inside rather than sliding off.

steps.text: Heat 2 tbsp coconut oil in a kadhai and fry the scored eggs with a pinch of turmeric and salt for 2 minutes, turning, until blistered and gold. Lift out.
steps.tip: Keep a lid handy. Eggs spit in hot oil.

steps.text: Add the remaining oil, then the sliced onions, ginger, garlic, green chillies and 2 sprigs of curry leaves with a pinch of salt.
Cook on medium-low for 20-25 minutes, stirring every few minutes, until the onions collapse to about a fifth of their volume and turn a deep glossy brown.
steps.tip: This is the entire dish and there is no shortcut. Twenty-five minutes, low and slow.

steps.text: Add the chilli powder, Kashmiri chilli, coriander powder, turmeric and pepper. Fry 90 seconds with a splash of water so the spices do not catch.
Stir in the tomatoes and cook 8 minutes until they break down completely and the oil pools at the edges.
steps.tip: Wait for the oil to separate. That is the signal the masala is cooked, not merely hot.

steps.text: Add 1/4 cup water, the garam masala and fennel powder, and simmer 3 minutes into a thick clinging masala.
Return the fried eggs, roll them in the masala and cook 3 minutes on low so they take on the colour.
Scatter over the last sprig of curry leaves, cover and rest 5 minutes off the heat before serving with appam or bread.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated; the masala improves but the whites toughen a little. Reheat over low heat with 2 tbsp water, turning the eggs gently.

recipes.name: Nadan Chicken Stew
recipes.subtitle: pale peppery chicken and potato stew in coconut milk, the classic appam partner

ingredients.note: the only heat that belongs here
400ml thin, 100ml thick

prepNotes: Stew is a white curry: no turmeric, no chilli powder, no browning. Keep the heat low the whole way through.
Separate your coconut milk before you start. Thin for cooking, thick for finishing. If using tinned, dilute 150ml with 250ml water for the thin.
Cut the potato into chunks no smaller than 4cm so they hold their shape through 25 minutes of simmering.

steps.text: Heat the coconut oil in a heavy pot over medium-low and add the cinnamon, cloves and cardamom. Fry 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the onion, ginger, garlic and green chillies with a pinch of salt. Cook 6-8 minutes until soft and glassy.
steps.tip: Do not let them colour. Any browning and it stops being a stew.

steps.text: Stir in the crushed pepper and fry 30 seconds.
Add the chicken and turn it in the aromatics for 3 minutes until the flesh turns opaque white.
Pour in the thin coconut milk, add the potato, carrot, curry leaves and salt, and bring to a bare simmer.
Cover and cook on low for 25 minutes, until the chicken pulls easily from the bone and the potato is soft at the centre.
steps.tip: A hard boil will curdle the coconut milk and toughen the chicken. Keep it at a lazy blip.

steps.text: Uncover and stir in the thick coconut milk. Warm through for 2 minutes without letting it boil.
Taste for salt and pepper, then rest covered for 10 minutes off the heat before serving with appam.
steps.tip: The stew tastes noticeably better after ten minutes of sitting. Build it into your timing.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated and improves overnight. Reheat over low heat, stirring, and add a splash of water. It thickens considerably when cold.

recipes.name: Nadan Mutton Curry
recipes.subtitle: slow-cooked mutton in a dark roasted-coconut and fennel gravy

ingredients.note: shoulder and leg with some bone for body
roasted dark and ground. This is the backbone

prepNotes: Bring the mutton to room temperature and pat it thoroughly dry. Wet meat steams instead of browning.
Marinate the mutton with the turmeric, half the chilli powder and 1 tsp salt for 30 minutes while you slice the shallots.
Slice the shallots as thin as you can manage; they are meant to melt into the gravy, not sit in it.

steps.text: Dry-roast the grated coconut in a heavy kadhai over medium-low heat for 10-12 minutes, stirring, until it is chocolate brown and smells nutty, then cool and grind with 100ml water to a smooth dark paste.
steps.tip: Grind this paste for a full 3 minutes. Gritty coconut paste is the most common flaw in this curry.

steps.text: Heat 3 tbsp coconut oil in a pressure cooker and fry the whole cinnamon, cloves and cardamom for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the sliced shallots and onion and fry over medium heat for 15 minutes until deeply browned and sweet. This is the longest active step and it cannot be shortened.
steps.tip: Pale onions make a thin, sharp curry. Wait for the colour of dark honey.

steps.text: Add the ginger, garlic and green chillies and fry 3 minutes until the raw smell lifts.
Lower the heat, add the coriander powder, kashmiri chilli, remaining chilli powder, fennel powder and black pepper and fry 90 seconds, sprinkling in a tablespoon of water if the spices catch.
steps.tip: A tablespoon of water at the first hint of sticking saves the whole masala from burning.

steps.text: Add the tomatoes and 2 sprigs of curry leaves and cook 5 minutes until the tomatoes break down and oil shows at the edges.
Stir in the marinated mutton and fry over high heat for 6-8 minutes until every piece is coated and the meat has tightened and browned.
Add 400ml water and the salt, close the cooker and cook on medium for 5 whistles, then let the pressure fall naturally, around 15 minutes.
Open the cooker, stir in the roasted coconut paste and simmer uncovered 15-20 minutes until the gravy is thick, dark and clings to the meat.
steps.tip: The gravy should coat a spoon heavily. If it is still loose, keep it on the heat rather than adding thickener.

steps.text: Stir in the garam masala, taste for salt, and take off the heat.
Heat the last tablespoon of coconut oil in a small pan, fry the remaining curry leaf sprig for 10 seconds and pour it over the curry.
Rest 15 minutes covered before serving with appam, kappa or rice.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated and 2 months frozen. Reheat gently on the stovetop with 2-3 tbsp water; the flavour is noticeably better on day two.

recipes.name: Neyyappam
recipes.subtitle: dark ghee-fried rice and jaggery fritters, crisp outside and soft within

ingredients.note: any short or medium grain works

ingredients.qty: 1/2 cup, cut into small thin slivers
ingredients.note: fried in ghee first, then folded through
traditional, and it stops the sweetness cloying
ghee is what makes it neyyappam; oil gives a lesser thing
for lift, added at the last moment

prepNotes: Soak the rice at least 4 hours, or overnight, then drain it thoroughly in a sieve for 15 minutes.
Make the batter and rest it 2-3 hours before frying. Unrested batter fries flat and heavy.
You need an appakara or aebleskiver pan for the classic shape; otherwise fry spoonfuls as small round fritters in a deep kadhai.

steps.text: Melt the jaggery with 100ml water over medium heat until dissolved, about 5 minutes, then strain through a sieve and cool to lukewarm.
steps.tip: Cool the syrup before it meets the rice. Hot syrup part-cooks the batter and it will never rise.

steps.text: Grind the drained rice with the cooled jaggery syrup and the remaining 50ml water to a thick, smooth batter. Thicker than dosa batter, roughly the consistency of cake batter.
Beat in the crushed cardamom, dry ginger powder and salt, then cover and rest the batter 2-3 hours at room temperature.
Heat 2 tbsp ghee in a small pan and fry the coconut slivers for 3-4 minutes until golden at the edges, then fry the sesame for 20 seconds.
Fold the fried coconut, sesame and all the ghee from that pan into the rested batter.
Stir in the baking soda if using, right before frying, and do not let the batter sit after this.
Heat the remaining ghee in a kadhai over medium heat until a drop of batter rises to the surface within 3 seconds without browning instantly.
steps.tip: Too hot and the outside darkens while the centre stays raw batter. Medium heat, patiently.

steps.text: Drop in tablespoons of batter, 4-5 at a time, and fry 3 minutes until the undersides are deep mahogany.
Flip each one and fry a further 2-3 minutes until puffed, dark and firm at the edges.
steps.tip: Test one first. If it collapses on flipping, the batter is too thin. Beat in a tablespoon of rice flour before continuing.

steps.text: Lift onto a rack to drain and cool, and let the ghee come back to temperature between batches.
Serve at room temperature, when the outside has crisped and the inside stays soft.

recipes.storage: Keeps a week in an airtight tin at room temperature and up to 3 weeks refrigerated. No reheating needed. Bring back to room temperature before eating.

recipes.name: Olan
recipes.subtitle: ash gourd and cowpeas simmered in thin coconut milk, barely spiced on purpose

ingredients.qty: 400g, peeled and cut into 4cm thin slices

ingredients.note: red cowpeas (van payar) are traditional
300ml thin, 100ml thick, see prep notes
raw, stirred in at the end

prepNotes: Soak the cowpeas 6 hours or overnight. They stay firm otherwise and will not cook alongside the gourd.
If you are using tinned coconut milk, dilute 100ml with 200ml water to stand in for the second and third pressings, and keep 100ml undiluted for the finish.
Olan carries no onion, garlic, mustard or chilli powder. The restraint is the dish, resist adding any.

steps.text: Boil the soaked cowpeas in 2 cups of water for 20-25 minutes until soft but still holding their shape. Drain, keeping a little of the cooking water.
steps.tip: Squeeze one between your fingers. It should give completely with no chalky centre.

steps.text: Put the ash gourd slices in a wide pan with the slit chillies, salt and just enough water to come halfway up.
Simmer uncovered 8 minutes until the gourd turns translucent at the edges and a knife slides through without resistance.
steps.tip: Ash gourd goes from firm to mush in about two minutes. Check early.

steps.text: Add the cooked cowpeas and the thin coconut milk. Bring to a bare simmer.
Cook 5 minutes on low, shaking the pan rather than stirring so the gourd slices stay whole.
Pour in the thick coconut milk and the curry leaves. Warm through for 1 minute only.
steps.tip: Do not let it boil after the thick milk goes in or it will split into oily flecks.

steps.text: Take off the heat, stir in the raw coconut oil and cover for 5 minutes before serving.
steps.tip: The raw oil is the signature aroma of olan. Use good unrefined coconut oil.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated. Reheat very gently over low heat without boiling; it will thicken as it sits, so loosen with a spoonful of water.

recipes.name: Parippu Curry
recipes.subtitle: soft moong dal in coconut and cumin, the first course of a sadya

ingredients.note: cherupayar parippu
goes into the paste

prepNotes: Dry-roast the moong dal in a pan for 4-5 minutes until it smells nutty and a few grains turn pale gold. This is what separates parippu curry from ordinary dal.
Rinse the roasted dal in two changes of water before cooking.
Grind the coconut, green chillies, cumin and garlic to a fine paste with 1/3 cup water while the dal cooks.

steps.text: Pressure cook the rinsed dal with 2.5 cups water and the turmeric for 3 whistles, then rest until the pressure drops.
steps.tip: It should be completely collapsed. Undercooked parippu curry has a raw beany edge that no amount of coconut hides.

steps.text: Whisk the cooked dal smooth with a ladle, adding hot water until it is the consistency of thin cream.
Stir in the ground coconut paste and the salt.
Simmer on low for 6-8 minutes, stirring often, until the raw coconut smell disappears and it thickens slightly.
steps.tip: Coconut catches on the base easily. Stir and keep the flame low.

steps.text: Heat the coconut oil in a small pan and pop the mustard seeds, about 30 seconds.
Add the sliced shallots, broken red chillies and curry leaves and fry 2 minutes until the shallots brown.
Pour the tempering over the dal and cover for 5 minutes so the curry leaf aroma settles in.
Serve over hot rice as the first course of the meal, with a papadam crushed over the top.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated. It sets almost solid when cold. Reheat with plenty of hot water, whisking, until it pours again.

recipes.name: Pazham Pori
recipes.subtitle: ripe plantain slices in a turmeric-gold batter, the four o'clock teashop snack

ingredients.note: use ripe nendran plantains. Catalogued here as raw-banana
for crispness
for the classic yellow
or neutral oil

prepNotes: The plantains must be properly ripe. Skin heavily blackened, flesh soft and sweet. Underripe nendran is starchy and the snack falls flat.
Make the batter 10 minutes ahead and let it rest so the flour hydrates; it will cling better to the slippery banana.
The batter should be the thickness of pouring cream: thick enough to coat the back of a spoon, thin enough to drip off in a steady ribbon.

steps.text: Whisk the maida, rice flour, turmeric, sugar, salt and crushed cumin together in a bowl.
Add the water gradually, whisking, until you have a smooth lump-free batter. Rest 10 minutes.
steps.tip: Add the last of the water a tablespoon at a time. Flours vary and a thin batter slides straight off.

steps.text: Peel the plantains and slice each lengthwise into 3-4 flat strips about 8mm thick.
steps.tip: Too thin and they disintegrate in the oil; too thick and the centre stays firm.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a kadhai to 175C. A drop of batter should rise and sizzle within 3 seconds without browning instantly.
Dip a strip into the batter, let the excess run off, and lower it gently into the oil.
Fry 3-4 at a time for 2 minutes, until the underside is set and pale gold.
steps.tip: Crowding the pan drops the oil temperature and the fritters drink oil instead of frying.

steps.text: Turn and fry a further 2 minutes until both sides are deep gold and the surface has stopped bubbling hard.
Lift onto a rack, not paper, so the underside stays crisp. Repeat with the rest.
Serve hot with strong black tea.

recipes.storage: Eat within an hour. They soften as they sit. Leftovers can be crisped in a hot oven for 5 minutes, but they will never be as good as the first batch.

recipes.name: Pulissery
recipes.subtitle: soured yogurt and coconut curry, gently spiced and never boiled

ingredients.note: a day-old yogurt is ideal
or raw banana, cut the same way
whole seeds, not dried leaves

prepNotes: Take the yogurt out of the fridge 30 minutes ahead. Cold yogurt hitting a hot pan splits immediately.
Whisk the yogurt completely smooth with 1/2 cup water before it goes anywhere near heat. Any lump will curdle.
Grind the coconut, green chillies, cumin and turmeric to a fine paste with 4 tbsp water. Fine matters: a gritty paste makes a gritty curry.

steps.text: Cook the ash gourd with the salt and 1/2 cup water in a wide pan, covered, for 8 minutes until soft and translucent.
Stir in the ground coconut paste and simmer 4 minutes on low, until the raw coconut smell has gone.
Take the pan off the heat completely and let it cool for 3 minutes.
steps.tip: This pause is what keeps the yogurt from splitting. Do not skip it.

steps.text: Pour in the whisked yogurt, stirring as you go.
Return to the lowest possible heat and warm, stirring constantly, for 3-4 minutes until it just steams and thickens slightly.
steps.tip: The instant you see a bubble, pull it off. Boiled pulissery separates and cannot be rescued.

steps.text: Taste for salt and set aside covered.
Heat the coconut oil in a small pan, pop the mustard seeds, then add the fenugreek seeds, broken red chillies and curry leaves and fry 20 seconds.
steps.tip: Fenugreek burns bitter fast. It should darken only a shade.

steps.text: Pour the tempering over the curry and cover for 5 minutes before serving with rice.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated and the sourness deepens. Reheat only to lukewarm over the lowest heat, or serve at room temperature as they do in Kerala.

recipes.name: Pumpkin Erissery
recipes.subtitle: mashed pumpkin and cowpeas under a lid of dark roasted coconut

image.credit: Vernon Chan from Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia

ingredients.note: red cowpeas
half for the paste, half for the roast

prepNotes: Soak the cowpeas overnight, or at least 6 hours. Unsoaked they take twice as long as the pumpkin and the dish falls apart waiting for them.
Grind half the grated coconut with the green chillies, garlic, half the cumin and the turmeric to a smooth paste with 3 tbsp water.
Keep the other half of the coconut dry and loose for roasting. It must not be damp or it will steam rather than brown.

steps.text: Boil the soaked cowpeas in 2 cups water for 20 minutes until tender. Do not drain.
Add the pumpkin cubes, chilli powder and salt to the same pan with a little more water if needed. Cook covered 10 minutes until the pumpkin is soft enough to crush against the side of the pan.
Mash roughly with the back of a ladle, leaving some cubes whole for texture.
steps.tip: Erissery is a mash, not a puree. Stop while you can still see pieces.

steps.text: Stir in the ground coconut paste and simmer 5 minutes on low until it loses its raw smell and thickens.
In a separate kadhai, heat the coconut oil and pop the mustard seeds, about 30 seconds.
Add the broken red chillies, curry leaves and the remaining cumin seeds and fry 20 seconds.
Add the reserved grated coconut and roast on medium-low, stirring constantly, for 5-6 minutes until it is a deep even brown and smells nutty.
steps.tip: This is the whole point of erissery and it turns from brown to burnt in seconds. Stand over it.

steps.text: Pour the roasted coconut tempering over the pumpkin, stir once, and rest 5 minutes before serving.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated. Reheat gently with a splash of water; the roasted coconut aroma fades, so a fresh spoonful of the tempering revives it.

recipes.name: Puttu
recipes.subtitle: steamed cylinders of rice flour layered with coconut, eaten hot with kadala curry

ingredients.note: coarse puttu podi if available
added a sprinkle at a time

prepNotes: If your rice flour is not pre-roasted, dry-roast it in a pan on low for 6-8 minutes until it smells toasty and feels warm but takes no colour. Cool completely before wetting it.
The moisture level is everything. The flour is right when a fistful holds its shape when squeezed but crumbles apart cleanly when you poke it.
Rest the wetted flour 10 minutes before steaming so the water distributes evenly.

steps.text: Dissolve the salt in the warm water.
Sprinkle the salted water over the rice flour a tablespoon at a time, rubbing it through with your fingertips after each addition.
steps.tip: Never pour. Poured water makes lumps that steam into hard pellets.

steps.text: Stop when the flour feels like damp sand and holds a shape in your fist. You may not need all the water.
Pass the whole lot through a coarse sieve or break the lumps by rubbing between your palms, then rest 10 minutes.
Bring water to a rolling boil in the base of the puttu maker or steamer.
Load the mould: a tablespoon of grated coconut at the bottom, then loose flour to two-thirds, then coconut, then flour, finishing with coconut. Do not press down.
steps.tip: Packing the flour is the classic mistake. Loose layers steam through; packed ones come out dense.

steps.text: Steam 7-8 minutes from when a steady plume comes out of the top.
Push the puttu out onto a plate with the handle of a wooden spoon and serve immediately with kadala curry or ripe banana.
steps.tip: Puttu hardens as it cools. Steam it in batches and eat each one as it comes.

steps.text: Fold in both long sides by 3cm, spread paste on the folded edges, then roll from the wide end into a tight cylinder. Seal the end with paste. Make 4 rolls.

prepNotes: Jowar has no gluten, so the dough is bound by hot water and kneading alone. The water must be at a rolling boil, not merely hot.
Clear a patch of clean, dry counter. Bhakri is patted out flat on the surface, not rolled with a pin.

steps.text: As soon as it is cool enough to touch, knead firmly for 5 minutes with the heel of your hand until the dough is smooth and shows no cracks when you press it.

steps.text: Divide into 6 balls and keep them covered with a damp cloth.
Dust the counter with jowar flour, flatten a ball with your palm, then pat it out into a 15cm disc by pressing and rotating with the flat of your fingers.

steps.text: Brush the loose flour off, lift the bhakri on your palm and lay it onto the hot tawa.
Smear the top surface with water using your fingers and cook 1 minute, until the wet film dries and the underside shows pale brown patches.

steps.text: Add the turmeric and chilli powder, count to five, and pour in the kat immediately so the spices do not burn.

recipes.name: Kolhapuri Chicken Rassa
recipes.subtitle: thin, fiery red chicken curry built on roasted coconut and dagad phool

ingredients.qty: 800g, on the bone, cut into curry pieces
3 medium, 2 for the masala and 1 for the gravy

for the red without wrecking anyone

prepNotes: Marinate the chicken with the turmeric, half the ginger-garlic and 1 tsp salt for 30 minutes in the refrigerator.

steps.text: Grind the ginger and garlic to a paste and rub half of it into the chicken with the turmeric and salt. Leave 30 minutes.
Dry-roast the grated dried coconut over low heat for 5 minutes until it is dark brown and smells toasted, then tip it out immediately.
steps.tip: Dark brown, not black. Burnt coconut makes the whole pot bitter and there is no fixing it.

steps.text: In the same pan, dry-roast the cumin, black pepper, cloves, cinnamon, black cardamom, stone flower, poppy seeds and sesame for 2 minutes until fragrant. Cool completely.

Heat the remaining oil in a heavy pan with the bay leaf, add the last onion, finely chopped, and cook 8 minutes until golden.
Add the remaining ginger-garlic paste, fry 1 minute, then add the chicken and sear over high heat for 5 minutes until the pieces are opaque all over.
Stir in the ground masala and fry over medium heat for 8 to 10 minutes, scraping the base, until it darkens and oil pools at the sides.

steps.text: Pour in the water, season with salt, bring to a boil then simmer uncovered 25 minutes until the chicken is tender and a red film of oil floats on the surface.

ingredients.qty: 3 large bunches (about 200g), leaves and tender stems, finely chopped

traditional; leave out for a nut-free version

prepNotes: Wash the coriander the night before and dry it completely. Even spread out on a towel for an hour works. Wet leaves make a batter that will not set.

steps.text: Chop the coriander finely, stems included, and squeeze it in your fist. It should feel dry, not release green water.
Mix the coriander with the besan, rice flour, crushed peanut, 1 tbsp sesame, green chilli, ginger, garlic, turmeric, chilli powder, coriander powder, asafoetida, sugar and salt.

steps.text: Stir in 1 tbsp oil, scrape into a greased 15cm tin and level the top.

recipes.name: Maharashtrian Basundi
recipes.subtitle: milk cooked down by half until it is thick, grainy and the colour of ivory

ingredients.note: the whole dish is the milk, so use the best you can get

ingredients.qty: a generous pinch, soaked in 2 tbsp warm milk

prepNotes: Use the widest, heaviest pan you own. A wide surface is what reduces milk in an hour rather than two.
Rinse the pan with cold water and leave a film of it before pouring in the milk. It makes the base far less likely to catch.
Soak the saffron in warm milk for 15 minutes so it gives up its colour before it goes in.

steps.text: Bring the milk to a boil in a wide heavy pan, then drop the heat to a steady low simmer.
Simmer 45-55 minutes, stirring every 3-4 minutes and scraping the base and the sides with a flat spatula.
steps.tip: Scrape the cream that sticks to the sides back into the milk each time. That is what makes basundi grainy rather than merely thick.

steps.text: Keep going until the milk has reduced by half and coats the back of a spoon in a thick ivory layer.
steps.tip: Judge by volume, not the clock. Mark the starting level on your spatula handle if it helps.

steps.text: Stir in the sugar and simmer 8 more minutes. The milk will loosen at first and then thicken again.
steps.tip: Adding sugar early slows the reduction and risks scorching. Wait until the milk is already thick.

steps.text: Add the crushed cardamom, the saffron milk and the scraping of nutmeg and simmer 2 minutes.
Take off the heat and cool to room temperature, stirring occasionally to stop a skin forming.
Chill at least 3 hours; it thickens noticeably as it cools.
Serve cold in small bowls, scattered with the slivered almonds and pistachios, with hot puris alongside if it is a festival day.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated in a covered container. Serve cold; if it has set too stiff, loosen with 2 tbsp cold milk and stir well.

prepNotes: Oil a flat plate or tray before you start cooking the besan. The mixture sets fast and there is no time to hunt for one.

steps.text: Dry-roast the dried coconut, poppy seeds, stone flower, dried red chillies, black pepper, cloves and cinnamon over low heat for 6-7 minutes, until the coconut is dark gold and the chillies smell smoky.

Blend 2 roughly chopped onions with the garlic and ginger and 3 tbsp water to a smooth paste.
Heat 6 tbsp oil in a heavy pan. Fry the sliced onions over medium heat 12-14 minutes until deep brown, not black.

for raja mircha, the Naga king chilli; two fresh bird's-eye chillies alongside gets you closer
not traditional everywhere, but common in Kohima kitchens
fresh or brined; rinse brined shoot twice

Pour in the rest of the water, add salt, cover and simmer very gently 45 minutes. Check at 30 minutes and add a splash if it looks dry.
Add the bamboo shoot and the green chillies and simmer uncovered 10 minutes more.
The pork is ready when a piece of skin gives completely under a spoon and the gravy has reduced to a thick, glossy few centimetres in the base.
steps.tip: If it is still chewy, it needs time, not heat. Go another 15 minutes covered on low.

steps.text: Stir in the remaining ginger julienne and the spring onion, rest 5 minutes off the heat, and serve with plain sticky rice.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated and improves overnight as the ferment settles into the fat. Lift off the set fat cap, reheat gently on the stovetop, and add fresh ginger and spring onion at the end.

recipes.name: Bai
recipes.subtitle: the mizo pot of greens and pumpkin, barely seasoned and softened with an alkaline pinch

ingredients.note: any sturdy local green does. This is what most kitchens use
fermented bamboo shoot is the classic addition; rinse brined shoot well or it dominates
the corm; peel it under running water and cook it right through
stands in for chingal, the alkaline water Mizo cooks filter through wood ash; the catalogue has no chingal and this is the closest thing

prepNotes: Bai has no onion, no garlic and no oil. That is not an omission. The point is the taste of the vegetables themselves, so buy them fresh and cut them the same day.
A quarter teaspoon of baking soda is plenty. Too much and the greens go slimy and the pot smells faintly of soap.
Peel colocasia under running water and rinse your hands after; the raw corm can itch.

steps.text: Bring the water to a boil in a wide pot with the salt, slit chillies and ginger.
Add the colocasia, if using, and boil 10 minutes. It takes longer than everything else and must be cooked right through.
steps.tip: Undercooked colocasia is unpleasantly scratchy in the throat. Give it the full time.

steps.text: Add the pumpkin and boil 6 minutes, until the edges have just started to soften.
Add the beans and bamboo shoot and cook 4 minutes.
Pile in the mustard greens, push them under the liquid and cook 4 minutes, until they have collapsed and turned dark.
Stir in the baking soda and simmer 3 minutes more. The greens will soften noticeably and the broth thickens a little.
steps.tip: It goes in at the end. Added at the start it strips the colour out of the greens.

steps.text: Crush a few pieces of pumpkin against the side of the pot to thicken the liquid, taste for salt, and serve hot with rice and a chilli chutney.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated, though the alkali keeps working and the greens will be softer on day two. Reheat gently on the stovetop with a splash of water; do not boil hard.

recipes.name: Bilahi Pitika
recipes.subtitle: fire-roasted tomatoes mashed with raw mustard oil, onion and green chilli

ingredients.note: unheated. The raw pungency is the whole point of a pitika
standing in for bhut jolokia, which the catalogue has no id for; the local chilli is many times hotter, so use a fraction of one if you have it
only if the tomatoes turn out sweet rather than sour

prepNotes: Choose tomatoes that are properly ripe and a little soft. Firm supermarket tomatoes roast into something watery and bland.
Chop the onion, chilli and coriander before you start roasting, so everything goes into the warm pulp at once.
Mustard oil goes in raw here. If yours is very sharp, warm it to smoking point, cool it fully, and use it cold.

steps.text: Set the tomatoes directly on a gas flame over medium heat and turn them with tongs every couple of minutes, 8-10 minutes in all, until the skins blister black and split and the flesh sags.
steps.tip: A flame, not a pan. The smoky char is half the flavour. Under a hot grill for 15 minutes is the next best thing.

steps.text: Drop the hot tomatoes into a bowl and cover it for 5 minutes.
steps.tip: The trapped steam loosens the skins so they slip off instead of tearing.

steps.text: Peel away and discard the skins, tipping every drop of juice back into the bowl.
Mash with a fork or your fingers to a coarse, lumpy pulp.
steps.tip: Stop while there are still recognisable pieces. Blended smooth it becomes a sauce, not a pitika.

steps.text: Fold in the raw mustard oil and salt and leave it 2 minutes.
Stir in the onion, green chilli and coriander. Taste, and add the lemon juice only if it tastes flat.
Serve at room temperature in a heap beside plain rice, with dal poured over the rice.

recipes.storage: Best within a couple of hours. The mashed tomato keeps 2 days refrigerated, but the onion goes limp and grey. Hold it back and stir fresh onion, chilli and coriander in just before serving.

recipes.name: Chakhwi
recipes.subtitle: Tripuri bamboo shoot stew with raw papaya and a low, savoury note of dried fish

ingredients.note: fermented shoot is traditional; fresh boiled shoot works and is milder
the nearest catalogued stand-in for berma, Tripura's fermented dried fish; toast it hard before use and expect a saltier, cleaner flavour than the original

ingredients.qty: 1 tbsp, slaked in 3 tbsp cold water
ingredients.note: gives the broth just enough body to cling
Tripuri cooking uses very little oil, and the dish is often made with none at all

prepNotes: Toast and crumble the dried fish first, in a separate pan, before anything else goes on the stove.
If your bamboo shoot is fresh, boil it in a change of water for 10 minutes and drain, or the stew will be harsh.
Raw papaya must be genuinely raw and green. A half-ripe one turns to mush and sweetens the pot.

steps.text: Dry-toast the dried fish over low heat for 3 minutes until brittle and strongly fragrant, then crumble it.
Warm the oil in a deep pan and fry the garlic and ginger for 1 minute until they smell sweet.
Add the bamboo shoot and cook 4 minutes, until the sharp raw smell softens.
steps.tip: Do not lean over the pan at this point. Bamboo shoot is aggressive in the first two minutes.

steps.text: Stir in the crumbled fish and the turmeric and cook 1 minute.
Add the papaya, potato and water, bring to a boil, then simmer uncovered 20 minutes until the papaya turns translucent at the edges.
Add the beans and green chillies and simmer 6 minutes more.
Stir in the slaked rice flour and cook 2 minutes, until the broth thickens just enough to leave a film on the spoon.
steps.tip: Slake it in cold water first. Dry flour tipped into hot broth lumps instantly.

steps.text: Season with salt (the dried fish has done much of the work) scatter the coriander and serve with rice.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated. The papaya softens further overnight, which most people prefer. Reheat to a bare simmer and loosen with a little water.

recipes.name: Chamthong
recipes.subtitle: the manipuri everyday vegetable stew, clear and light and lifted by fermented fish

ingredients.note: any soft local green does; this is what goes in at home
stands in for ngari, Manipuri fermented fish. Dry-roast it first; the catalogue carries no ngari
chamthong is a near-oilless broth; this is all it gets

prepNotes: Dry-roast the dried fish for 3 minutes over low heat before it goes in. Straight from the packet it makes the broth muddy.
Cut the vegetables to roughly the same size and add them in order of hardness. This stew is boiled, not layered with fat, so timing is the only thing keeping it from turning to soup.
Chamthong is deliberately plain. Resist adding garlic or masala: it is meant to sit next to eromba and a chilli chutney, not compete with them.

steps.text: Dry-roast the dried fish 3 minutes over low heat until brittle and toasty, then break it into rough pieces.
Bring the water to a boil in a wide pot with the onion, ginger, green chillies, roasted fish and salt. Boil 5 minutes.
Add the potato and pumpkin and boil 8 minutes, uncovered, until the potato is nearly done.
steps.tip: Uncovered. A lid makes the greens go grey later and dulls the whole pot.

steps.text: Add the beans and cook 4 minutes.
Add the cabbage and cook 3 minutes, until it has just wilted but still has a bite.
Stir in the amaranth greens and the tablespoon of oil and cook 2 minutes more.
steps.tip: The oil goes in at the end; it sits on top as a few bright beads rather than dissolving into the broth.

steps.text: Taste for salt, scatter over the spring onion and serve hot in bowls alongside rice.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated. Reheat only to a bare simmer. A hard boil turns the pumpkin to purée and the greens to sludge. Add the spring onion fresh each time.

recipes.name: Chhurpi Soup
recipes.subtitle: fermented cheese simmered with greens, the Sikkimese winter bowl

ingredients.note: standing in for soft chhurpi, the fermented yak cheese

prepNotes: Chhurpi is yak or cow milk cheese, fermented and either eaten soft or dried into a block hard enough to chew for hours.
Paneer is the honest substitute available here. It gives the texture but not the sourness, so the bamboo shoot is doing more work than usual.

steps.text: Fry the onion, garlic and ginger in the oil until soft.
Add the bamboo shoot and cook 5 minutes.
Add the water, bring to a boil and simmer 10 minutes.
Add the cheese and the green chillies and simmer 8 minutes until it softens and begins to melt at the edges.
Stir in the spinach, cook 3 minutes, and season heavily with pepper and salt.

recipes.name: Doh Khleh
recipes.subtitle: khasi pork salad. Boiled meat tossed hot with onion, chilli and a lot of lemon

ingredients.qty: 500g belly or shoulder, in one piece

ingredients.note: doh khleh should be properly sharp
black sesame is what is used in Meghalaya; the catalogue's sesame is the same seed, so roast it a shade darker
for the boiling water

prepNotes: Boil the pork in one piece and dice it after. Diced first, it dries out and loses its bounce.
Slice the onion paper-thin and salt it while the pork boils. Twenty minutes of sitting takes the harshness out.
Dress the salad while the pork is still warm. Cold meat will not take up the lemon.

steps.text: Bring the water to a boil with the bay leaf and a generous tablespoon of salt, lower in the pork and simmer 35 minutes.
Test it with a skewer. It should go in easily but the meat should still hold together, not shred.
steps.tip: Boil it past this point and the salad turns to threads.

steps.text: Meanwhile toss the sliced onion with a big pinch of salt and leave it in a bowl for 20 minutes.
Roast the sesame in a dry pan 2 minutes, until it pops and smells toasted, then grind it coarsely.
Lift the pork out, rest it 5 minutes, then cut it into 1.5cm dice, fat and all.
While it is still warm, toss the pork with the onion and any liquid in its bowl, the ginger, green chilli and crushed black pepper.
Add the lemon juice and check the salt. The boiling water has seasoned the meat already, so taste before adding more.
steps.tip: Add the lemon to warm meat, not hot: straight off the boil it just evaporates.

steps.text: Fold in the ground sesame and coriander and serve at room temperature, on its own or with plain rice.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated but the onion softens and the lemon fades. Bring it to room temperature and refresh with a squeeze of lemon and fresh coriander; do not reheat.

recipes.name: Doh Neiiong
recipes.subtitle: Khasi pork stewed in ground black sesame until the gravy turns dark and nutty

ingredients.qty: 700g belly and shoulder mixed, in 3cm cubes with the fat left on

ingredients.note: black sesame is what gives the gravy its colour; white seeds work but the dish stays grey-brown
barely any is needed. The pork renders plenty of its own fat

prepNotes: Ask for pork with a decent fat cap. Lean pork gives a thin, gritty gravy. The fat is what carries the sesame.
Grind the sesame with a little water into a paste, not a dry powder, and do it before you start cooking.
Bring the pork to room temperature so it browns instead of stewing when it hits the pan.

steps.text: Dry-roast the sesame seeds in a heavy pan over low heat for 4-5 minutes, shaking constantly, until they start to pop and smell strongly nutty.
steps.tip: Black seeds hide their colour, so go by smell and sound. Burnt sesame turns the whole dish bitter and there is no rescuing it.

steps.text: Cool the seeds completely, then blend with the chopped onion and 4 tbsp water to a thick, slightly coarse paste.
steps.tip: Cooling first matters. Warm seeds go oily and smear instead of grinding.

steps.text: Put the pork in a pan with the turmeric, 1 tsp salt, the bay leaf and 300ml of the water. Bring to a boil and simmer covered 20 minutes, skimming the grey foam off the top.
Heat the oil in a kadhai and fry the sliced onion for 8 minutes until deep gold and shrunken.
Add the ginger and garlic and cook 2 minutes until the raw smell is gone.
Lift the pork out of its liquor into the kadhai, keeping the liquor. Add the cracked pepper and fry hard for 8 minutes, turning, until the cubes take on brown edges and the pan looks dry.
Stir in the sesame paste and cook 3 minutes, then add the reserved pork liquor and the remaining 200ml water.
steps.tip: Scrape the base as you add the liquid. Everything stuck there is flavour.

steps.text: Simmer uncovered 20-25 minutes, stirring every few minutes, until the gravy darkens, thickens enough to coat the pork, and fat beads at the rim.
steps.tip: Sesame catches on the base the moment you stop stirring. Keep the heat low.

steps.text: Add the green chillies, check the salt, and simmer 5 minutes more.
Rest 10 minutes off the heat before serving with plain rice.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated and tastes better on day two. The gravy sets solid when cold. Reheat over low heat with 3-4 tbsp water, stirring, until it loosens. Freezes well for a month.

recipes.name: Eromba
recipes.subtitle: manipuri mash of boiled vegetables, fierce chilli and fermented fish, eaten with rice

ingredients.note: stands in for ngari, the Manipuri fermented fish; the catalogue has no ngari, and dried fish rinsed and dry-roasted gives the closest savoury weight
for umorok, the local king chilli; use three if you want to live
the nearest thing to maroi napakpi, the Manipuri hill chive

prepNotes: Rinse the dried fish twice in warm water and pat it dry before roasting, or the eromba comes out salty and rank rather than savoury.
Eromba is a mash, not a curry. It should hold its shape on the spoon. Boil the vegetables in as little water as will cover them.
Everything gets pounded together at the end, so cut the vegetables large; they only need to be soft.

steps.text: Dry-roast the dried fish in a small pan over low heat for 3 minutes, turning, until it smells toasty and goes brittle. Crumble it and set aside.
steps.tip: Low heat and keep it moving. Scorched dried fish tastes of nothing but burnt.

steps.text: Roast the dried red chillies in the same pan 40 seconds a side, until they darken and puff slightly. Pound them to a coarse paste with a pinch of salt.
steps.tip: Open a window. Roasting this many chillies will clear the room.

steps.text: Boil the potato in the water for 8 minutes.
Add the eggplant and beans and boil 8 minutes more, until everything is completely tender and the potato is starting to fall apart.
Drain, keeping about 100ml of the cooking water.
Mash the vegetables roughly in the pot with the back of a ladle, leaving some lumps.
Work in the crumbled fish, the chilli paste and salt, adding the reserved water a spoon at a time until it is thick and scoopable.
Fold in the spring onion and coriander off the heat and serve at room temperature with hot rice.
steps.tip: The greens go in raw at the end. Cooked, they lose the sharp note the mash is built around.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated. Serve at room temperature rather than reheated; if it has stiffened, loosen it with a tablespoon of warm water and fresh chopped spring onion.

recipes.name: Galho
recipes.subtitle: Naga one-pot of rice cooked down with smoked pork and bitter greens into a soft porridge

ingredients.qty: 400g smoked pork or fatty belly, in 2cm cubes
ingredients.note: smoked pork is what makes galho taste like galho; with plain belly, add an extra dried chilli and a little more pepper
any sturdy bitter green. Naga kitchens use whatever the garden gives
standing in for raja mircha, the Naga king chilli, which has no catalogue id; the real thing would be one chilli, deseeded, and still fiercer
adds body and a faint stickiness

prepNotes: If your pork is heavily smoked and salty, soak it in warm water for 20 minutes and taste before salting the pot.
Rinse the rice until the water runs almost clear. You want a soft porridge, not glue.
Wash the greens in two changes of water. Grit at the bottom of the pot ruins the dish.

steps.text: Put the pork, onion, garlic, ginger, dried chillies and 800ml of the water in a pressure cooker and cook for 15 minutes at pressure, or simmer covered for 45 minutes.
Release the pressure, open up, and skim off any heavy fat sitting on the surface, leaving a thin slick behind.
steps.tip: Leave some fat. It is what makes the rice glossy rather than pasty.

steps.text: Add the rinsed rice, the colocasia and the remaining 700ml water. Bring back to a boil.
Simmer uncovered on low for 20 minutes, stirring every 4 or 5 minutes and scraping the base, until the grains have burst and swollen.
steps.tip: Stirring is not optional. Rice sinks and scorches, and the burnt taste goes right through the pot.

steps.text: Stir in the greens a handful at a time. They will look like far too much and will collapse within 2 minutes.
Cook another 8 minutes until the greens are tender and the whole thing is the consistency of loose porridge.
Add the cracked pepper and salt to taste. Remember the smoked pork has already salted it.
Take it off the heat, cover, and let it sit 5 minutes. It thickens noticeably. Loosen with hot water and serve in bowls.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated and sets almost solid. Reheat in a pan with 100ml water per portion, breaking it up with a spoon until it flows again. Do not freeze. The rice goes mealy.

recipes.name: Gundruk ko Jhol
recipes.subtitle: sour Sikkimese greens broth, thin and hot, drunk alongside a plate of rice

ingredients.note: gundruk (dried fermented leaf) has no catalogue id; fresh mustard greens plus the vinegar below get you the closest available approximation of its sourness
replaces the sourness the fermentation would have supplied; add it at the end, off the boil
the bitter note that marks out a Sikkimese jhol; a scant quarter teaspoon, no more

prepNotes: Wash the greens in two changes of water and shake them dry. Wet leaves steam rather than fry.
Measure the fenugreek carefully. A heaped spoon turns the whole pot bitter and cannot be fixed.
This is a broth to drink, not a curry. Keep it thin.

steps.text: Heat the mustard oil until it smokes, then take it off the heat for 30 seconds.
Add the fenugreek seeds and dried chillies and fry for 15 seconds only, until the seeds turn one shade darker.
steps.tip: Fenugreek burns fast and goes acrid. Count the seconds out loud.

steps.text: Add the onion, garlic and ginger and cook 3 minutes until the onion is translucent.
Stir in the chopped greens and cook 4 minutes, pressing them down, until they have wilted right down and turned dark.
Add the tomato and turmeric and cook 3 minutes until the tomato has slumped.
Add the potato and the water, bring to a boil, then simmer uncovered 12 minutes until the potato is soft enough to crush against the side.
Crush 3 or 4 pieces of potato into the broth to give it the faintest body, and season with salt.
steps.tip: Just a few pieces. Any more and it becomes soup rather than jhol.

steps.text: Take the pan off the heat, stir in the vinegar, and stand 2 minutes before ladling out.
steps.tip: Vinegar boiled in tastes flat; added off the heat it stays bright.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated and the sourness settles nicely. Reheat to a bare simmer and add a few drops more vinegar before serving to wake it back up.

recipes.name: Hanhor Mangkho
recipes.subtitle: assamese duck stewed slowly with ash gourd, peppery and lean rather than creamy

ingredients.qty: 1kg, on the bone, cut into curry pieces

ingredients.note: the traditional partner; it drinks up the fat
pepper carries this curry, not chilli powder, crush it fresh

prepNotes: Duck carries a lot of fat under the skin. Dry-fry the pieces first with no oil for a few minutes and pour off what renders, or the curry sits under a slick.
Grind the ginger and garlic fresh into a coarse paste. A duck this strongly flavoured flattens shop-bought paste.
Ash gourd goes in only for the last stretch. Added early it dissolves completely.

steps.text: Put the duck pieces in a dry heavy pot over medium heat and cook 6 minutes, turning, until fat pools in the base. Pour that fat off and set the duck aside.
steps.tip: This one step is the difference between a clean curry and a greasy one.

steps.text: Heat the mustard oil in the same pot until it smokes, cool it a minute, then fry the bay leaf, cinnamon, cloves and black cardamom for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the sliced onion and cook 12 minutes over medium heat, until deep gold and shrunk to a third of its volume.
steps.tip: Do not rush this. Pale onion leaves the curry thin and sweetish.

steps.text: Stir in the ginger and garlic paste and fry 3 minutes, until the raw smell goes and the oil starts to separate at the edges.
Add the turmeric and crushed black pepper, stir for 20 seconds, then return the duck and toss to coat every piece.
Fry the duck in the masala 8 minutes, scraping the base as it catches, until the pieces are browned all over.
Pour in the hot water, add salt, cover and simmer very gently 45 minutes, until a skewer goes into the thigh with no resistance.
Add the ash gourd and green chillies and simmer uncovered 15 minutes more, until the gourd is translucent and the gravy has reduced to a coating consistency.
steps.tip: Translucent, not collapsed. Check at 10 minutes, it can go from firm to mush quickly.

steps.text: Rest 10 minutes off the heat before serving with plain rice.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated and is better on the second day. Skim the set fat from the top before reheating, then warm gently on the stovetop with a few spoons of water.

recipes.name: Jadoh
recipes.subtitle: khasi rice cooked through with pork, ginger and black pepper, meghalaya's one-pot meal

ingredients.qty: 300g short-grain, washed until the water runs clear
ingredients.note: Khasi red rice is what is used at home; any short-grain rice works

ingredients.qty: 400g belly or shoulder with its fat, cut into 1cm dice

ingredients.note: jadoh is a gingery dish; do not cut this back
only to start the pork off; it renders plenty of its own

prepNotes: Wash the rice until the water runs clear and soak it 20 minutes, then drain it well. Wet rice going into hot fat clumps.

Traditional jadoh is cooked with pig's blood, which is what gives it the dark colour you see in Shillong stalls. This version leaves it out; the turmeric version is common at home and in Khasi restaurants.
Get the pork diced small (1cm) so it cooks in the same time as the rice.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a heavy pot and fry the diced pork over medium-high heat for 8 minutes, until it has rendered its fat and the edges are browned and crisp.
steps.tip: Crowd the pot and it steams instead of browning. Use a wide pan and give it room.

steps.text: Add the bay leaves and sliced onion and cook 8 minutes in the pork fat, until the onion is gold and sticky.
Stir in the ginger and garlic and fry 2 minutes, until the raw edge has gone.
Add the turmeric and crushed black pepper and stir for 30 seconds.
Tip in the drained rice and toss gently for 3 minutes, until every grain is coated and glossy and the rice smells toasted.
steps.tip: Fold rather than stir. A spoon dragged through soaked rice snaps the grains.

steps.text: Pour in the hot water, add the green chillies and salt, and bring to a fast boil.
As soon as the water level drops to the surface of the rice, cover tightly, drop the heat to its lowest and cook 12 minutes undisturbed.
steps.tip: No peeking. Lifting the lid lets out the steam that is doing the cooking.

steps.text: Take it off the heat and rest, still covered, 10 minutes. Fluff with a fork, scatter over the spring onion and serve.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated. Reheat covered with a tablespoon of water sprinkled over the top, on low heat or in a steamer, so the grains soften rather than dry out.

recipes.name: Kinema
recipes.subtitle: fermented soybeans cooked with tomato and chilli, pungent and deeply savoury

ingredients.note: standing in for kinema, fermented whole soybeans; the flavour is milder but the base is right

prepNotes: Kinema is a Limbu and Nepali ferment of the eastern Himalaya, close kin to Japanese natto. It smells strong and tastes savoury rather than sour.

Add the onion, garlic, ginger and green chillies and cook until soft.
Add the turmeric and tomato and cook down until the oil separates, about 8 minutes.
Add 150ml water and simmer 5 minutes into a thick, spoonable curry.
Season and finish with coriander. Serve with rice.

recipes.name: Masor Jhol
recipes.subtitle: the everyday Assamese fish curry, thin and turmeric-yellow with potato and tomato

ingredients.qty: 600g rohu or any firm river fish, cut into 2cm steaks on the bone

prepNotes: Rub the fish with turmeric and salt and leave it 10 minutes before frying. It firms the surface so the pieces do not break in the pan.
Bring the fish to room temperature first. Cold pieces stick and tear.
This is a thin curry, not a thick one. It should pool around the rice rather than sit on it.

steps.text: Rub the fish with 1/2 tsp of the turmeric and 1 tsp salt and set it aside for 10 minutes.
Heat the mustard oil in a kadhai until it smokes and the sharp smell fades, then take it off the heat for 30 seconds.
steps.tip: Raw mustard oil tastes bitter in a curry. Smoking it once fixes that.

steps.text: Fry the fish in the hot oil, 2 minutes a side, until the edges are set and pale gold. Lift out onto a plate.
steps.tip: You are firming the fish, not cooking it through. It finishes in the gravy.

steps.text: In the same oil, fry the potato quarters for 4 minutes until the cut faces are gold. Lift them out too.
Drop the panch phoron into the oil and let it crackle for about 20 seconds until the fennel seeds turn a shade darker.
Add the onion and cook 5 minutes until soft and just gold, then the ginger and garlic for 1 minute more, until the raw garlic smell goes.
Stir in the tomato, the remaining 1 tsp turmeric and the coriander powder, and mash it about for 4 minutes until the tomato collapses and oil beads at the edge of the pan.
Pour in the water, return the potato, bring to a boil and simmer 10 minutes until a knife goes into the potato without resistance.
Slide the fish back in with the green chillies and simmer uncovered 5 minutes. Do not stir. Shake the pan by the handle instead.
steps.tip: A spoon in the pan at this stage will shred the fish.

steps.text: Take it off the heat, rest 5 minutes, scatter the coriander leaves and serve with hot rice.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated and the flavour deepens overnight. Reheat gently in a wide pan without stirring; do not boil, or the fish falls apart.

recipes.name: Masor Tenga
recipes.subtitle: assam's daily sour fish curry, thin and lemon-bright rather than rich

ingredients.qty: 600g rohu or any firm river fish, cut into 2cm steaks

ingredients.note: the defining fat here. No other oil gives the same pungency
the everyday souring agent; dried thekera or elephant apple is used when in season
usual in home kitchens, and it thickens the broth a little
goes in off the heat

prepNotes: Rub the fish with half the turmeric and a good pinch of salt and leave it 15 minutes. This firms the surface so the steaks do not shred in the pan.
Heat mustard oil until it smokes and goes pale, then pull it off the heat for a minute before frying. Raw mustard oil tastes harsh and stays that way.
Tenga means sour. Tomato is what most Assamese kitchens use on a weekday; if you have dried thekera, use two pieces and cut back to one tomato.

steps.text: Heat the mustard oil in a wide pan until it smokes, take it off the heat for a minute, then fry the fish steaks 2 minutes a side until the edges are golden. Lift them out onto a plate.
steps.tip: Do not move them for the first 2 minutes. The skin sticks and tears if you fuss.

steps.text: In the same oil, crackle the fenugreek seeds for about 10 seconds, until they darken a shade and smell nutty.
steps.tip: Fenugreek turns bitter fast. Count to ten and move straight on.

steps.text: Slide in the potato wedges and fry 4 minutes, until the cut edges look translucent.
Add the tomato, the rest of the turmeric, the slit chillies and salt. Cook 5 minutes, pressing the tomato with the back of the spoon, until it slumps and gives up its water.
Pour in the water, bring to a boil and simmer 10 minutes uncovered, until the potato gives easily to a knife.
Slide the fish back in, spoon broth over each piece and simmer 4 minutes more. Shake the pan rather than stirring.
steps.tip: Stirring at this point breaks the fish into the broth.

steps.text: Take the pan off the heat, stir in the lemon juice and coriander, and let it sit 5 minutes before serving over plain rice.
steps.tip: Lemon goes in off the heat. Boiled, it flattens and turns faintly bitter.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated and the sourness deepens overnight. Reheat gently in a wide pan without stirring, loosening with a splash of water and a fresh squeeze of lemon.

recipes.name: Momos
recipes.subtitle: Steamed dumplings with a juicy filling, eaten with a fiery tomato-chilli chutney

ingredients.note: or finely chopped cabbage for a vegetarian version
for the chutney
for the chutney

prepNotes: Everything in the filling must be chopped very fine and kept raw. It cooks in the steamer, and any large piece will tear the wrapper.
Do not salt the filling until just before you fill: salt draws water out of the cabbage and makes the dough soggy.

steps.text: Knead the flour with water and a pinch of salt into a firm, smooth dough. Rest 30 minutes covered.
Mix the filling ingredients with the oil and pepper. Salt it only when you are ready to fill.
Roll the dough very thin and cut 8cm rounds, keeping the edges thinner than the centre.
steps.tip: Thin edges, thicker middle. Otherwise the pleated top is doughy.

steps.text: Place a spoon of filling in each, then pleat and seal into a half-moon or a gathered purse.
Steam in a greased steamer for 10-12 minutes. The wrappers turn translucent and stop looking floury.
steps.tip: Do not crowd them; they swell and stick together.

steps.text: For the chutney, boil the tomatoes and dried chillies, then blend with garlic and salt. Serve alongside.

recipes.storage: Best straight from the steamer. Uncooked momos freeze well on a tray for a month. Steam from frozen, adding 4 minutes. Cooked ones go rubbery.

recipes.name: Muya Awandru
recipes.subtitle: tripura's oil-free bamboo shoot pot, thickened with rice flour and pungent with dried fish

ingredients.qty: 300g, fresh or brined, rinsed twice and sliced thin

ingredients.note: stands in for berma, the dry fermented fish at the heart of Tripuri mui borok cooking; the catalogue carries no berma
the thickener. Slake it in cold water before it goes anywhere near the pot
Tripuri food is genuinely hot; four is a compromise

ingredients.qty: 800ml, plus 4 tbsp cold for the slurry

prepNotes: Brined bamboo shoot needs rinsing twice and a 5-minute boil in fresh water before you start, or the whole pot tastes only of brine.
Slake the rice flour in 4 tbsp of cold water and stir it smooth before it goes in. Tipped in dry it seizes into lumps that never dissolve.
This is cooked without a drop of oil, which is the defining habit of mui borok. Do not be tempted to start with a tempering.

steps.text: Rinse the bamboo shoot twice, cover with fresh water, boil 5 minutes and drain.
steps.tip: Skip this and the sourness of the brine flattens everything else in the pot.

steps.text: Dry-roast the dried fish in a small pan over low heat 3 minutes, until brittle and toasty, then break it into pieces.
Bring the 800ml of water to a boil with the crushed ginger, garlic, green chillies, roasted fish and salt. Boil 5 minutes so the broth takes on the flavours.
Add the drained bamboo shoot and the potato and simmer 12 minutes, uncovered.
Add the beans and cook 5 minutes, until the potato is soft enough to break with a spoon.
Stir the rice flour into 4 tbsp cold water until completely smooth, with no dry specks.
steps.tip: Cold water only. Warm water starts cooking the flour in the cup.

steps.text: Pour the slurry into the simmering pot in a thin stream, stirring the whole time, and cook 4 minutes until the liquid turns glossy and coats the back of a spoon.
Taste for salt and heat, stir in the coriander and serve hot with plain rice.
steps.tip: It thickens further as it cools. Take it off the heat looser than you want it.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated but sets firm as the rice flour cools. Reheat on low with 3-4 tbsp of water, stirring until it loosens back to a coating consistency.

recipes.name: Naga Smoked Pork with Bamboo Shoot
recipes.subtitle: Smoked pork simmered with fermented bamboo shoot and raja mircha

image.alt: Naga smoked pork with bamboo shoot

ingredients.note: raja mircha traditionally, use far less

prepNotes: Naga cooking uses very little oil and few spices; the flavour is carried by smoke, fermentation and heat. Adding garam masala here would be a mistake.
Fermented bamboo shoot is pungent. Rinse it, and add it in stages, tasting as you go.

steps.text: Rinse the fermented bamboo shoot in two changes of water and drain.
Put the smoked pork in a pot with the ginger, garlic, chillies and just enough water to cover. Bring to a boil.
steps.tip: No oil. The pork renders plenty of its own.

steps.text: Simmer covered 45-60 minutes until the pork is tender and the water has reduced by half.
Add the bamboo shoot and the onion and tomato if using, and cook a further 15 minutes.
steps.tip: Taste before adding all the bamboo. Its sourness varies enormously between batches.

steps.text: Season with salt only at the end; smoked pork is already salty.
Serve with plain rice and a raw chilli on the side.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated and improves. Freezes 2 months.
