recipes.name: Nga Thongba
recipes.subtitle: Manipuri fish curry, thin and ginger-sharp, built on a small hit of fermented fish

ingredients.qty: 600g firm freshwater fish, cut into 3cm pieces

ingredients.note: the nearest catalogued thing to ngari, the Manipuri fermented fish this dish is built on; toast it hard and use it sparingly. It is saltier and less funky than the real thing
the local umorok is far hotter and has no catalogue id; add a pinch of chilli powder if you want closer to the real heat

prepNotes: Toast the dried fish before anything else and keep it aside. Done in the curry pan it makes everything taste of it.
Rub the fish with a little turmeric and salt while you chop, so it firms up.
Manipuri curries carry very little oil and no thickener. Resist the urge to reduce this into a gravy.

steps.text: Dry-toast the dried fish in a small pan over low heat for 3 minutes, until it is brittle and smells strongly nutty. Crumble it and set it aside.
steps.tip: Toasting takes the raw edge off. Untoasted, it dominates everything.

steps.text: Rub the fish pieces with 1/2 tsp of the turmeric and 1 tsp salt and leave them while you prepare the rest.
Heat the mustard oil until it smokes, rest it off the heat 30 seconds, then fry the fish 90 seconds a side just to set the surface. Lift it out.
In the same oil cook the onion 4 minutes until translucent, then add the garlic and half the ginger for 1 minute.
Add the tomato and the remaining 1/2 tsp turmeric and cook 4 minutes, pressing the tomato until it breaks down.
Stir in the crumbled toasted fish and cook 1 minute. The smell should turn savoury rather than sharp.
Pour in the water, bring to a boil and simmer 8 minutes uncovered so it stays thin but tastes concentrated.
Slide the fish back in with the green chillies and the rest of the ginger. Simmer 5 minutes without stirring, tilting the pan instead.
steps.tip: Salt only now. The dried fish has already brought a lot of it.

steps.text: Off the heat, scatter the spring onion and coriander and stand 3 minutes before serving with rice.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated. Reheat gently in a wide pan, never at a rolling boil. The broth stays good even when the fish has softened, so leftovers are best spooned over rice.

recipes.name: Omita Khar
recipes.subtitle: the alkaline assamese opener. Raw papaya simmered soft, plain and cleansing

ingredients.qty: 500g, peeled, deseeded and cut into 3cm cubes

ingredients.note: stands in for khar, the alkaline water filtered through sun-dried banana-peel ash; the catalogue has no khar and this is the standard urban substitute
fried till golden, the upper-Assam habit

prepNotes: A quarter teaspoon of baking soda is the ceiling for this quantity. More and the dish turns soapy and slippery on the tongue. There is no fixing it once it is in.
Soak the whole urad 30 minutes and drain it thoroughly on a cloth, or it will spit in the hot oil.
Khar is eaten first, at the very start of an Assamese meal, with plain rice and nothing sour alongside it.

steps.text: Heat the mustard oil in a heavy pan until it smokes, then let it cool for a minute.
Fry the drained urad 2 minutes until deep gold and lift it out with a slotted spoon. Keep it for the end.
steps.tip: It should crackle, not brown in seconds. If it darkens instantly the oil is still too hot.

steps.text: Drop in the slit chillies and let them blister 30 seconds.
Add the papaya, turmeric and salt and toss 3 minutes, until the cut edges look glassy.
Pour in the water, cover and simmer 12 minutes, until a fork goes through a cube with no resistance.
Stir in the baking soda and simmer uncovered 5 minutes. It will foam up and settle, and the liquid turns faintly silky.
steps.tip: Add it at the end, never at the start. Early alkali collapses the papaya to mush.

steps.text: Crush four or five cubes against the side of the pan to thicken the broth, then scatter over the fried urad and coriander and serve at once.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated, and the alkali keeps softening the papaya, so it will be looser on day two. Reheat gently with a splash of water; add the fried urad fresh if you want the crunch back.

recipes.name: Ooti
recipes.subtitle: Manipuri dried peas simmered soft with bamboo shoot and finished with burnt chilli oil

ingredients.note: stands in for kaanjeer, the ash-filtered water Manipuri kitchens use; it does the same job of collapsing the peas
fermented soibum if you can find it, otherwise fresh boiled shoot

ingredients.qty: 4, chopped, whites and greens kept separate

prepNotes: Soak the dried peas in plenty of cold water for at least 8 hours, or overnight. They will roughly double.
If your bamboo shoot is fresh rather than fermented, boil it in a change of water for 10 minutes first to take off the bitterness.
The soda goes in at the start with cold water, never into a hot pan.

steps.text: Drain the soaked peas and pressure cook them with 800ml of the water, the baking soda and 1 tsp salt, 5 whistles, or about 20 minutes at pressure.
Let the pressure drop on its own, open up, and crush about a quarter of the peas against the side of the pan.
steps.tip: This is what gives ooti its body. Do not blend it. You want soft whole peas suspended in a thick liquor.

steps.text: Add the bamboo shoot and the remaining 400ml water and simmer uncovered for 15 minutes. The sourness sharpens as it reduces.
Stir in the spring onion whites and the green chillies and simmer another 10 minutes, until the stew coats the back of a spoon.
Check the consistency: it should pour thickly, not sit in a mound. Loosen with hot water if it has gone too far.
In a small pan heat the mustard oil until it smokes, take it off the heat for 20 seconds, then drop in the dried red chillies for 20 seconds until they darken and smell toasty.
steps.tip: Chillies go from toasted to acrid in about ten seconds. Have the pan of ooti right beside you.

steps.text: Pour the chilli oil over the ooti and stir it through once, leaving streaks.
Scatter the spring onion greens and coriander, rest 5 minutes off the heat, and serve with rice.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated and thickens considerably as it sits. Reheat with a good splash of water and re-check the salt. Make the chilli oil fresh each time.

recipes.name: Pika Pila
recipes.subtitle: Apatani bamboo shoot pickle, fiercely sour and hot, eaten a spoonful at a time

ingredients.qty: 300g fermented bamboo shoot, very finely chopped
150g pork fat or very fatty belly, finely diced

ingredients.note: standing in for the local king chilli, which the catalogue has no id for; two king chillies would do the work of all eight of these
backs up the sourness of the ferment

prepNotes: Squeeze the chopped bamboo shoot out over a bowl and keep 2 tbsp of the liquor. It is intensely sour and goes back in at the end.
Sterilise the jar you plan to store this in: wash, then dry it in a low oven for 10 minutes.
Everything must be chopped fine and evenly. This is a relish eaten by the teaspoon, not a curry.

steps.text: Render the diced pork fat in a dry pan over low heat for about 12 minutes, until the pieces are shrunken and gold and swimming in clear fat.
steps.tip: Low and slow. Rushed on high heat the fat browns bitter and the crackling stays chewy.

steps.text: Lift the crisp pieces out with a slotted spoon and set them aside, leaving the fat in the pan.
Fry the dried chillies in the fat for 30 seconds until they darken and the kitchen makes you cough.
Add the ginger and garlic and cook 2 minutes until pale gold.
Stir in the squeezed bamboo shoot, turmeric and salt and cook 8 minutes over medium heat, stirring often, until the liquid has dried off and it no longer smells raw.
steps.tip: Keep it moving. Bamboo shoot sticks and scorches the moment the pan goes dry.

steps.text: Return the crackling, pour in the raw mustard oil, the lemon juice and the reserved bamboo liquor, and cook 2 minutes more.
Taste for salt and sourness. It should be sharp enough to make you flinch.
Cool completely, uncovered, before spooning into the jar and pressing down so the oil covers the surface.
steps.tip: Jarring it warm traps steam, and steam is what makes a pickle go mouldy.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 weeks refrigerated in a sterilised jar with the oil covering the top. Always use a dry spoon. Serve a teaspoon per person alongside rice and a plain boiled vegetable.

recipes.name: Poita Bhat
recipes.subtitle: cooked rice soaked overnight until faintly sour, eaten cold with mustard oil and onion

ingredients.note: joha or any local non-basmati; long, slender basmati stays too separate to sour properly

ingredients.qty: 1.5 litres for boiling, plus more to cover the rice overnight

ingredients.note: the pitika that is nearly always served alongside

prepNotes: The rice has to sit under water overnight, 8 to 12 hours at room temperature. Start it the evening before.
This is a hot-weather dish and it souring is the point. But it wants a cool room, not a warm kitchen. In real heat, 8 hours is plenty.
Use an earthen or glass bowl if you have one. Metal picks up a tinny edge from the sour water.

steps.text: Boil the rice in the 1.5 litres of water for 15-18 minutes, until the grains are soft and just past the point you would normally stop.
steps.tip: Slightly overcooked is correct here. Firm rice never softens properly in the soak.

steps.text: Drain and spread the rice in a wide bowl. Leave it uncovered until it is completely cool to the touch, about 30 minutes.
steps.tip: Covering it hot traps steam and the rice sours in a stale, unpleasant way.

steps.text: Pour in cold water to cover the rice by about 3cm, cover the bowl loosely and leave it overnight.
Next morning the water should smell faintly sour and clean, a little like buttermilk. Pour off most of it, keeping 3-4 tbsp in the bowl.
steps.tip: If it smells sharp, yeasty or off, throw it out. The soak has gone too far.

steps.text: Break the clumped rice up with your fingers until it is loose again.
Fold through the raw mustard oil and salt.
Stir in the onion, green chilli and coriander, and squeeze over the lemon.
Serve cold, with the mashed potato and a green chilli on the side.

recipes.storage: Eat the morning it is ready. Once soured, the rice keeps only a few hours and does not refrigerate well. The texture goes chalky. Cook a fresh batch rather than saving it.

recipes.name: Sanpiau
recipes.subtitle: Mizo rice porridge under a drift of toasted rice powder, coriander and black pepper

ingredients.note: toasted to a sandy brown. This is the topping that defines the dish, not a thickener for the porridge

ingredients.qty: 1 large bunch, about 40g, very finely chopped

prepNotes: Chop the coriander just before serving. Chopped early it goes dark and loses the fresh smell the dish depends on.
Grind the pepper coarsely and fresh. Pre-ground pepper disappears into the porridge.
Sanpiau is eaten hot from a bowl as a street snack, so have the toppings ready before the porridge is done.

steps.text: Bring the rice and water to a boil, then turn the heat right down.
Simmer 25 minutes, stirring every few minutes and scraping the base, until the grains have burst and the whole thing is a loose porridge the consistency of thin oatmeal.
steps.tip: It should pour, not mound. Add hot water whenever it starts to hold its shape.

steps.text: Season with salt and keep it hot on the lowest heat.
Meanwhile dry-roast the rice flour in a small pan over low heat for 6-8 minutes, stirring without stopping, until it is sandy brown and smells like popcorn.
steps.tip: It goes from tan to burnt in under a minute at the end. Do not walk away, and do not raise the heat.

steps.text: Tip the toasted flour onto a cold plate and spread it out to cool. It only stays loose and powdery once cold.
Dry-roast the chillies in the same pan for 40 seconds until brittle, then crush them coarsely.
Ladle the porridge into bowls, loosening it with hot water if it has thickened while standing.
Top each bowl with a heaped teaspoon of the toasted rice powder, then a thick layer of coriander, the spring onion, the pepper and a pinch of crushed chilli.
steps.tip: Do not stir it in at the pan. The layered toppings hitting the hot porridge in the bowl is the whole experience.

steps.text: Serve with a lemon wedge to squeeze over at the table.

recipes.storage: The porridge keeps 2 days refrigerated and sets firm; reheat with plenty of water until it flows again. Store the toasted rice powder separately in a jar for up to a month, and always cut the coriander fresh.

recipes.name: Sel Roti
recipes.subtitle: crisp-edged ring of fried fermented rice batter, lightly sweet and cardamom-scented

ingredients.note: some households use water; milk gives a softer crumb inside the crisp shell

prepNotes: Soak the rice in cold water for at least 8 hours, or overnight. It has to be fully softened or the batter will be gritty.
The batter then rests 3-4 hours in a warm spot to ferment. Plan for most of a day, or soak overnight and fry in the afternoon.
Have a wide, deep pan and a long skewer or chopstick ready before you start frying. The rings are turned with the skewer, not tongs.

steps.text: Drain the soaked rice thoroughly and spread it on a cloth for 15 minutes until the surface looks dry.
steps.tip: Wet rice means a slack batter, and slack batter will not hold a ring in hot oil.

steps.text: Grind the rice in batches with the milk and only as much of the water as it takes to move the blades, to a thick, completely smooth batter.
steps.tip: Grind longer rather than adding water. The batter should fall from a spoon in a heavy ribbon.

steps.text: Beat in the sugar, melted ghee, ground cardamom, cloves and salt, then beat by hand for a good 5 minutes.
steps.tip: That beating aerates the batter, and aeration is what gives sel roti its light inside.

steps.text: Cover and leave in a warm place for 3-4 hours, until the batter has risen slightly and smells faintly sweet and sour.
Heat the oil in a kadhai to about 170C. A drop of batter should sink briefly, then rise within 3 seconds.
steps.tip: Too hot and the ring browns before the middle sets; too cool and it drinks oil and goes heavy.

steps.text: Pour the batter into a squeeze bottle or a piping bag. Working quickly, pipe a 12cm ring onto the surface of the oil, joining the ends.
Let it fry undisturbed 1 minute, until it floats free and the top loses its shine.
Turn it with a skewer through the hole and fry another 2 minutes until both sides are a deep reddish gold.
Drain on a wire rack, not paper, and fry the rest one or two at a time.
Cool at least 10 minutes before eating. The crispness only arrives as they cool.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days at room temperature in a tin, and stays edible for a week. Refresh in a dry pan over low heat for a minute a side; do not refrigerate, which makes them leathery.

recipes.name: Singju
recipes.subtitle: manipur's raw-vegetable salad bound with roasted gram flour and loud with chilli

ingredients.qty: 250g, shredded as finely as you can manage

ingredients.note: dry-roasted; this is the binder that makes singju singju
stands in for thoiding, the perilla seed used in Manipur, which the catalogue does not carry. Roast and grind it the same way
for ngari, the fermented fish; roast and crumble it

prepNotes: Shred the cabbage on the day and keep it dry. Washed and not spun out, the water thins the gram flour and the salad slumps.
Roast the besan, sesame, chilli and dried fish ahead. All four can be done in the same pan, in that order, in under ten minutes.
Dress it at the last minute. Singju is assembled to be eaten within about twenty minutes.

steps.text: Dry-roast the besan over low heat for 4 minutes, stirring constantly, until it turns a shade darker and smells nutty. Tip it straight out of the pan.
steps.tip: It goes from nutty to burnt in about fifteen seconds at the end. Do not walk away.

steps.text: Roast the sesame in the same pan 2 minutes until the seeds start popping, then grind them coarsely.
Roast the dried red chillies 40 seconds a side until they darken, and pound them coarse.
Roast the dried fish 3 minutes over low heat until brittle, then crumble it fine.
Toss the cabbage, radish and spring onion in a wide bowl with the salt and leave 5 minutes.
Squeeze the vegetables gently with your hands and pour off any water that has come out.
steps.tip: This is the step people skip, and it is why home singju often goes soggy.

steps.text: Scatter over the roasted besan, ground sesame, crumbled fish and pounded chilli, and mix with your fingers until every shred is coated and the flour has stopped looking powdery.
Add the lemon juice and coriander, toss once more and serve immediately as a side or an evening snack.

recipes.storage: Eat within the hour. The gram flour draws water and the salad wilts. The roasted besan, sesame, chilli and fish keep a week in an airtight jar, so make that mix ahead and shred the cabbage fresh.

recipes.name: Thukpa
recipes.subtitle: sikkim's hand-torn noodle soup, chicken broth thick with vegetables and pepper

ingredients.note: for hand-pulled noodles; 300g of ready wheat noodles works if you would rather not

ingredients.qty: 400g boneless thigh, cut into thin strips
1.2 litres for the broth, plus about 120ml for the dough

prepNotes: Make the dough first and let it rest 30 minutes before you touch it again. Unrested, it springs back and you will fight it the whole time.
Have every vegetable cut before the broth goes on. Once the noodles are in, this dish moves in under five minutes.
Cook the noodles in the soup, not separately. The starch they release is what gives thukpa its body.

steps.text: Mix the maida with 1/2 tsp salt and enough water (about 120ml) to make a firm, slightly stiff dough. Knead 8 minutes until smooth, then cover and rest 30 minutes.
steps.tip: Firmer than a chapati dough. A soft dough tears into shapeless scraps in the broth.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large pot and fry the onion, garlic and ginger 5 minutes over medium heat, until the onion is soft and the garlic smells sweet.
Add the chicken strips and fry 5 minutes, until they have lost their pink and picked up a little colour at the edges.
Stir in the turmeric, chilli powder and crushed black pepper for 20 seconds, then add the tomato and cook 5 minutes until it collapses.
Pour in the 1.2 litres of water, add salt, and simmer 15 minutes with the lid ajar.
While it simmers, roll the rested dough out to about 2mm and cut or tear it into ribbons roughly 2cm wide and 10cm long. Dust them with flour and keep them separate.
steps.tip: Torn edges hold the broth better than knife-cut ones, which is why thenthuk is torn by hand.

steps.text: Add the carrot to the simmering broth and cook 3 minutes.
Drop the noodles in a few at a time, stirring so they do not clump, and boil 4 minutes until they float and turn from chalky to translucent.
steps.tip: A few at a time, into moving liquid. Dumped in together they weld into a single mass.

steps.text: Add the cabbage and spinach and cook 2 minutes more, until the spinach has just wilted.
Taste for salt and pepper, ladle into deep bowls and finish with spring onion and coriander.

recipes.storage: Best eaten straight away. The noodles keep swelling and drink the broth. If you want leftovers, cook and store the broth separately for up to 3 days and boil fresh noodles into a reheated portion.

recipes.name: Aloo Potala Rasa
recipes.subtitle: potato and pointed gourd in a thin, cumin-scented tomato gravy, made without onion or garlic

ingredients.note: potala, or parwal

prepNotes: Scrape the pointed gourd lightly with a knife rather than peeling it. The skin holds the flavour and stops the pieces going mushy.
Puree the tomatoes and grate the ginger before you start. With no onion or garlic in this dish, the tomato has to be fried properly and that needs your full attention.
Cut the potato into quarters, not smaller; they should stay in recognisable pieces in the thin gravy.

steps.text: Heat the mustard oil in a kadhai until it smokes, then lower the flame for 30 seconds.
Fry the halved pointed gourd on medium for 5 minutes, turning, until blistered and lightly browned. Lift out and set aside.
steps.tip: Frying them separately keeps them firm; boiled straight into the gravy they go limp.

steps.text: In the same oil add the bay leaf and cumin seeds and let them sizzle 15 seconds.
Add the grated ginger and slit green chillies and fry 1 minute.
Add the potato quarters and fry 4 minutes until the edges are golden.
Pour in the tomato puree with the turmeric, cumin powder, coriander powder, chilli powder and salt. Fry 6-8 minutes until the oil beads at the edges.
steps.tip: Do not shortcut this. Underfried tomato leaves the gravy tasting sour and raw.

steps.text: Add the water, bring to a boil, then cover and simmer 12 minutes until the potato is tender.
Return the fried pointed gourd and simmer uncovered 5 minutes. The gravy should stay thin. This is a rasa, not a thick curry.
Stir in the garam masala, scatter the coriander leaves and rest 5 minutes off the heat before serving with rice.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated. Reheat on the stovetop with 3 tbsp water; the pointed gourd softens further overnight but the flavour deepens.

recipes.name: Arisa Pitha
recipes.subtitle: deep-fried jaggery and rice flour discs crusted with sesame, chewy in the middle

ingredients.note: traditionally soaked rice ground fresh; fine rice flour works

prepNotes: Sieve the rice flour and dry-roast it in a pan over low heat for 4 minutes, just until warm and loose. Do not let it colour.
The kneaded dough must rest at least 4 hours, ideally overnight, before shaping; it firms up and stops sticking.
Keep a small bowl of oil beside you for shaping. Arisa dough is worked with oiled palms, never with flour.

steps.text: Melt the jaggery with the water in a pan over medium heat, stirring until dissolved, then strain out any grit.
Boil the syrup 5 to 6 minutes until a drop pressed between finger and thumb pulls a single short thread as they part.
steps.tip: Undercooked syrup gives a dough that will not hold its shape in the oil. Test twice before you trust it.

steps.text: Take the syrup off the heat, add the pinch of salt and the cardamom, and let it cool 2 minutes.
Pour the hot syrup over the roasted rice flour in a wide bowl and mix with a spoon until it comes together as a shaggy mass.
When it is cool enough to handle, knead 5 minutes with oiled hands into a smooth dough the softness of an earlobe.
Cover and rest at least 4 hours or overnight at room temperature.
steps.tip: Skipping the rest is the usual failure. Fresh dough spreads and disintegrates in hot oil.

steps.text: Divide into 14 balls, flatten each between oiled palms into a 7cm disc, and press one side firmly into the sesame seeds.
Heat the oil in a kadhai to medium. A scrap of dough should rise slowly and sizzle steadily, not fizz violently.
steps.tip: Too hot and the outside darkens while the centre stays raw and sticky. Medium and patient is the rule.

steps.text: Slide in 2 or 3 discs sesame-side down and fry 3 minutes a side, spooning oil over, until deep reddish brown.
Lift onto a rack, not paper, and let them cool completely; they firm from soft to chewy as they cool.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 weeks in an airtight tin at room temperature and gets chewier with time. Do not refrigerate. The jaggery weeps and the crust goes soggy.

recipes.name: Badi Chura
recipes.subtitle: crushed fried lentil dumplings pounded with raw onion, chilli and mustard oil

ingredients.note: Odia badi are sun-dried urad dal dumplings; buy them ready-made

prepNotes: Chop the onion as fine as you can manage and leave it uncovered for 5 minutes so some of the raw bite blows off.
Have a mortar and pestle or a heavy rolling pin ready. This dish is defined by texture and a blender will powder it.

steps.text: Heat the mustard oil in a small kadhai over medium until it shimmers and smells sharp.
Fry the badi, turning often, for 4 to 5 minutes until they are deep chestnut brown all over and float lightly.
steps.tip: Keep the heat at medium. On high they blacken outside while the middle stays chalky and raw-tasting.

Pound the garlic and green chillies with 1/4 tsp of the salt into a rough, wet paste.
Break the cooled badi into the mortar and crush to coarse gravel, leaving a few pea-sized pieces for bite.
steps.tip: Stop while it still looks uneven. Powdered badi turns pasty once the oil goes in.

steps.text: Tip the crushed badi into a bowl with the chopped onion, the garlic-chilli paste and the remaining salt.
Pour over 1 tbsp of the warm frying oil straight from the pan and rub everything together with your fingers.
Squeeze in the lemon, fold through the coriander, taste for salt and serve at once alongside pakhala or plain rice.
steps.tip: Make it minutes before eating. Left standing, the onion waters and the badi goes soft.

recipes.name: Besara
recipes.subtitle: mixed vegetables in a sharp ground-mustard gravy, pungent enough to make your eyes water

ingredients.qty: 2 tbsp, soaked in warm water 20 minutes
ingredients.note: the whole dish is named for this
ground into the mustard paste
2 for the paste, 1 slit for the pot

prepNotes: Soak the mustard seeds in warm water for at least 20 minutes before grinding. Unsoaked seeds grind unevenly and taste bitter rather than hot.
Grind the mustard with the garlic, 2 green chillies and a pinch of salt to a fine paste with 4 tbsp water. Salt in the grinder keeps the paste from turning bitter.
Cut the vegetables into even 2-3cm pieces so nothing collapses while the slower pieces cook.

steps.text: Grind the soaked mustard seeds, garlic, 2 green chillies and a pinch of salt to a smooth paste with 4 tbsp water. Set aside.
steps.tip: Grind in short bursts. Long continuous grinding heats the paste and makes it acrid.

steps.text: Heat the mustard oil in a kadhai until it smokes, then lower the flame for 30 seconds.
Add the panch phoron and broken dried red chillies. When the seeds pop and the chillies darken, about 20 seconds, add the slit green chilli.
Add the potato and raw banana and fry 3 minutes, stirring, until the surfaces turn matte.
Add the pumpkin, eggplant and drumstick with the turmeric and salt. Fry 2 minutes more.
Pour in the water, bring to a boil, cover and simmer 12 minutes until the potato is nearly tender.
Lower the flame to its weakest setting and stir in the mustard paste. Do not let it boil hard from here on.
steps.tip: Boiling ground mustard hard is the classic besara mistake. It turns the gravy bitter within a minute.

steps.text: Simmer uncovered on low for 6-8 minutes, until the raw smell of the mustard has gone and the gravy coats a spoon.
Taste for salt, stir in the coriander leaves and take off the heat. Rest 5 minutes before serving with rice.

recipes.name: Chakuli Pitha
recipes.subtitle: soft fermented rice and urad pancakes, thicker and paler than a dosa

ingredients.note: helps the batter ferment and browns the edges
feeds the ferment

prepNotes: Soak the rice in one bowl and the urad dal with the fenugreek seeds in another, both in plenty of water, for 6 hours.
Grind the dal first with 150ml water until it is white, fluffy and holds a peak; then grind the rice with 200ml water to a fine batter with the faintest grit.
Combine the two, beat in the sugar with your hand for a minute, cover loosely and ferment 8 to 10 hours in a warm spot until risen and bubbly.
Salt the batter only after fermenting. Salt slows the rise.

steps.text: Stir the salt into the fermented batter and let it down with water until it is the consistency of thick cream, thicker than dosa batter.
steps.tip: Stir gently. Beating hard knocks out the air you spent all night building.

steps.text: Heat a flat tawa over medium until a drop of water skitters and vanishes in about 2 seconds.
Rub the surface with half an onion or a scrunched paper towel dipped in oil and wipe off the excess.
Pour a ladleful into the centre and spread it with the back of the ladle in one slow spiral to about 15cm. Chakuli is meant to be thick and soft, not lace-thin.
steps.tip: One pass only. Going back over a setting batter tears holes in it.

steps.text: Drizzle 1/2 tsp oil around the rim and cook 2 minutes, until the top loses its shine and small holes open across the surface.
Flip and cook the second side 1 minute, until it is set and speckled pale gold.
steps.tip: Chakuli should stay soft and blond. If it is crisp and brown you have the tawa too hot.

steps.text: Slide it off and repeat, wiping and re-oiling the tawa between each one and dropping the heat a notch if they start browning too fast.
Stack them under a cloth as you go so they steam each other soft, and serve hot with ghuguni or a mustardy vegetable curry.

recipes.storage: The batter keeps 3 days refrigerated and gets tangier each day; bring it to room temperature before using. Cooked chakuli keep 1 day wrapped in a cloth and reheat in 30 seconds on a warm tawa.

recipes.name: Chhatu Rai
recipes.subtitle: mushrooms simmered in a hot mustard and poppy seed gravy, a monsoon favourite

ingredients.note: the closest stand-in for wild monsoon chhatu
gives the gravy body

prepNotes: Soak the mustard seeds and poppy seeds together in warm water for 20 minutes, then grind with 2 green chillies and 3 tbsp water into a fine paste.
Wipe the mushrooms with a damp cloth instead of washing them; soaked mushrooms leak water and refuse to brown.
Crush the garlic and ginger to a coarse paste in a mortar rather than a blender. You want texture in this gravy.

steps.text: Heat the mustard oil in a kadhai until it smokes lightly, then lower to medium-high.
Add the mushrooms with 1/2 tsp salt and fry hard for 6 to 7 minutes, without stirring much, until they have given up their water and the edges are browned.
steps.tip: Wait through the wet stage. Mushrooms boil in their own liquid first and only brown after it evaporates.

steps.text: Scoop the mushrooms out and set aside, leaving the oil in the pan.
Crackle the panch-phoron in the same oil for 20 seconds until it pops and smells nutty.
Add the crushed garlic and ginger and fry for 2 minutes until the raw edge goes and the paste turns straw coloured.
Stir in the tomato, turmeric, chilli powder and cumin powder and cook for 5 minutes, pressing with the spoon, until the tomato breaks down and oil beads at the sides.
steps.tip: That ring of separated oil is the signal the masala is done. Rush it and the gravy tastes raw.

steps.text: Return the mushrooms, pour in the water, and simmer uncovered for 6 minutes.
Drop the heat to its lowest, stir in the mustard-poppy paste and the remaining slit green chilli, and cook 4 minutes at a bare simmer.
steps.tip: Do not boil after the mustard goes in. It turns bitter fast and never comes back.

steps.text: Taste for salt, take off the heat and finish with the coriander and a teaspoon of raw mustard oil.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated. Reheat on low heat only, adding a splash of water; a hard reboil will make the mustard bitter.

recipes.name: Chhena Poda
recipes.subtitle: Odisha's baked cheesecake: fresh chhena and sugar caramelised until the top is almost burnt

ingredients.note: separate from the sugar above

prepNotes: Poda means burnt. The dark, almost-scorched top is the dish, not a mistake. Pull it out pale and it is just baked cheese.
Chhena for this should be soft and moist. Unlike rasgulla, do not hang it dry.

steps.text: Curdle the milk with lemon juice, strain through muslin and rinse briefly. Hang only 20 minutes. It should stay moist.
Knead the chhena smooth, then work in the sugar, rava, cardamom, nuts and raisins. Rest 15 minutes so the rava swells.
Caramelise the 2 tbsp sugar in a ghee-greased tin and let it set at the bottom.
steps.tip: Traditionally the batter sits on a lining of sal leaves, which is where the smoky note comes from.

steps.text: Pour in the batter and bake at 180C for 50-60 minutes, until the top is deep brown to nearly black and a skewer comes out clean.
steps.tip: Go further than instinct says. Brown is not enough.

steps.text: Cool completely in the tin (at least 2 hours) before turning out.
Serve at room temperature in wedges.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated and firms as it sits. Bring back to room temperature before serving; cold chhena poda tastes flat.

recipes.name: Chhena Tarkari
recipes.subtitle: soft fresh cheese in a light gingered tomato gravy, no onion, no garlic, straight out of the temple kitchen

ingredients.note: or fresh chhena, drained and pressed only lightly so it stays soft
the only aromatic in the dish, so use it generously
added at the end
softens the gravy the way cream would

prepNotes: If you are using shop paneer, soak the cubes in hot salted water for 10 minutes before you start. It brings back the softness that chhena has naturally.
Puree the tomatoes smooth and keep them ready; with no onion in the pan, the tomato has to be fried properly to build the base.
Grate the ginger rather than chopping it so it melts into the gravy.

steps.text: Heat the ghee in a kadhai and add the bay leaf and cumin seeds. They should sizzle on contact and smell toasty in about 15 seconds.
Add the grated ginger and slit green chillies and fry 1 minute, until the raw ginger smell lifts.
Pour in the tomato puree with the turmeric, cumin powder and coriander powder. Stand back, it will spit.
Fry the puree on medium heat for 8-10 minutes, stirring, until it darkens to brick red and the ghee separates at the edges.
steps.tip: This is the whole dish. Undercooked tomato tastes raw and thin, and there is no onion here to hide behind.

steps.text: Add the water and salt, bring to a boil, then simmer 5 minutes.
Slide in the paneer cubes, add the sugar, and simmer very gently for 6 minutes, spooning gravy over them.
steps.tip: Never boil paneer hard. It tightens into rubber. A lazy bubble at the edge is all you want.

steps.text: Stir in the milk and the garam masala and warm through for 1 minute without boiling.
Take off the heat, scatter the coriander leaves and rest 5 minutes before serving with rice or roti.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated. Reheat covered on a low flame with 3 tbsp water; the paneer firms up in the fridge and softens again as it warms.

recipes.name: Chingudi Tarkari
recipes.subtitle: everyday prawn and potato curry, thin-gravied and heavy on mustard oil

ingredients.note: stirred in at the end

prepNotes: Toss the prawns with 1/2 tsp turmeric and 1/2 tsp salt and leave 10 minutes; pat them dry before they go in the pan.
Have the hot water ready in a kettle. This curry comes together fast once the masala is fried.
If using frozen prawns, thaw them fully and squeeze out the water, or the gravy will taste washed out.

steps.text: Heat the mustard oil in a kadhai until it smokes, then lower to medium and let it settle for 30 seconds.
Fry the prawns for 90 seconds, just until they turn opaque pink and curl loosely, then lift them straight out.
steps.tip: Undercook them here on purpose. They finish in the gravy, and a prawn cooked twice through goes tight and squeaky.

steps.text: Add the potato cubes to the same oil and fry 5 minutes until patched with gold, then set them aside too.
Crackle the bay leaf and cumin seeds in the remaining oil for 20 seconds.
Add the onion and cook 7 to 8 minutes over medium heat until it is soft and properly browned at the edges.
steps.tip: This is the only slow step. Pale onion gives a thin, sharp gravy.

steps.text: Stir in the garlic and ginger and fry 90 seconds until the raw smell is gone.
Add the tomato with the remaining turmeric, chilli powder, cumin powder and coriander powder and cook 6 minutes, until the mixture pulls together and oil beads at the edges.
Return the potato, pour in the hot water with 1 tsp salt, cover and simmer 12 minutes until the potato is tender to a knife tip.
Slide the prawns back in with the slit green chillies and simmer just 3 minutes.
Stir in the garam masala, take off the heat, scatter the coriander and rest 5 minutes before serving with rice.

recipes.name: Chungdi Malai
recipes.subtitle: prawns simmered in coconut milk, mildly spiced and faintly sweet, Odisha's most coaxing curry

ingredients.qty: 500g medium, shelled and deveined, tails on

ingredients.note: the traditional fat here; use oil if you prefer
for colour without heat

prepNotes: Rub the shelled prawns with 1/4 tsp turmeric and 1/2 tsp salt and rest 10 minutes. Rinse and pat dry before cooking.
Grind the onion to a smooth paste with no water. Wet onion paste will not brown properly and the gravy stays raw-tasting.
Shake the tin of coconut milk before opening, and keep it out of the fridge. Cold coconut milk splits when it hits a hot pan.

steps.text: Heat 1 tbsp ghee in a kadhai and sear the prawns on high for 45 seconds a side, until they just turn pink. Lift them out at once.
steps.tip: Prawns cook in under two minutes total. Anything more and they go to rubber, so undercook them here. They finish in the gravy.

steps.text: Add the remaining 2 tbsp ghee and drop in the bay leaves, cinnamon, cardamom and cloves. Fry 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the onion paste and fry on medium for 8-10 minutes, stirring often, until it turns pale gold and stops smelling raw.
steps.tip: This is the longest step and the one people cut short. Wait for the paste to pull away from the pan in a mass.

steps.text: Stir in the ginger and garlic pastes and cook 2 minutes more.
Add the turmeric, kashmiri chilli and salt with 2 tbsp water and fry 1 minute so the spices do not scorch.
Lower the flame and pour in the coconut milk. Add the sugar and slit green chillies.

steps.text: Simmer gently, uncovered, for 6-8 minutes until the gravy thickens enough to coat a spoon.
Return the prawns with any juices, add the garam masala, and simmer 2 minutes only.
Take off the heat and rest 5 minutes covered before serving with plain rice.

recipes.name: Dahi Baigana
recipes.subtitle: fried eggplant rounds folded into cool tempered yogurt, sharp with mustard oil

ingredients.note: rounds off the sourness
use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free

prepNotes: Toss the eggplant rounds with the turmeric and 1/2 tsp salt and leave 10 minutes; they weep a little and soak up less oil.
Take the yogurt out of the fridge 30 minutes ahead. Cold yogurt splits the moment warm tempering hits it.
Whisk the yogurt smooth with 2 tbsp water before you light the stove.

steps.text: Heat 3 tbsp mustard oil in a kadhai until it just begins to smoke, then take it off the heat for 30 seconds to lose the raw pungency.
Fry the eggplant in a single layer over medium heat, 3 to 4 minutes a side, until bronzed and collapsing at the centre.
steps.tip: Do not crowd the pan. Two batches of properly browned eggplant beat one batch of steamed grey slices.

steps.text: Drain the rounds on paper and leave them to cool to room temperature.
Whisk the yogurt with the sugar and 1/4 tsp salt until it pours off the spoon in a smooth ribbon.
Wipe the pan, heat the remaining 1 tbsp mustard oil and crackle the mustard seeds, then the cumin, about 20 seconds.
Add the broken red chillies, curry leaves and asafoetida and stand back. They spit for 10 seconds, then go quiet.
Take the pan off the heat and let the tempering cool for 2 minutes until it stops sizzling.

steps.text: Stir the green chilli and ginger into the yogurt, then pour in the warm tempering and fold once or twice.
Lay the eggplant in a shallow dish, spoon the yogurt over, and rest 15 minutes so the rounds drink it up.
Scatter the coriander and serve at room temperature with rice or pakhala.

recipes.name: Dahi Pakhala
recipes.subtitle: Odia fermented rice in water with yogurt, eaten cold in the hot months

image.alt: Dahi pakhala, Odia fermented rice with yogurt

ingredients.note: day-old rice is traditional and better

prepNotes: Real pakhala is rice left in water overnight to ferment lightly, which gives it a faint sourness and, in the Odia summer, a cooling effect. The quick version below skips the overnight step.

For the traditional version, cover the cooked rice with water and leave it in the refrigerator 8-12 hours, then proceed from step 2. It is fermented on the counter in Odia homes, and cooked rice held warm is exactly the conditions Bacillus cereus wants, so this version moves it to the fridge. It sours more slowly and more mildly there; give it the full 12 hours.
Serve cold. This is a hot-weather dish and warm pakhala misses the point.

steps.text: Put the cooled rice in a bowl, add the water and lightly crush some of the grains with your fingers to cloud the liquid. For the traditional version, this is where you leave it overnight.
Whisk the yogurt smooth and stir it through with salt, the ginger and green chilli. It should be soupy, not thick; add more water if needed.
Heat the oil in a small pan. Splutter the mustard seeds, then add the dried chilli, curry leaves and asafoetida.
Pour the tempering over the pakhala, add a squeeze of lemon and scatter with coriander.
Chill at least 30 minutes before eating. Serve with something fried and salty alongside; fried fish, badi chura or a simple potato bharta are the usual partners.

recipes.storage: Eat the same day. The fermentation continues in the fridge and it turns increasingly sour after about 24 hours. Do not leave it out of the refrigerator for more than two hours at any point. Do not freeze.

recipes.name: Dalma

image.alt: A bowl of Odia dalma, lentils cooked with vegetables

ingredients.note: rinsed until the water runs clear
use oil to keep it vegan

prepNotes: Dalma has no onion or garlic at all. The flavour comes from the roasted cumin-chilli powder added at the end, so do not skip that step.

steps.text: Meanwhile, dry roast half the cumin seeds and one dried chilli in a small pan over medium heat until the cumin darkens a shade and smells toasty, about 90 seconds. Cool, then grind to a coarse powder.

recipes.name: Ghanta Tarkari
recipes.subtitle: a big pot of mixed vegetables and chana dal with coconut, cooked for festivals without onion or garlic

ingredients.note: 1 tsp whole, 1/2 tsp for the coconut paste

prepNotes: Soak the chana dal at least 2 hours, or overnight if you can. It has to be tender at the same moment the vegetables are, and it is the slowest thing in the pot.

steps.tip: Stop while the dal still has bite. It cooks another 15 minutes with the vegetables.

Add the remaining grated ginger and the slit green chillies and fry 1 minute.

steps.text: Simmer uncovered 10 minutes until the gravy thickens and the yam is completely soft.

recipes.name: Kanika
recipes.subtitle: fragrant sweet ghee rice from the Jagannath temple kitchen, studded with cashew and raisin

ingredients.note: temple kanika uses fine short-grain local rice; basmati works
kanika is mildly sweet, not a dessert
for the pale gold colour
finish only

prepNotes: Rinse the rice in three changes of water until it runs clear, then drain in a colander for 20 minutes so the grains dry off.
Boil the 500ml of water and keep it hot. Cold water added to toasted rice makes it gummy.
Measure the sugar out before you start; it goes in at a moment when you cannot leave the pan.

steps.text: Heat 3 tbsp of the ghee in a heavy pan over medium and add the bay leaf, cinnamon, cloves, cardamom and peppercorns; they should swell and smell sweet in about 30 seconds.
steps.tip: Keep the heat at medium. Scorched whole spices turn the whole pot bitter and there is no rescuing it.

steps.text: Add the cashew halves and raisins and fry for 1 minute, until the cashews are pale gold and the raisins puff up.
Lift the cashews and raisins out with a slotted spoon onto a plate, leaving the whole spices behind.
Tip in the drained rice and the turmeric and toast gently for 3 to 4 minutes, until every grain looks glassy and slicked with ghee.
steps.tip: Fold with the back of a spoon rather than stirring. Soaked-and-drained rice snaps easily at this stage.

steps.text: Pour in the hot water, add the salt, and bring to a rolling boil.
Cover, drop to the lowest heat and cook undisturbed for 12 minutes, until the water is gone and the top grains are just tender.

steps.text: Fold the sugar through with a fork along with the fried cashews and raisins, the remaining 1 tbsp ghee and the grated nutmeg.

recipes.name: Khaja
recipes.subtitle: layered flaky pastry fried and dipped in sugar syrup, sold in stacks outside the Puri temple

ingredients.qty: 60g melted for the dough, plus 3 tbsp for the layering paste

ingredients.note: for the sata paste that makes the layers separate
for the syrup

ingredients.qty: 150ml for the dough, plus 200ml for the syrup

ingredients.note: or more ghee if you are being traditional

prepNotes: Rub the 60g melted ghee into the flour until a fistful holds its shape when squeezed. This moyan is what makes khaja short rather than hard.
Rest the dough a full 30 minutes under a damp cloth. Unrested dough springs back and the layers will not roll thin.
Beat the 3 tbsp ghee with the rice flour into a smooth white paste before you begin rolling. This sata is what separates the layers in the hot oil.
Make the syrup while the khaja fry so it is warm at the same moment they come out.

steps.text: Rub the melted ghee and salt into the maida for 3 minutes, then add the 150ml water a little at a time to make a firm, tight dough. Knead 6 minutes.
steps.tip: Firm, not soft. A slack dough will not hold its layers.

steps.text: Cover with a damp cloth and rest 30 minutes.
Beat the 3 tbsp ghee with the rice flour to a smooth, spreadable white paste.
Divide the dough in two. Roll each half into a thin rectangle about 2mm thick and spread the sata paste evenly right to the edges.
Roll each rectangle up tightly into a log, pressing as you go to expel air pockets.
steps.tip: Air pockets blow the layers apart in the oil. Roll tight and press along the seam.

steps.text: Cut each log into 2cm slices. Lay each slice cut-side up and press it flat with your palm, then roll very lightly into an oval about 8cm long. You should see the spiral of layers on the face.
Boil the 350g sugar with 200ml water and the cardamom for 8-10 minutes to a one-thread syrup, then keep it warm on the lowest flame.
steps.tip: One thread: a drop between thumb and finger pulls a single strand when you part them. Thicker and it will crystallise on the khaja.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a kadhai to low-medium. A scrap of dough should take a full 30 seconds to float up.
Fry the khaja in small batches for 7-9 minutes, turning often, until they are pale gold and the layers have visibly fanned open.
steps.tip: Low and slow is the entire technique. Fast frying browns the outside and leaves the inner layers doughy.

steps.text: Drain briefly, then dip each hot khaja in the warm syrup for 30 seconds, turning once, and lift onto a rack.
Leave to set for 30 minutes until the syrup coating turns matte and crisp.

recipes.storage: Keeps 10 days in an airtight tin at room temperature. Never refrigerate. The syrup weeps and the layers go soft.

recipes.name: Macha Besara
recipes.subtitle: rohu steaks in a hot, sour ground-mustard gravy, the Sunday fish curry of coastal Odisha

ingredients.qty: 600g rohu or katla, cut into 2cm-thick steaks
ingredients.note: any firm freshwater fish on the bone

ingredients.qty: 2 tbsp, soaked in warm water 20 minutes

ingredients.note: 3 for the paste, 2 sliced
1 tsp for rubbing the fish, 1/2 tsp for the gravy
4 for frying the fish, 1 for the gravy

prepNotes: Rub the fish steaks with 1 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt then cover and refrigerate 15 minutes. This firms the flesh so it does not break in the pan.
Soak the mustard seeds 20 minutes, then grind with 3 garlic cloves, 2 green chillies and a pinch of salt to a fine paste with 4 tbsp water.
Pat the fish dry just before frying. Wet fish sticks to the pan and tears when you turn it.

steps.text: Grind the soaked mustard, garlic, green chillies and a pinch of salt to a smooth paste with 4 tbsp water. Set aside.
Heat 4 tbsp mustard oil in a kadhai until it smokes. Fry the turmeric-rubbed fish in one layer, 3 minutes a side, until a light crust forms.
steps.tip: Do not move the fish for the first 3 minutes. It releases from the pan on its own once the crust sets.

steps.text: Lift the fish out onto a plate. Pour off all but about 1 tbsp of the oil.
Add the panch phoron to the hot oil and let it crackle 20 seconds, then add the sliced garlic and 2 slit green chillies.
Add the chopped tomato with 1/2 tsp turmeric, the chilli powder and salt. Cook 6 minutes, mashing, until the tomato collapses and the oil separates.
Pour in the water and bring to a boil, then simmer 5 minutes.
Drop the flame to its lowest and stir in the mustard paste. Simmer uncovered 5 minutes without letting it boil.
steps.tip: A hard boil after the mustard goes in makes the gravy bitter. Keep it barely trembling.

steps.text: Slide the fried fish back in, spoon gravy over each piece, and simmer 4 minutes more.
Take off the heat, scatter the coriander leaves and rest 10 minutes before serving. The fish keeps absorbing gravy as it stands.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated. Reheat on the lowest flame in a wide pan without stirring, tilting the pan to baste the fish instead; stirring breaks the steaks apart.

recipes.name: Machha Ghanta
recipes.subtitle: fish head cooked down with roasted moong dal and mixed vegetables into a thick one-pot stew

ingredients.qty: 400g rohu head and collar, or thick steaks, cut into 6 pieces

prepNotes: Rub the fish with 1/2 tsp turmeric and 1/2 tsp salt and leave 15 minutes while you cut the vegetables.
Dry-roast the moong dal in a pan over low heat for 5 minutes until it smells like toast and turns a shade darker, then rinse and drain it.
Cut all the vegetables to a similar 2cm size so they finish together.

steps.text: Heat 3 tbsp mustard oil until smoking, drop to medium and fry the fish pieces 2 minutes a side until the skin is set and golden.
steps.tip: Do not move the fish for the first 2 minutes or the skin tears and sticks. It releases itself when it is ready.

steps.text: Lift the fish out, and when it is cool enough to handle break the head into large pieces and flake the collar meat off the bone.
Add the remaining 2 tbsp oil to the same pan and crackle the panch-phoron, bay leaves and red chillies for 20 seconds.
Stir in the garlic and ginger and fry 90 seconds until the raw smell lifts.
Add the potato, raw banana and pumpkin with the turmeric, cumin powder, coriander powder and 1 tsp salt, and fry 5 minutes until the pieces are coated and glossy.
Tip in the roasted moong dal and stir for 2 minutes so each grain takes on oil.
Pour in the hot water, add the eggplant and the slit green chillies, bring to a boil then cover and simmer 20 minutes.
Uncover and check: the dal should be soft but still holding shape and the liquid reduced by about half.
steps.tip: Ghanta means a jumble, not a soup. Keep cooking uncovered until a spoon drawn through leaves a brief track.

steps.text: Fold the flaked fish and head pieces back in and simmer 5 minutes more, stirring gently so the fish stays in pieces.
Take off the heat, scatter the coriander and rest 10 minutes before serving with plain rice.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated in a covered container. Reheat on the stovetop with 3 tbsp water over low heat; do not microwave on full power, the fish goes rubbery.

recipes.name: Mahura
recipes.subtitle: yam, pumpkin and colocasia in mustard with crumbled badi, the festival curry of western Odisha

ingredients.note: urad dal badi, the dried dumplings sold as 'bori', fry them first
rounds off the mustard

prepNotes: Colocasia and yam make some hands itch. Rub your palms with a little mustard oil before peeling them, or wear gloves.
Soak the mustard seeds 20 minutes, then grind with 2 green chillies, the cumin seeds and a pinch of salt into a fine paste with 4 tbsp water.
Fry the badi first and set them aside. They go back in at the end so they stay chewy rather than dissolving.
This is a no-onion-garlic dish cooked for festivals and offerings; the mustard and jaggery carry all of it.

steps.text: Heat 1 tbsp mustard oil and fry the crushed badi over medium heat for 2 minutes until deep brown and smelling nutty. Lift out and reserve.
steps.tip: Badi burn in seconds once they colour. Stand over them.

steps.text: Add the remaining 2 tbsp oil to the same kadhai and heat until it smokes, then lower the flame.
Add the panch phoron and let it crackle 20 seconds.
Add the yam, colocasia, potato and raw banana. Fry 4 minutes, turning, until the cut faces are lightly golden.
steps.tip: Colocasia goes slimy if it steams before it fries. Give it dry heat first.

steps.text: Add the pumpkin, slit green chilli, turmeric and salt and toss for 2 minutes.
Pour in the water, bring to a boil, cover and simmer 15 minutes until the yam is tender to a knife.
Turn the flame to its lowest, stir in the mustard paste and the jaggery, and simmer uncovered 8 minutes.
steps.tip: Keep it below a rolling boil or the mustard turns bitter.

steps.text: Return the fried badi, stir once and simmer 3 minutes more so they drink up the gravy but keep their bite.
Rest 5 minutes off the heat before serving with plain rice.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated. Reheat gently on the stovetop with a splash of water; the badi will be softer on day two, which many people prefer.

recipes.name: Mudhi Mansa
recipes.subtitle: Baripada's peppery mutton curry eaten by the fistful with puffed rice

ingredients.note: puffed rice, served alongside
the signature heat of this dish

prepNotes: Marinate the mutton with the turmeric, half the crushed garlic, the ginger and 1 tsp salt for at least 1 hour in the refrigerator, or overnight.
Take the meat out of the fridge 30 minutes before cooking so it browns instead of steaming.
Buy the puffed rice fresh and keep the bag sealed. Stale mudhi goes leathery and ruins the dish.

steps.text: Heat the mustard oil in a pressure cooker until it smokes, then lower to medium and add the bay leaves, cinnamon, cardamom and cloves for 30 seconds.
Add the sliced onion and fry 12 to 14 minutes, stirring often, until deep brown and shrunk to a third of its volume.
steps.tip: This is where the colour of the gravy comes from. Stop at golden and the curry will look and taste thin.

steps.text: Stir in the remaining garlic and fry 1 minute, then add the tomato and cook 5 minutes until it collapses.
Add the chilli powder, coriander powder and cumin powder with 3 tbsp water and fry 3 minutes until oil separates at the edges.
Tip in the marinated mutton and brown it over high heat for 8 minutes, turning the pieces so every side catches.
steps.tip: Do not add water here. Let the meat sear in the masala until it stops sticking on its own.

steps.text: Add the potato halves, the crushed black pepper and 1/2 tsp salt and stir for 2 minutes.
Pour in the hot water, close the cooker and cook on high for 4 whistles, then on low for 12 minutes.
Let the pressure drop naturally, open, and check that the meat pulls from the bone with light pressure; if not, simmer uncovered 10 minutes more.
Simmer uncovered 5 to 8 minutes until the gravy coats a spoon but is still loose enough to soak into puffed rice.
steps.tip: Keep it wetter than a normal curry. It has to run through the mudhi rather than sit on top.

steps.text: Stir in the garam masala and coriander, rest 10 minutes, and serve in bowls with the puffed rice heaped alongside for crushing in by hand.

recipes.storage: The mutton keeps 3 days refrigerated and improves overnight; reheat on low with a splash of water. Never store it mixed with the puffed rice. Add that fresh at the table.

recipes.name: Rasabali
recipes.subtitle: fried chhena discs soaked in thick cardamom milk, the offering sweet of Kendrapara

ingredients.note: properly this is chhena from 2 litres of milk, drained but never pressed hard
for the rabri
100g for the milk, 50g for the syrup
binds the discs; this is wheat semolina, so the dish is not gluten-free
the traditional back-note; leave it out if you prefer
or a neutral oil, though ghee is traditional
for the light syrup

ingredients.qty: a pinch, soaked in 1 tbsp warm milk

prepNotes: The chhena must be fresh and soft. If you are using shop paneer, crumble it fine and knead it with the heel of your hand for a full 8 minutes until there is not a single lump and the mixture feels like dough.
Reduce the milk before you fry anything. It takes 30 minutes and cannot be hurried.
Rest the kneaded chhena dough 10 minutes covered before shaping. It shapes without cracking after resting.
Have the light sugar syrup made and warm before the discs come out of the ghee.

steps.text: Reduce the 1.5 litres of milk in a heavy pan over medium-low heat, scraping the sides down, for about 30 minutes until it has halved and thickened to a pourable rabri.
steps.tip: Scrape the skin off the sides back into the milk every few minutes. That is what gives rasabali its grain.

steps.text: Stir 100g sugar, the crushed cardamom, the pepper and the saffron milk into the reduced milk. Simmer 3 minutes and take off the heat.
Separately dissolve 50g sugar in 300ml water and bring to a boil to make a thin syrup. Keep it warm.
Knead the crumbled paneer with the rava for 8 minutes until smooth and dough-like, with no grains visible. Rest 10 minutes covered.
steps.tip: If the dough cracks when you flatten a ball, it needs more kneading, not more rava.

steps.text: Divide into 12 balls and flatten each into a disc about 5cm across and 1cm thick, with smooth unbroken edges.
Heat the ghee in a kadhai to medium-low. A scrap of dough should rise slowly and take 20 seconds to colour.
steps.tip: Hot ghee is the classic failure: the outside browns in seconds while the middle stays raw and the disc bursts.

steps.text: Fry the discs in batches, 4-5 minutes, turning once, until they are an even deep reddish-brown. They will puff slightly.
Drop each fried disc straight into the warm syrup and leave 10 minutes to soften and swell.
Lift the discs out, squeeze them very gently against the side of the bowl to shed excess syrup, and slide them into the warm rabri.
Rest at least 2 hours so the discs drink the milk all the way through. Serve cool, not chilled.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated in a covered box, and is better on day two. Serve cool or at room temperature; do not reheat, as the discs disintegrate.

recipes.name: Saga Bhaja
recipes.subtitle: amaranth greens stir-fried hard in mustard oil with garlic and dried chilli, done in ten minutes

ingredients.qty: 2 large bunches (about 400g), leaves and tender stems, chopped
ingredients.note: leutia saga; spinach works if you cannot get it

prepNotes: Wash the greens in three changes of water (amaranth holds grit in the leaf folds) then drain them properly and spread on a cloth for 10 minutes. Wet greens steam instead of frying.
Chop the stems separately from the leaves; the stems go in first.
Salt only at the very end. Salted greens release water immediately and you lose the fry.

steps.text: Heat the mustard oil in a wide kadhai until it smokes, then lower the flame for 30 seconds.
Add the mustard seeds and let them pop, about 15 seconds.
Add the sliced garlic and broken red chillies and fry until the garlic is pale gold at the edges, about 1 minute.
steps.tip: Gold, not brown. Brown garlic will taste burnt against the greens.

steps.text: Throw in the chopped stems and the slit green chillies and fry 2 minutes on high.
Add the leaves in two handfuls, letting the first wilt before the second goes in. Keep the flame high.
Add the turmeric and stir-fry 4-5 minutes uncovered, tossing often, until the water the leaves throw off has cooked away.
steps.tip: Do not cover the pan at any point. Trapped steam turns this into a soggy mash.

steps.text: Salt to taste, toss once more and take off the heat immediately.

recipes.storage: Eat within a few hours; greens dull and darken quickly. It keeps a day refrigerated but reheating makes it watery, so serve leftovers at room temperature.

recipes.name: Saja Pakhala
recipes.subtitle: same-day watered rice with lemon, ginger and a mustard tempering, eaten cool on the hottest afternoons

ingredients.note: Odia arua or any non-basmati short grain

ingredients.qty: 1.5 litres for cooking, plus 700ml cold for the pakhala

prepNotes: This is the fresh, curd-free version made and eaten the same day, not the overnight fermented basi pakhala.
Cook the rice loose and slightly soft, and do not drain away all the starch water. The torani is the point of the dish.
The rice must cool to room temperature before the cold water goes in. Hot rice makes a gluey pakhala.
Everything served alongside (fried fish, saga bhaja, a fried papad) should be salty and hot to contrast the cool rice.

steps.text: Boil the washed rice in 1.5 litres of water for 12-14 minutes, uncovered, until the grains are soft and just starting to swell open.
steps.tip: Cook it two minutes past what you would want for a normal plate of rice. Firm grains never soften once they are in cold water.

steps.text: Drain off the excess starch water into a bowl and keep it. Spread the rice in a wide dish.
Let the rice cool to room temperature, about 40 minutes. Do not rush it in the fridge.
Add 700ml cold water plus the reserved starch water to the rice, along with the salt. It should be soupy, with the grains floating loose.
Stir in the lemon juice, half the julienned ginger and the slit green chillies.
Heat the mustard oil in a small pan until it smokes, then lower the flame for 30 seconds.
Add the mustard seeds, cumin seeds and curry leaves. When the mustard pops and the leaves crisp, about 20 seconds, pour the whole tempering over the rice.
steps.tip: Pour it in while it is still spitting. The noise it makes hitting the cold rice is the sign you did it right.

steps.text: Stir once, scatter over the remaining ginger and the coriander leaves, and let it sit 15 minutes before eating.

recipes.storage: Eat the same day, ideally within a few hours. It keeps overnight refrigerated and will taste faintly sour by morning, which is closer to basi pakhala; do not reheat it.

recipes.name: Sajana Chhuin Rai
recipes.subtitle: drumsticks and potato in a pale, pungent ground-mustard gravy with no onion or garlic

ingredients.note: 2 for the paste, 2 slit for the pot
takes the edge off the mustard

prepNotes: Soak the mustard seeds in warm water for 20 minutes before grinding. Dry seeds grind bitter.
Peel the drumsticks lightly with a knife, taking off only the stringy outer skin, and cut them into finger lengths.
Grind the soaked mustard with 2 green chillies, a pinch of salt and 4 tbsp water into a smooth paste, using short pulses.

steps.text: Heat the mustard oil in a kadhai until it smokes faintly, then bring it down to medium.
Crackle the panch-phoron and broken red chillies for about 20 seconds, until the fenugreek in the mix darkens a shade.
steps.tip: Fenugreek goes from fragrant to acrid in seconds. The moment you smell it, move on.

steps.text: Add the potato, turmeric and 1/2 tsp salt and fry for 4 minutes until the cut edges take on gold patches.
Add the drumstick pieces and toss for 2 minutes so they pick up the oil.
Pour in the water, cover and simmer for 12 minutes, until a spoon scrapes the drumstick flesh out cleanly and the potato yields to a fork.
Turn the heat right down until the surface is barely moving, then stir in the ground mustard paste, the sugar and the cumin powder.
steps.tip: Never let the pot boil once the mustard is in. A hard boil makes it harsh and bitter within a minute.

steps.text: Hold at a bare simmer for 4 minutes; the gravy thickens slightly and loses its raw, nose-tingling smell.
Drop in the two slit green chillies and simmer 2 minutes more.
Take off the heat, stir through 1 tsp of raw mustard oil, and let it sit 5 minutes before serving with rice.
steps.tip: The raw oil at the end is what makes this taste Odia rather than merely mustardy.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated. Reheat gently on low with a splash of water and stop as soon as it is warm. Reboiling turns the mustard bitter.

recipes.name: Santula
recipes.subtitle: barely-spiced mixed vegetables stewed in their own water, the plainest good thing in an Odia kitchen

ingredients.note: gives the sweetness that balances the mustard oil
traditional, and it softens fast
stirred in off the heat

prepNotes: Cut every vegetable to roughly the same size so they finish together; the potato and raw banana are the slowest, so keep those pieces a touch smaller.
Santula has no onion or garlic and almost no ground spice, so the mustard oil has to be good. Heat it to smoking once and let it cool slightly before you cook in it.
This is a one-pot dish that wants to be left alone. Have everything cut before the oil goes on.

steps.text: Heat the mustard oil in a kadhai until it just smokes, then lower the flame and let it settle for 30 seconds.
steps.tip: Raw mustard oil tastes harsh and sinus-clearing; smoking it once takes that edge off.

steps.text: Add the panch phoron and let it crackle for about 20 seconds, until the fenugreek darkens a shade.
steps.tip: Fenugreek turns bitter fast. The moment it goes from pale to tan, move on.

steps.text: Add the slit green chillies and the potato and raw banana. Stir 2 minutes until the edges look chalky.
Add the pumpkin, eggplant, papaya, drumstick and tomato with the turmeric and salt. Toss to coat.
Pour in the water, bring to a boil, then cover and simmer on low for 15 minutes.
Uncover and check the potato with a knife tip; it should give with no resistance. Simmer uncovered 5 minutes more to thicken.
Mash three or four pieces of pumpkin against the side of the pan and stir through. That is what makes the broth cling.
steps.tip: Do not mash more than that or you lose the point of the dish, which is distinct pieces in a light liquor.

steps.text: Take off the heat, stir in the coriander leaves and rest 5 minutes before serving with rice.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated in a covered box. Reheat gently on the stovetop with 2 tbsp water; the eggplant will have softened further, which is fine.

recipes.name: Tomato Khajuri Khatta
recipes.subtitle: sweet-sour tomato and date relish tempered with panch phoron, served at the end of every Odia meal

ingredients.note: khajuri. Soak if they are dry
only if the tomatoes are on the sweet side

prepNotes: If your dates are hard, soak them in warm water for 15 minutes and drain before using.
Taste a tomato first. Sweet winter tomatoes need less jaggery and a squeeze of lemon at the end; sharp ones need the full 60g.
This is served at room temperature at the end of the meal, so make it early and let it sit.

steps.text: Heat the mustard oil in a small pan until it smokes, then lower the flame for 30 seconds.
Add the panch phoron and the broken red chillies. Let them crackle for 20 seconds until the fenugreek turns tan.
steps.tip: Fenugreek that goes dark brown will make the whole khatta bitter. This is the one moment to watch.

steps.text: Tip in the chopped tomato with the turmeric and salt. Stir once and cover.
Cook covered on medium for 8 minutes, until the tomatoes have completely collapsed.
Add the dates, raisins and water. Simmer uncovered 6 minutes so the dates plump and soften.
Stir in the jaggery and cook 6-8 minutes more, stirring now and then, until the mixture is glossy and a spoon dragged through leaves a track that closes slowly.
steps.tip: It thickens noticeably as it cools, so stop while it still looks slightly loose.

steps.text: Taste. Add the lemon juice if it needs sharpening, and adjust salt.
Cool to room temperature before serving alongside rice and dal.

recipes.storage: Keeps 5 days refrigerated in a clean glass jar. Serve at room temperature. Take it out 30 minutes ahead rather than reheating.

recipes.name: Aloo ke Gutke
recipes.subtitle: boiled potatoes tossed in smoking mustard oil and chilli until the edges crisp

ingredients.note: waxy potatoes hold their shape best
do not substitute. This is the flavour of the dish
stand-in for jakhya, the wild hill seed the catalogue does not carry
use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free
to finish

prepNotes: Boil the potatoes a few hours ahead and let them cool completely before peeling and cutting. Warm potatoes break up and turn to mash in the pan.
Cut the chunks large and uneven; the ragged faces are what catch and crisp.
This is a fast dish once the oil is hot, so have every spice measured out beside the stove.

steps.text: Heat the mustard oil in a kadhai over high heat until it smokes and the sharp smell mellows, about 2 minutes.
steps.tip: Under-heated mustard oil leaves a raw, throat-catching bitterness that no amount of cooking fixes later.

steps.text: Lower the heat to medium and crackle the mustard seeds until they pop, about 30 seconds, then add the cumin and broken red chillies.
Add the asafoetida and the slit green chillies and let them blister for 15 seconds.
Take the pan off the heat, stir in the turmeric, coriander powder and chilli powder, and count to five.
steps.tip: Powdered spices scorch instantly in oil this hot; the residual heat is enough to bloom them.

steps.text: Return to medium heat, tip in the potato chunks and salt, and toss until every piece is coated yellow.
Spread the potatoes in a single layer and leave them undisturbed for 4 minutes so a crust forms underneath.
steps.tip: Stirring constantly is the most common mistake. The potatoes need still contact with the pan to crisp.

steps.text: Turn them over in sections and fry another 5-6 minutes until the edges are brown and crisp in patches.
Squeeze over the lemon juice, scatter the coriander leaves and toss once.
Serve immediately, while the crust is still audible, with kumaoni raita or plain rice.

recipes.storage: Best eaten straight from the pan. Leftovers keep 2 days refrigerated; re-crisp in a dry hot pan for 5 minutes rather than microwaving, which turns them soft.

recipes.name: Arsa
recipes.subtitle: deep-fried rice flour and jaggery cakes, crisp at the rim and chewy in the middle

ingredients.note: hill cooks soak and grind their own rice; coarse shop flour works
mustard oil is traditional if you want the sharper hill version

prepNotes: The dough must rest overnight at room temperature, covered. This is not optional. The rest is what gives arsa its chew, and same-day dough fries hard and flat.
If you are grinding your own, soak the rice 6 hours, drain, dry in the shade for 2 hours until just damp, then grind coarse and sieve.
Have a bowl of cold water beside you for wetting your palms while shaping. The dough is very sticky.

steps.text: Melt the jaggery with 120ml water over low heat, stirring, until it dissolves, then strain out the grit through a fine sieve.
Return the syrup to the pan and boil until it reaches one-thread consistency. A drop lifted between finger and thumb pulls a single strand, about 6 minutes.
steps.tip: This is the make-or-break step. Under-cooked syrup gives soggy arsa; taken too far it sets hard and the dough will not come together.

steps.text: Pour the hot syrup over the rice flour in a wide bowl, add the sesame, fennel, cardamom and salt, and mix with a wooden spoon.
Once it is cool enough to handle, knead 4-5 minutes into a soft, sticky dough that just holds together.
Cover and rest at room temperature overnight, 8-10 hours.
Next day, wet your palms and shape walnut-sized pieces into flat discs about 6cm across and 1cm thick.
steps.tip: Keep re-wetting your hands. Dry palms tear the discs apart.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a kadhai to medium-low, about 160C. A scrap of dough should rise slowly after 4 seconds.
steps.tip: Hot oil browns the outside while the centre stays raw. Low and slow is the whole technique.

steps.text: Slide in 3-4 discs at a time and fry 6-8 minutes, spooning hot oil over them and turning once, until deep reddish brown.
Lift onto a rack and press each one gently with a slotted spoon to squeeze out oil. Cool completely before eating. They firm up as they sit.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 weeks in an airtight tin at room temperature, which is why arsa is made in batches for weddings and Diwali. Do not refrigerate; it goes hard and loses the chew.

recipes.name: Auriya Kaddu
recipes.subtitle: pumpkin in a sharp ground-mustard and yogurt gravy, the tangy course of a dham

ingredients.qty: 2 tbsp, soaked 2 hours and ground to a paste
ingredients.note: the auriya. This ground mustard is the whole dish
use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free
balances the bite of the mustard

prepNotes: Soak the mustard seeds 2 hours, then grind with 2 tbsp of the soaking water to a fine grey paste. Ground dry, they stay gritty and turn bitter.
Take the yogurt out of the fridge an hour ahead. Cold yogurt splits the moment it meets a hot pan.
Whisk the yogurt with the turmeric and chilli powder before it goes anywhere near the heat.

steps.text: Heat the ghee and mustard oil together until the mustard oil stops smelling raw, about 1 minute.
Crackle the fenugreek seeds and broken red chillies for 20 seconds, then add the hing.
steps.tip: Fenugreek goes from fragrant to bitter in about 10 seconds. Pull it the moment it turns reddish-brown.

steps.text: Add the pumpkin cubes and toss over medium heat 5 minutes until the edges catch a little colour.
Take the pan off the heat for a minute so it cools, then pour in the whisked spiced yogurt and stir continuously.
steps.tip: Off the heat and stirring. This is the only reliable way to stop the yogurt curdling.

steps.text: Return to a low flame and cook, stirring in one direction, until the yogurt loses its raw smell and thickens slightly, about 4 minutes.
Stir in the ground mustard paste, 200ml water and salt. Simmer uncovered 12 minutes until the pumpkin is tender at a knifepoint but not falling apart.
steps.tip: Never boil the mustard hard. Heat turns it acrid. A bare simmer only.

steps.text: Add the amchur and sugar, cook 2 minutes more and taste. It should be sour, mustardy and only faintly sweet.
Rest 5 minutes off the heat and serve with rice as part of a dham.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated. Reheat over the lowest flame with a spoon of water. A hard reheat splits the yogurt and sharpens the mustard.

recipes.name: Babru
recipes.subtitle: shimla-style fried breads packed with spiced ground urad dal, crisp outside and savoury through

ingredients.note: a little refined flour keeps the shell crisp rather than chewy

prepNotes: Soak the urad dal 4 hours, then drain it hard in a sieve for 10 minutes. Wet dal makes a sloppy filling that tears the dough.
The dough needs 30 minutes rest before rolling, so make it first and the filling while it sits.
Grind the dal coarse, not smooth - babru filling should be grainy.

steps.text: Mix the atta, maida, 1 tsp salt and the mustard oil, then add water gradually to a firm, smooth dough. Knead 6 minutes.
Cover and rest 30 minutes. The dough should press back slowly when poked.
Grind the drained urad dal with the green chillies and ginger to a coarse, dry paste, using at most 2 tbsp water.
steps.tip: If it looks like batter you have gone too far. Stop while you can still see broken grains.

steps.text: Heat 2 tbsp of the frying oil in a pan, crackle the cumin, ajwain and asafoetida, then add the dal paste.
Cook the dal on medium for 8 to 10 minutes, breaking up lumps, until it dries out and comes away from the pan in a single crumbly mass.
steps.tip: Filling that is still moist will steam inside the babru and burst it open in the oil.

steps.text: Stir in the coriander powder, chilli powder, amchur, crushed fennel, garam masala, salt and coriander leaves. Cook 2 minutes, then cool completely.
Divide the dough into 10 balls. Flatten each in your palm, cup it, put in a heaped tablespoon of cold filling, gather the edges over the top and pinch shut. Press flat.
Roll each stuffed ball gently to about 10cm across, working from the centre out with light pressure.
steps.tip: Press hard and the filling pushes through. If a tear opens, patch it with a scrap of dough.

steps.text: Heat the oil to 175C. Slide in two babrus at a time and press the centre lightly with a slotted spoon so they puff.
Fry 2 minutes a side until deep golden and blistered. Drain and serve hot with kaddu ka khatta or a tamarind chutney.

recipes.storage: Eat within a couple of hours while the shell is crisp. They keep a day in an airtight tin and revive in a 180C oven for 5 minutes; refrigeration makes them leathery.

recipes.name: Bhatt Ki Churkani
recipes.subtitle: kumaoni black beans roasted in mustard oil and simmered into a dark, smoky, rice-thickened gravy

ingredients.note: stands in for bhatt, the small Kumaoni black soybean; use bhatt if you can find it and skip the soaking in favour of a dry roast
the traditional thickener - churkani means the gravy, not the bean
compounded-free hing, both for the gluten and because jambu is hard to source outside the hills

prepNotes: Soak the beans overnight. If you have actual bhatt, dry roast them in a heavy pan for 5 minutes until they crackle and smell toasted, then cook them unsoaked.
Whisk the rice flour into 150ml cold water and leave it aside. Added dry to a hot pan it lumps immediately.
This is a mustard oil dish through and through - a neutral oil version tastes of nothing much.

steps.text: Heat 2 tbsp mustard oil in a heavy pan until it smokes, then cool it 20 seconds. Add the drained beans and roast them on medium for 6 to 7 minutes, stirring, until the skins wrinkle and blister.
steps.tip: This roast is where the smokiness comes from. Take it to the point where the pan smells nutty, just short of burnt.

steps.text: Transfer the beans to a pressure cooker with 800ml water and 1 tsp salt. Cook for 6 whistles and let the pressure fall naturally.
Heat the remaining 2 tbsp mustard oil in a kadhai to smoking, then cool briefly. Crackle the cumin and fenugreek seeds and the broken red chillies, 20 seconds.
steps.tip: Fenugreek goes bitter fast. Pull it off the heat the moment it browns.

steps.text: Add the asafoetida, then the crushed garlic, and fry 1 minute to pale gold.
Stir in the ginger and green chillies, then the turmeric, coriander powder and chilli powder. Fry 30 seconds.
Tip in the cooked beans with all their liquid and bring to a boil.
Stir the rice flour slurry once more and pour it in slowly while stirring hard. The gravy will thicken visibly within a minute.
steps.tip: Pour in a thin stream and keep the spoon moving, or you will be picking out lumps for the next ten minutes.

steps.text: Simmer uncovered on low for 15 minutes, stirring every couple of minutes, until the gravy turns glossy and dark and coats a spoon thickly.
Check the salt, scatter over the coriander leaves and serve with plain rice and a spoon of raw mustard oil on top if you like it sharp.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated and sets almost solid as it cools. Reheat on low with 100ml water, whisking to bring the thickened gravy back together.
