recipes.name: Chainsoo
recipes.subtitle: dark roasted black gram dal from the kumaon hills, smoky and heavy

ingredients.note: black gram with skin on, not the split white dal
the pungency is part of the dish
use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free
hill kitchens add this for warmth
to finish

prepNotes: Do not soak the urad. Chainsoo is built on dry-roasted dal, and wet dal will steam instead of colour.
Keep the hot water in a kettle beside the pan; adding cold water to the roasted paste makes it seize into lumps.
An iron kadhai gives the traditional near-black colour, but any heavy pan works.

steps.text: Dry-roast the whole urad in a heavy kadhai over medium heat for 10-12 minutes, stirring constantly, until the skins turn matte black-brown and the kitchen smells strongly nutty.
steps.tip: Take it a shade further than feels comfortable. Pale roasting gives a flat, raw-tasting dal. Stop the moment you smell any acrid edge.

steps.text: Cool the dal fully on a plate, 10 minutes, then grind to a coarse meal in a blender. The texture of semolina, not flour. Grinding it warm turns it pasty.
Heat the mustard oil in the same kadhai until it just begins to smoke, then lower the heat and let it settle for 30 seconds.
steps.tip: Mustard oil must be taken to smoking point or it stays bitter and raw.

steps.text: Crackle the cumin seeds and broken red chillies for 20 seconds, then add the asafoetida.
Add the garlic, ginger and green chilli and fry 2 minutes until the garlic is pale gold and no longer smells sharp.

Stir in the turmeric, coriander powder and chilli powder, then immediately tip in the ground urad. Fry on low heat for 6-8 minutes, stirring the whole time, until the meal darkens and loosens from the pan.
steps.tip: This is the step that makes or breaks chainsoo. The roasted meal must fry in the oil, not sit in it.

steps.text: Pour in the hot water a ladleful at a time, whisking after each addition so no lumps form. Add salt.
Simmer uncovered on low heat for 25-30 minutes, stirring every 5 minutes, until the dal is the colour of wet slate and thick enough to coat a spoon.
steps.tip: It thickens a lot as it cools. Leave it looser than you think you want.

steps.text: Stir in the dry ginger powder and garam masala, cook 2 minutes more, then rest off the heat for 5 minutes.
Scatter the coriander leaves and serve hot over plain rice with a spoon of mustard oil on top.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated and thickens into a solid block. Reheat gently with a generous splash of hot water, whisking to bring it back to a pourable dal.

recipes.name: Chana Dal Dham
recipes.subtitle: sweet-sour chana dal from the dham feast, no onion or garlic anywhere in it

ingredients.note: the botis of Himachal cook dham entirely in ghee
use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free
saunth, the dham cook's stand-in for fresh ginger
extra sourness if the tamarind is mild

prepNotes: Soak the chana dal 3 hours. Unsoaked dal softens unevenly, and dham dal has to hold its shape rather than collapse.
Soak 20g tamarind in 100ml hot water for 20 minutes, then squeeze and strain to get the 2 tbsp of pulp.
Dham is cooked without onion or garlic by tradition, so all the depth has to come from the ghee, the hing and the long tempering. Do not shortcut those.

steps.text: Pressure cook the drained dal with 750ml water, the turmeric and 1 tsp salt for 2 whistles, then lower the flame and give it 6 minutes more.
steps.tip: You want grains that yield when pressed but still look like grains.

steps.text: Heat the ghee in a heavy pan until it thins and shimmers, then add the cumin. It should crackle within 3 seconds.
Drop in the hing and count to five. It will foam and smell nutty, not acrid.
steps.tip: If it darkens past pale gold the whole pot turns bitter. Pull the pan off the heat if it moves fast.

steps.text: Stir in the coriander powder, chilli powder and dry ginger powder off the heat for 20 seconds so they bloom without burning.
Pour in the cooked dal with its liquid and bring to a simmer, 5 minutes.
Add the tamarind pulp and the jaggery and simmer uncovered 15 minutes, stirring now and then, until the gravy coats the back of a spoon.
steps.tip: Taste at 10 minutes. It should land sour first, sweet second. Add jaggery a teaspoon at a time.

steps.text: Crush in the anardana and the garam masala, simmer 3 minutes more, then check the salt.
Rest the pot off the heat for 10 minutes before serving. Scatter the coriander leaves and serve with plain rice.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated and tastes better on day two. Reheat gently with 3-4 tbsp water. It thickens hard as it cools.

recipes.name: Chana Madra
recipes.subtitle: chickpeas simmered slowly in whisked yogurt until the gravy is silky, faintly sour and heavy with whole spice

ingredients.note: sour, day-old curd is better than fresh
madra is a generous dish; do not cut this below 4 tbsp
stabilises the yogurt so it will not split
use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free
sonth carries the warmth that ginger root would in a plains curry
colour without heat
the Chamba touch, a sweet note against the sour curd

prepNotes: Soak the chickpeas overnight in plenty of water. They should more than double.
Take the yogurt out of the fridge an hour ahead. Cold yogurt splits the moment it meets hot ghee.
Whisk the yogurt with the besan and a pinch of salt until there is not a single lump, then keep the whisk in the bowl - you will use it again.

steps.text: Pressure cook the drained chickpeas with 500ml water and 1 tsp salt for 4 whistles, then let the pressure drop by itself. They should crush easily between finger and thumb but still hold their shape.
steps.tip: Undercooked chana will never soften later - the acid in the yogurt sets them hard.

steps.text: Heat the ghee in a heavy kadhai until it thins and shimmers. Add the cumin, cinnamon, black cardamom, green cardamom, cloves and bay leaves and let them swell and crackle, about 40 seconds.
Add the asafoetida, count to five, then take the pan off the heat entirely and let it cool for a full minute.
steps.tip: This off-heat pause is the whole trick of madra. Yogurt going into ripping-hot ghee will curdle every time.

steps.text: Pour in the whisked yogurt, return to the lowest possible flame and stir continuously in one direction for 8 to 10 minutes, until the yogurt loses its raw smell and thickens to the consistency of pouring cream.
steps.tip: Do not stop stirring and do not cover the pan until the yogurt has come to a boil once.

steps.text: Stir in the coriander powder, fennel powder, dry ginger, turmeric and kashmiri chilli. Cook 3 minutes more - the gravy will turn glossy and the ghee will start to bead at the edges.
Add the drained chickpeas along with 150ml of their cooking water. Season with salt.
Simmer uncovered on low for 20 to 25 minutes, stirring every few minutes, until the gravy coats the back of a spoon and a clear rim of ghee sits around the edge of the pan.
steps.tip: That ring of separated ghee is how Chamba cooks judge madra is done.

steps.text: Fold in the almonds and raisins and cook 3 minutes so the raisins plump.
Finish with the garam masala, cover and rest off the heat for 10 minutes before serving with plain rice.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated and genuinely improves on day two. Reheat very gently on low with a splash of water - a hard boil will break the yogurt.

recipes.name: Gahat ki Dal
recipes.subtitle: slow-cooked horse gram, nutty and mineral, the winter dal of every hill house

ingredients.note: gahat or kulthi; pick over for grit before soaking
just a few seeds. More turns it bitter
use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free

prepNotes: Soak the horse gram in plenty of water for at least 8 hours or overnight. It is the hardest pulse in the Indian kitchen and unsoaked it will hold you at the stove for hours.
Do not throw away the soaking water if you like the dish strong; hill cooks often cook the dal in it. Discard it if you find gahat heavy to digest.
Have the tempering ingredients chopped before you open the cooker. The dal is added straight into the hot masala.

steps.text: Drain the soaked horse gram and pressure-cook it with the litre of water and the turmeric for 6 whistles, then let the pressure drop naturally, about 15 minutes.
steps.tip: Naturally releasing pressure lets the grains finish softening; quick-releasing leaves them chalky in the middle.

steps.text: Check a grain. It should crush easily between finger and thumb. If not, cook 3 more whistles.
Heat the mustard oil in a wide pan until it smokes lightly, then lower the heat.
Crackle the cumin and fenugreek seeds for 20 seconds, then add the asafoetida.
steps.tip: Fenugreek burns in seconds and goes acridly bitter. Get the next ingredient in fast.

steps.text: Add the garlic and fry 2 minutes to pale gold, then the ginger and green chilli for 1 minute more.
Add the tomatoes with the coriander powder and chilli powder. Cook 8 minutes on medium until the tomatoes collapse and oil beads at the edge of the masala.
steps.tip: Wait for the oil to separate. The raw tomato taste hangs around in the finished dal otherwise.

steps.text: Tip in the cooked horse gram with all its liquid and the salt. Bring to a boil.
Simmer uncovered on low for 20-25 minutes, mashing a ladleful of grains against the side of the pan halfway through to thicken the broth.
Stir in the dry ginger powder and take off the heat.
Rest 5 minutes, scatter coriander leaves and serve with rice or mandua roti.

recipes.storage: Keeps 4 days refrigerated and improves on the second day. Reheat on the stovetop with a little hot water; the dal drinks up liquid as it sits.

recipes.name: Jhangora ki Kheer
recipes.subtitle: barnyard millet simmered slowly in milk with jaggery and cardamom, grainy and gentle

ingredients.note: stand-in for jhangora, the barnyard millet the catalogue does not carry; use samak millet if you can find it
or 120g sugar
for toasting the grain

ingredients.qty: a pinch, soaked in 1 tbsp warm milk

prepNotes: Rinse the grain in three changes of water until it runs clear, then soak 20 minutes and drain. This is soaking time, not cooking time.
Grate the jaggery and keep it ready; it must go in off the heat at the very end.
Use a heavy-based pan. Kheer sticks and scorches in a thin one, and burnt milk cannot be rescued.

steps.text: Toast the drained grain in the ghee over medium heat for 2 minutes until each grain is glossy and smells faintly nutty.
Pour in the milk, bring to a boil, then drop the heat to its lowest setting.
steps.tip: Watch it as it comes up. Milk climbs the pan and boils over in seconds.

steps.text: Simmer uncovered for 35-40 minutes, stirring every 4-5 minutes and scraping the bottom and sides of the pan with a flat spoon.
steps.tip: Scrape the base every single time. A skin of milk left sitting there will catch and taint the whole pot.

steps.text: Keep going until the grains are soft and swollen and the milk has reduced by about a third, coating the spoon thickly.
Stir in the almonds and raisins and cook 3 minutes more, until the raisins plump.
Take the pan off the heat and let it stand for 8-10 minutes, until you can comfortably hold a hand against the side of the pan.
steps.tip: This wait is not optional. Jaggery added to near-boiling milk will curdle it instantly.

steps.text: Stir in the grated jaggery until fully dissolved, then the crushed cardamom and the saffron milk.
Taste and add a little more jaggery if you want it sweeter, then rest 10 minutes for the flavours to settle.
Serve warm, or chill 2 hours and serve cold. It thickens considerably in the fridge.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated in a covered container. It sets firm when cold; loosen with 3-4 tbsp of warm milk and stir well before serving. Do not reheat over high heat.

recipes.name: Kaapa
recipes.subtitle: garhwali spinach thickened with gram flour, garlicky and eaten by the bowl with rice

ingredients.note: the thickener. No cream or dairy goes into kaapa
whole seeds, not kasuri methi
use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free

prepNotes: Wash the spinach in three changes of water. Hill spinach comes in gritty and grit in kaapa is unforgiveable.
Whisk the besan into 200ml cold water until completely smooth before you start cooking, and leave it aside. Lumps will not come out later.
Blanch and blend the spinach only if you want it smooth; many Garhwali homes leave it coarse and chopped.

steps.text: Blanch the spinach in boiling water for 90 seconds, drain and plunge into cold water to fix the colour.
steps.tip: Ninety seconds, no more. Overcooked spinach goes olive and dull.

steps.text: Squeeze out the excess water and either chop it fine or pulse it briefly in a blender to a coarse puree.
Heat the mustard oil until it smokes, cut the flame for a minute, then crackle the cumin and fenugreek seeds for 20 seconds.
steps.tip: Fenugreek turns bitter quickly. The moment it reddens, move on.

steps.text: Add the hing, red chillies, garlic, ginger and green chillies and fry 2 minutes until the garlic is golden.
Stir in the turmeric and coriander powder, then pour in the smooth besan slurry, whisking continuously.
Cook the besan mixture on a low flame for 6-8 minutes until it thickens and stops smelling of raw flour.
steps.tip: Raw besan is the single most common fault in kaapa. Give it the full 8 minutes.

steps.text: Add the spinach, the remaining 200ml water and salt. Simmer uncovered 10 minutes until it is thick enough to hold a ridge from the spoon.
Finish with the lemon juice off the heat and serve with hot rice.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated. Reheat gently with a splash of water; the colour dulls on day two but the flavour improves.

recipes.name: Kaddu Ka Khatta
recipes.subtitle: pumpkin cooked down with tamarind, pomegranate seed and jaggery into the sharp sour dish that cuts a dham

ingredients.qty: 700g, cut into 3cm cubes with the skin left on
ingredients.note: the skin keeps the pieces from disintegrating
heat it to smoking first to take off the raw pungency
use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free

ingredients.qty: 2 tbsp thick pulp, from a lime-sized ball soaked in hot water

ingredients.note: dried pomegranate seed, the sourness Himachal actually uses

prepNotes: Soak the tamarind in 100ml hot water for 20 minutes, then squeeze and strain out the pulp.
Grind the anardana coarsely in a mortar just before cooking - ready-ground powder goes flat within weeks.
Do not peel the pumpkin. The skin holds the cubes together through a long simmer.

steps.text: Heat the mustard oil in a kadhai until it smokes faintly and the sharp smell drops away, about 2 minutes. Take it off the heat for 20 seconds to cool slightly.
steps.tip: Raw mustard oil tastes acrid. Smoking it once is the whole difference.

steps.text: Add the fenugreek seeds and let them darken to a nut brown, no more than 15 seconds, then the cumin.
steps.tip: Fenugreek turns bitter the second it goes past brown - have the cumin in your hand ready.

steps.text: Stir in the asafoetida, then immediately add the turmeric, chilli powder, coriander powder and dry ginger. Fry 20 seconds.
Tip in the pumpkin and toss to coat every piece in the spiced oil. Fry on medium for 5 minutes until the edges start to catch.
Pour in 300ml water, add salt, cover and simmer 12 to 15 minutes until a knife slides into a cube with no resistance.
Add the tamarind pulp, the ground anardana and the jaggery. Stir gently - from here on you want the cubes intact.
Simmer uncovered 8 to 10 minutes, mashing four or five pieces against the side of the pan, until the gravy thickens to a loose chutney that clings to the pumpkin.
steps.tip: Taste now and balance: it should read sour first, sweet second, never cloying. More jaggery or more tamarind, a spoon at a time.

steps.text: Finish with garam masala and coriander leaves. Serve at room temperature alongside rice and madra.

recipes.storage: Keeps 4 days refrigerated and the sourness settles and deepens. Serve cold or at room temperature; it is not a dish that wants reheating, though a minute on low is fine.

recipes.name: Kafuli
recipes.subtitle: garhwali spinach and fenugreek greens thickened to a silky, sour-edged green curry

ingredients.note: fresh fenugreek leaves
thin, slightly sour
the traditional thickener; besan also works
use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free
drizzled over each bowl

prepNotes: Wash the greens in three changes of water. Hill spinach carries a lot of grit, and one gritty mouthful ruins the dish.
Whisk the rice flour into the cold buttermilk before it goes anywhere near heat, and leave it 10 minutes so no dry specks remain.
Bring the buttermilk to room temperature so it is less likely to split when it hits the hot pan.

steps.text: Bring 200ml water to a boil, add the spinach and methi leaves, and blanch for 3 minutes until they wilt down and turn deep green.
Drain, keeping the green cooking water, and cool the greens under cold running water for 30 seconds.
steps.tip: The cold shock keeps the colour bright; skip it and the curry goes olive-brown.

steps.text: Blend the greens with the green chillies, ginger and 4 tbsp of the reserved water to a coarse purée. Leave a little texture rather than making it smooth.
Whisk the rice flour into the buttermilk until completely smooth and set aside.
Heat the mustard oil in a pan until it smokes lightly, then lower the heat and crackle the cumin and fenugreek seeds for 20 seconds.
Add the asafoetida and garlic and fry 2 minutes until pale gold.
Stir in the turmeric and coriander powder, then add the green purée and the salt. Cook 5 minutes on medium, stirring, until it darkens and tightens.
Turn the heat to its lowest setting and pour in the buttermilk mixture in a slow stream, stirring continuously in one direction.
steps.tip: Adding cold buttermilk to a hot pan without stirring will curdle it into grains. Low heat, slow stream, constant stirring.

steps.text: Simmer very gently for 10-12 minutes, stirring often, until the curry thickens enough to hold a line drawn across the back of a spoon.
steps.tip: Do not let it boil hard at any point after the buttermilk goes in.

steps.text: Taste for salt, rest 3 minutes off the heat, and serve in bowls with a teaspoon of ghee floated on top, alongside rice.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated. Reheat over low heat only, stirring, and add a splash of water. A hard boil will split the buttermilk.

recipes.name: Khatta Meat
recipes.subtitle: chamba mutton curry made sour with pomegranate seed and dried mango, thin and fiercely spiced

ingredients.note: shoulder and neck give the best gravy
the defining sourness. Do not substitute lemon
rounds off the sourness without sweetening the curry

prepNotes: Bring the mutton to room temperature for 30 minutes before cooking. Cold meat straight from the fridge seizes in hot oil.
Grind the anardana coarsely in a dry grinder just before you cook. Pre-ground pomegranate seed goes flat and stale within weeks.
Heat the mustard oil to smoking point and let it cool for a minute before you start. Raw mustard oil is harsh and this curry has nowhere to hide it.

steps.text: Heat the mustard oil until it smokes, cut the flame for 60 seconds, then return it to medium.
Crackle the cumin, black cardamom, cinnamon, cloves and bay leaf for 30 seconds until the cardamom smells smoky.
Add the sliced onion and fry 10-12 minutes to a deep even brown, stirring often.
steps.tip: Brown, not black. Burnt onion turns the whole curry bitter and there is no fixing it.

steps.text: Stir in the ginger and garlic pastes and fry 2 minutes until the raw smell lifts.
Add the mutton and brown it hard over high heat for 8 minutes, stirring so every piece takes colour.
steps.tip: Do this in two batches if your pan is crowded. Steamed meat gives a pale, thin curry.

steps.text: Lower the heat, add the turmeric, coriander powder, chilli powder and salt, and fry 4 minutes until oil beads at the edges.
Pour in 600ml water, bring to a boil, then pressure cook 4 whistles and rest until the pressure drops on its own, about 20 minutes.
Open the cooker, stir in the ground anardana and the amchur, and simmer uncovered 12 minutes. The gravy stays deliberately thin.
steps.tip: Add the sour agents only now. Cooking them under pressure makes them dull and slightly bitter.

steps.text: Add the jaggery and garam masala, simmer 3 minutes, taste for salt and sourness.
Rest 10 minutes off the heat, scatter the coriander and serve with steamed rice.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated, better on the second day once the anardana settles. Reheat over low heat with a splash of water; do not boil hard or the meat tightens.

recipes.name: Kullu Trout
recipes.subtitle: whole river trout crisped in mustard oil with ajwain and a hard squeeze of lemon

ingredients.qty: 2 whole trout, about 300g each, cleaned and slashed 3 times a side
ingredients.note: catalogued simply as fish. Use trout, or any firm river fish
carom is the hill cook's fish spice; it cuts the oiliness
for colour without heat

ingredients.qty: 1, half juiced and half in wedges

ingredients.note: a light dusting for extra crust

prepNotes: Pat the fish bone dry inside and out with kitchen paper. Any surface water and the marinade slides off and the skin steams instead of crisping.
Marinate 20 minutes only. Lemon juice on a delicate river fish for longer than that starts to cure the flesh and it goes chalky.
Bring the fish to room temperature before it hits the pan.

steps.text: Mix the turmeric, kashmiri chilli, chilli powder, ajwain, black pepper, ginger, garlic, lemon juice and salt into a thick paste.
Rub the paste over the fish and well into the slashes and the cavity. Rest 20 minutes.
steps.tip: Push it into the cuts with your fingers. That is the only way seasoning reaches the flesh of a whole fish.

steps.text: Dust each fish lightly with rice flour on both sides and shake off the excess.
Heat the mustard oil on a heavy tawa until it smokes, then cut the heat to medium for a minute.
Lay the fish in away from you and fry undisturbed for 5 minutes.
steps.tip: Do not poke it. The skin releases from the pan by itself when the crust has formed.

steps.text: Turn once with a wide spatula and fry the second side 4-5 minutes until the thickest part flakes at a fork.
Lift onto a warm plate, rest 2 minutes, scatter coriander and serve with lemon wedges and hot rice.

recipes.storage: Best eaten within the hour. The crust softens fast. Leftovers keep 1 day refrigerated; flake the cold flesh into a salad rather than reheating.

recipes.name: Kumaoni Raita
recipes.subtitle: grated cucumber in yogurt sharpened with ground mustard until it stings the nose

ingredients.note: thick set curd, not runny
yellow or brown; this is the defining flavour
for dusting on top
for the tempering
for grinding the mustard

prepNotes: Grate the cucumber and squeeze out the liquid 15 minutes before you mix, or the raita will turn watery within the hour.
Grind the mustard seeds fresh with a little water. Pre-ground mustard powder has lost the volatile heat that gives this raita its kick.
Take the yogurt out of the fridge 20 minutes ahead; fridge-cold yogurt mutes the mustard.

steps.text: Soak the mustard seeds in the 2 tbsp water for 10 minutes, then grind with the green chillies and turmeric to a smooth, bright yellow paste in a blender.
steps.tip: The paste should smell so sharp it makes your eyes water. If it does not, grind another minute.

steps.text: Squeeze the grated cucumber firmly in your fist over the sink and discard the liquid.
Whisk the yogurt in a bowl until completely smooth with no lumps, about 1 minute.
Fold in the mustard paste a teaspoon at a time, tasting as you go, until the raita is as pungent as you want it.
steps.tip: Add it gradually. Too much ground mustard turns bitter and there is no way back.

steps.text: Stir in the squeezed cucumber, the salt and the black salt.
Heat the mustard oil in a small pan until it smokes, drop in the broken red chilli for 10 seconds, and pour the tempering over the raita.
Chill for at least 20 minutes so the mustard heat settles into the yogurt.
steps.tip: Straight after mixing the mustard sits on top as a raw burn; 20 minutes rounds it out.

steps.text: Dust with chilli powder, scatter the coriander leaves and serve cold with aloo ke gutke or rice.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated in a covered box, though the mustard heat fades after the first day. Do not freeze; the yogurt splits. Stir before serving.

recipes.name: Mandua ki Roti
recipes.subtitle: dark finger millet flatbread, earthy and faintly sweet, soft only while hot

ingredients.note: mandua is finger millet, sold as ragi flour
for smearing; use mustard oil for a dairy-free version
for dusting, since millet dough sticks

prepNotes: Boil the water before you start. Millet has no gluten and only hot water will gelatinise the starch enough to make a workable dough.
Rest the dough 15 minutes under a cloth; it firms up and stops cracking at the edges when you pat it out.
Have the tawa heating while the dough rests, and keep a damp cloth ready to hold the finished rotis.

steps.text: Mix the ragi flour and salt in a heatproof bowl and make a well in the centre.
Pour in the boiling water all at once and stir hard with a wooden spoon for 30 seconds until it comes together as a shaggy, steaming mass.
steps.tip: Water that has gone off the boil gives a crumbly dough that will not hold a round. Use it straight from the kettle.

steps.text: Cover and leave 10 minutes, until cool enough to handle but still warm.
Knead in the bowl for 4-5 minutes with the heel of your hand until the dough is smooth, dark and slightly tacky. It should not crack when you press a ball flat.
steps.tip: Knead it warm. Cold millet dough will never come smooth however long you work it.

steps.text: Rest the dough covered with a damp cloth for 15 minutes.
Divide into 8 balls. Dust a work surface with rice flour and pat each ball out with your palm into a 15cm round about 4mm thick, turning as you go.
steps.tip: Patting by hand works far better than a rolling pin here; a pin drags and tears the dough.

steps.text: Heat a tawa over medium-high until a drop of water skitters across it.
Lay a roti on the tawa and cook 60-70 seconds until the surface dulls and small pale spots appear.
Flip and cook the second side 60 seconds, pressing the edges gently with a folded cloth until it puffs in patches and dark freckles form.
steps.tip: Millet rotis rarely balloon fully like wheat ones. Patchy puffing is the right result.

steps.text: Smear with ghee, stack in a cloth-lined box, and repeat with the rest.
Serve hot with gahat ki dal or chainsoo.

recipes.storage: Best within an hour of making. They stiffen as they cool; wrap in foil and warm on a hot tawa for 30 seconds a side. Dough keeps 1 day refrigerated, brought back to room temperature before rolling.

recipes.name: Mash Ki Dal
recipes.subtitle: whole black urad cooked down thick and buttery over a mustard oil base, the everyday hill dal

ingredients.note: gives body and a little sweetness
stirred in at the end, not cooked in
compounded-free hing keeps this gluten-free

prepNotes: Soak the urad and chana dal together for at least 6 hours. Unsoaked whole urad takes an hour of pressure and still eats chalky.
Chop the onion fine - in the hills this dal is not blended, so the onion has to melt into it.
Have the ghee at room temperature; it goes in off the heat at the end.

steps.text: Pressure cook the drained dals with 900ml water, the turmeric and 1 tsp salt for 5 whistles, then 15 minutes on the lowest flame. Let the pressure drop naturally.
steps.tip: The dal is ready when a grain smears to paste between your fingers with no grit at the centre.

steps.text: Heat the mustard oil in a kadhai until it smokes lightly, then cool it 20 seconds off the flame.
Crackle the cumin, add the asafoetida, then the garlic. Fry 40 seconds until it just turns pale gold.
steps.tip: Garlic past gold goes bitter and there is nothing in this dal to hide it behind.

steps.text: Add the onion and cook on medium, stirring, for 10 to 12 minutes until it is properly brown at the edges and sweet-smelling.
Stir in the ginger and green chillies, then the coriander powder, chilli powder and dry ginger. Fry 30 seconds.
Add the tomatoes and cook 6 to 8 minutes, pressing them down, until they break completely and the oil pulls away to the sides.
Pour the cooked dal into the masala. Simmer uncovered 15 to 20 minutes on low, stirring and mashing against the pan, until it thickens enough to hold a furrow behind the spoon.
steps.tip: This long open simmer is what separates hill mash dal from a thin plains dal. Do not shortcut it.

steps.text: Check the salt, sprinkle over the garam masala and take off the heat.
Stir in the raw ghee and the coriander leaves and cover for 5 minutes before serving with rice or a hot roti.
steps.tip: Adding the ghee off the heat keeps its aroma; cooked in, it just disappears.

recipes.storage: Keeps 4 days refrigerated and thickens to a paste. Loosen with hot water and reheat on low, then add a fresh half-spoon of ghee before serving.

recipes.name: Mittha
recipes.subtitle: saffron sweet rice studded with raisin, almond and apricot, the dish that closes every dham

ingredients.note: long grain matters here - the rice must stay separate

ingredients.qty: a generous pinch, soaked in 2 tbsp warm water

ingredients.note: the Lahaul touch; dried apricot is the fruit these valleys actually grow

prepNotes: Soak the rice 30 minutes, then drain it in a sieve for a full 10 minutes. Wet rice will clump and this dish lives on separate grains.
Steep the saffron in 2 tbsp of warm - not boiling - water for 15 minutes so it gives up all its colour.
Have the sugar weighed out. It goes in after the rice is nearly cooked, and by then there is no time to measure.

steps.text: Heat 4 tbsp of the ghee in a heavy pot. Fry the almonds until pale gold, about 90 seconds, then the raisins until they puff, 20 seconds. Lift both out and set aside.
steps.tip: Raisins burn in seconds and turn bitter. Watch them, do not walk away.

steps.text: Into the same ghee add the cardamom, cloves and cinnamon and let them sizzle for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the drained rice and fry gently for 3 minutes, turning with a flat spoon, until every grain is glossy and a few have turned opaque white.
steps.tip: Turn, do not stir. Broken grains go mushy later.

steps.text: Pour in 550ml water with the pinch of salt and half the saffron liquid. Bring to a hard boil.
Drop the heat to low, cover and cook 10 minutes until the water is absorbed and the rice is about three-quarters done - still firm at the core.
steps.tip: This stage is the one that decides the dish. Add sugar to fully cooked rice and it goes sticky; add it too early and the rice never softens.

steps.text: Sprinkle the sugar evenly over the surface, add the apricots, and do not stir. Cover and cook on the lowest heat 8 minutes - the sugar will melt and be drawn down through the rice.
Uncover, drizzle over the last tablespoon of ghee and the remaining saffron water, and fold through once with a fork.
Fold in the fried almonds, raisins and the coconut slivers. Cover and rest off the heat 10 minutes.
Fluff once more with a fork and serve warm, in small portions - it is richer than it looks.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated, where it will firm up. Reheat covered with 1 tbsp of water and a little ghee on low, or steam 5 minutes; it is also good cold.

recipes.name: Patrode
recipes.subtitle: colocasia leaves layered with spiced gram flour, steamed into rolls and fried in slices

ingredients.note: catalogued as colocasia. You want the leaves, arbi patta, not the corm
keeps the paste from going rubbery
the acid that neutralises the itch in the leaves
use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free
for the final tempering

prepNotes: Choose young colocasia leaves. Old ones carry far more calcium oxalate and will leave your throat scratching however much tamarind you use.
Shave the thick central rib flat with a knife on the underside of each leaf, or the rolls will not lie flat.
Soak 30g tamarind in 150ml hot water for 20 minutes and strain to get the 3 tbsp of pulp. Do not skip it. It is doing chemistry, not just flavour.
The steamed rolls must cool completely, ideally 2 hours or overnight, before you slice them. Warm rolls crumble.

steps.text: Wipe the leaves clean and shave down the raised central ribs so each leaf lies flat.

Whisk the besan, rice flour, tamarind pulp, jaggery, ajwain, turmeric, chilli powder, coriander powder, cumin powder, hing and salt with enough water to make a thick spreadable paste, about the consistency of peanut butter.
steps.tip: Too thin and it runs out of the rolls in the steamer. It should cling to a spoon turned sideways.

steps.text: Lay a leaf shiny side down, spread a thin even layer of paste over it, and lay a second leaf on top facing the opposite way. Build stacks of 4 leaves.
steps.tip: Thin layers. A thick smear steams into a wet, gummy centre.

steps.text: Fold the two long sides of each stack inward, spread a little more paste on the folds, then roll up tightly from the base into a firm log.
Steam the rolls seam side down for 25-30 minutes, until a knife pushed into the centre comes out clean.
Cool the rolls completely, at least 2 hours, then cut into 1.5cm thick slices.
steps.tip: Cold rolls cut cleanly. This is the difference between neat rounds and a broken mess.

steps.text: Heat the mustard oil in a kadhai until it smokes, cut the heat for a minute, then pop the mustard seeds and sesame.
Lay the slices in a single layer and shallow fry 3 minutes a side until crisp and browned at the edges.
Drain, scatter with coriander leaves and serve hot with tea, or with rice and dal as part of a meal.

recipes.storage: The steamed rolls keep 4 days refrigerated unsliced and freeze for a month. Slice and fry straight from cold. Fried slices are best eaten the same day.

recipes.name: Rajma Madra
recipes.subtitle: red kidney beans in a thick soured-yogurt gravy, the dham version that eats richer than chana madra

ingredients.note: the small dark Chamba beans if you can get them
insurance against splitting
compounded-free hing keeps the dish gluten-free

prepNotes: Soak the rajma at least 10 hours, ideally overnight. Beans that have not swollen to twice their size will not cook through.
Bring the yogurt to room temperature and whisk it with the besan until it pours like thin cream.
Have the whole spices measured into one small bowl - once the ghee is hot they all go in together.

steps.text: Pressure cook the drained rajma with 700ml fresh water and 1 tsp salt for 6 to 7 whistles, then let the pressure fall naturally. A bean should collapse when pressed, with the skin still intact.
steps.tip: Never add the yogurt to half-cooked beans. Acid stops rajma softening dead.

steps.text: Heat the ghee in a heavy pan until it shimmers. Add cumin, black cardamom, green cardamom, cinnamon, cloves and bay leaves; they will foam and smell sweet within 30 to 40 seconds.
Add the asafoetida, then pull the pan off the flame and let it cool a full minute.
steps.tip: Hot ghee plus cold yogurt equals a grainy, broken gravy. The pause is not optional.

steps.text: Return the pan to the lowest heat and pour in the yogurt, stirring without pause for 8 to 10 minutes until it thickens and the raw sourness cooks off.
Stir in the coriander, fennel, dry ginger, turmeric and kashmiri chilli. Cook 3 minutes until the gravy turns a deep ochre and glossy.
Tip in the rajma with about 200ml of its cooking liquor and season with salt.
Crush a small ladleful of the beans against the side of the pan and stir back in - this thickens the gravy without flour.
steps.tip: Six or seven crushed beans is plenty; any more and you lose the texture.

steps.text: Simmer uncovered 25 minutes on low, stirring often, until the ghee separates and rises in a clear rim.
Sprinkle over the garam masala, cover and rest 10 minutes off the heat before serving with steamed rice.

recipes.storage: Refrigerates well for 3 days and thickens as it sits. Loosen with hot water and reheat on the lowest flame, stirring; do not let it boil hard or the yogurt will separate.

recipes.name: Sepu Vadi
recipes.subtitle: fried urad dal dumplings soaked soft in a spinach and yogurt gravy, the dish that marks a proper kangra dham

ingredients.note: thickens the gravy and holds the yogurt together
use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free

prepNotes: Soak the urad dal 5 hours. Drain it thoroughly - wet dal grinds into a batter that will not hold a shape.
Grind the dal with as little water as possible, then beat it by hand for 4 to 5 minutes until a spoonful floats in a glass of water. This aeration is what makes the vadis light.
Bring the yogurt to room temperature and whisk it with the besan so the gravy will not split.

steps.text: Grind the drained urad dal to a thick, coarse paste with the green chillies and grated ginger, using no more than 3 tbsp water.
steps.tip: Coarse, not silky. Sepu vadi should have a little bite left in it.

steps.text: Beat the paste vigorously for 4 to 5 minutes with salt until it lightens in colour and passes the float test.
Heat the frying oil to 170C. Drop in flat spoonfuls of the batter, four or five at a time, and fry 4 to 5 minutes until deep gold and firm. Drain on paper.
steps.tip: Too hot and the outside browns while the inside stays raw batter. A dropped bit should rise steadily, not violently.

steps.text: Cut each fried vadi in half through its thickness. This is what lets it drink up the gravy.
Boil the spinach in 200ml water for 4 minutes, then blend it to a smooth green puree with its liquid.
Heat the ghee in a kadhai, crackle the cumin, add the asafoetida and take the pan off the heat for a minute to cool.
On the lowest flame pour in the yogurt-besan mixture and stir continuously for 8 minutes until it thickens and stops smelling raw.
steps.tip: One direction, no stopping, low heat. If it splits there is no fixing it.

steps.text: Stir in the coriander powder, turmeric, kashmiri chilli, fennel and dry ginger, then the spinach puree and 200ml water. Season and simmer 8 minutes.
Slide in the halved vadis, cover and simmer very gently 10 minutes until they swell and turn spongy but still hold together.
steps.tip: Stir as little as possible now - a soaked vadi falls apart if you push it around.

steps.text: Finish with garam masala and coriander leaves and rest 5 minutes before serving with rice.

recipes.storage: Best the day it is made, while the vadis still have some structure. Keeps 2 days refrigerated; reheat covered on the lowest flame with a little water, without stirring.

recipes.name: Siddu
recipes.subtitle: steamed wheat buns risen slow and stuffed with crushed walnut and poppy seed, eaten swimming in ghee

image.alt: Siddu, the steamed stuffed bread of the hills

ingredients.note: sours the dough and helps it rise; yeast is traditional in Kullu, this is the everyday shortcut
for serving, and this is not the place to be shy
the Kullu filling; the nuts should be gritty, not powdered

prepNotes: The dough needs 3 hours in a warm place. In a cold kitchen sit the covered bowl over a pan of hand-hot water.
Dry roast the poppy seeds in a pan until they smell nutty and start popping, about 2 minutes, then cool before crushing.
Crush the walnuts in a mortar or under a rolling pin. A blender turns them to oily paste.

steps.text: Mix the atta, baking soda and 1 tsp salt. Work in the yogurt, then the lukewarm water a little at a time, to a soft dough slightly stickier than roti dough. Knead 8 minutes.
steps.tip: Softer than you think is right. A stiff dough steams into a dense brick.

steps.text: Oil the surface, cover with a damp cloth and leave in a warm spot for 3 hours. It should look puffed and feel airy, not doubled like bread.
Meanwhile mix the crushed walnuts, roasted poppy seeds, mustard oil, green chilli, ginger, coriander leaves, ajwain, cumin powder, chilli powder, black pepper and salt into a damp, crumbly filling.
Knock the dough back gently and divide into 8 balls. Do not knead it hard again.
Roll each ball into a 12cm disc. Put 2 heaped tbsp of filling on one half, fold over into a half moon and press the curved edge firmly, then pleat it shut with your fingers.
steps.tip: Seal properly or the filling weeps out and the siddu collapses in the steamer.

steps.text: Rest the shaped siddus, covered, for 15 minutes while the steamer comes up to a rolling boil.
Grease the steamer plate, arrange the siddus with 2cm between them and steam on high for 18 to 20 minutes.
steps.tip: Do not lift the lid before 15 minutes - the drop in steam makes them sink.

steps.text: Test with a skewer through the thickest part: it should come out clean and dry. Give them 3 more minutes if not.
Take them out, split the tops slightly and pour a tablespoon of melted ghee over each. Serve hot with mash dal or a chutney.

recipes.storage: Best within a few hours. Keeps 2 days refrigerated; re-steam 6 to 8 minutes to bring back the softness, or slice and pan-fry in ghee. Do not microwave - they go rubbery.

recipes.name: Thechwani
recipes.subtitle: crushed radish and potato simmered with hill spices, coarse-textured and peppery

ingredients.note: the fat white winter mooli, or use colocasia in the same way
use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free

prepNotes: Thechwani takes its name from thechna, to crush. The vegetables are pounded or hand-crushed into rough pieces, never cut into neat cubes.
Crush the radish and potato just before cooking; radish weeps water and goes limp if it sits.
If you use colocasia instead of radish, oil your hands before handling it to avoid the itch.

steps.text: Crush the radish and potato in rough 3cm pieces. Put them on a board and press down with the flat of a heavy knife, or pound with a pestle, so they split with ragged faces.
steps.tip: Those torn surfaces are the whole point: they hold masala the way a clean cut never will.

steps.text: Heat the mustard oil in a pressure cooker until it smokes lightly, then lower the heat.
Crackle the cumin and fenugreek seeds for 20 seconds, add the asafoetida, then the garlic, ginger and green chilli.
Fry 2-3 minutes until the garlic is gold and the raw smell is gone.
Stir in the turmeric, coriander powder and chilli powder off the heat for 10 seconds, then return to the flame.
Add the crushed radish and potato with the salt and fry on medium-high for 8 minutes, stirring, until the radish loses its sharp smell and starts to catch on the base.
steps.tip: This dry frying is what stops the radish tasting raw and watery in the finished dish. Do not shorten it.

steps.text: Pour in the water, close the cooker and cook for 3 whistles, then release the pressure naturally, about 10 minutes.
Open, mash a few pieces of potato against the side to thicken the gravy, and simmer uncovered 8-10 minutes until it clings rather than pools.
Stir in the dry ginger powder and crushed black pepper and cook 2 minutes more.
steps.tip: Dry ginger and pepper go in at the end so their warmth stays sharp rather than cooking flat.

steps.text: Rest 5 minutes, scatter coriander leaves and serve with rice or roti.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated; the flavour deepens overnight. Reheat on the stovetop with 2-3 tbsp of water.

recipes.name: Tudkiya Bhath
recipes.subtitle: chamba pahari rice cooked through with chana dal, potato and yogurt until every grain carries the masala
prepNotes: Soak the chana dal 2 hours and the rice 30 minutes, separately. They cook at very different speeds and the soaking is what brings them together.
Drain the rice in a sieve for 10 minutes before it goes in the pan so it fries rather than steams.
Whisk the yogurt to a pouring consistency and keep it out of the fridge.

steps.text: Heat the ghee and mustard oil together in a heavy pot until shimmering. Add the bay leaves, black cardamom, cinnamon, cloves and cumin and let them crackle for 30 seconds.
Add the sliced onion and fry on medium-high for 10 minutes until brown at the edges and shrunken to a third of its volume.
steps.tip: Real colour here is where the dish gets its depth. Pale onion gives a flat bhath.

steps.text: Stir in the garlic, ginger and green chillies and fry 1 minute until the raw smell goes.
Add the turmeric, coriander powder and kashmiri chilli, then the tomato. Cook 5 minutes until the tomato collapses and oil beads at the edge.
Take the pot off the heat for 30 seconds, then pour in the whisked yogurt on low and stir constantly for 4 minutes until it thickens and stops looking curdled.
steps.tip: Straight from fridge to hot pan is how this splits. Room temperature yogurt, low flame, keep stirring.

steps.text: Add the drained chana dal and potato cubes with 150ml water. Cover and simmer 10 minutes - the dal should be half done, still with a bite.
Fold in the drained rice as gently as you can and fry 2 minutes so each grain is coated.
Pour in 450ml hot water, add salt generously and the mint, and bring to a hard boil. Taste the water - it should be a shade saltier than you want the finished rice.
Cover tight, drop to the lowest flame and cook 12 minutes without lifting the lid.
Rest off the heat 10 minutes, then fork through with the garam masala and coriander leaves. Serve with plain yogurt.
steps.tip: Never stir with a spoon while it is hot - a fork lifted from the edge keeps the grains whole.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated. Reheat covered with 2 tbsp of water sprinkled over, on low or in a steamer, so the grains soften rather than dry out.

nutrition.caveat: Whey poured away when the milk is curdled means much of the weighed input is never eaten, so the real figures are likely lower.

recipes.name: Akoori on Toast
recipes.subtitle: soft-scrambled spiced eggs piled on buttered toast
prepNotes: Akoori is defined by being underdone. It should pour slightly, not hold its shape.
Everything else is cooked before the eggs go anywhere near the pan.

steps.text: Soften the onion in the butter, add the ginger, green chilli and turmeric and cook 2 minutes.
Add the tomato and cook just until it slumps, 2 minutes.
Beat the eggs with the cream and salt and pour them in over low heat.
Stir slowly and constantly, taking the pan off the heat every few seconds.
steps.tip: Off the heat repeatedly. That is how you get curds this soft.

steps.text: Pull it off while still visibly wet, fold in the coriander and pile onto the hot toast.
steps.tip: It carries on cooking on the plate. Wet in the pan is right.

recipes.storage: Eat immediately. Scrambled eggs do not keep or reheat.

recipes.name: Akuri
recipes.subtitle: soft-scrambled eggs loose with onion, chilli and coriander, eaten on buttered pav

ingredients.note: keeps the curd soft

prepNotes: Take the eggs out of the fridge 15 minutes ahead; cold eggs seize into hard lumps.
Chop the onion far finer than feels necessary. Coarse pieces stay raw and crunch against the soft egg.
Have the toast or pav ready before you start. Akuri waits for nobody.

steps.text: Beat the eggs with the milk, black pepper and salt just until streaky, about 15 strokes.
steps.tip: Over-beating aerates the eggs and they set spongy rather than creamy.

steps.text: Melt the butter in a small kadhai over medium-low heat until it foams but does not brown.
Add the onion and cook 4 minutes until soft and translucent, with no colour on it at all.
Stir in the ginger and green chilli and cook 1 minute until fragrant.
Add the turmeric and cumin powder, then the tomato, and cook 2 minutes until the tomato slumps but still holds shape.
steps.tip: Deseeding the tomato matters. The jelly makes akuri watery.

steps.text: Drop the heat to its lowest setting and pour in the eggs.
Push the eggs slowly from the edges to the centre with a flat spoon for 3 to 4 minutes, forming large soft curds.
steps.tip: Stop while it still looks slightly underdone and glossy. Carryover heat finishes it in the 30 seconds it takes to reach the table.

steps.text: Fold through the coriander leaves off the heat and serve immediately on buttered pav or toast.

recipes.storage: Akuri does not keep. Eat it within minutes of cooking. Refrigerated leftovers turn rubbery and weep water, and no reheating fixes it.

recipes.name: Berry Pulao
recipes.subtitle: saffron rice layered over spiced chicken, studded with sharp sour-sweet dried fruit

ingredients.note: for soaking the saffron
stand in for barberries, tossed in lemon juice for sourness
the second half of the sour-sweet fruit

prepNotes: Soak the basmati in cold water for 30 minutes, then drain in a colander for 10 minutes. This is the difference between separate grains and a clump.
Marinate the chicken in the yogurt, ginger-garlic paste, garam masala and salt for at least 1 hour, or overnight.
Steep the saffron in the warm milk for 20 minutes; it should stain the milk deep orange.
Toss the raisins and slivered apricot with the lemon juice and leave 15 minutes so they turn properly tart.

steps.text: Fry the sliced onion in 4 tbsp ghee over medium heat for 15 minutes until dark brown and crisp, drain on paper, and set a third aside for the garnish.
Fry the cashews in the same ghee for 1 minute until golden and set aside.
Add the marinated chicken to the pan with two thirds of the fried onion and cook uncovered 20 minutes over medium heat until the yogurt tightens around the meat.
steps.tip: If the yogurt splits, keep going and stir. It comes back together as the water cooks off.

steps.text: Stir in half the mint and coriander and cook 3 minutes more, then set the chicken aside off the heat.
Bring 3 litres of water to a rolling boil with the cinnamon, cloves, cardamom, bay leaf, black pepper and 2 tbsp salt.
steps.tip: Salt it like pasta water. This is the rice's only chance to be seasoned.

steps.text: Add the drained rice and boil 4 to 5 minutes, until a grain crushes between your fingers but still has a hard white core.
steps.tip: Seventy percent cooked, no more. The rice finishes on dum and mush is irreversible.

steps.text: Drain the rice immediately and spread it on a tray to stop the cooking.
Layer the chicken in a heavy pot, then the rice, then the lemon-soaked raisins and apricots, the reserved fried onion, cashews and the rest of the herbs.
Drizzle over the saffron milk and the remaining 1 tbsp ghee, seal the pot with a tight lid or foil, and cook on the lowest heat 20 minutes, or in a 160C oven for 25.
Rest 10 minutes sealed, then open and lift the pulao from the sides with a flat spoon so the layers stay visible.
steps.tip: Never stir it round. Fold and lift, or the grains break.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated. Reheat covered with 2 tbsp water sprinkled over, on low heat or in a 150C oven for 15 minutes, so the rice steams rather than dries.

recipes.name: Bhida Par Eeda
recipes.subtitle: okra fried dry with onion and eggs cracked over the top

ingredients.qty: 400g, wiped dry and cut into 2cm rounds

prepNotes: Wash the okra a good hour ahead and dry every pod with a cloth. Any water left on them turns the dish slimy.
Use a knife and board that are completely dry for the same reason.
Bring the eggs to room temperature.

steps.text: Heat 3 tbsp of the oil in a wide kadhai and fry the okra over high heat, undisturbed for the first 3 minutes so it sears rather than steams.
steps.tip: Do not stir constantly and do not cover the pan. Both make it slimy.

steps.text: Keep frying 8-10 minutes, turning occasionally, until the pieces are browned at the edges and no longer sticky. Lift them out onto a plate.
Add the last tbsp of oil and fry the onion until golden, 8 minutes.
Add the garlic and green chilli and fry 1 minute.
Stir in turmeric, chilli powder, cumin and coriander powder for 30 seconds.
Return the okra with salt, toss 2 minutes to coat, then spread it into an even layer.
Make four hollows and crack in the eggs. Season with salt and black pepper.
Cover and cook on low 7-9 minutes until the whites are set and the yolks still run.
steps.tip: If your lid does not fit well, add a tablespoon of water at the pan edge to raise steam.

steps.text: Squeeze over the lemon, scatter the coriander leaves and serve hot with rotli.

recipes.storage: Eat the same day. The okra will not stay crisp; leftovers keep 1 day refrigerated and are best reheated uncovered in a hot pan.

recipes.name: Chelo Kebab
recipes.subtitle: minced kebabs over buttered rice with a raw egg yolk, the Bombay club dish

ingredients.note: squeeze it, or the kebabs fall apart
traditionally raw on the hot rice; cook them if you prefer

ingredients.qty: a pinch, soaked in warm milk

prepNotes: Borrowed from Iranian chelo kabab and kept alive by Bombay's Irani restaurants. The butter, the saffron rice and the yolk are all part of it.
A raw yolk on hot rice is traditional. If you would rather not, a soft-cooked yolk does the same job.

steps.text: Mix the mince with the squeezed onion, ginger, garlic, pepper, chilli powder and salt. Knead 5 minutes until sticky.
steps.tip: The kneading develops the bind. Under-worked mince crumbles off the skewer.

steps.text: Rest the mixture in the refrigerator 30 minutes, then shape onto skewers in long flat kebabs.
Cook the rice, drain, and fold through half the butter and the saffron milk.
Grill or pan-fry the kebabs on high 4 minutes a side until charred outside and just cooked within.
Serve the kebabs on the rice, dot with the remaining butter and slide a yolk on top of each plate.

recipes.storage: The kebabs keep 2 days refrigerated. Cook the rice fresh and add the yolk at the table, never in advance.

recipes.name: Dar Ni Pori
recipes.subtitle: flaky ghee pastry packed with sweet lentil paste, made for Navroze and weddings

ingredients.note: for the dough, the filling and the frying
enriches the filling

prepNotes: Make the filling a day ahead if you can. It firms up in the fridge and is far easier to enclose cold.
The dough needs a full 30 minutes covered rest before rolling, or it will fight you and tear.
Work with 60g of dough and 60g of filling per pori. Weigh them, because uneven parcels burst.

steps.text: Pressure cook the toor dal with 500ml water for 4 whistles, until completely soft, then drain off every drop of liquid.
steps.tip: Wet dal makes a filling that will not hold. Drain it hard and dry it out in the pan if you must.

steps.text: Blend or mash the dal to a smooth paste while still warm.
Cook the dal paste with the sugar and 2 tbsp ghee over low heat, stirring, 15-18 minutes, until it pulls away from the pan in one mass.
steps.tip: Keep stirring and keep the heat low. Sugar and dal catch on the base and taste burnt through the whole batch.

steps.text: Take it off the heat and fold in the ground almonds, pistachios, khoya, cardamom, nutmeg and rose water. Cool completely, then divide into 8 balls.
For the dough, rub 60g melted ghee and the salt into the maida until it clumps when squeezed, then add the water a little at a time to make a firm, smooth dough.
Knead 5 minutes, coat with a spoon of ghee, cover and rest 30 minutes.
Divide the dough into 8, roll each into a 12cm disc, place a filling ball in the centre and gather the edges over the top, pinching them shut.
Flatten each parcel gently and roll it out to about 18cm, sealed side down, using light even pressure.
steps.tip: Roll from the centre outward and stop the moment the filling shows through. A burst pori leaks sugar into the pan.

steps.text: Cook on a medium tawa 2-3 minutes a side until pale gold flecks appear.
Spoon a tablespoon of ghee around each pori and fry 1-2 minutes more per side until deep golden and crisp.
Cool on a rack. They crisp as they cool and are traditionally cut into wedges.

recipes.storage: Keeps a week in an airtight tin at room temperature and a month refrigerated. Warm briefly on a dry tawa before serving to bring back the crispness.

recipes.name: Dhansak
recipes.subtitle: sunday mutton simmered into a purée of four dals and gourds, sour and gently hot

image.alt: Parsi dhansak with caramelised brown rice

ingredients.qty: 700g, shoulder on the bone, cut into 4cm pieces
ingredients.note: bone is what makes the gravy
the backbone of the dal mix
red pumpkin, for sweetness
the bitter note that defines dhansak
the sliced one is for the brown onion garnish
stand in for dhansak masala

prepNotes: Rinse the four dals together and soak them 45 minutes; they cook far more evenly.
Bring the mutton to room temperature 30 minutes ahead so it browns instead of steaming.
Soak the tamarind in hot water while the dals cook, then squeeze and strain out the fibres.

steps.text: Pressure cook the drained dals with the pumpkin, eggplant, methi leaves, chopped onion, tomato, turmeric and 1 litre of water for 5 whistles, about 20 minutes.
steps.tip: The vegetables melt away. That is the point. Do not keep them chunky.

steps.text: Meanwhile heat 3 tbsp oil in a heavy pan and brown the mutton in two batches over high heat, 5 minutes a batch.
steps.tip: Crowding the pan is the single most common mistake; the meat will grey instead of crusting.

steps.text: Pound the garlic, ginger and green chilli to a coarse paste and fry it in the same pan for 2 minutes, until the raw smell lifts.
Add the cinnamon, cloves, cardamom, black pepper, coriander powder, cumin powder, chilli powder and garam masala and fry 90 seconds, splashing in 2 tbsp water when it catches.
Return the mutton, add 200ml water, cover and simmer 45 minutes until a knife slides into the meat with no resistance.
Cool the dal mixture slightly, fish out any large spice pieces, and blend to a smooth, pourable purée.
steps.tip: Blend it hot and it will spit. Wait ten minutes, and leave the lid vented.

steps.text: Pour the purée over the mutton, add the tamarind extract, jaggery and salt, and simmer uncovered 20 minutes, stirring every few minutes.
steps.tip: It sticks readily once thick. Use a flat wooden spoon and scrape the base.

steps.text: Taste and balance. It should land sour first, then sweet, then hot. Add tamarind or jaggery a teaspoon at a time.
Fry the sliced onion in the remaining 2 tbsp oil until dark brown and crisp, about 10 minutes over medium heat.
Rest the dhansak 10 minutes off the heat, then top with the fried onion, mint and coriander leaves.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated and freezes well for 2 months. It thickens overnight. Loosen with hot water and reheat gently, as a fast reheat scorches the dal.

recipes.name: Jardaloo Ma Gosht
recipes.subtitle: mutton braised with dried apricots until the gravy turns sweet, sour and dark

ingredients.note: Hunza apricots with the stone in are the traditional choice
for colour without more heat
cane vinegar if you have it

ingredients.qty: 2 medium, cut into fine matchsticks and fried crisp
ingredients.note: the sali topping

prepNotes: Soak the apricots in 200ml warm water for 30 minutes. Keep the soaking water. It goes into the gravy.
Bring the mutton to room temperature and pat it dry, or it will steam rather than brown.
If you are making sali at home, soak the potato matchsticks in cold water 15 minutes, dry them thoroughly, then fry in batches.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a heavy pan and fry the cinnamon and cloves for 30 seconds, until the cloves swell.
Add the sliced onion and cook over medium heat until deep brown, 18-20 minutes, stirring so the edges do not catch.
steps.tip: This is where the colour of the dish comes from. Brown, never black. Burnt onion turns the whole gravy bitter.

steps.text: Stir in the ginger and garlic paste and fry 2 minutes, until the raw smell goes.
Add turmeric, coriander, cumin, chilli powder and Kashmiri chilli. Fry 40 seconds with a splash of water so they do not scorch.
Add the mutton and brown it hard for 8 minutes, until the pieces are sealed and the oil separates at the edges.
Add the tomato and salt, cover, and cook 10 minutes until the tomato collapses into the masala.
Pour in the water, bring to a boil, then simmer covered 55-65 minutes until the mutton is tender. In a pressure cooker, 4 whistles then 10 minutes on low.
Add the soaked apricots with their water, the jaggery and the vinegar. Simmer uncovered 12 minutes.
steps.tip: Add the apricots this late or they dissolve. You want them whole and plump against the meat.

steps.text: Taste and balance: it should read sweet first, then sour, then hot. Adjust with a little more jaggery or vinegar.
steps.tip: Balancing is the whole recipe. Do it off the heat, a teaspoon at a time.

steps.text: Stir in the garam masala, rest 5 minutes off the heat, and pile the fried sali on top just before serving.
steps.tip: Sali goes on at the table. Sat in the gravy it goes soft in two minutes.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated and tastes better on day two. Reheat gently with a splash of water; fry fresh sali rather than reheating old.

recipes.name: Kheema Par Eeda
recipes.subtitle: spiced mutton mince with eggs baked into the surface, soft yolks over dry kheema

ingredients.note: for cracking over the eggs

prepNotes: Use a wide pan with a lid. You need enough surface area to sit four eggs apart from each other.
Bring the eggs to room temperature so the whites set evenly on the hot kheema.
The kheema must be dry before the eggs go on. Wet mince makes the whites run together into a puddle.

steps.text: Heat the ghee in a wide kadhai and fry the onion until golden brown, 12 minutes.
Add ginger, garlic and green chilli and fry 2 minutes.
Add turmeric, chilli powder, coriander and cumin powder, and fry 30 seconds.
Add the mince and break it up with the back of a spoon, frying 8 minutes until it loses all pinkness and starts to catch.
steps.tip: Break the lumps early. Once the mince sets in clumps you will not get it smooth again.

steps.text: Add the tomato and salt and cook 6 minutes until the tomato disappears into the mince.
Add the water, cover, and simmer 12 minutes, then uncover and cook off every trace of liquid, about 5 minutes.
steps.tip: Dry means dry. Tilt the pan and no gravy should run.

steps.text: Stir through the garam masala, coriander leaves and mint, then level the surface and press four shallow wells with the back of a spoon.
Crack an egg into each well, season with salt and the coarse black pepper.
Cover and cook on the lowest heat 8-10 minutes, until the whites are opaque and the yolks still wobble.
steps.tip: Check at 8 minutes. A minute too long and you lose the runny yolk that makes the dish.

steps.text: Bring the pan to the table and serve with pav or rotli.

recipes.storage: Best eaten straight away for the soft yolks. Leftover kheema alone keeps 2 days refrigerated; reheat and crack fresh eggs onto it.

recipes.name: Kolmi no Patio
recipes.subtitle: prawns in a thick red tamarind masala that is fiery, sour and sweet at once

ingredients.note: for colour

prepNotes: Soak the dried red chillies in hot water for 20 minutes before grinding, or the masala will stay gritty.
Toss the prawns with 1/2 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt and leave 15 minutes, then rinse and pat dry.
Squeeze the tamarind and strain out the fibres and seeds before you begin cooking.

steps.text: Grind the soaked chillies, garlic, ginger, cumin seeds, kashmiri chilli and 2 tbsp of the soaking water to a smooth red paste.
steps.tip: Grind it properly smooth. Patio should be a paste-thick masala, not a chunky curry.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a kadhai and fry the curry leaves for 20 seconds until they crackle and go translucent.
Add the onion and cook 10 minutes over medium heat until soft and pale gold.
Add the ground masala and fry 6 to 8 minutes, stirring constantly, until the oil pools around the edges and the raw garlic smell disappears.
steps.tip: This is the whole dish. Under-fried masala tastes harsh no matter how much jaggery you add later.

steps.text: Stir in the turmeric, coriander powder and tomato and cook 6 minutes until the tomato has collapsed completely.
Add the tamarind extract, jaggery, vinegar and salt and simmer 5 minutes to a thick, glossy masala.
Taste and balance the three points. Sour, sweet, hot. It should be assertive on all three, since the prawns will mute it.
Slide in the prawns, stir to coat, and cook 3 to 4 minutes only, until they curl and turn opaque.
steps.tip: Prawns go rubbery the moment they overcook. Take the pan off the heat while they still look barely done.

steps.text: Rest 5 minutes off the heat, scatter with coriander leaves, and serve with plain rice or rotli.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated. Reheat only until warm through. A second full simmer will toughen the prawns. The masala base alone freezes 2 months.

recipes.name: Lagan nu Custard
recipes.subtitle: the dense baked wedding custard, caramel-topped and heavy with nutmeg and cardamom
prepNotes: Reduce the milk well ahead. This is the step that takes the time, and rushing it gives a loose, watery custard.
Bring the eggs to room temperature so they blend into the warm milk without scrambling.
Preheat the oven to 160C a full 20 minutes before baking, and set a tray of hot water on the lower shelf.

steps.text: Boil the milk in a wide heavy pan and simmer 30 minutes, stirring often, until reduced to about 600ml.
steps.tip: Scrape the sides back in as it reduces. Those caramelised scrapings are where the flavour lives.

steps.text: Stir in the condensed milk and sugar and simmer 5 minutes more, then take off the heat and cool to lukewarm.
Beat the eggs until just smooth, with no strands of white remaining.
Pour a ladle of the warm milk into the eggs while whisking, then repeat twice before adding the eggs back into the pan.
steps.tip: Tempering is not optional. Tip cold eggs into hot milk and you get sweet scrambled egg.

steps.text: Whisk in the ground cardamom, nutmeg and rose water.
Strain the mixture through a fine sieve into a ghee-rubbed baking dish about 25cm across.
steps.tip: Straining catches the inevitable few threads of cooked egg and is what makes the texture silky.

steps.text: Scatter the slivered almonds and pistachios over the surface.
Bake at 160C for 45 to 55 minutes, until the edges are set and the centre wobbles like a soft jelly when nudged.
steps.tip: A cracked, puffed surface means it went too far. Pull it while the middle still moves.

steps.text: If the top has not browned, run it under a hot grill for 2 minutes until patched with dark caramel spots.
Cool completely at room temperature, at least 3 hours, before cutting into squares.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate up to 4 days, covered. Serve chilled or at room temperature. It is never reheated, and it firms up and tastes better on the second day.

recipes.name: Machhi No Saas
recipes.subtitle: pomfret poached in a pale sweet-sour sauce thickened with egg and rice flour

ingredients.qty: 600g pomfret or seer, cut into 4 steaks

ingredients.note: the traditional thickener
cane vinegar

prepNotes: Rub the fish steaks with salt and a squeeze of the vinegar and leave 20 minutes, then rinse and pat dry.
Grind the garlic, green chilli, cumin seeds and ginger to a fine paste with 2 tbsp water before you start cooking.
Slake the rice flour in 4 tbsp cold water and keep it beside the stove. Added dry it will lump instantly.

steps.text: Heat the oil and cook the onion gently until soft and translucent but not coloured, 8 minutes.
steps.tip: Saas is a pale sauce. Brown onion here and it will look and taste wrong.

steps.text: Add the ground garlic-chilli-cumin paste and fry 2 minutes, until it stops smelling raw.
Pour in the water with salt, bring to a simmer, and cook 5 minutes.
Stir in the slaked rice flour and simmer 4 minutes, stirring, until the sauce coats a spoon lightly.
Slide in the fish steaks in a single layer and poach on low 8-10 minutes, spooning sauce over rather than turning them.
steps.tip: Turning breaks the steaks. Baste instead.

steps.text: Lift the fish out onto a serving dish and keep it warm.
Beat the eggs with the vinegar until smooth.
Take the pan off the heat, wait a minute, then trickle in the egg-vinegar mixture in a thin stream while whisking hard.
steps.tip: Off the heat and slowly. Straight into a boiling pan the egg scrambles and the sauce is ruined.

steps.text: Return to the lowest heat with the sugar and stir 2 minutes until the sauce thickens to a thin custard. It must not boil.
Taste for the sweet-sour balance, pour over the fish, scatter with coriander and serve with plain boiled rice.

recipes.storage: Eat the same day. Refrigerated it keeps 1 day; reheat over the gentlest heat or in a bain-marie, as a boil will split the egg-thickened sauce.

recipes.name: Margi Na Farcha
recipes.subtitle: chicken marinated overnight, dipped in beaten egg and fried crisp for wedding lunches

ingredients.qty: 800g, 8 bone-in thigh and drumstick pieces, skin off

ingredients.note: into the egg batter

prepNotes: Slash each piece of chicken to the bone twice and marinate overnight, or at least 4 hours, refrigerated.
Take the chicken out of the fridge 30 minutes before frying so it cooks through evenly.
Beat the eggs only when the chicken is cooked and cooling. Batter beaten too early goes flat.

steps.text: Mix the ginger and garlic paste, all the ground spices, the vinegar, lemon juice and salt into a thick marinade.
Rub it hard into the slashed chicken, working it into the cuts, and refrigerate overnight.
steps.tip: The cuts matter. Without them the marinade sits on the surface and the meat inside tastes of nothing.

steps.text: Tip the chicken with all its marinade into a wide pan, add the water, cover, and cook over medium heat 18-20 minutes, turning once.
Uncover and cook off the liquid until the pieces are coated in a thick, almost dry masala. Cool completely on a plate.
steps.tip: The chicken must be cool and dry, or the egg coating slides off in the oil.

steps.text: Beat the eggs with a pinch of salt and the chopped coriander until pale and frothy.
Heat the oil in a kadhai to 175C. A drop of batter should rise and sizzle in 3 seconds.
Dip a chicken piece in the egg, let the excess drip for two seconds, and lower it into the oil away from you.
Fry 2-3 pieces at a time for 3-4 minutes, spooning egg over any bald patches, until the coating is golden and puffed.
steps.tip: Crowding drops the oil temperature and the coating turns greasy instead of crisp.

steps.text: Drain on a rack, not paper, so the underside stays crisp.
Serve hot with lemon wedges and a plate of rotli, or alongside pulao dal.

recipes.storage: Best within an hour of frying. The cooked, unfried masala chicken keeps 2 days refrigerated. Bring it to room temperature and egg-fry to order.

recipes.name: Mawa Cake
recipes.subtitle: dense cardamom cake made with reduced milk, sold by every Irani bakery

ingredients.note: mawa; it is what makes this a mawa cake and not a sponge
generous; the cake should smell of it across the room

prepNotes: Mawa cake is deliberately dense. If it comes out light and airy, something has gone wrong.
Crumble the khoya finely and warm it slightly so it blends rather than sitting in lumps.

steps.text: Cream the butter and sugar until pale, then beat in the crumbled khoya.
Add the eggs one at a time, beating well between each.
Fold in the flour, soda and ground cardamom, then loosen with the milk to a thick dropping consistency.
steps.tip: Fold, do not beat. Beating at this stage is what makes it rise like a sponge, which is not what this is.

steps.text: Pour into a lined tin, scatter the almonds and bake at 170C for 40 minutes.
Test with a skewer at the centre; a few moist crumbs are right, wet batter is not.
Cool completely in the tin before cutting.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate it in an airtight tin, up to a week. Mawa is milk boiled down to a solid and there is egg in it besides, so the fridge is the default rather than the hot-weather exception. It is better on day two. Bring it back to room temperature before eating.

recipes.name: Mutton Pulao Dal
recipes.subtitle: brown-rice mutton pulao served with a smooth toor dal, the Sunday lunch of Parsi homes

ingredients.note: caramelised, for the brown colour of the rice
for the dal

prepNotes: Soak the rice 30 minutes and drain it in a colander for 15 more, so the grains are damp but not wet.
Make the caramel first and have it cool in a cup: 2 tbsp sugar melted in a dry pan to a dark mahogany, killed with 2 tbsp hot water.
The dal and the pulao cook in parallel. Start the dal first. It can sit while the rice steams.
Take the mutton out of the fridge 30 minutes ahead.

steps.text: For the dal, pressure cook the toor dal with the tomato, turmeric, half the chilli powder, salt and 700ml water for 5 whistles, then blend smooth and keep warm.
steps.tip: Blend it properly. Parsi dal is silk, not a textured tadka dal.

steps.text: Heat 2 tbsp ghee, crackle the cumin seeds, add 1 sliced onion and fry to deep gold, then pour this over the dal.
For the pulao, heat 4 tbsp ghee in a heavy pot and fry the remaining sliced onion until dark brown, 20 minutes. Lift out half and reserve for the top.
steps.tip: Twenty minutes on medium, not ten on high. Rushed onion is bitter and pale in the same breath.

steps.text: Add cinnamon, cloves, cardamom, black cardamom, bay leaves and peppercorns to the pot and fry 1 minute.
Add the ginger and garlic paste, fry 2 minutes, then add the mutton and brown it 8 minutes.
Add the rest of the chilli powder, salt and 700ml water. Pressure cook 4 whistles, or simmer covered 60 minutes, until the mutton is tender.
Strain the meat from the stock. Measure the stock and make it up with water to 900ml. This is what the rice will drink.
steps.tip: Getting the liquid right is the difference between separate grains and porridge.

steps.text: Bring the stock to a boil with the caramel, the garam masala and salt. It should taste slightly too salty on its own.
Stir in the drained rice and the mutton, boil hard 4 minutes until craters appear on the surface, then cover tightly and cook on the lowest heat 15 minutes.
Rest, still covered, for 10 minutes off the heat before opening.
steps.tip: Do not lift the lid early. The last of the steam is what finishes the top layer of rice.

steps.text: Fork the rice through gently, scatter the reserved brown onion and coriander over, and serve with the hot dal in a bowl alongside.

recipes.storage: Rice and dal both keep 2 days refrigerated, stored separately. Reheat the rice covered with a sprinkle of water; loosen the dal with water and bring it back to a bare simmer.

recipes.name: Papeta Ma Gosht
recipes.subtitle: everyday mutton and potato stew, gently spiced and thickened by the potatoes themselves
prepNotes: Cut the potatoes big (quarters, not chunks) or they will disintegrate before the mutton is done.
Keep the peeled potatoes in cold water until they go into the pan so they do not grey.
Take the mutton out of the fridge 30 minutes ahead.

steps.text: Heat the oil and fry the chopped onion over medium heat until soft and pale gold, about 10 minutes.
steps.tip: This is a gentler dish than jardaloo ma gosht. Do not brown the onion hard.

steps.text: Add ginger and garlic paste with the slit green chillies and fry 2 minutes.
Add turmeric, chilli powder, coriander and cumin powder. Fry 30 seconds.
Add the mutton and brown 6 minutes, turning the pieces so each face colours.
Add the tomato and salt and cook 8 minutes until the tomato has broken down and the oil rises.
Pour in the water and simmer covered 45 minutes, or pressure cook 3 whistles and release naturally.
Add the potatoes, cover, and cook 20 minutes more until a knife slides through them with no resistance.
steps.tip: Crush two potato pieces against the side of the pan. That is what thickens the gravy.

steps.text: Stir in the garam masala and simmer uncovered 5 minutes to reduce to a pouring consistency.
Finish with coriander leaves and the lemon juice, and rest 5 minutes before serving with rotli or plain rice.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated. Reheat over low heat with a little water; the potatoes soak up gravy overnight, so expect to loosen it.

recipes.name: Papeta par Eeda
recipes.subtitle: eggs baked on a bed of soft spiced potatoes, the everyday parsi supper

ingredients.qty: 500g, peeled and cut into thin matchsticks

ingredients.note: neutral oil works, but ghee is the traditional fat

prepNotes: Cut the potato into fine even matchsticks. Thick pieces stay hard while the eggs overcook waiting for them.
Rinse the cut potato and dry it well so it fries rather than steams.
Use a wide pan you can cover, so all the eggs sit in a single layer on the potato.

steps.text: Heat the ghee in a wide kadhai and fry the sliced onion 6 minutes until soft and lightly golden.
Add the green chilli and cook 1 minute.
Stir in the turmeric, cumin powder and chilli powder and fry 30 seconds.
Add the potato matchsticks with 1 tsp salt and toss until every strand is coated yellow.
Sprinkle over 3 tbsp water, cover, and cook 12 to 14 minutes on low, shaking the pan every few minutes.
steps.tip: Shake rather than stir. Stirring breaks the potato into mash.

steps.text: Uncover and check. A matchstick should give completely under a spoon but the mass should still be loose, not sticky.
Fold in half the coriander leaves, then flatten the potato into an even bed and make five shallow wells with the back of a spoon.
Crack one egg into each well, season with salt and black pepper, cover, and cook on the lowest heat 6 to 8 minutes.
steps.tip: Cover it. The steam is what sets the tops. Lift the lid at 6 minutes and check; the whites should be opaque and the yolks still liquid.

steps.text: Scatter the remaining coriander over and bring the pan straight to the table with pav or rotli.

recipes.storage: Best eaten straight from the pan. Leftover potato base keeps 2 days refrigerated and reheats well in a covered pan. Cook fresh eggs on it rather than reheating set ones.
