recipes.name: Sindhi Biryani
recipes.subtitle: sharply sour, chilli-hot mutton biryani layered with potato, yogurt and dried fruit

image.alt: Sindhi biryani with potato and plum

ingredients.note: Sindhi biryani is meant to be hot
stands in for the aloo bukhara (dried plums) traditionally used. Same sweet-sour job, slightly less tart

ingredients.qty: a good pinch, soaked in 3 tbsp warm milk
3 litres for the rice, plus 1 cup

prepNotes: Marinate the mutton in the yogurt, ginger, garlic, chilli powder and turmeric for at least 1 hour, or overnight refrigerated.
Wash the rice until the water runs clear, then soak it 30 minutes and drain. Skipping this gives you broken, sticky grains.
Fry the birista (browned onion) first and set it aside. It goes into both the masala and the layers.
Bring the marinated meat to room temperature 20 minutes before cooking so the yogurt does not split on contact with the hot pan.

steps.text: Fry the sliced onion in the oil over medium heat, 15-18 minutes, stirring, until deep brown and shrunken. Drain on paper and reserve.
steps.tip: Pull them out a shade lighter than you want. They darken as they cool, and burnt birista turns the whole biryani bitter.

steps.text: In the same oil, crackle the cumin, bay leaf, cinnamon, cloves, cardamom and black cardamom for 30 seconds.
Add the marinated mutton and fry on high for 6-8 minutes, until the yogurt has dried onto the meat and the fat runs clear at the edges.
steps.tip: Keep the heat high and do not cover it yet, or the meat stews grey instead of catching colour.

steps.text: Stir in the tomato, coriander powder, half the green chilli, half the mint and coriander, and two-thirds of the birista. Cook 5 minutes until the tomato collapses.
Add 1 cup water and salt, close the cooker and cook 4 whistles, then 12 minutes on low. Release the pressure and boil off any thin liquid. The masala should be thick and clinging.
Fry the halved potatoes in a little oil until golden on the cut faces, then fold them into the meat with the dried apricot and cook 5 minutes.
Meanwhile bring 3 litres of well-salted water to a rolling boil, add the drained rice and cook 5-6 minutes only. A grain should snap in two when pressed, still white at the core. Drain immediately.
steps.tip: This is the moment biryani is won or lost. Seventy percent cooked, no more; it finishes on the dum.

steps.text: Spread half the rice over the meat in a heavy pot, scatter the remaining birista, mint, coriander and green chilli, then the rest of the rice.
Drizzle over the saffron milk, kewra water and ghee.
Seal the pot with a tight lid, cook 2 minutes on high, then set it on the lowest possible heat (or a tawa under the pot) for 25 minutes.
steps.tip: No peeking. Every lift of the lid loses the steam that is cooking the top layer.

steps.text: Rest 10 minutes off the heat, then open and lift the rice from the sides with a flat spoon rather than stirring.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated. Reheat portions covered with 1 tbsp water over low heat or in a steamer for 10 minutes. A microwave dries the grains and toughens the mutton.

recipes.name: Sindhi Chicken Curry
recipes.subtitle: chicken in a yogurt and onion gravy, sharp with green chilli and garam masala
prepNotes: Marinate the chicken with the yogurt, half the ginger-garlic paste, turmeric and salt for 30 minutes in the refrigerator.
Whisk the yogurt until completely lump-free before it goes anywhere near the chicken, or it will split into curds in the pan.
Slice the onions thin and even so they brown at the same rate.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a kadhai and fry the onion 12 minutes over medium heat, until deep golden brown and shrunken to a third of its volume.
steps.tip: This is the backbone of the gravy. Pull it off pale and the curry tastes thin all the way through.

steps.text: Add the remaining ginger-garlic paste and the green chilli, and fry 1 minute.
Add the tomato and cook 8 minutes, mashing with the back of the spoon, until it breaks down and oil pools at the edges.
Stir in the chilli powder, coriander powder and cumin powder and fry 30 seconds. No longer, or they scorch.
Turn the heat to low and add the marinated chicken with all its yogurt, stirring continuously for the first 2 minutes.
steps.tip: Low heat and constant stirring are what stop the yogurt splitting. Once it is incorporated you can relax.

steps.text: Raise the heat and fry the chicken 8 minutes until the pieces are opaque and the masala clings to them.
Add the water and salt, bring to a boil, then cover and simmer 18 minutes until the chicken is tender at the bone.
Uncover and reduce 5 minutes to the gravy consistency you want.
Stir in the garam masala and lemon juice, rest 5 minutes covered, then finish with coriander leaves.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated. Reheat over low heat with a splash of water; the yogurt gravy can split if you boil it hard from cold.

recipes.name: Sindhi Dodo
recipes.subtitle: thick pearl millet flatbread studded with onion and green chilli, eaten with ghee

ingredients.note: buy it fresh. Bajra flour goes rancid within weeks

prepNotes: Use warm water, not cold. Bajra has no gluten to hold it together and warm water helps the starch bind the dough.
Chop the onion very fine. Coarse pieces tear the dodo apart the moment you try to pat it out.
Rest the dough 10 minutes before shaping so the flour hydrates fully and the dough stops crumbling.
Keep a bowl of water beside the tawa for wetting your palms while patting.

steps.text: Mix the bajra flour, onion, green chilli, coriander leaves, ajwain and salt in a wide bowl.
Add the warm water a little at a time, working with your knuckles, until you have a firm dough that just holds together when squeezed.
steps.tip: Bajra dough never becomes smooth and elastic like wheat. Stop when it holds a ball without cracking apart.

steps.text: Cover and rest the dough 10 minutes.
Divide into 6 balls. Wet your palms and pat one ball out on a sheet of plastic or a damp cloth into a disc about 12cm across and 6mm thick.
steps.tip: Pat, do not roll. A rolling pin cracks bajra dough at the edges; wet fingertips seal any cracks as they form.

steps.text: Heat the tawa over medium heat until a drop of water skitters across it.
Lift the disc on your palm and lay it flat on the tawa. Cook 2 minutes until the underside sets and dulls in colour.
Flip and cook 2 minutes more, then press the edges down with a folded cloth so the whole surface contacts the pan.
steps.tip: Pressing the edges is what makes a dodo puff slightly and cook through the thick middle.

steps.text: Flip once more and cook 1 minute until brown spots appear and the bread feels firm rather than doughy at the centre.
Smear generously with ghee and repeat with the remaining dough.
Serve hot with curd, garlic chutney or leftover sai bhaji.

recipes.storage: Best eaten straight off the tawa. They keep 1 day wrapped in a cloth and are traditionally reheated on the tawa, never in a microwave, which turns them leathery.

recipes.name: Sindhi Kadhi
recipes.subtitle: roasted gram flour and tamarind curry thick with drumstick and okra, the Sunday lunch of every Sindhi house

ingredients.note: roasting this properly is the whole dish
whole seeds, not kasuri methi
use compounded-free hing if you need this strictly gluten-free
fried separately so it does not go slimy

ingredients.qty: walnut-sized ball, soaked in 100ml hot water

prepNotes: Soak the tamarind in 100ml hot water for 20 minutes, then squeeze and strain out the pulp.
Cut all the vegetables before you start. Once the besan is roasted the pot moves quickly.
Keep the 1.2 litres of water hot on a second burner. Cold water into hot besan is how lumps happen.

steps.text: Heat 3 tbsp oil in a kadhai, crackle the fenugreek seeds and cumin, then the mustard seeds, curry leaves and hing.
steps.tip: Fenugreek turns bitter fast, 10 seconds, until it just darkens, then move on.

steps.text: Tip in the besan and roast on low heat, stirring constantly, 8-10 minutes until it is sandy-brown and smells like toasted biscuit.
steps.tip: This is the step people rush. Pale besan gives a raw, pasty kadhi no amount of simmering will fix.

steps.text: Add the tomato, ginger and green chilli and cook 3 minutes until the tomato slumps.
Take the pan off the heat and pour in the hot water in a thin stream, whisking hard the whole time until smooth.
steps.tip: Off the heat and whisking is the anti-lump insurance. If lumps form anyway, pass it through a sieve now.

steps.text: Return to the heat, add the turmeric, chilli powder and salt, and bring to a boil. Simmer 10 minutes. It will thin out and then start to body up.
Add the drumstick and carrot and simmer 10 minutes.
Add the cluster beans and potato and simmer another 12-15 minutes, until a knife slides into the potato with no resistance.
Meanwhile fry the okra in the remaining 1 tbsp oil over high heat for 5-6 minutes, until the cut edges are dry and no longer ropy.
steps.tip: Never boil okra straight into the kadhi. Frying it first is the difference between kadhi and glue.

steps.text: Stir in the tamarind pulp and the fried okra and simmer 5 minutes. Taste: it should be assertively sour against the nutty besan.
Scatter the coriander over and let it stand 10 minutes off the heat before serving with plain rice or bhuga chawal.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated and tastes better on day two. It thickens as it sits. Loosen with hot water and reheat gently, but add the okra fresh if you want it firm.

recipes.name: Sindhi Seero
recipes.subtitle: coarse semolina halwa, heavy with ghee and cardamom, made for every good occasion

ingredients.note: seero is not a dish to make lean
for a softer set

prepNotes: Bring the water, milk and sugar to a boil in a separate pan and keep it simmering. The syrup must be hot when it meets the rava or the halwa turns lumpy.
Sliver the almonds and have the cardamom crushed before you start roasting. Once the rava is in the ghee you cannot step away.
Use a heavy kadhai. Thin pans scorch the rava on one side while the rest is still pale.

steps.text: Bring the water, milk and sugar to a boil in a saucepan, stir until the sugar dissolves, and keep it on the lowest heat.
Melt the ghee in a heavy kadhai over low heat and fry the raisins for 30 seconds until they puff, then lift them out.
Fry the slivered almonds in the same ghee for 1 minute until pale gold, and lift them out too.
Add the rava to the ghee and roast over low-medium heat for 10-12 minutes, stirring constantly.
steps.tip: Go by smell and colour: it should turn the shade of wet sand and smell toasted, like biscuits. This is the whole flavour of the dish.

steps.text: Add the pinch of salt and the crushed cardamom and stir for 30 seconds.
Take the kadhai off the heat and pour in the hot syrup in a steady stream, stirring hard with your other hand.
steps.tip: Off the heat and pouring slowly. It will spit violently. Stand back and keep the spoon moving or it will seize into lumps.

steps.text: Return to low heat and cook 6-8 minutes, stirring, until the rava has drunk all the liquid and the mass pulls cleanly away from the sides of the pan.
Stir in most of the fried almonds and raisins, keeping some back.
Cover and rest off the heat for 5 minutes so the grains swell and soften fully.
steps.tip: Skipping this rest leaves a faintly gritty seero. It costs five minutes.

steps.text: Fluff with a fork, scatter the reserved nuts and raisins, and serve warm.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated. It firms up solid when cold. Reheat portions covered with 1 tbsp milk, or steam for 5 minutes to bring back the soft texture.

recipes.name: Sindhi Teevan
recipes.subtitle: everyday mutton and potato curry with a thin, tomato-sharp gravy

ingredients.note: they thicken the gravy as much as they feed you

prepNotes: Take the mutton out of the fridge 30 minutes ahead so it browns instead of stewing.
Puree the tomatoes rather than chopping them. Teevan gravy should be smooth and pourable, thin enough to eat with rice.
Halve the potatoes and hold them in cold water so they do not discolour while the meat browns.

steps.text: Heat the oil in the pressure cooker and crackle the cumin, bay leaf, cinnamon and black cardamom for 30 seconds.
steps.tip: The cumin should sizzle the moment it lands. If it sits silent the oil is too cool and the spices will stew.

steps.text: Add the onion and fry 10 minutes over medium heat until evenly golden brown.
Stir in the ginger and garlic pastes and cook 90 seconds, until the raw smell lifts.
Add the mutton and brown over high heat 8 minutes, turning the pieces so every side catches colour.
Add the turmeric, chilli powder, coriander powder and salt, and stir for 1 minute to coat the meat.
Pour in the tomato puree and cook 10 minutes, until it darkens to brick red and oil separates at the sides.
steps.tip: Undercooked tomato leaves a sour, tinny edge that no amount of simmering later will fix.

steps.text: Add the water, close the cooker and cook on high pressure 15 minutes, about 3 whistles. Release the pressure naturally.
Open, add the potatoes, and simmer uncovered 15-18 minutes until a knife slides through them with no resistance.
steps.tip: Adding potatoes at the start turns them to mush; they need only the last stretch.

steps.text: Taste for salt, stir in the garam masala, and simmer 2 more minutes.
Scatter the coriander leaves and serve with plain rice or phulka.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated. The potatoes soften further on standing, so reheat gently with a splash of water and do not stir hard.

recipes.name: Sindhi Tomato Chutney
recipes.subtitle: slow-cooked sweet and sour tomato relish with garlic and a mustard tempering

ingredients.note: or the juice of 1 lemon at the end
for colour more than heat

prepNotes: Use properly ripe tomatoes. Underripe ones stay sour and watery no matter how long you cook them down.
Soak the tamarind in 3 tbsp warm water for 15 minutes and press the pulp through a sieve before you start.
Sterilise the jar you will store it in. A wet or dirty jar will spoil the chutney within days.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a heavy pan and crackle the mustard seeds until they pop, about 40 seconds.
steps.tip: Wait for the popping to actually start. Unpopped mustard seeds taste raw and faintly bitter.

steps.text: Add the cumin, nigella, crushed fennel and broken red chillies, and fry 20 seconds.
Add the sliced garlic and ginger and fry 1 minute until the garlic is just golden at the edges.
Tip in the tomatoes with the turmeric, kashmiri chilli and salt, and stir well.
Cook uncovered over medium heat for 15 minutes, stirring every few minutes, until the tomatoes have collapsed and lost their raw smell.
Stir in the jaggery and tamarind pulp and cook 12 minutes more, until the chutney darkens and thickens.
steps.tip: The test: draw a spoon through the middle of the pan and the trail should stay open for a second before closing.

steps.text: Taste and balance. More jaggery if it is too sharp, more tamarind if it is flat.
Take off the heat and cool completely in the pan before jarring.
steps.tip: Jarring it warm creates condensation in the lid, which is exactly how chutney grows mould.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 weeks refrigerated in a sterilised jar. Always use a dry spoon. It thickens as it chills and is served cold or at room temperature.

recipes.name: Tidali Dal
recipes.subtitle: three lentils cooked together into one soft, garlicky everyday dal

ingredients.note: use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free

prepNotes: Soak the chana dal separately for 30 minutes. It is the toughest of the three and will otherwise still be firm when the moong has dissolved.
Rinse all three dals until the water runs clear, four or five changes. Cloudy dal foams over in the cooker.
Add salt only after the dal is cooked; early salt keeps the chana dal grainy.

steps.text: Drain the soaked chana dal and pressure cook all three dals with the water, turmeric and green chilli for 12 minutes, about 3 whistles.
steps.tip: Let the pressure drop on its own. Forcing it makes the dal watery and grey.

steps.text: Open the cooker and whisk the dal briefly. You want the moong broken down but the chana still holding as distinct grains.
Heat the oil in a small pan and crackle the cumin seeds for 20 seconds.
Add the asafoetida and the sliced garlic and fry 1 minute until the garlic is golden but not brown.
steps.tip: Garlic goes from gold to bitter in about 15 seconds. Pull it the moment it colours.

steps.text: Add the onion and ginger and fry 6 minutes until the onion is soft and lightly browned.
Stir in the tomato and chilli powder and cook 6 minutes until the tomato collapses to a jammy mass.
Pour the tempering into the dal, add salt, and simmer 8 minutes so the flavours settle.
steps.tip: If it thickens past a pourable consistency, loosen it with hot water, never cold.

steps.text: Stir in the garam masala and lemon juice off the heat.
Scatter the coriander leaves and serve with plain rice.

recipes.storage: Keeps 4 days refrigerated and thickens considerably. Reheat with 1/4 cup hot water per portion and re-check the salt.

recipes.name: Chettinad Chicken Curry

ingredients.note: thigh and drumstick hold up better than breast
sambar onions, not big onions
Indian gingelly oil, not toasted East Asian sesame oil
or 4 tbsp whole coriander seeds, dry-roasted and ground with the rest
kalpasi, the black lichen that gives Chettinad masala its smoke
to finish

prepNotes: Rub the chicken with the turmeric and 1 tsp salt then cover and refrigerate it 20 minutes while you roast the masala.

steps.text: Dry-roast the red chillies, coriander powder, black pepper, cumin, fennel, poppy seeds, cinnamon, cloves, star anise and stone flower in a dry pan over low heat for 4-5 minutes.
steps.tip: Low heat only. The moment the fennel smells sweet and the pan starts to smoke faintly, take it off. Burnt pepper cannot be rescued.

steps.text: Add the grated coconut to the same pan and roast a further 3 minutes until it turns the colour of weak tea.
Cool the mixture completely, then grind to a fine powder, add 100ml water and grind again to a smooth thick paste.
steps.tip: Grinding hot spices steams the jar and gives you a gummy paste instead of a fine one.

steps.text: Heat the gingelly oil in a kadhai and add the bay leaf and curry leaves; they will spit for a few seconds.
Add the shallots and fry over medium heat for 8 minutes until soft and browning at the edges.

Add the tomatoes and cook 5 minutes until they collapse and the oil starts to separate at the sides.
Stir in the ground masala paste and fry on low for 6-8 minutes, scraping the base, until the oil rises dark red around the edges.
steps.tip: This fry-down is the whole dish. Under-fry it and the curry tastes of raw spice powder.

steps.text: Add the chicken and turn it in the masala for 5 minutes so every piece is coated and sealed.
Pour in 200ml water, season with salt, cover and simmer 20-25 minutes until the chicken is tender and the gravy clings.
steps.tip: Chettinad kuzhambu is a coating gravy, not a soup. If it looks thin, uncover and boil hard for 3 minutes.

steps.text: Rest off the heat 5 minutes, then scatter the coriander leaves and serve with rice or dosai.

recipes.name: Chettinad Eral Masala

ingredients.note: gingelly oil; the Chettinad kitchen fat
or 1 large onion, finely sliced
for the ground masala
2 tbsp whole seeds, dry-roasted, if you have them
the backbone of the dish
kalpasi; the smoky note nothing else gives
or fresh coconut

prepNotes: Grind the masala fresh. This is the whole difference between Chettinad and a generic South Indian prawn curry. Pre-ground powders taste flat here.
Pat the prawns bone dry and salt them 10 minutes before cooking so they do not weep into the masala.

steps.text: Dry-roast the red chillies, coriander, pepper, fennel, cumin, stone flower, star anise, cinnamon, cloves, cardamom and poppy seeds in a dry pan over low heat, 4-5 minutes.
steps.tip: Low heat and constant movement. The fennel should smell sweet, not scorched. Burnt masala cannot be rescued.

steps.text: Add the grated coconut to the same pan and roast a further 2 minutes, until it turns the colour of milky tea. Cool completely.

steps.tip: Cool before grinding or the blender steams and you get a gritty paste.

steps.text: Heat the gingelly oil in a kadhai and fry the curry leaves for 10 seconds until they blister.
Add the shallots and cook over medium heat until soft and gold at the edges, about 8 minutes.
Stir in the crushed garlic and ginger and fry 2 minutes, until the raw smell goes.

steps.tip: This frying stage is where the raw edge goes. Undercook it and the curry tastes powdery.

steps.text: Pour in 150ml water, bring to a simmer and cook 4 minutes to a thick, clinging gravy.
Slide in the prawns, cover and cook 3-4 minutes, until they curl and turn opaque. Turn off the heat immediately.

steps.text: Finish with lemon juice and coriander leaves, and rest 5 minutes before serving with rice or dosai.

recipes.name: Chettinad Idiyappam
recipes.subtitle: steamed rice-flour string hoppers, soft as lace, eaten with coconut and curry

ingredients.note: roasted idiyappam flour if you can find it
for the dough and for greasing the plates
scattered on the hoppers
only if serving with sweet coconut milk

prepNotes: You need an idiyappam press (sevai nazhi) with the finest plate, and a steamer with flat perforated trays.

steps.text: Bring the water to a rolling boil with the salt and 1 tbsp of the coconut oil.
Pour the boiling water over the flour all at once and mix with the handle of a wooden spoon until there is no dry flour left.
steps.tip: All at once, not in stages. Dribbling water in gives you lumps you will never knead out.

steps.text: Cover and let it sit 5 minutes so the flour drinks the water.

steps.tip: If it cracks, sprinkle in hot water a spoon at a time. If it sticks, dust with a little dry flour.

steps.text: Grease the steamer plates with coconut oil and scatter a teaspoon of grated coconut on each.
Fill the press, and squeeze the dough onto the plates in overlapping spirals, one layer thick.
Steam 6-8 minutes, until the strands turn from chalky white to glossy and translucent at the edges.
steps.tip: Over-steaming makes them wet and they clump. Pull them the moment they look glossy.

steps.text: Rest 2 minutes before lifting them off. They firm up and release cleanly.
Repeat with the rest of the dough, keeping it covered between batches.
Serve warm with the remaining grated coconut, and a mutton or chicken kuzhambu, or with sweetened coconut milk.

Drain it thoroughly and let it sit in the colander 10 minutes; wet dal needs extra water to grind and gives flat vadas.

Add the salt only just before frying; salted batter goes watery within minutes.

steps.text: Grind the drained dal with 2 to 3 tbsp of ice-cold water, in short bursts, to a thick fluffy paste.
steps.tip: Every extra spoon of water costs you crispness. Scrape down rather than adding more.

steps.text: Beat the batter with your hand for 3 minutes until it lightens in colour and feels aerated.
Test it by dropping a pinch into a bowl of water. It should float within seconds.
steps.tip: If it sinks, beat for another 2 minutes; unaerated batter fries dense.

steps.text: Fold in the pepper, cumin, ginger, chilli, curry leaves, coriander, hing and salt.
Heat the oil to 170C. A drop of batter should rise steadily, not shoot to the surface.
Wet your palm, take a lime-sized ball of batter, flatten it and make a hole through the centre with a wet thumb.
Slide the vada off your palm into the oil from close to the surface, and fry 4 or 5 at a time.
Fry 4 to 5 minutes, turning once, until deep gold and the sizzle drops to a quiet crackle.
steps.tip: That quietening means the water has cooked out and the shell has set.

steps.text: Drain on a rack rather than paper so the underside stays crisp, and serve immediately with coconut chutney.

recipes.storage: Best within the hour. Leftovers keep a day refrigerated; refresh in a 180C oven for 6 minutes rather than a microwave, which turns them leathery.

recipes.name: Milagu Kuzhambu
recipes.subtitle: a dark, peppery tamarind gravy roasted from whole spices, the household cure-all

ingredients.qty: a lime-sized ball, soaked in 300ml hot water

ingredients.note: the whole point of the dish; do not reduce it
for the roast, not for body
stirred into the roasted spices at the end
use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free
rounds off the tamarind
the quantity is deliberate; this gravy is preserved by its oil

prepNotes: Soak the tamarind in hot water for 20 minutes, then squeeze it out and strain. Discard the fibres and seeds.
Roast the spices on a genuinely low flame. This is the step the whole dish rests on and it cannot be hurried.
Milagu kuzhambu tastes better the day after it is made. Consider cooking it a day ahead.

steps.text: Dry roast the peppercorns, the three dals, the red chillies and fenugreek seeds in a kadhai over low heat for 6 to 8 minutes until the dals are reddish gold and the pepper smells sharp.
steps.tip: If the fenugreek darkens past honey brown the whole pot turns bitter. It is the first thing to burn.

steps.text: Turn off the heat, stir in the coriander powder and one sprig of curry leaves, and let the residual heat toast them for 30 seconds.
Cool completely, then grind to a fine powder in a dry blender.
steps.tip: Grind only when cold. Warm spices smear into a paste in the jar.

steps.text: Heat the sesame oil in the same kadhai and crackle the mustard seeds, then add the remaining curry leaves and the asafoetida.
Pour in the strained tamarind water with the turmeric and salt and bring to a rolling boil.
Boil hard, uncovered, for 8 minutes to cook out the raw edge of the tamarind.
Whisk the ground spice powder with 60ml water to a slurry and stir it in.
steps.tip: Making a slurry first stops the powder from seizing into lumps in the hot liquid.

steps.text: Simmer 10 to 12 minutes over low heat until the gravy thickens and the oil separates and floats in a dark ring on top.
steps.tip: The floating oil is the finish line. Take it off any earlier and it will not keep.

steps.text: Stir in the jaggery, cook 2 minutes more and take off the heat.
Serve a spoonful over hot rice with a poriyal and a papad.

recipes.storage: Because of the oil and tamarind this keeps 10 days refrigerated in a glass jar, and improves for the first three. Always spoon it out with a dry spoon. Reheat only the portion you need.

recipes.name: More Kuzhambu
recipes.subtitle: sour yogurt curry with ground coconut and cumin, never boiled

ingredients.note: fresh sweet yogurt gives a flat curry
okra or chow chow are the other usual choices
ground with the coconut; this is what stops the yogurt splitting
adds a rounder body to the paste
any more and the curry turns bitter
use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free

prepNotes: Soak the raw rice and toor dal together for 20 minutes so they grind smooth.
Take the yogurt out of the fridge early. Cold yogurt hitting a hot pan splits immediately.
Whisk the yogurt with 1/2 cup water until there is no lump left anywhere.

steps.text: Simmer the ash gourd in 1 cup water with the turmeric and salt for 8 minutes, until translucent at the edges.
Grind the coconut, cumin, green chilli, soaked rice and toor dal with 1/2 cup water to a very smooth paste.
steps.tip: Any grit left in the paste will be obvious in the finished curry.

steps.text: Add the paste to the cooked gourd and simmer 6 minutes, until the raw rice smell disappears.
Take the pan off the heat and let it stop bubbling completely, about 2 minutes.
Pour in the whisked yogurt, stirring constantly as it goes.
Return to the lowest possible heat and warm it only until steam rises and it thickens slightly.
steps.tip: The moment it boils, the yogurt curdles into grains. Take it off before you think you should.

steps.text: Check the salt and take it off the heat entirely.
Heat the coconut oil, pop the mustard seeds, add the fenugreek, red chilli, curry leaves and hing.
steps.tip: Fenugreek burns black in seconds. Add it after the mustard has finished popping.

steps.text: Pour the tempering over and serve with hot rice and a dry poriyal.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated and gets sourer. Reheat only to warm on the lowest heat, stirring; it will split if it boils.

recipes.name: Murukku
recipes.subtitle: spiralled rice flour crisps, the snack tin that is never empty

ingredients.note: the roasted dal is what makes it crisp rather than hard
or ghee; the fat is what stops it being a jaw-breaker

prepNotes: The dough should be soft enough to press and stiff enough to hold a spiral. Too soft and it breaks in the oil.
Fry on steady medium. High heat browns the outside while the inside stays raw and chewy.

steps.text: Dry roast the urad dal until it smells nutty and turns pale gold, cool, and grind to a fine flour.
Mix both flours with the sesame, cumin, asafoetida, salt and softened butter, rubbing until it resembles crumbs.
Add water a little at a time to a smooth, soft dough. Do not let it get sticky.
Press spirals directly onto a greased sheet using a murukku press with the star plate.
Slide them into medium-hot oil and fry until the bubbling stops and they turn pale gold, about 5 minutes.
steps.tip: When the hissing stops, the water has gone and they are done. Colour alone will mislead you.

steps.text: Drain on paper and cool completely before storing.
steps.tip: Completely. Stored warm they go soft overnight.

recipes.name: Mutton Chukka Varuval
recipes.subtitle: slow-cooked mutton fried down dry until every piece is coated in black masala

ingredients.note: shoulder or leg
gingelly oil
or 2 onions, finely sliced
one for the pot, two for the finish
half in the masala, half at the end
kalpasi
for the pressure cooker

prepNotes: Chukka means dry. The mutton is cooked soft first, then fried until the gravy has vanished into a coating. Plan for two stages and do not shortcut the second.
Bring the mutton to room temperature for 30 minutes before cooking; cold meat straight from the fridge seizes and takes longer to tenderise.
Goat, not lamb, if you can get it. The flavour holds up to this much pepper.

steps.text: Dry-roast the chillies, coriander, fennel, cumin, stone flower, star anise, cinnamon, cloves and 1 tsp of the pepper over low heat for 5 minutes, until fragrant and a shade darker. Cool and grind fine with the coconut.
steps.tip: Roast on the lowest flame you can hold. Scorched kalpasi turns the whole dish bitter.

steps.text: Pressure cook the mutton with turmeric, half the crushed garlic and ginger, one sprig of curry leaves, salt and 250ml water for 5 whistles, then 15 minutes on low.
Release the pressure naturally and check: the meat should give when pressed with a spoon. If not, cook 2 more whistles.
steps.tip: Do not proceed with tough mutton. No amount of frying later will soften it.

steps.text: Drain the mutton, keeping the stock. Heat the gingelly oil in a kadhai and fry the remaining curry leaves 10 seconds.
Add the shallots and fry over medium heat until deep brown at the edges, about 10 minutes.
Add the rest of the garlic and ginger, fry 2 minutes, then add the ground masala and fry 4 minutes with a splash of the stock.
Tip in the drained mutton and toss so every piece is coated. Add 100ml of the reserved stock.
Now fry it down over medium-low heat, stirring every couple of minutes, for 20-25 minutes, until the liquid is gone and the masala clings darkly to the meat.
steps.tip: This is the whole dish. Stop while it is still glossy and slightly sticky, not powder-dry.

steps.text: Crush in the remaining 1 tsp pepper off the heat, scatter the coriander leaves and rest 5 minutes.
steps.tip: Pepper added at the end stays sharp and floral; pepper cooked from the start goes flat.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated and tastes better on day two. Reheat dry in a hot pan for 3-4 minutes; a microwave steams it and loses the crust.

recipes.name: Mutton Kola Urundai
recipes.subtitle: deep-fried mince and lentil balls, dense and heavy with pepper and fennel

ingredients.note: lean; too much fat and the balls fall apart
the binder and the texture
the signature note of kola urundai
kalpasi
insurance if the mix is loose

prepNotes: Soak the chana dal 1 hour, then drain it thoroughly. Wet dal makes a mix that will not hold its shape.
Boil the mince with turmeric and salt for 10 minutes and drain it well before grinding. Cooking first is what gives kola urundai its tight, dense bite.
Chill the ground mixture 20 minutes before rolling. Cold mix rolls smooth and does not crack in the oil.

steps.text: Boil the minced mutton with the turmeric, salt and 100ml water for 10 minutes, until it is cooked and dry. Drain and cool.
Dry-roast the pepper, fennel, cumin, chillies, cloves, cinnamon, star anise and stone flower for 3 minutes over low heat, then cool.
Grind the drained chana dal coarsely with the roasted spices. You want texture, not a paste.
steps.tip: Grind dry. Adding water here is the single most common reason kola urundai disintegrate in the oil.

steps.text: Add the cooked mince, shallots, garlic, ginger, curry leaves, coconut and coriander leaves and pulse to a thick, sticky mass.
Check the bind by rolling one ball. If it cracks or sags, work in the rice flour a spoon at a time. Chill 20 minutes.
Roll into smooth balls the size of a small lime, about 18 of them, pressing firmly.
Heat the oil to 170C. A pinch of the mix should rise in 3 seconds without browning instantly.
steps.tip: Too hot and the outside blackens while the middle stays raw-tasting; too cool and they soak up oil and break.

steps.text: Fry in batches of 5-6 for 5-6 minutes, turning, until deep mahogany brown and firm.
Drain on paper and rest 3 minutes before eating.

recipes.name: Nandu Rasam
recipes.subtitle: thin, fiercely peppery crab broth drunk from a tumbler before the meal

ingredients.note: shells cracked; the shell carries the flavour

ingredients.qty: small lime-sized ball, soaked in 400ml warm water
10 cloves, lightly crushed with skin on

ingredients.note: half ground with cumin, half crushed at the end
use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free
for the tempering
gingelly oil

prepNotes: Ask the fishmonger to clean the crabs but keep the shells cracked and the claws on. Almost all the flavour of nandu rasam comes out of the shell.
Soak the tamarind in warm water 20 minutes and squeeze it out well; the rasam should be sour enough to make you blink.
Rasam must never boil hard once the tamarind water is in. It goes cloudy and bitter.

steps.text: Pound the pepper, cumin, dried chillies and 4 of the garlic cloves coarsely in a blender. Pulse it, do not powder it.
steps.tip: Coarse pepper floats and perfumes the broth. Fine powder sinks and makes it muddy.

steps.text: Boil the crab pieces in 600ml water with turmeric and salt for 10 minutes. Skim the grey foam off the top.
steps.tip: Skimming is what keeps the finished rasam clear.

steps.text: Lift the crab out and set aside; keep the cooking liquor.
Add the tamarind water, crushed tomatoes, remaining garlic, one sprig of curry leaves and half the pounded masala to the crab liquor.
Simmer uncovered 12 minutes, until the raw sourness of the tamarind has gone and the liquid smells sweet at the edges.
Return the crab, add the rest of the pounded masala and bring just to the point of frothing. Bubbles at the rim, no rolling boil. Turn it off.
steps.tip: The moment a rasam boils it loses its top note. Catch it at the froth.

steps.text: In a small pan heat the gingelly oil, crackle the mustard seeds, add the fenugreek, asafoetida and remaining curry leaves, and pour it over.
Cover and rest 5 minutes, then stir through the coriander leaves and serve hot with rice, or on its own in small steel tumblers.

recipes.name: Paal Paniyaram
recipes.subtitle: fried rice-and-urad dumplings soaked in warm sweet coconut milk

ingredients.note: idli rice or any short grain
the paal; fresh-pressed if you can
or 120g sugar
adjust to how sweet your jaggery is
a few pieces fried in the oil for the top
or a neutral oil
for grinding and melting the jaggery

prepNotes: Soak the rice and urad dal separately for 4 hours. They grind to different textures and must be ground apart.
The batter needs to be thick enough to drop from a spoon and hold a round shape. Thinner and the dumplings flatten and drink oil.
A short 2-3 hour ferment at room temperature gives a lighter dumpling, but this version works unfermented too if you are in a hurry.
Warm the coconut milk gently and never boil it. It splits and turns grainy.

steps.text: Grind the soaked urad dal with 50ml water to a light, fluffy paste, 4-5 minutes in the blender.
steps.tip: The urad should almost double in volume and feel airy. This is where the softness comes from.

steps.text: Grind the soaked rice separately with 50ml water to a slightly grainy paste, like fine semolina.
Fold the two together with the salt to a thick dropping batter. Rest 30 minutes.
Melt the jaggery in 100ml water over low heat, then strain out the grit.
steps.tip: Jaggery always carries sand and fibre. Straining is not optional.

steps.text: Warm the coconut milk with the strained jaggery syrup, the crushed cardamom and the sugar over the lowest heat, until it just steams. Take it off and keep it warm.
steps.tip: Do not let it bubble. Boiled coconut milk splits and the dish is ruined.

steps.text: Heat the coconut oil in a kadhai to 170C. Fry the coconut pieces for 30 seconds until gold and lift them out.
Drop in teaspoons of batter, 8-10 at a time, and fry 4-5 minutes, turning, until they puff and turn even gold.
steps.tip: Keep the heat medium. Rushed at high heat they brown outside and stay raw and sour in the middle.

steps.text: Drain briefly, then drop the hot dumplings straight into the warm sweetened coconut milk.
Let them soak at least 20 minutes, until they have swollen and gone soft all the way through.
Serve warm or at room temperature, topped with the fried coconut.

recipes.storage: Best the day it is made. Keeps 2 days refrigerated, though the dumplings go softer and denser. Bring back to room temperature or warm very gently; do not boil.

recipes.name: Paruppu Payasam
recipes.subtitle: moong dal pudding sweetened with jaggery and finished in coconut milk

ingredients.note: roasting is what gives payasam its nutty depth
dark jaggery for colour and a deeper taste
the traditional finish; it keeps the sweetness from cloying

prepNotes: Dry-roast the moong dal on low heat for 5 minutes until golden and fragrant, then rinse and drain it.
Melt the jaggery with 1/2 cup water and strain it. Jaggery almost always carries grit.
Keep the thick coconut milk aside and do not let it near a boil later.

steps.text: Pressure cook the roasted dal with 2 cups water for 4 whistles until completely soft.
Mash the cooked dal lightly with a ladle, leaving some texture.
Melt the jaggery with 1/2 cup water on low heat, then strain out the sediment.
Add the strained jaggery syrup to the dal and simmer 8 minutes until it thickens and darkens.
steps.tip: Cooking the jaggery into the dal, rather than just stirring it in, is what makes it taste finished.

steps.text: Stir in the thin coconut milk and simmer 3 minutes more.
Take the pan off the heat and let it stop bubbling before adding the thick coconut milk.
steps.tip: Thick coconut milk splits into curds if it boils. Off the heat, always.

steps.text: Stir in the cardamom and dry ginger powder.
Heat the ghee in a small pan and fry the coconut slivers to gold, then the cashews, then the raisins until they puff.
steps.tip: They brown at different speeds, so add them in that order, about 20 seconds apart.

steps.text: Pour the ghee and fried garnish over the payasam and serve warm.

steps.tip: No flip. It cooks through from one side.

ingredients.qty: 1 cup raw, cooked firm and spread out to cool
large lime-sized ball, soaked in 1.5 cups hot water

bitter if you use more

recipes.name: Sakkarai Pongal
recipes.subtitle: rice and moong dal cooked soft in jaggery syrup with cardamom and fried cashew

ingredients.note: dark kolhapuri or paagu vellam, not sugar
this is a ghee dish; do not cut it back
the traditional finishing note alongside cardamom
cooks the rice softer than water alone

prepNotes: Dry roast the moong dal for 3 minutes before cooking it. The raw smell has to go, and it is what makes pongal smell like pongal.
Grate the jaggery rather than chopping it so it dissolves evenly.
Have the ghee warm and ready; cold ghee added to hot pongal seizes into streaks.

steps.text: Dry roast the moong dal in a pan over medium heat for 3 minutes until it smells nutty and turns a shade darker.
Wash the rice and roasted dal together, then pressure cook with the milk and 500ml water for 5 whistles.
steps.tip: Five whistles, not three. Sakkarai pongal wants the grains collapsed, not separate.

steps.text: Let the pressure fall naturally, open, and mash the rice and dal together with a ladle until creamy.
Meanwhile melt the jaggery with 150ml water in a separate pan over medium heat, stirring, then strain through a sieve to remove grit.
steps.tip: Always strain jaggery. Even good blocks carry sand and cane fibre.

steps.text: Boil the strained syrup 4 minutes until it thickens slightly and coats a spoon.
Pour the hot syrup into the mashed rice and stir over low heat for 8 to 10 minutes until the mixture pulls away from the sides of the pan.
steps.tip: Keep the flame low from here on. Jaggery scorches on the base and the burnt taste spreads through the whole pot.

steps.text: Fry the cashews, coconut slivers and raisins in 2 tbsp of the ghee until the nuts are golden and the raisins plump, then tip them in with their ghee.
Stir in the remaining ghee a spoonful at a time, along with the crushed cardamom and dry ginger powder.
Cook 2 minutes more until glossy, then serve warm.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated. It sets firm when cold, so reheat with 2 tbsp milk and an extra spoon of ghee, stirring until it loosens back to a soft spoonable mass.

recipes.name: Sambar
recipes.subtitle: Toor dal and vegetables in a tamarind broth, built on freshly ground sambar powder

ingredients.note: sambar onions
or sesame oil

prepNotes: Cook the tamarind broth and the vegetables together before the dal goes in. Vegetables added to dal never take on the sourness properly.
Sambar powder loses its aroma quickly. If yours has been open six months, it is doing very little.

steps.text: Pressure cook the toor dal with turmeric until completely soft, then whisk it smooth.
Simmer the tamarind extract with the shallots, tomato and harder vegetables, the sambar powder and salt for 12-15 minutes.
steps.tip: Cook the raw edge off the tamarind before the dal goes in.

steps.text: Add quicker vegetables like okra for the last 5 minutes.
Stir in the whisked dal and enough hot water to reach a pourable consistency. Simmer 8 minutes; do not boil hard.
Temper mustard seeds, fenugreek, dried chilli, curry leaves and asafoetida in oil and pour it in.
Add jaggery if the tamarind is sharp, finish with coriander, and rest 10 minutes before serving.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated and thickens; loosen with hot water. Freezes 2 months, though okra softens.

recipes.name: Seedai
recipes.subtitle: small rice flour spheres fried crisp for Krishna Jayanthi
prepNotes: Seedai has a reputation for bursting in the oil. Two things cause it: air pockets in the balls and undissolved salt.
Dissolve the salt in the water before it touches the flour, and roll each ball smooth with no cracks.

steps.text: Sieve the flours together. Dissolve the salt and asafoetida in a little water and add that, not dry salt.
steps.tip: Undissolved salt crystals are the classic cause of a seedai exploding.

steps.text: Rub in the butter and coconut, then bring together into a stiff dough with water.
Roll small marble-sized balls, keeping each one completely smooth with no cracks.
steps.tip: A crack is where the steam gets in. Roll them properly.

steps.text: Spread the balls on a cloth and air-dry 20 minutes.
Fry a small batch on medium first as a test. If it holds, fry the rest until the bubbling stops.
steps.tip: Test batch first, and stand back from the pan for the first minute.

steps.text: Drain and cool completely.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 weeks in an airtight tin at room temperature. The coconut is what limits it; beyond that it can turn.

recipes.name: Thattai
recipes.subtitle: flat, crisp rice discs studded with dal and curry leaf

ingredients.note: the studs; they should stay whole and crunchy

prepNotes: Thattai means flat. They are pressed thin by hand between plastic sheets, not rolled.
Prick each disc before frying or it puffs into a ball.

steps.text: Mix the flours, soaked chana dal, torn curry leaves, sesame, asafoetida, chilli powder, salt and butter.
Add water gradually to a stiff dough. It should not be sticky.
Take small balls and flatten each between two greased plastic sheets into thin discs.
Prick each disc several times with a fork.
steps.tip: This is not optional. Unpricked thattai balloons and cooks unevenly.

steps.text: Fry on medium until the bubbling subsides and they are pale gold and rigid, about 4 minutes.
Drain and cool completely before storing.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 weeks in an airtight tin at room temperature. If they soften, 5 minutes in a low oven brings them back.

recipes.name: Thayir Vadai
recipes.subtitle: fried urad dal vadas soaked soft in seasoned yogurt, cold and gently spiced

ingredients.note: use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free
thick, fresh and not sour
loosens the yogurt and keeps it mild

ingredients.qty: 1.5 litres warm, for soaking the vadas

prepNotes: Soak the urad dal 3 hours. Any longer and the batter absorbs oil like a sponge.
Grind the batter with as little water as you can manage. Ice cold water, a tablespoon at a time.
Whisk the yogurt with the milk and salt an hour ahead and keep it refrigerated so it is properly cold when the vadas go in.

steps.text: Drain the soaked dal thoroughly and grind to a thick, fluffy white batter, adding cold water a tablespoon at a time. A blob dropped in water should float.
steps.tip: The float test is not optional. A batter that sinks makes dense, oily vadas.

steps.text: Beat the batter by hand for 2 minutes to aerate it, then fold in the green chilli, ginger, crushed pepper, chopped curry leaves, asafoetida and salt.
Heat the oil to 170C. Wet your palm, flatten a lime-sized ball of batter on it and make a hole through the centre with your thumb.
Slide the vadas into the oil, 4 at a time, and fry 4 to 5 minutes turning once, until pale gold, not dark.
steps.tip: Fry these lighter than you would a standalone medu vada. They have to soften in yogurt later.

steps.text: Drain on paper, then drop the hot vadas straight into a bowl of warm salted water for 15 minutes.
Lift each vada out and press it gently between your palms to squeeze out the water. It should feel like a wrung sponge.
steps.tip: Squeeze firmly but slowly, or the vada tears in half.

steps.text: Arrange the vadas in a single layer in a shallow dish and pour the cold yogurt-milk mixture over them.
Refrigerate at least 2 hours so the vadas drink up the yogurt and swell.
Just before serving, heat 1 tbsp of the frying oil and crackle the mustard seeds, red chillies and remaining curry leaves, and pour it over.
Dust with chilli powder, scatter the coriander and serve cold.

recipes.storage: Best on the day it is assembled. Keeps 2 days refrigerated but the vadas slump and the yogurt turns sour after that. Never freeze. Serve straight from the fridge.

recipes.name: Thengai Sadam
recipes.subtitle: leftover rice tossed through toasted coconut, dals and curry leaves

ingredients.note: day-old rice, grains separate
use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free

prepNotes: Cook the rice at least 2 hours ahead, spread it on a wide plate and let it cool completely. Warm rice turns this to mush.
Grate the coconut fresh. Desiccated coconut will not give the moisture this dish needs.

steps.text: Spread the cooled rice on a wide plate, sprinkle with salt and 1 tbsp of the coconut oil, and separate the grains with your fingers.
steps.tip: Oiling the rice before anything else is added keeps the grains from clumping later.

steps.text: Dry roast the grated coconut in a kadhai over low heat for 4 to 5 minutes until it just turns pale gold and smells toasted. Set aside.
steps.tip: Stop while it is blonde. Brown coconut tastes of caramel and overwhelms the dish.

steps.text: Heat the remaining coconut oil in the same kadhai and crackle the mustard seeds.
Add the urad dal, chana dal and cashews and fry until all three are golden, about 2 minutes.
Add the red chillies, slit green chillies, ginger, curry leaves and asafoetida and fry 30 seconds until the leaves crisp.
Return the toasted coconut to the pan and stir for 1 minute so it takes up the tempering.
Turn off the heat, tip in the rice and fold everything together gently with a flat spatula.
steps.tip: Fold, do not stir. A spoon breaks the grains and you lose the texture entirely.

steps.text: Cover and let it sit 5 minutes so the flavours settle, then check the salt and serve.

recipes.storage: Traditionally this travelled all day, which is why it exists, but cooked rice is the one dish where that habit carries real risk. Cool it quickly, spread out, and refrigerate within two hours; it keeps 3 days. If it is going in a lunchbox, pack it cold with an ice block. Bring it back to room temperature rather than microwaving, which dries the coconut out.

recipes.name: Tomato Chutney
recipes.subtitle: deep red cooked chutney, tangy and hot, for idli and dosa

ingredients.note: ripe and red, not pink
byadgi for colour, guntur for heat
skip it if the tomatoes are very sour
use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free

prepNotes: Chop the tomatoes coarsely. They break down anyway.
Cool the fried mixture fully before grinding, or the chutney will froth and taste raw.
Keep 1 tbsp of the oil back for the final tempering.

steps.text: Heat 3 tbsp sesame oil and fry the urad dal and chana dal until golden, about 90 seconds.
Add the red chillies and fry 20 seconds until they darken and swell, then lift out the dals and chillies.
steps.tip: Removing them now stops the chillies burning while the tomatoes cook down.

steps.text: In the same oil, cook the onion and garlic until the onion is soft and edged with brown, about 6 minutes.
Add the tomatoes, tamarind and salt and cook on medium heat for 10 minutes.
Keep going until the tomatoes lose all shape and the oil pools red at the sides of the pan.
steps.tip: Underdone tomato is the single reason this chutney tastes thin.

steps.text: Cool the mixture completely, then grind it with the reserved dals and chillies to a coarse paste, no water.
Heat the last 1 tbsp oil, pop the mustard seeds, then add the curry leaves and hing.
Pour the tempering over the chutney and stir it through.

recipes.storage: Keeps 5 days refrigerated in a clean jar. The sesame oil preserves it. Serve at room temperature; it also freezes for a month.

recipes.name: Upma
recipes.subtitle: soft savoury semolina with crackling dal, ginger and curry leaves

ingredients.note: coarse bombay rava, not the fine idli variety
brightens the whole pan

prepNotes: Dry-roast the rava on low heat for 4 minutes until it smells toasty and moves loosely in the pan, then tip it out.
Boil the water and keep it on a low flame. It must go in hot or the upma turns lumpy.
Have everything chopped before you start; the tempering to the finish takes six minutes.

steps.text: Heat the oil and pop the mustard seeds until they jump and quieten.
Add the urad dal and chana dal and fry until both turn a light red-gold, about 90 seconds.
steps.tip: The dals are what give upma its crunch; pale dal means no texture.

steps.text: Add the cashews, green chilli, ginger and curry leaves and fry 30 seconds until the leaves crisp.
Add the onion and cook until soft and translucent, about 4 minutes, no browning.
Pour in the boiling water with the salt and let it come back to a rolling boil.
Lower the heat and add the roasted rava in a thin steady stream with one hand while stirring hard with the other.
steps.tip: Dumping it in all at once is exactly how you get lumps.

steps.text: Keep stirring for 2 minutes until the mixture pulls away from the sides of the pan.
Cover and steam on the lowest heat for 3 minutes, then turn off and rest 2 minutes.
Fluff with a fork, squeeze over the lemon and scatter the coriander.

recipes.storage: Best within a few hours. Refrigerate up to 2 days and revive by steaming with 2 tbsp water sprinkled over; microwaving dries it out.

recipes.name: Uttapam
recipes.subtitle: thick fermented pancake with onion and tomato pressed into the top

ingredients.note: parboiled idli rice, not raw table rice
helps the ferment and browns the surface
deseeding stops the topping going soggy

prepNotes: Soak the rice and the dal separately. They grind to different textures and must be ground apart.
Ferment the batter 8 to 12 hours in a warm place; in a cold kitchen use a switched-off oven with the light on.
Do not stir the risen batter vigorously before use. Fold gently once so it keeps its air.
Chop the toppings fine and keep them dry in a bowl, ready to scatter.

steps.text: Grind the urad dal and fenugreek with about 3/4 cup cold water to a light, fluffy paste.
Grind the rice separately with 3/4 cup water to a batter with a fine sandy grain still in it.
steps.tip: That slight grain is what gives uttapam its body. A silk-smooth batter spreads too thin.

steps.text: Mix the two by hand with the salt, in wide circular strokes, for 2 minutes.
Cover and leave to ferment 8 to 12 hours until risen by half and smelling pleasantly sour.
steps.tip: A batter that has risen and fallen back is over-fermented. Use it, but expect a sharper taste.

steps.text: Heat a tawa on medium until a flick of water dances and evaporates in about 2 seconds.
Pour a ladle of batter and spread it only slightly, to a thick round about 12cm across.
steps.tip: Uttapam is meant to be thick. Resist the urge to spread it like a dosa.

steps.text: Scatter a handful of onion, tomato, chilli, coriander and curry leaves over the wet surface and press them in with the back of the ladle.
Drizzle a teaspoon of sesame oil around the edge and cook 3 minutes until the base is golden and the top has set matte.
Flip and cook 90 seconds on the topping side to caramelise the onion, then serve straight from the pan.

recipes.storage: The batter keeps 4 days refrigerated and grows sourer each day. Cooked uttapam is best immediately; reheat on a dry tawa, never in a microwave.

recipes.name: Vatha Kuzhambu
recipes.subtitle: dark, oily tamarind gravy with shallots, spiked with fenugreek

ingredients.qty: large lime-sized ball, soaked in 2 cups hot water

ingredients.note: sambar onions; they stand in for the sun-dried vathal
the quantity is not a typo. This curry sits under a layer of oil
the signature bitterness; measure it exactly
use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free
rounds off the sourness
only if it refuses to thicken

prepNotes: Soak the tamarind in hot water 20 minutes and strain out about 2 cups of extract.
Peel the shallots and leave them whole. They should stay recognisable in the finished gravy.
This curry needs a long slow reduction, so start it before the rice.

steps.text: Heat the sesame oil in a kadhai and pop the mustard seeds.
Add the fenugreek seeds and chana dal and fry 20 seconds until the fenugreek turns reddish.
steps.tip: Fenugreek that goes dark brown makes the whole pot bitter, pull it early.

steps.text: Add the red chillies, curry leaves and hing and let them crackle.
Add the whole shallots and garlic and fry 5 minutes until the shallots are browned in patches and glossy.
Stir in the sambar powder and turmeric and fry 30 seconds in the oil.
Pour in the tamarind extract with the salt and jaggery and bring to a simmer.
Simmer uncovered on low heat for 20 to 25 minutes, stirring occasionally.
It is done when the volume has dropped by a third and the sesame oil floats clear on top.
steps.tip: That floating oil is the whole test. Until it appears, the tamarind still tastes raw.

steps.text: If it is still thin after 25 minutes, stir in the slaked rice flour and cook 2 minutes more.
Rest 10 minutes off the heat and serve with rice, a spoon of sesame oil and a poriyal.

recipes.storage: Keeps a week refrigerated and improves for the first three days. The oil seals it. Reheat gently; do not freeze.

recipes.name: Vellai Paniyaram
recipes.subtitle: pale lacy rice-and-urad fritters, crisp at the rim and soft in the middle

ingredients.note: pacharisi or any raw short-grain rice
to tighten the batter if needed
helps the rim colour without browning the whole fritter
stirred into the batter for aroma

prepNotes: Soak the rice and urad dal together for 4 hours; they grind more evenly than when soaked apart for this batter.
Grind and rest the batter 30 minutes before frying. Unrested batter spreads and tears in the oil.
Vellai means white, so this batter is not fermented and the fritters should stay pale. Keep the oil at a steady medium.

steps.text: Drain the soaked rice and dal and grind with 150ml water to a very smooth batter, stopping to scrape down twice.
steps.tip: Smoothness matters here, unlike kandarappam. Any grit and the lacy rim will not form.

steps.text: Beat in the salt, sugar and coconut oil, then rest the batter 30 minutes covered.
Check the consistency: it should ribbon off the spoon and settle back in about 3 seconds. Tighten with rice flour if it is thinner than that.
Heat the oil in a kadhai to a steady medium. A drop of batter should sink briefly, then rise within 3 seconds without browning.
steps.tip: If the oil browns the batter, it is too hot. These are meant to stay white with only a blush of gold.

steps.text: Wet a small ladle, pour a ladleful of batter from about 10cm above the oil so it spreads into a disc.
Fry 2 minutes, spooning hot oil over the top, until the edges frill up and turn lacy.
Turn once and fry 90 seconds more until the fritter is puffed and set but still pale.
steps.tip: One turn only. Repeated flipping collapses the puff.

steps.text: Lift onto a rack, salt lightly if you like, and fry the rest three or four at a time.
Serve hot with a thin coconut chutney or, in the Chettinad way, alongside a peppery mutton kuzhambu.

recipes.storage: Eat within an hour. They soften as they cool. The unfried batter keeps 2 days refrigerated; bring it back to room temperature and whisk before frying.

recipes.name: Ven Pongal
recipes.subtitle: soft rice and moong dal loaded with ghee, black pepper and cumin

ingredients.note: roasting is what stops it tasting like plain khichdi
half in the pot, half poured over at the end
use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free

prepNotes: Dry-roast the moong dal on low heat for 4 minutes until it smells nutty and turns a shade darker, then rinse it.
Crush the pepper coarsely in a mortar. Whole peppercorns are unpleasant to bite and ground pepper disappears.
Have the ghee tempering ready before the cooker is opened; pongal stiffens as it cools.

steps.text: Pressure cook the rice and roasted dal with 5 cups water and the salt for 5 whistles.
steps.tip: Five cups looks like far too much water. It is not. Pongal should be sloppy.

steps.text: Let the pressure fall on its own, then open and mash the mixture with a ladle until it is soft and shapeless.
Keep it on the lowest heat while you make the tempering, stirring so the base does not catch.
Heat the ghee in a small pan and fry the cashews to pale gold, about 40 seconds.
Add the cumin seeds and crushed pepper and let them sizzle for 20 seconds.
steps.tip: Pepper that fries too long turns acrid, 20 seconds, no more.

steps.text: Add the ginger, curry leaves and hing and fry until the leaves crisp.
Pour the whole tempering into the pongal and fold it through.
Check the consistency and loosen with hot water until it falls off the ladle in a thick sheet.
Serve immediately with the remaining ghee spooned over, alongside coconut chutney.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated but sets firm. Reheat with 1/2 cup hot water per portion, mashing until it flows again, and add a spoon of fresh ghee.
